06.03.1064.t:
Rural Esquesing, Halton Hills

This community covers the rural part of the former Esquesing Township. The township was surveyed in 1818 and opened to settlement in 1819, and early settlements grew along Trafalgar Road and the York to Guelph Road (now Highway 7). The name is thought to come from a Mississauga word for Bronte Creek. In 1974 Esquesing was joined with Georgetown and Acton to form Halton Hills.

Rural Esquesing is generally bounded by 22 Side Road and Nassagaweya-Esquesing Town Line to the north, Fourth Line to the east, 5 Side Road to the south and the Milton boundary to the west, and covers approximately 5,272 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), Dufferin Aggregates (quarry), Boston Presbyterian Church Cemetery and Mansewood United Presbyterian Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Middle Sixteen Mile Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Scotch Block Reservoir. Glencairn Golf Club and Greystone Golf Club are located in the area.

09.10.0020.t:
Snake Island, Georgina Islands

Snake Island is a small island in southern Lake Simcoe, named after the Chippewa leader Snake. It was set aside as a reserve in 1830, together with Georgina and Fox islands, and some Chippewa families stayed there under Snake's leadership. The island is part of the reserve lands of the Chippewas of Georgina Island First Nation and has only unpaved roads.

Snake Island is generally bounded by Lake Simcoe to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 264 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Snake Island.

The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe.

06.01.1033.t:
Harrison, Milton

Harrison is named after Thomas and Elizabeth Harrison, who settled the land after arriving from England in approximately 1820. It was planned in 2004 as part of the Sherwood Survey, Milton's first major expansion of new urban neighbourhoods. It is also known as Hawthorne Village South, after the Mattamy Homes community, and construction began in approximately 2007.

Harrison is generally bounded by Derry Road to the north, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the east, Louis St. Laurent Avenue to the south and Tremaine Road to the west, and covers approximately 179 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Harrison includes Optimist Park, Speyer Park and Gastle Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

08.09.0040.t:
Blue Mountains, Blue Mountains

The Town of The Blue Mountains was formed on January 1, 1998, when the Town of Thornbury merged with Collingwood Township. Thornbury was first incorporated in 1831 and became separate from Collingwood Township in 1887. The town is named for the Blue Mountain on the Niagara Escarpment, where the Blue Mountain ski resort was founded in 1941 by Jozo Weider and Gordon Peter Campbell. Resort and recreational housing has grown around the foot of the escarpment since then, alongside the older communities of Thornbury and Craigleith.

Blue Mountains is generally bounded by Georgian Bay to the north and the Grey Highlands boundary and Osprey-The Blue Mountains Townline to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 27,456 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a wastewater treatment plant and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Blue Mountains includes Pretty River Valley Provincial Park, Craigleith Provincial Park and Petun Conservation Area, and Silver Creek, the Pretty River and Black Ash Creek run through or along the community. Monterra is located in the area. Other notable landmarks include Scenic Caves and Historic Snowbridge - Resort Homes by Blue Mountain Resort.

08.07.0045.t:
Grey Highlands, Grey Highlands

Grey Highlands was formed on January 1, 2001, when the Village of Markdale and the townships of Artemesia, Euphrasia and Osprey were amalgamated. The former Village of Flesherton had already merged into Artemesia Township in 1998. The municipality includes hamlets such as Eugenia, Ceylon, Maxwell, Singhampton, Priceville, Kimberley and Feversham. It is largely rural, with farmland and the Niagara Escarpment along the Beaver Valley.

Grey Highlands is generally bounded by the Blue Mountains boundary to the north, County Road 124/124 to the east, the Melancthon boundary to the south and the Southgate boundary to the west, and covers approximately 37,766 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a quarry or aggregate pit, South Line Union Cemetery and McIntyre Pioneer Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Beaver River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Brewster's Lake and Perry's Pond.

11.01.0090.t:
Little Britain, Kawartha Lakes

Little Britain was established in 1834 by Harrison Haight, who built its first mill in 1837. First postmaster Robert Whiteside named it after his birthplace, Little Britain, Pennsylvania, and the post office opened in 1853. It was part of Mariposa Township and remains largely agricultural. It became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

The boundary of Little Britain follows local streets, lot lines and natural features rather than major roads, and the community covers approximately 56 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Little Britain includes Fairground exhibition ground. Residents are served by one school and the Little Britain branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library.

06.01.1027.t:
Clarke, Milton

Clarke is named after Samuel Clarke, who settled this part of Trafalgar Township in 1834 and was a farmer, municipal politician and founder of the Halton Journal in 1855. The Town of Milton created the neighbourhood in 1998 as part of the Bristol Survey urban expansion. Construction began in 2003.

Clarke is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) to the north, James Snow Parkway to the east, Derry Road to the south and Thompson Road to the west, and covers approximately 231 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Clarke includes Clarke Neighourhood Park (South), Clarke Neighbourhood Park (North) and Trudeau Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

11.01.0060.t:
Manilla, Kawartha Lakes

Manilla grew from a post office opened in 1837 in Jacob Ham's log store. It had several earlier names, including Ham's Corners, before a public meeting chose Manilla in 1851, after Manilla, Indiana. By 1881 it had a steam flour mill, a rake factory and several stores. The village straddles the boundary between Durham Region and the City of Kawartha Lakes (formed January 1, 2001).

Manilla is generally bounded by Simcoe Street to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 154 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 7 and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Manilla includes Manilla Park.

11.01.0070.t:
Oakwood, Kawartha Lakes

Oakwood was named for the oak forest in the area. It had a post office from 1843 and a Mariposa Township hall built in 1845, which remained the township's municipal focus. The village served the surrounding farm community. It became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

The boundary of Oakwood follows local streets, lot lines and natural features rather than major roads, and the community covers approximately 112 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 7. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Oakwood includes Oakwood Community Centre Park, Thorndyke Park and Oakwood Memorial park. Residents are served by the Oakwood branch of the Kawartha Lakes Library.

06.01.1025.t:
Bowes, Milton

Bowes is named after the brothers Thomas and Joseph Bowes, who settled in the area in 1824. The Town of Milton created the neighbourhood in 2004 as part of the Boyne Survey, together with Cobban, Ford and Walker. It lies between Louis St. Laurent Avenue and Britannia Road, and Thompson Road and Fourth Line; construction began in approximately 2015.

Bowes is generally bounded by Louis St. Laurent Avenue to the north, James Snow Parkway to the east, Britannia Road to the south and Thompson Road to the west, and covers approximately 326 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a quarry or aggregate pit and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bowes includes Omagh Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

06.01.1026.t:
Cobban, Milton

Cobban is named after Dr. James Cobban, who came to Milton from Aberdeen, Scotland, in 1837 and was the area's first medical doctor. The Town of Milton created the neighbourhood in 2004 as part of the Boyne Survey, together with Bowes, Ford and Walker. The land was farmland until construction began in approximately 2015.

Cobban is generally bounded by Louis St. Laurent Avenue to the north, Thompson Road to the east, Britannia Road to the south and Regional Road 25 to the west, and covers approximately 217 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Omagh Presbyterian Church Cemetery and Bowes Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Sixteen Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

11.01.0311.t:
Bexley, Kawartha Lakes

Bexley is a former township in the northwest of Victoria County, likely named for Nicholas Vansittart, Baron Bexley. It was surveyed in the early 1830s, and its first settler, Admiral Vansittart, received a grant on the west shore of Balsam Lake in 1834. Coboconk, founded in 1851, became its main centre. The township became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Bexley is generally bounded by Bexley-Laxton Boundary Road to the north, Balsam Lake to the south and Victoria Road and Fenel Road to the west, and covers approximately 16,569 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bexley includes Indian Point Provincial Park, Balsam Lake Provincial Park and Coboconk Park, and the Talbot River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Balsam Lake and Raven Lake. Residents are served by one school and the Coboconk branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library.

11.01.0300.t:
Omemee, Kawartha Lakes

Omemee grew up around William Cottingham's mills on the Pigeon River and was first called Williamstown, then Metcalfe. In 1857 it was renamed Omemee, a Mississauga word for pigeon, and the Port Hope, Lindsay and Beaverton Railway arrived the same year. It became a shipping point for timber and grain. It was an incorporated village until it became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Omemee is generally bounded by the Pigeon River to the east and Highway 7 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 217 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 7. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Omemee includes Omemee Municipal Park, and the Pigeon River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Omemee branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library.

06.01.1028.t:
Coates, Milton

Coates is named after James and Elizabeth Coates, early settlers who arrived in 1836. The Town of Milton created the neighbourhood in 1998 as part of the Bristol Survey urban expansion, on former Trafalgar Township farmland between Derry Road and Louis St. Laurent Avenue. Construction began in 2005.

Coates is generally bounded by Derry Road to the north, Thompson Road to the east, Louis St. Laurent Avenue to the south and Regional Road 25 to the west, and covers approximately 208 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Coates.

Green space in Coates includes Coates Neighbourhood Park South, Bristol District Park and Coates Neighbourhood Park North. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

11.01.0321.t:
Manvers, Kawartha Lakes

Manvers is a former township in the south of the City of Kawartha Lakes, named after Charles Pierrepont, 1st Earl Manvers. It was established in 1816, with land grants to Loyalists, former soldiers and others. It was part of Durham County until 1974, when it moved to Victoria County. Its communities include Bethany, Janetville and Pontypool, and it became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Manvers is generally bounded by Mount Horeb Road to the north, Dranoel Road to the east, Boundary Road and Regional Road 20 to the south and Manvers-Scugog Townline and Nesbitt Line to the west, and covers approximately 30,039 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), John M. Turner Memorial Highway, a landfill site, a hydro transformer station and a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a quarry or aggregate pit. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Manvers includes Fleetwood Creek Conservation Area, Ganaraska Forest 2 and Pontypool Park, and the Pigeon River and Fleetwood Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Scugog. Wolf Run Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Bethany branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library.

46.03.0447.t:
447 - Cushman/Industrial, St. Catharines

This area is named after Cushman Road and is largely made up of industrial and commercial land in St. Catharines. It was originally part of Grantham Township, which was surveyed between 1787 and 1789 and settled by Loyalists. The land was annexed by the city in 1961. Manufacturing has long been the city's main industry, reflected in its motto "Industry and Liberality".

447 - Cushman/Industrial is generally bounded by the Niagara-on-the-Lake boundary and Welland Avenue to the north and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 222 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a hydro transformer station (Bunting TS) and industrial lands (approximately 65% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Welland Canal runs through or along the community.

11.01.0312.t:
Carden, Kawartha Lakes

Carden is a former township in the northwest corner of Victoria County. It was named by Lieutenant-Governor Sir John Colborne after Captain John Surman Carden, a naval officer at Corunna in 1809. Its communities included Dalrymple, Carden and Rohallion. Carden merged with Dalton Township in 2000 and became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Carden is generally bounded by Victoria Road to the east, Portage Road to the south and Mara-Carden Boundary Road and Kirkfield Road to the west, and covers approximately 26,154 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and a quarry or aggregate pit. Along or just beyond its edges are a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Carden includes Carden Alvar Provincial Park and Queen Elizabeth II Wildlands Provincial Park, and the Head River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Dalrymple Lake and Canal Lake. Residents are served by one school.

11.01.0220.t:
Pontypool, Kawartha Lakes

Pontypool was named by settlers James Leigh and John Jennings after Pontypool, Wales. A sawmill operated by 1865, and a post office opened in 1881; locals long called the place Jennings' Mills. The Canadian Pacific Railway line built in the 1880s spurred its growth as a village. It was part of Manvers Township and became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Pontypool is generally bounded by Telecom Road to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 351 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are a quarry or aggregate pit. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Pontypool includes Pontypool Park and Pontypool Park 2.

11.01.0313.t:
Eldon, Kawartha Lakes

Eldon is a former township in the west of Victoria County, named after John Scott, Earl of Eldon, a British Lord Chancellor. It was surveyed in 1826 and settled from approximately 1827 by Scottish immigrants and Loyalists. Its communities include Kirkfield, Glenarm and Woodville. It became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Eldon is generally bounded by Portage Road to the north, Fenel Road to the east, Woodville Road to the south and Simcoe Street to the west, and covers approximately 23,079 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, GoodLight Solar Project, Simcoe Solar Energy Centre 1, a quarry or aggregate pit, Glenarm Solar Farm and Argyle Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Simcoe Solar Energy Centre 3 and SparkleLight Solar Farm. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Staples River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Mitchell Lake and Goose Lake. Residents are served by the Kirkfield branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library.

11.01.0270.t:
Bobcaygeon, Kawartha Lakes

Bobcaygeon's name is believed to come from an Ojibway term describing the shallow rapids or narrows. Thomas Need arrived in 1833, built mills and a store, and laid out the village. Construction of the first lock on the Trent-Severn Waterway began here in 1833. It was incorporated as a village in 1876, merged with Verulam Township in 2000 and became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Bobcaygeon is generally bounded by Pigeon Lake to the east and Sturgeon Lake to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 608 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bobcaygeon includes Tommy Anderson Park and Bobcaygeon Beach Park, and the Bobcaygeon River and Trent–Severn Waterway run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Pigeon Lake. Residents are served by one school and the Bobcaygeon branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library.

11.01.0319.t:
Verulam, Kawartha Lakes

Verulam is a former township named after James Walter Grimston, Earl of Verulam. It was surveyed in 1831, and lots went on sale in 1832, with settlement starting at Bobcaygeon under Thomas Need. Lumbering came first, followed by dairy farming south of Sturgeon Lake and later cottage tourism. Verulam merged with Bobcaygeon in 2000 and became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Verulam is generally bounded by Kawartha Lakes Road 49 to the east and Colony Road and Pigeon Lake to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 25,717 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a quarry or aggregate pit, a landfill site, a hydro transformer station and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Hawkers Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Sturgeon Lake and Emily Lake. Eganridge Resort, Country Club & Spa and Sturgeon Point Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by one school and the Dunsford branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library.

06.01.1029.t:
Dempsey, Milton

Dempsey is named after John Dempsey, an Irish immigrant who arrived in 1836, built Winding Sixteen Farm, and whose family ran some of Milton's early businesses. The Town of Milton created the neighbourhood in 1998 as part of the Bristol Survey, between Highway 401 and the railway, and Thompson Road and James Snow Parkway. Construction began in 2002.

Dempsey is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, James Snow Parkway to the east, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) to the south and Thompson Road to the west, and covers approximately 247 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Dempsey includes Lions Sport Park, Woodward Woodlot and Dempsey Neighbourhood Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Main branch of the Milton Public Library.

11.01.0320.t:
Emily, Kawartha Lakes

Emily is a former township in the southeast of Victoria County, named after Emily Charlotte, daughter of Lord George Lennox. It was surveyed in 1818 and 1819, and settlers brought by Peter Robinson arrived from Ireland in 1825. Its communities include Omemee, Downeyville and Fowlers Corners. It became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Emily is generally bounded by Pigeon Lake and Colony Road to the north, Boundary Road to the east and Hayes Line to the south, and covers approximately 27,085 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 7, a landfill site and Emily Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a quarry or aggregate pit. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Emily includes Emily Provincial Park and Omemee Municipal Park, and the Pigeon River and Emily Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Pigeon Lake. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Omemee branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library.

11.01.0140.t:
Fenelon Falls, Kawartha Lakes

Fenelon Falls was first called Cameron's Falls and was renamed after Fenelon Township. The village grew around the falls between Cameron and Sturgeon lakes and was incorporated in 1874. The Victoria Railway arrived in 1876, and construction of the lock began in 1885. It became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Fenelon Falls is generally bounded by Louisa Street to the north, Sturgeon Lake and Francis Street to the east, County Road 8 to the south and Cameron Lake to the west, and covers approximately 832 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Fenelon Falls includes Fenelon Beach. The community includes or fronts onto Cameron Lake and Sturgeon Lake. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Fenelon Falls branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library.

11.01.0314.t:
Fenelon, Kawartha Lakes

Fenelon is a former township in Victoria County, named after François de Salignac de la Mothe-Fénelon, a missionary in New France. Settlement was only beginning by 1842. Its communities include Cameron, Cambray, Sturgeon Point and Fenelon Falls. It became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Fenelon is generally bounded by Balsam Lake and Northline Road to the north and Fenel Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 26,494 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a quarry or aggregate pit, Lindsay Solar Farm, Penn Energy - Ridgefield Solar Project, a landfill site and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Fenelon includes Ken Reid Conservation Area, Fenelon Falls Fairground and Fenelon Beach, and Martin Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Sturgeon Lake and Cameron Lake. Byrnell Golf Course and Meadow Oaks Golf are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Fenelon Falls branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library.

11.01.0050.t:
Woodville, Kawartha Lakes

Woodville was once called Irish Corners and took its name when its post office opened under postmaster John Morrison. The Toronto and Nipissing Railway passed through in 1871 and helped it grow. It became a police village in 1878 and was incorporated in 1884. It became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Woodville is generally bounded by Windmere Road to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 298 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school and the Woodville branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library.

11.01.0315.t:
Dalton, Kawartha Lakes

Dalton is a former township in northern Victoria County, named after English scientist John Dalton. Logging and farming drove its early growth, with settlement along the Old Monck Road colonization route. Several late 19th-century logging villages are now abandoned, while Sebright, Sadowa and Uphill remain. Dalton merged with Carden in 2000 and became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Dalton is generally bounded by Rama-Dalton Boundary Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 15,771 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Sadowa Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Dalton includes Queen Elizabeth II Wildlands Provincial Park, and the Head River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Cranberry Lake and Young Lake. Residents are served by the Dalton branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Old Monck Road.

11.01.0318.t:
Somerville, Kawartha Lakes

Somerville is a former township in the northeast of Victoria County. The origin of its name is uncertain, with several possible namesakes recorded. Kinmount, first called Burnt River Crossing and renamed in 1859, was its seat and an early site of Icelandic settlement. Forestry was the early economy, and the area became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Somerville is generally bounded by Kawartha Lakes Road 49 and County Road 121 to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 29,023 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Balsam Lake Solar Farm and Burnt River Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Burnt River and Union Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Four Mile Lake.

11.01.0316.t:
Ops, Kawartha Lakes

Ops is a former township in the centre of Victoria County, named after the Roman goddess of plenty. It was surveyed in 1824, and Irish families, including Peter Robinson settlers in 1825, were among the first settlers. It surrounds the Town of Lindsay and includes Reaboro and Fleetwood. It became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Ops is generally bounded by Mount Horeb Road to the south and Opmar Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 25,443 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 7, a wastewater treatment plant, Central East Correctional Centre, a hydro transformer station (LIndsay TS), a landfill site, Riverside Cemetery and St. Mary's Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Ops includes Pioneer Park, Lindsay Memorial Park and Elgin Park, and the Scugog River and Stony Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Scugog. Lindsay Golf and Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 14 schools and the Lindsay branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library. Shopping is available at Lindsay Square. Ross Memorial Hospital, Three Sixty Health and Fleming College - Frost Campus are also located in the community.

11.01.0170.t:
Lindsay, Kawartha Lakes

Lindsay began as Purdy's Mills, where the Purdy family built a dam and mills on the Scugog River from 1827 to 1830. The town site was laid out in 1834, and the name is said to come from an assistant to surveyor John Huston. Lindsay was incorporated as a town in 1857 and grew as a railway, lumber and farming centre. It was the largest centre of Victoria County and became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Lindsay is generally bounded by Verulam Road to the east and Highway 35 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,586 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 7, a wastewater treatment plant, Central East Correctional Centre and industrial lands (approximately 8% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are St. Mary's Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lindsay includes Pioneer Park, Elgin Park and Logie Park, and the Scugog River and Jenning's Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 11 schools and the Lindsay branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library. Shopping is available at Lindsay Square. Ross Memorial Hospital and Three Sixty Health are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Old Mill Park.

11.01.0317.t:
Laxton/Digby/Longford, Kawartha Lakes

Laxton, Digby and Longford is a former township in the north of Victoria County, formed from three original townships. Digby was named after a Captain Digby who served at Corunna in 1809, and Longford after the Irish county. Longford was surveyed in 1861 and logged by John Thomson for his mill at Longford Mills. Norland is the main community, and the area became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Laxton/Digby/Longford is generally bounded by Bexley-Laxton Boundary Road to the south and Victoria Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 27,682 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Pine Grove Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Laxton/Digby/Longford includes Queen Elizabeth II Wildlands Provincial Park, Ward Memorial Park and Mud Turtle Dam Park, and the Head River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Head Lake and Shadow Lake. Monck's Landing Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by the Norland branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library.

11.01.0190.t:
Janetville, Kawartha Lakes

Janetville is a hamlet in the former Manvers Township. Manvers was named after Charles Pierrepont, 1st Earl Manvers, and was established in 1816 with land grants to Loyalists and former soldiers. The township was part of Durham County until 1974, when it moved to Victoria County. It became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

The boundary of Janetville follows local streets, lot lines and natural features rather than major roads, and the community covers approximately 158 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Janetville Creek runs through or along the community.

11.01.0322.t:
Mariposa, Kawartha Lakes

Mariposa is a former township in the southwest of Victoria County; mariposa is the Spanish word for butterfly. It was surveyed in 1820, with settlement starting approximately 1827 and Scottish settlers arriving approximately 1831. Its rich soil made it the leading farm township in the county. Communities include Oakwood, Little Britain and Manilla, and it became part of the City of Kawartha Lakes on January 1, 2001.

Mariposa is generally bounded by Woodville Road to the north, Opmar Road to the east, Lake Scugog to the south and Simcoe Street to the west, and covers approximately 34,321 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 7, a landfill site, Bedard Sand & Gravel Ltd (quarry), Bedard- White Rock Pit, Simcoe Solar Energy Centre 3 and Friends Cemetery est. 1844. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Mariposa includes Fairground exhibition ground, Oakwood Community Centre Park and Thorndyke Park, and Mariposa Brook runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Scugog and Goose Lake. Oliver's Nest Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools, the Oakwood branch of the Kawartha Lakes Library and the Little Britain branch of the Kawartha Lakes Public Library.

07.01.1930.t:
Allison, Hamilton

Allison is a residential neighbourhood on the south Hamilton Mountain, near Upper James Street and Rymal Road West. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960. The south Mountain, beyond the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway, was among the later parts of the city to be built up.

Allison is generally bounded by Rymal Road to the north, Jacqueline Boulevard and Upper Wellington Street to the east, a hydro corridor to the south and Upper James Street to the west, and covers approximately 51 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor and Mount Hamilton Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 2.2 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Allison is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

04.16.0040.t:
Sugarbush, Oro-Medonte

Sugarbush is a residential community in the Township of Oro-Medonte. The townships of Oro and Medonte were incorporated in 1850 and were amalgamated, with the Hawkestone Police Village, to form the Township of Oro-Medonte on January 1, 1994. The surrounding area was settled for farming in the 19th century.

Sugarbush is generally bounded by Horseshoe Valley Road to the north and Huronwood Drive to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 287 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Sugarbush.

Green space in Sugarbush includes Sweet Water Park.

06.01.1050.t:
Brookville/Haltonville, Milton

Brookville is a hamlet in the former Nassagaweya Township. Settlement began in approximately 1831, and the community was first called Nassagaweya and then Easterbrook, after Thomas Easterbrook, the township's first reeve; the name Brookville keeps part of that name. A town hall was built in 1875 and the area was the site of the Nassagaweya Fall Show. Haltonville is a nearby former Nassagaweya hamlet. Both became part of the Town of Milton in 1974.

Brookville/Haltonville is generally bounded by 15 Side Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 222 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Nassagaweya Presbyterian Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brookville/Haltonville includes Brookville Park. Residents are served by one school.

46.09.0220.t:
220 - Oldfield, Niagara Falls

Oldfield is a residential area of the City of Niagara Falls. It takes its name from Oldfield Road, a local road. It lies within the former Stamford Township, which was surveyed in approximately 1782 and settled by Loyalists, mainly from New York. The township was first called Mount Dorchester and was renamed Stamford in the early 1790s. Stamford Township was amalgamated with the City of Niagara Falls in 1963.

220 - Oldfield is generally bounded by McLeod Road to the north, a hydro corridor and Thundering Waters Boulevard to the east and Oldfield Road and Dorchester Road to the west, and covers approximately 163 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 220 - Oldfield includes Crimson Park and Wilson Park. Thundering Waters Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by one school.

46.04.0103.t:
103 - River, Niagara-on-the-Lake

The River area lies along the Niagara River between the Old Town and Queenston. It is part of the former Niagara Township, settled by Loyalists from the 1780s. Niagara Township merged with the Town of Niagara in 1970 to form the Town of Niagara-on-the-Lake.

103 - River is generally bounded by East & West Line and Niagara River Parkway to the north, Line 6 Road and Niagara Parkway to the south and Concession 2 to the west, and covers approximately 1,159 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of 103 - River.

103 - River is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

46.04.0108.t:
108 - Virgil, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Virgil is a community just southwest of the Old Town of Niagara-on-the-Lake. It was a settlement of the former Niagara Township and has a large Mennonite community that came from Russia in the early to mid-20th century. Virgil became part of the Town of Niagara-on-the-Lake when the town and township merged in 1970.

108 - Virgil is generally bounded by East & West Line and Hunter Road to the north, Concession 2 to the east, Line 7 Road to the south and Concession 6 to the west, and covers approximately 2,601 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Methodist United Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 108 - Virgil includes Centennial Sports Park, and Four Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

46.09.0218.t:
218 - West Wood, Niagara Falls

West Wood is a residential area of the City of Niagara Falls. It is in the western part of the city. It lies within the former Stamford Township, which was surveyed in approximately 1782 and settled by Loyalists, mainly from New York. The township was first called Mount Dorchester and was renamed Stamford in the early 1790s. Stamford Township was amalgamated with the City of Niagara Falls in 1963.

218 - West Wood is generally bounded by Lundy's Lane to the north, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the east, McLeod Road to the south and Kalar Road to the west, and covers approximately 281 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW), a hydro transformer station and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school and the Community Centre branch of the Niagara Falls Public Library.

46.01.0541.t:
541 - Grimsby West, Grimsby

This is the western part of the Town of Grimsby, below the Niagara Escarpment. Grimsby was founded by United Empire Loyalists in 1790 at The Forty, took the name of the English port of Grimsby in 1816, became a village in 1876 and became a town in 1922. Most local orchards were replaced by housing between the 1950s and 1980s, and growth has continued since because of the town's location between Hamilton and St. Catharines.

541 - Grimsby West is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the east and the Hamilton boundary to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,037 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), a cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 8% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and the Grimsby Water Treatment Plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 541 - Grimsby West includes Woolverton Conservation Area, Beamer Memorial Conservation Area and Peach King Centre, and Forty Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

46.09.0216.t:
216 - Dorchester, Niagara Falls

Dorchester takes its name from Dorchester Road. The area was first surveyed in approximately 1782 as Mount Dorchester, after Guy Carleton, 1st Baron Dorchester, and Dorchester Road is one of the few places that keeps that name today. The township was renamed Stamford in the early 1790s and was amalgamated with the City of Niagara Falls in 1963.

216 - Dorchester is generally bounded by Lundy's Lane to the north, Stanley Avenue and Ferry Street to the east, Dunn Street to the south and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and a hydro corridor to the west, and covers approximately 326 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a hydro transformer station (Murray TS) and Drummond Hill Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 216 - Dorchester includes A.G. Bridge Park and Brookfield Park, and the Chippawa-Queenston Power Canal runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

46.04.0104.t:
104 - Rural, Niagara-on-the-Lake

This area covers the farmland of the former Niagara Township, an area of orchards, vineyards and wineries. The township's settlements included Colemans, Homer, McNab, Queenston, St. Davids and Virgil. Niagara Township merged with the Town of Niagara in 1970 to form the Town of Niagara-on-the-Lake.

104 - Rural is generally bounded by Carlton Street and Line 4 Road to the north, Concession 6 to the east, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and the General Brock Parkway to the south and the St. Catharines boundary to the west, and covers approximately 2,221 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and St Catharines / Niagara District Airport (YCM). Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW), the General Brock Parkway and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Six Mile Creek and Eight Mile Creek run through or along the community.

46.04.0102.t:
102 - Lakeshore, Niagara-on-the-Lake

The Lakeshore area lies along Lake Ontario west of the Old Town. It is part of the former Niagara Township, a largely agricultural area of orchards and vineyards. Niagara Township merged with the Town of Niagara in 1970 to form the Town of Niagara-on-the-Lake.

102 - Lakeshore is generally bounded by Lake Ontario to the north, Concession 6 and 4 Mile Creek Road to the east, Carlton Street and Line 4 Road to the south and Read Road to the west, and covers approximately 2,693 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Four Mile Creek, Six Mile Creek and Eight Mile Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

46.04.0105.t:
105 - St. Davids, Niagara-on-the-Lake

St. Davids is a former village at the foot of the Niagara Escarpment in the south part of Niagara-on-the-Lake. It was settled by Loyalists after the American Revolution and was part of Niagara Township. The village became part of the Town of Niagara-on-the-Lake when the town and township merged in 1970.

105 - St. Davids is generally bounded by Line 7 Road to the north, Concession 2 to the east, the General Brock Parkway to the south and Concession 6 to the west, and covers approximately 1,509 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the General Brock Parkway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Four Mile Creek runs through or along the community. St. David's Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by one school.

46.01.0542.t:
542 - Grimsby East, Grimsby

This is the eastern part of the Town of Grimsby, below the Niagara Escarpment. Grimsby was founded by United Empire Loyalists in 1790 at The Forty and named after the English port of Grimsby in 1816. It became a village in 1876, a town in 1922, and merged with North Grimsby Township in 1970. Most local orchards were replaced by housing between the 1950s and 1980s.

542 - Grimsby East is generally bounded by the Lincoln boundary to the east and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 663 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) and Queen's Lawn Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and the Baker Road Pollution Control Plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 542 - Grimsby East includes Centennial Park, Sherwood Hills Park and Dorchester Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Grimsby Public Library, and transit is provided by the Grimsby VIA Rail station. West Lincoln Memorial Hospital is also located in the community.

46.09.0217.t:
217 - Arad/Fallsview, Niagara Falls

Fallsview is the hotel and tourist district on the high ground overlooking the Horseshoe Falls. Its high-rise hotels, casino and attractions reflect tourism, which is the main part of the city's economy. The area is part of the City of Niagara Falls, which was formed in 1904 and expanded to take in Stamford Township in 1963.

217 - Arad/Fallsview is generally bounded by Dunn Street and Stanley Avenue to the east and McLeod Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 260 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 217 - Arad/Fallsview includes Prince Charles Park, C.B Wright Park and Westfield Park, and the Chippawa-Queenston Power Canal runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

46.01.0055.t:
055 - Grimsby Escarpment, Grimsby

This area covers the part of Grimsby on and near the Niagara Escarpment, much of it in the former Township of North Grimsby. Grimsby was settled by United Empire Loyalists from 1790 at a place called The Forty and took the name of the English port of Grimsby in 1816. North Grimsby merged with the Town of Grimsby in 1970 when the Regional Municipality of Niagara was formed. The area is mainly rural, with fruit farms, wineries and escarpment woodland.

055 - Grimsby Escarpment is generally bounded by the Lincoln boundary to the east, Twenty Road to the south and the Hamilton boundary to the west, and covers approximately 11,986 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision), Niagara Road 12 Landfill (landfill), a hydro transformer station, Grimsby Regional Airport and Grimsby Mountain Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 055 - Grimsby Escarpment includes Southward Park, Beamer Memorial Conservation Area and Alway Community Centre, and Twenty Mile Creek, Forty Mile Creek and Spring Creek run through or along the community.

46.03.0463.t:
463 - Rural Eighth, St. Catharines

This is the rural area along Eighth Avenue in the southwest part of St. Catharines. The area lies in the west end of St. Catharines, on land that was part of Louth Township until 1970. That year, under the creation of the Regional Municipality of Niagara, the part of Louth east of Fifteen Mile Creek was transferred to the city. The transfer included the hamlet of Power Glen and part of Rockway. The area remains largely rural.

463 - Rural Eighth is generally bounded by St Paul Street to the north, First Street Louth to the east, Pelham Road and the Thorold boundary to the south and the Lincoln boundary to the west, and covers approximately 1,102 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 463 - Rural Eighth includes Rockway Conservation Area and Short Hills Provincial Park, and Fifteen Mile Creek and Twelve Mile Creek run through or along the community.

46.04.0106.t:
106 - Queenston, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Queenston was first settled in the 1770s by Loyalists and was first called Lower Landing. Lieutenant Governor Simcoe named it Queenston, and it grew at the north end of the portage around Niagara Falls. The Battle of Queenston Heights was fought here on October 13, 1812, and the village was destroyed in 1813. It became part of Niagara-on-the-Lake in 1970.

106 - Queenston is generally bounded by Line 6 Road to the north, the General Brock Parkway and York Road to the south and Concession 2 to the west, and covers approximately 831 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the General Brock Parkway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 106 - Queenston includes Queenston Heights Park. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Laura Secord Homestead and Lewiston-Queenston Bridge.

46.04.0101.t:
101 - Town, Niagara-on-the-Lake

The Old Town was founded in 1781 as Butlersburg, a British military base and Loyalist refuge. As Newark, it was the first capital of Upper Canada from 1792 to 1797, and it was renamed Niagara in 1798. American forces burned the town during the War of 1812, and it was rebuilt afterward. The name Niagara-on-the-Lake became official in 1970, and the historic district was named a National Historic Site in 2003.

101 - Town is generally bounded by Lake Ontario and 4 Mile Creek Road to the north, East & West Line to the south and Hunter Road to the west, and covers approximately 1,352 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include St. Andrews (cemetery). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 101 - Town includes Fort George National Historic Site, Veterans Memorial Park and Simcoe Park, and Two Mile Creek, Three Mile Creek and Four Mile Creek run through or along the community. Niagara-on-the-Lake Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by one school and the Niagara-On-The-Lake Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Queen Street historic district, Fort George and Fort Mississauga.

46.07.0558.t:
558 - Confederation Heights, Thorold

Confederation Heights is a residential area of the City of Thorold. The land was part of Thorold Township, which was first surveyed in 1788. The township was absorbed by the Town of Thorold when the Regional Municipality of Niagara was formed in 1970. Thorold became a city in 1975.

558 - Confederation Heights is generally bounded by St Davids Road to the north, Collier Road to the east, Decew Road to the south and Merrittville Highway to the west, and covers approximately 378 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 406, Highway 58 and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 558 - Confederation Heights includes Confederation South Park and Hutt Park. Residents are served by one school.

46.01.0540.t:
540 - Grimsby Beach, Grimsby

Grimsby Beach is on the Lake Ontario shore. It grew from Grimsby Park, a Methodist camp founded in 1859 that drew over 50,000 visitors in 1884. The park went bankrupt by 1909, ran as an amusement park until approximately 1950, and its land was then sold for cottages. Some of the original painted cottages, known as the Gingerbread Houses, still stand.

540 - Grimsby Beach is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the east and Lake Ontario to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 580 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Grimsby Water Treatment Plant and the Baker Road Pollution Control Plant. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 540 - Grimsby Beach includes Fifty Point Conservation Area, Biggar Lagoon Wetlands and Forty Mile Creek Park, and Forty Mile creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

46.04.0107.t:
107 - Glendale, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Glendale is in the south part of Niagara-on-the-Lake, near the Queen Elizabeth Way. It is part of the former Niagara Township, which merged with the Town of Niagara in 1970. It is now home to a Niagara College campus and a large outdoor shopping mall that opened in 2014.

107 - Glendale is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the north, the Niagara Falls boundary and the General Brock Parkway to the east and the Welland Canal and Glendale Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 743 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW), the General Brock Parkway and Warner Methodist Burying Ground. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) and the CN rail line (CN Grimsby Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Eight Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Niagara College - Niagara-on-the-Lake Campus is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Outlet Collection at Niagara.

46.09.0219.t:
219 - Forestview, Niagara Falls

Forestview is a residential area of the City of Niagara Falls. It lies within the former Stamford Township, which was surveyed in approximately 1782 and settled by Loyalists, mainly from New York. The township was first called Mount Dorchester and was renamed Stamford in the early 1790s. Stamford Township was amalgamated with the City of Niagara Falls in 1963.

219 - Forestview is generally bounded by Beaverdams Road and Garner Road to the north, Kalar Road and Lundy's Lane to the east, McLeod Road to the south and Thorold Townline Road to the west, and covers approximately 989 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Stamford Subdivision) and a hydro transformer station. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 219 - Forestview includes Kalar Sports Park. Niagara Falls Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

46.09.0205.t:
205 - Church's Lane, Niagara Falls

Church's Lane is a residential area of the City of Niagara Falls. It takes its name from Church's Lane, a local road. It lies within the former Stamford Township, which was surveyed in approximately 1782 and settled by Loyalists, mainly from New York. The township was first called Mount Dorchester and was renamed Stamford in the early 1790s. Stamford Township was amalgamated with the City of Niagara Falls in 1963.

205 - Church's Lane is generally bounded by the General Brock Parkway to the north, the Chippawa-Queenston Power Canal to the south and St Paul Avenue and Townline Road Niagara to the west, and covers approximately 1,411 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), the CN rail line (Stamford Subdivision), the CN rail line (CN Grimsby Subdivision), the CN rail line, the General Brock Parkway, a wastewater treatment plant, Sir Adam Beck II Generating Station, a hydro transformer station (Stanley TS) and industrial lands (approximately 32% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 205 - Church's Lane includes Niagara Glen Nature Reserve, Niagara Parks Botanical Gardens and M F Ker Park, and the Chippawa-Queenston Power Canal runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Sir Adam Beck Reservoir. Whirlpool Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Other notable landmarks include Butterfly Conservatory.

46.09.0206.t:
206 - Stamford, Niagara Falls

Stamford takes its name from Stamford Village, a community dating to 1783 and the largest settlement in the former Stamford Township. The township was surveyed in approximately 1782, settled by Loyalists, and named Stamford in the early 1790s after Stamford in Lincolnshire, England. The Stamford Meeting House was built in 1787 and later became Stamford Presbyterian Church. Stamford Township was amalgamated with the City of Niagara Falls in 1963.

206 - Stamford is generally bounded by Dorchester Road and St Paul Avenue to the north and Thorold Stone Road and Portage Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 353 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (CN Grimsby Subdivision), the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) and a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the General Brock Parkway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 206 - Stamford includes Russell Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Stamford Centre branch of the Niagara Falls Public Library.

46.09.0207.t:
207 - Casey, Niagara Falls

Casey is a residential area of the City of Niagara Falls. It lies within the former Stamford Township, which was surveyed in approximately 1782 and settled by Loyalists, mainly from New York. The township was first called Mount Dorchester and was renamed Stamford in the early 1790s. Stamford Township was amalgamated with the City of Niagara Falls in 1963.

207 - Casey is generally bounded by the Niagara-on-the-Lake boundary to the north, Dorchester Road to the east, Thorold Stone Road to the south and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the west, and covers approximately 453 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) and the CN rail line (CN Grimsby Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and Warner Methodist Burying Ground. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 207 - Casey includes SCVFA Firemens Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

46.09.0208.t:
208 - Mt. Carmel, Niagara Falls

Mt. Carmel is a residential area of the City of Niagara Falls. It is in the northwest part of the city. It lies within the former Stamford Township, which was surveyed in approximately 1782 and settled by Loyalists, mainly from New York. The township was first called Mount Dorchester and was renamed Stamford in the early 1790s. Stamford Township was amalgamated with the City of Niagara Falls in 1963.

208 - Mt. Carmel is generally bounded by Mountain Road to the north, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the east, Thorold Stone Road to the south and Kalar Road to the west, and covers approximately 267 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school.

46.09.0209.t:
209 - Beaverdams, Niagara Falls

Beaverdams is a residential area of the City of Niagara Falls. It is named after Beaverdams Road, which follows the historic route toward the Beaver Dams area west of the city. It lies within the former Stamford Township, which was surveyed in approximately 1782 and settled by Loyalists, mainly from New York. The township was first called Mount Dorchester and was renamed Stamford in the early 1790s. Stamford Township was amalgamated with the City of Niagara Falls in 1963.

209 - Beaverdams is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the north, Kalar Road to the east, Beaverdams Road to the south and Thorold Townline Road and the Thorold boundary to the west, and covers approximately 1,590 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), a landfill site and a quarry or aggregate pit. Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and Warner Methodist Burying Ground. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 209 - Beaverdams includes Shriner's Creek Conservation Area, and Ten Mile Creek runs through or along the community.

46.09.0210.t:
210 - Downtown, Niagara Falls

Downtown Niagara Falls is the older commercial core of the city along Queen Street. It lies within the former Town of Clifton, incorporated in 1856 and renamed Niagara Falls in 1881. In 1904 the town merged with the Village of Niagara Falls (the former Drummondville) to form the City of Niagara Falls. Stamford Township joined the city in 1963 and Chippawa followed in 1970.

Ridley takes its name from Ridley College, an independent school founded in 1889 by Anglican clergymen as Bishop Ridley College. The school's first campus burned in 1903 and it was rebuilt on its present site on Ridley Road. The surrounding area was annexed to St. Catharines in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, along with Western Hill.

459 - Ridley is generally bounded by Highway 406 to the north, St Paul Street to the south and First Street Louth to the west, and covers approximately 283 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 21% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 406. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Twelve Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school, and transit is provided by the St. Catharines GO Station.

46.03.0452.t:
452 - Haig, St. Catharines

Haig is one of the recognized communities of St. Catharines. It lies on land that was mostly outside the original town and was added to the city through annexations in the twentieth century, including the 1961 annexation of Grantham Township, Merritton and Port Dalhousie. Much of the city's housing was built during its post-war growth, when the population more than doubled between 1951 and 1961.

452 - Haig is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and Carlton Street to the east and Twelve Mile Creek to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 188 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transformer station (Carlton TS) and industrial lands (approximately 8% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 452 - Haig includes Torosian Park, and Twelve Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

46.03.0456.t:
456 - Oakdale, St. Catharines

Oakdale is one of the recognized communities of St. Catharines and takes its name from Oakdale Avenue. The area lies outside the original town and was added to the city through twentieth-century annexations, including the 1961 amalgamation with Grantham Township, Merritton and Port Dalhousie. It was built up mainly during the city's post-war growth.

456 - Oakdale is generally bounded by Queenston Street and Westchester Crescent to the north, Hartzel Road to the east and Highway 406 and Merritt Street to the south, and covers approximately 244 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 406 and a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 456 - Oakdale includes Eastmount Park. Garden City Golf Course is located in the area.

46.03.0457.t:
457 - Old Glenridge, St. Catharines

Old Glenridge is an older residential area southwest of downtown St. Catharines. Glenridge and Western Hill were annexed to the city in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The area was built up as an early residential extension of the city.

457 - Old Glenridge is generally bounded by Highway 406 to the east, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) to the south and Twelve Mile Creek to the west, and covers approximately 204 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) and Highway 406 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 457 - Old Glenridge includes Burgoyne Woods Park and Partridge Park, and Twelve Mile Creek runs through or along the community. St. Catharines Golf & Country Club is located in the area.

46.07.0556.t:
556 - Allanburg/Thorold South, Thorold

Allanburg is a community on the Welland Canal in the City of Thorold. The sod-turning ceremony for the first Welland Canal was held here on November 30, 1824. Thorold South, nearby, has long been an industrial area. Both became part of the expanded Town of Thorold when it absorbed Thorold Township in 1970.

556 - Allanburg/Thorold South is generally bounded by Thorold Townline Road and the Niagara Falls boundary to the north and the Welland Canal and Davis Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 833 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), Highway 58, Thorold Power Plant, a hydro transformer station, a cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 16% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Niagara Detention Centre and a landfill site. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 556 - Allanburg/Thorold South includes McAdam Park and Allanburg Community Park, and the Welland Canal runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

46.07.0559.t:
559 - Cataract Road, Thorold

This area is named after Cataract Road in the City of Thorold. It lies on land that was part of Thorold Township, first surveyed in 1788. The township was absorbed by the Town of Thorold in 1970, when the Regional Municipality of Niagara was formed. Thorold became a city in 1975.

559 - Cataract Road is generally bounded by Lake Gibson and Decew Road to the north, the Welland Canal to the east, Highway 20 and Canboro Road to the south and the Pelham boundary to the west, and covers approximately 3,283 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 406 and Pleasantview Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 559 - Cataract Road includes Short Hills Provincial Park, St. John's Conservation Area and Lake Gibson Recreation Area, and Twelve Mile Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Gibson and Lake Gibson Reservoir. Brock University is also located in the community.

46.07.0561.t:
561 - Port Robinson, Thorold

Port Robinson grew as a port on the first Welland Canal. It was originally called Port Beverley and was named after Sir John Beverley Robinson, Attorney General of Upper Canada when the canal was built. Its post office opened in 1835. The canal divides the community, and a seasonal pedestrian ferry has operated since 1977, after the lift bridge was destroyed in 1974.

561 - Port Robinson is generally bounded by Highway 20 and Lundy's Lane to the north, Thorold Townline Road to the east, the Welland River to the south and the Welland Canal to the west, and covers approximately 1,529 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Stamford Subdivision), the CN rail line, a hydro transformer station (Allanburg TS) and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Welland River and the Welland Canal run through or along the community.

46.07.0560.t:
560 - Rolling Meadows, Thorold

Rolling Meadows is a residential area of the City of Thorold. The land was formerly part of Thorold Township, which was first surveyed in 1788 and was mostly farmland. The township was absorbed by the Town of Thorold in 1970, and Thorold became a city in 1975.

560 - Rolling Meadows is generally bounded by Davis Road to the north, Thorold Townline Road to the east and Highway 20 to the south, and covers approximately 480 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Niagara Detention Centre. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

560 - Rolling Meadows is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

46.06.0663.t:
663 - North Pelham, Pelham

North Pelham is the northern, largely rural part of the Town of Pelham in Niagara Region. Pelham Township was laid out in the late 1780s and named in the 1790s; the name is linked to the Pell family's Pelham Manor in New York, lost by Loyalist Pells during the American Revolution. The area includes the Short Hills and the hamlet of Effingham, and has long been used for farms, orchards and rural homes. In 1970 Pelham Township, the Village of Fonthill and part of Thorold Township were merged to form the Town of Pelham.

663 - North Pelham is generally bounded by the Lincoln boundary to the north, the Thorold boundary to the east, Highway 20 to the south and Victoria Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 5,601 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 663 - North Pelham includes Short Hills Provincial Park and St. John's Conservation Area, and Fifteen Mile Creek, Twelve Mile Creek and Sixteen Mile Creek run through or along the community. Peninsula Lakes Golf Course and Lookout Point Country Club are located in the area.

46.02.0984.t:
980 - Lincoln-Jordan/Vineland, Lincoln

This area covers the villages of Jordan and Vineland and their surroundings. Mennonites from the United States founded Jordan and Vineland from 1799, and Vineland's First Mennonite Church (1801) is the oldest Mennonite congregation in Canada. Jordan's harbour at the mouth of Twenty Mile Creek made it a shipping centre for timber, grain and fruit. The area became part of the Town of Lincoln on January 1, 1970.

980 - Lincoln-Jordan/Vineland is generally bounded by Lake Ontario to the north, Fifteen Mile Creek and the St. Catharines boundary to the east, Spring Creek Road and the Pelham boundary to the south and Cherry Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 7,230 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a quarry or aggregate pit and a hydro transformer station. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 980 - Lincoln-Jordan/Vineland includes Louth Conservation Area, Balls Falls Conservation Area and Rockway Conservation Area, and Sixteen Mile Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Jordan Harbour and Sixteen Mile Pond. Twenty Valley Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Rittenhouse branch of the Lincoln Pelham Public Library.

46.02.0981.t:
