981 - Lincoln Lake, Lincoln

This area covers the Lake Ontario shoreline of the Town of Lincoln. Early European settlers were former Butler's Rangers, and the land was used mainly for fruit farming. Jordan Harbour, at the mouth of Twenty Mile Creek, was an early shipping point. The area became part of the Town of Lincoln, formed on January 1, 1970.

981 - Lincoln Lake is generally bounded by Cherry Avenue and Lakeshore Road to the east and Lake Ontario to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,591 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW), a hydro transformer station (Beamsville TS) and industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 981 - Lincoln Lake includes Town Hall Park, and Bartlett Creek and Thirty Mile Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. Residents are served by one school.

46.02.0982.t:
982 - Beamsville, Lincoln

Beamsville is named after Loyalist Jacob Beam, who founded the settlement in 1788. By 1869 it was a village of approximately 550 people on the Great Western Railway. In 1917 a Royal Flying Corps aerial fighting school operated east of town. On January 1, 1970, the Town of Beamsville was merged with Clinton Township and part of Louth Township to form the Town of Lincoln.

982 - Beamsville is generally bounded by Cherry Avenue to the east and Fly Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 3,945 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), a quarry or aggregate pit and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 982 - Beamsville includes Cave Springs Conservation Area, Mountainview Conservation Area and Angelina Macri Prokich Park, and Konkle Creek and Thirty Mile Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Fleming branch of the Lincoln Public Library.

46.02.0983.t:
983 - Escarpment, Lincoln

This area covers the Niagara Escarpment lands of the Town of Lincoln, south of the lakeshore villages. Early settlers built mills at places such as Glen Elgin (now Ball's Falls) and Tintern. The area was historically part of Clinton and Louth townships and is mainly farmland, vineyards and rural homes. It became part of the Town of Lincoln on January 1, 1970.

983 - Escarpment is generally bounded by Fly Road to the north, Cherry Avenue to the east, 20 Mile Road to the south and the Grimsby boundary to the west, and covers approximately 4,403 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision) and a quarry or aggregate pit. Along or just beyond its edges are St. Ann's Community Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 983 - Escarpment includes Beamsville Lions Park, and Twenty Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Twenty Valley Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by one school.

43.04.0010.t:
Rural Blandford-Blenheim, Blandford-Blenheim

Rural Blandford-Blenheim covers farmland in the Township of Blandford-Blenheim in Oxford County. The township was formed in 1975 by joining the former Blandford and Blenheim townships, which Lieutenant Governor Simcoe named after English places in the 1790s. Blenheim Township was granted to Thomas Watson in 1793, and settlement around Princeton followed by 1795. The area has remained largely agricultural, with small villages such as Drumbo, Plattsville and Princeton.

The boundary of Rural Blandford-Blenheim follows local streets, lot lines and natural features rather than major roads, and the community covers approximately 3,501 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Rural Blandford-Blenheim.

Rural Blandford-Blenheim is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

02.07.0441.t:
Junction/Onward Willow, Guelph

The Junction takes its name from the meeting point of the Grand Trunk Railway and the Galt and Guelph Railway in west-central Guelph. The arrival of these railways in the mid-1800s led to new housing in the area, which runs west of Edinburgh Road to Silvercreek Parkway, the former city limit. Onward Willow is the adjoining residential area to the west.

Junction/Onward Willow is generally bounded by the Guelph/Eramosa boundary and a hydro corridor to the north and Highway 6 and Edinburgh Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 591 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (Campbell Transformer Station (Guelph)) and industrial lands (approximately 32% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Goderich Subdivision rail line, Highway 6, Dolime Quarry and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Junction/Onward Willow includes Norm Jary Park, Silver Creek Park and Howitt Creek Flood Protection Facility, and the Speed River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. Shopping is available at Willow West.

04.14.0070.t:
Gilford, Innisfil

Gilford is a village near Cook's Bay on Lake Simcoe, in the southeast of Innisfil. It began in 1853 with the opening of a Northern Railway station, and Thomas Maconchie opened a sawmill the same year. A post office followed in 1854, a Methodist church in 1861 and a community hall in 1874. It became part of the Town of Innisfil on January 1, 1991.

Gilford is generally bounded by Shore Acres Drive to the north, Lake Simcoe to the east and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and Gilford Road to the west, and covers approximately 83 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe.

02.07.0310.t:
Kortright West, Guelph

This area in south-west Guelph is named after Kortright Road, which runs through it. It was largely built up with suburban housing from the 1980s onward, as the city expanded south and west. Guelph itself was founded in 1827 by John Galt of the Canada Company and became a city in 1879.

Kortright West is generally bounded by Stone Road to the north, Gordon Street to the east, Hanlon Creek to the south and Highway 6 to the west, and covers approximately 532 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 6 and the Hanlon Expressway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Kortright West includes Preservation Park, Hanlon Creek Park and University Village Park, and Hanlon Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Scottsdale branch of the Guelph Public Library. University of Guelph is also located in the community.

02.07.0360.t:
Victoria North, Guelph

This area in north-east Guelph is named after Victoria Road, which runs through it. It was largely built up with suburban housing in the later 20th century and after. Guelph itself was founded in 1827 by John Galt of the Canada Company and became a city in 1879.

Victoria North is generally bounded by the Speed River to the north, the Guelph/Eramosa boundary to the east, Victoria Road and Eramosa Road to the south and Woodlawn Road to the west, and covers approximately 382 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Woodlawn Memorial Park (cemetery) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Victoria North includes Brant Park, Wilson Farm Park and Dakota Park, and the Speed River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

02.07.0290.t:
Grange Road, Guelph

This area in Guelph's east end is named after Grange Road, which runs through it. The east end was largely built up with suburban subdivisions in the later 20th century and after. Guelph itself was founded in 1827 by John Galt of the Canada Company and became a city in 1879.

Grange Road is generally bounded by Speedvale Avenue and Eramosa Road to the north, the Guelph/Eramosa boundary and Davis Street to the east, York Road to the south and Victoria Road to the west, and covers approximately 746 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Goderich Subdivision rail line. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Grange Road includes Eastview Community Park, Peter Misersky Park and St. James Sports Fields, and Clythe Creek and Hadati Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the East Side branch of the Guelph Public Library.

12.05.0021.t:
Cavan-Monaghan, Cavan Monaghan

Cavan Monaghan is a largely rural township in Peterborough County. Cavan and Monaghan townships were surveyed in 1817 and named after Irish counties, the home of many early settlers. On January 1, 1998, Cavan Township, North Monaghan Township and the Village of Millbrook merged as Cavan-Millbrook-North Monaghan. The name was shortened to Cavan Monaghan in 2007. Hamlets include Ida, Mount Pleasant, Cedar Valley and Springville.

Cavan-Monaghan is generally bounded by the Peterborough boundary and Parkhill Road to the north, the Otonabee River to the east, Whitfield Road to the south and Highway 7 to the west, and covers approximately 3,874 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), John M. Turner Memorial Highway, Highway 7 and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Otonabee River and Cavan Creek run through or along the community. Heron Landing Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Bruce Johnston branch of the Cavan Monaghan Public Library.

12.06.0011.t:
Otonabee-South Monaghan, Otonabee-South Monaghan

The Township of Otonabee-South Monaghan in Peterborough County was formed on January 1, 1998, by merging the former Otonabee and South Monaghan townships. Otonabee takes its name from the Otonabee River, and the area was settled for farming in the 19th century. The township is largely rural, with hamlets such as Keene (the municipal seat), Bailieboro, Cameron and Lang. It lies along the north shore of Rice Lake, an area with a long history of Indigenous settlement.

Otonabee-South Monaghan is generally bounded by the Douro-Dummer boundary and the Peterborough boundary to the north, Rice Lake to the south and County Road 28 and the Otonabee River to the west, and covers approximately 35,327 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), Highway 7, a landfill site, a quarry or aggregate pit, a hydro transformer station and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Otonabee-South Monaghan includes Harold Town Conservation Area and Mark S. Burnham Provincial Park, and the Otonabee River and Wood Duck Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Rice Lake. Residents are served by the Stewart Hall branch of the Otonabee South Monaghan Public Library and the Bailieboro branch of the Otonabee-South Monaghan Public Library.

12.17.0101.t:
Selwyn, Selwyn

Selwyn is a township in Peterborough County, first settled in approximately 1822. Ennismore and Smith townships were merged in 1998, and in 2001 they were joined with the Village of Lakefield and part of Douro-Dummer to form Smith-Ennismore-Lakefield. The township was renamed Selwyn on January 15, 2013. It includes Lakefield, Bridgenorth, Ennismore, Buckhorn and Young's Point, as well as many lakeside areas along the Trent-Severn Waterway.

Selwyn is generally bounded by Buckhorn Lake and Lower Buckhorn Lake to the north, the Douro-Dummer boundary and Katchewanooka Lake to the east, the Peterborough boundary to the south and Pigeon Lake to the west, and covers approximately 36,753 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 7, a quarry or aggregate pit, a landfill site and a hydro transformer station (Dobbin TS). Along or just beyond its edges are Hillside Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Selwyn includes Selwyn Conservation Area, Skyline Park and Ennismore Robert E. Young Recreation Complex, and the Otonabee River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Chemong Lake and Buckhorn Lake. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools, the Ennismore branch of the Selwyn Public Library and the Lakefield branch of the Selwyn Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Trent-Severn Waterway.

12.09.0011.t:
Douro-Dummer, Douro-Dummer

Douro-Dummer is a rural township in Peterborough County, on the Trent-Severn Waterway. The Rice Lake Treaty of 1818 opened the land for settlement. Dummer Township was surveyed in 1823, and both townships were largely settled by 1841. Douro and Dummer townships merged on January 1, 1998. Communities include Warsaw, Douro and Young's Point.

Douro-Dummer is generally bounded by the Selwyn boundary and Katchewanooka Lake to the north, the Otonabee-South Monaghan boundary to the south and Douro Ninth Line to the west, and covers approximately 24,986 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Hillside Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a quarry or aggregate pit. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Douro-Dummer includes Trent-Severn Lock 25, and the Otonabee River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Katchewanooka Lake. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Other notable landmarks include Young's Point.

12.10.0011.t:
North Kawartha, North Kawartha

North Kawartha is a township in northern Peterborough County. It was formed on January 1, 1998, by amalgamating the Townships of Burleigh and Anstruther with the Township of Chandos, and was called Burleigh-Anstruther-Chandos until December 1999. Its communities include the village of Apsley and the hamlets of Burleigh Falls, Woodview, Big Cedar and Glen Alda. The area is mainly lakes, cottages and forest.

North Kawartha is generally bounded by the Selwyn boundary to the south and the Trent Lakes boundary to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 22,277 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of North Kawartha.

Green space in North Kawartha includes Kawartha Highlands Provincial Park. The community includes or fronts onto Cox Lake and Triangle Lake.

12.18.0101.t:
Trent Lakes, Trent Lakes

Trent Lakes is a lake and cottage municipality in Peterborough County. Early settlement was based on lumber camps and farming, and the area became a camping and cottage destination after the Second World War. Galway-Cavendish and Harvey townships were amalgamated on January 1, 1998, and the municipality was renamed Trent Lakes in 2013 after the Trent-Severn Waterway.

Trent Lakes is generally bounded by the North Kawartha boundary to the east, Buckhorn Lake to the south and Kawartha Lakes Road 49 to the west, and covers approximately 80,230 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a quarry or aggregate pit, Buckhorn Landfill (landfill) and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Trent Lakes includes Kawartha Highlands Provincial Park and Wolf Island Provincial Park, and Union Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Pigeon Lake and Buckhorn Lake. Six Foot Bay G&CC is located in the area. Residents are served by one school, the Helen Bowen branch of the Trent Lakes Public Library and the Main branch of the Trent Lakes Public Library.

12.05.0022.t:
Cavan Twp, Cavan Monaghan

This area is the former Cavan Township, west of Peterborough. Cavan and Monaghan townships were surveyed by John Deyell in 1817 and named after counties in Ireland, the home of many early settlers. The township moved from Durham County to Peterborough County in 1974. In 1998 it merged with the Village of Millbrook and North Monaghan Township, and the municipality was renamed Cavan Monaghan in 2007.

Cavan Twp is generally bounded by Hayes Line to the north, County Road 28 and Highway 7 to the east, the Port Hope boundary and Eagleson Line to the south and Dranoel Road and Glamorgan Road to the west, and covers approximately 26,885 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), John M. Turner Memorial Highway, a quarry or aggregate pit, a landfill site, St Paul's Anglican Cemetery, Grace Presbyterian Cemetery and Gardiner's United Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 7. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Cavan Twp includes Millbrook Conservation Area, Millbrook Fair Grounds and Ganaraska Forest 2, and Baxter Creek, Squirrel Creek and Jackson Creek run through or along the community. Baxter Creek Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Millbrook branch of the Cavan Monaghan Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Peterborough Speedway.

12.05.0023.t:
Millbrook Village, Cavan Monaghan

Millbrook is the main village of Cavan Monaghan. It began in 1816, when John Deyell built the first sawmill on the stream. Most of the downtown along King and Tupper Streets was rebuilt after a fire in 1875. The village lost population in the 1880s as families moved west, and it merged into the Township of Cavan-Millbrook-North Monaghan in 1998.

The boundary of Millbrook Village follows local streets, lot lines and natural features rather than major roads, and the community covers approximately 222 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Millbrook Village.

Green space in Millbrook Village includes Millbrook Conservation Area and Millbrook Fair Grounds, and Baxter Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Millbrook branch of the Cavan Monaghan Public Library.

02.07.0300.t:
Kortright East, Guelph

This area in south-central Guelph is named after Kortright Road, which runs through it. It was largely built up with suburban housing in the later 20th century as the city expanded south of the university. Guelph itself was founded in 1827 by John Galt of the Canada Company and became a city in 1879.

Kortright East is generally bounded by Stone Road to the north, Victoria Road to the east, Arkell Road to the south and Gordon Street to the west, and covers approximately 373 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Kortright East.

Green space in Kortright East includes Arboretum Nature Reserve, Macalister Park and Jubilee Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. University of Guelph is also located in the community.

02.07.0160.t:
Kortright Hills, Guelph

Kortright Hills is a residential area in south-west Guelph, near the Speed River and surrounding conservation lands. Most homes were built in the 1980s and early 1990s, with small new developments since. It takes its name from Kortright Road. Guelph itself was founded in 1827 by John Galt of the Canada Company and became a city in 1879.

Kortright Hills is generally bounded by the Speed River and Highway 6 to the north, the Hanlon Expressway to the east, Forestell Road and Downey Road to the south and the Puslinch boundary to the west, and covers approximately 538 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 12% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, the Hanlon Expressway and Highway 6. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Kortright Hills includes Mollison Park, Woodland Glen Park and Phelan Conservation Area, and Hanlon Creek and the Speed River run through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

02.07.0380.t:
Willow West/Sugarbush/West Acres, Guelph

This community is a residential area in the west end of Guelph, named after local streets and subdivisions such as Willow Road. Guelph was founded in 1827 by John Galt of the Canada Company and became a city in 1879. The west end grew as the city expanded onto former Guelph Township farmland, with most housing here built in the second half of the 20th century.

Willow West/Sugarbush/West Acres is generally bounded by the Guelph/Eramosa boundary to the north and Highway 6 to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,219 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision), the Guelph Wastewater Treatment Plant and industrial lands (approximately 26% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 6 and Dolime Quarry. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Willow West/Sugarbush/West Acres includes Margaret Greene Park, Stephanie Park and Castlebury Park, and the Speed River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the West End branch of the Guelph Public Library. Conestoga College - Guelph Campus is also located in the community.

02.08.0020.t:
Aberfoyle, Puslinch

Aberfoyle was named by John McFarlane, who came from Aberfoyle in Perthshire, Scotland, in 1841 and ran the first general store. The area was earlier called Schatzville, after George Schatz, who built mills here in 1831. Aberfoyle was settled in the 1840s on Brock Road (old Highway 6), and its post office opened in 1854. It is the administrative centre of the Township of Puslinch.

Aberfoyle is generally bounded by Brock Road to the north and Gilmour Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 114 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Aberfoyle Pit lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Aberfoyle includes Puslinch Community Park. Residents are served by one school and the Puslinch branch of the Wellington County Library.

02.07.0390.t:
York/Watson Industrial Park, Guelph

This area in the east end of Guelph takes its name from York Road and Watson Parkway (formerly Watson Road). The York Road corridor near the Eramosa River has long been one of the city's manufacturing districts, and industrial development later extended east toward Watson Parkway. Guelph was founded in 1827 by John Galt of the Canada Company and became a city in 1879.

York/Watson Industrial Park is generally bounded by York Road to the north, the Guelph/Eramosa boundary and Skyway Drive to the east, the Puslinch boundary to the south and Victoria Road to the west, and covers approximately 522 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Goderich Subdivision rail line, Cargill Proteins (industrial plant) and industrial lands (approximately 19% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Eramosa River runs through or along the community.

02.08.0030.t:
Morriston, Puslinch

Morriston is a village on Highway 6 in the Township of Puslinch. The area was settled in the 1830s and many of its early residents were German. By 1857 the village had its own volunteer fire company. Morriston has remained a small village serving the surrounding rural area.

Morriston is generally bounded by Calfass Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 134 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 6. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Morriston is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

02.04.0040.t:
Belwood, Centre Wellington

Belwood is a village on the north shore of Lake Belwood, in the former West Garafraxa Township. It began around 1850 and was called Skeenville after early postmaster George Skeen. It was surveyed into lots and renamed Douglas around 1860, and became Belwood in 1885. The Shand Dam created Lake Belwood in 1942, and the area joined Centre Wellington in 1999.

Belwood is generally bounded by Sideroad 9 to the south and Lake Belwood to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 256 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Belwood.

Green space in Belwood includes Douglas Park and Maple Park, and the Grand River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Belwood.

02.04.0020.t:
Elora/Salem, Centre Wellington

Elora was founded in 1832 by Captain William Gilkison, who opened a sawmill and store at the falls of the Grand River. Its name came from his brother's ship, which was named after the Ellora Caves in India. Elora became a village in 1858. Salem, on Irvine Creek to the northwest, was founded in 1845 by Sem Wissler and has since grown together with Elora. Both became part of Centre Wellington in 1999, and newer subdivisions have been added since.

Elora/Salem is generally bounded by the Grand River to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 760 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Elora/Salem.

The Grand River runs through or along the community.

02.04.0030.t:
Fergus, Centre Wellington

Fergus was founded in 1833 by Adam Fergusson and James Webster, who bought approximately 7,000 acres on the Grand River. It was first called Little Falls and was named after Fergusson. It became a village in 1858 and a town in 1953. Fergus joined the Township of Centre Wellington in 1999 and has grown with new subdivisions since then.

Fergus is generally bounded by the Grand River to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,355 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Fergus.

The Grand River runs through or along the community.

02.04.0060.t:
Rural Centre Wellington West, Centre Wellington

This is the rural western part of the Township of Centre Wellington. Centre Wellington was formed on January 1, 1999, by merging Fergus, Elora, the townships of Nichol, Pilkington and West Garafraxa, and part of Eramosa Township. The rural area was settled from the 1830s and remains mostly farmland with small hamlets such as Inverhaugh and Aboyne.

Rural Centre Wellington West is generally bounded by the Guelph/Eramosa boundary and Sideroad 6 to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 10,700 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Grand River and Cox Creek run through or along the community.

02.08.0031.t:
Rural Puslinch West, Puslinch

Rural Puslinch West covers the western farmland of the Township of Puslinch, between Guelph and Cambridge. The township was surveyed from 1828 to 1832 and named after Puslinch House in Devon, England, birthplace of Lady Colborne. Settlers arrived in the 1830s, many by the Stone Road from Dundas, and the township was incorporated in 1850. The area includes Badenoch, near the site of a large pre-contact Neutral (Attawandaron) village.

Rural Puslinch West is generally bounded by the Guelph/Eramosa boundary and the Guelph boundary to the north, the Hanlon Expressway and Downey Road to the east, Wellington Road 34 to the south and the Speed River to the west, and covers approximately 3,967 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Hanlon Expressway, Glenchristie Quarry, a landfill site and Howitt Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and Spencer Pit. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Speed River and Irish Creek run through or along the community.

02.07.0350.t:
St. Patrick's Ward, Guelph

St. Patrick's Ward lies east of the Speed River and north of the Eramosa River, near downtown Guelph. It was first called Ward One, then East Ward, then St. Patrick's Ward. Early factories used water power from the rivers, which gave it an industrial and working-class character. In the mid-20th century it became known as "the Ward", largely because of its growing Italian community.

St. Patrick's Ward is generally bounded by Elizabeth Street to the north, Victoria Road to the east, the Eramosa River to the south and the Speed River to the west, and covers approximately 191 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Goderich Subdivision rail line and industrial lands (approximately 20% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in St. Patrick's Ward includes Eramosa River Park, York Road Park and Lyon Park, and the Eramosa River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

02.07.0340.t:
St. George's, Guelph

St. George's Park is a residential area north of downtown Guelph, on higher ground once known as Horsman's Hill after local business owner John Horsman. The steep ground slowed development until the 1850s. The area is known for large estate homes such as Wyoming, Gilnockie, Tyrcathlen and Maplebank.

St. George's is generally bounded by Eramosa Road to the north, Victoria Road to the east, Elizabeth Street to the south and the Speed River to the west, and covers approximately 209 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are the Goderich Subdivision rail line. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in St. George's includes Franchetto Park, St. George's Park and Green Meadows Park, and the Speed River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

02.06.0020.t:
Eden Mills, Guelph/Eramosa

Eden Mills is a hamlet on the Eramosa River. It began in 1842 when the Kribbs family built a mill, and the place was first known as Kribbs Mill. In 1846 the new mill owner renamed it Eden Mills. A Toronto Suburban Railway stop served the village from 1917 to 1930. It was part of Eramosa Township, which merged with Guelph Township in 1999 to form Guelph/Eramosa.

Eden Mills is generally bounded by the Milton boundary to the south and Barden Street and Wellington Road 29 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 189 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Eden Mills includes Memorial Park, and the Eramosa River and Blue Springs Creek run through or along the community.

02.07.0370.t:
Village By The Arboretum, Guelph

Village by the Arboretum is a residential community for older adults in south-east Guelph, next to the University of Guelph Arboretum. It was mostly built in the 1990s, with condominiums, townhomes and detached bungalows set around ponds and walking trails. The University of Guelph grew from the Ontario Agricultural College, founded in 1874, and became a university in 1964.

Village By The Arboretum is generally bounded by Stone Road to the north, Zaduk Place and Elmridge Drive to the east, Lorna Drive to the south and Monticello Crescent and Hands Drive to the west, and covers approximately 48 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Village By The Arboretum.

Other notable landmarks include University of Guelph Arboretum.

07.01.1890.t:
Rymal, Hamilton

Rymal is an area of the south Hamilton Mountain named for Rymal Road. The road is named after William Rymal, an early settler who owned land on the Mountain. The area was once part of Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages until 1960. Specific records on the build-out of the neighbourhood were not found.

Rymal is generally bounded by Stone Church Road to the north, Chippewa Trail to the east, Rymal Road to the south and Upper Ottawa Street to the west, and covers approximately 86 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 81% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Rymal is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

02.06.0031.t:
Rural Guelph/Eramosa East, Guelph/Eramosa

This is the rural eastern part of Guelph/Eramosa Township, largely within the former Eramosa Township. Eramosa was first settled in 1821, mainly by Scottish and Irish settlers, on land purchased from the Mississaugas. The name comes from an Indigenous word, Un-ne-mo-sah, often translated as "dog" or "black dog". Eramosa and Guelph townships merged in 1999 to form Guelph/Eramosa.

Rural Guelph/Eramosa East is generally bounded by Wellington Road 22 to the north, Eramosa-Erin Townline and Wellington Road 26 to the east, Highway 7 to the south and Highway 6 and the Guelph boundary to the west, and covers approximately 19,793 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision) and Johnston Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Woodlawn Memorial Park (cemetery) and Marymount Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Guelph/Eramosa East includes Guelph Lake Conservation Area, Rockwood Conservation Area and Guelph Lake Sports Fields, and the Eramosa River and the Speed River run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Guelph Lake. Guelph Lakes Golf and Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Rockwood branch of the Wellington County Library.

02.06.0032.t:
Rural Guelph/Eramosa West, Guelph/Eramosa

This is the rural western part of Guelph/Eramosa Township, largely within the former Guelph Township. Guelph Township was first settled in 1825, and in 1827 the Canada Company resettled Scottish emigrants known as the La Guayrans on land here. The area has remained mainly agricultural with scattered hamlets. Guelph and Eramosa townships merged in 1999 to form Guelph/Eramosa.

Rural Guelph/Eramosa West is generally bounded by the Centre Wellington boundary to the north, Highway 6 to the east and the Guelph boundary to the south, and covers approximately 9,648 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision), the Goderich Subdivision rail line, Spencer Pit, Dolime Quarry, Marymount Cemetery and Jesuit Cemetrary (cemetery). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 6, Glenchristie Quarry and the Guelph Wastewater Treatment Plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Ellis Creek, Hopewell Creek and the Speed River run through or along the community. Residents are served by the Wellington County Library, Marden Branch.

02.06.0030.t:
Rockwood, Guelph/Eramosa

Rockwood is the main village in Guelph/Eramosa Township, on the Eramosa River. Settlement in this part of Eramosa Township began in the 1820s and centred on a community first called Brotherstown, later renamed Rockwood. River-powered mills and limestone quarrying formed the early economy. Eramosa Township merged with Guelph Township in 1999 to form Guelph/Eramosa.

Rockwood is generally bounded by Edgar Bonner Avenue to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 359 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision) and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rockwood includes Rockwood Conservation Area, Rockmosa Park and Lloyd Dyer Park, and the Eramosa River and Richardson Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Rockwood branch of the Wellington County Library.

02.03.0030.t:
Rural Mapleton, Mapleton

Rural Mapleton covers the farmland and hamlets of the Township of Mapleton in Wellington County. The land was part of the Queen's Bush and was surveyed in the 1840s: Peel Township in 1843 and Maryborough Township in 1849. The Grand Trunk Railway arrived in the early 1870s, with stations at Alma, Goldstone, Drayton and Moorefield. Mapleton was formed on January 1, 1999, from Peel, Maryborough and the Village of Drayton.

Rural Mapleton is generally bounded by the Wellington North boundary to the north and the Centre Wellington boundary to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,065 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Rural Mapleton.

Rural Mapleton is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

02.07.0320.t:
Pineridge/Westminster Woods, Guelph

Pine Ridge and Westminster Woods are newer residential areas in Guelph's south end, near Highway 401 access. Pine Ridge was built first, followed by Westminster Woods, and both have continued to grow in the 2000s and 2010s. Part of Guelph's south end was annexed from Puslinch Township in 1993 for future growth.

Pineridge/Westminster Woods is generally bounded by Arkell Road to the north, Victoria Road to the east, Maltby Road to the south and Gordon Street to the west, and covers approximately 720 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Pineridge/Westminster Woods.

Green space in Pineridge/Westminster Woods includes Orin Reid Park, Clair Park and Westminster Woods Park. The community includes or fronts onto Hall's Pond. Springfield Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Westminister Square branch of the Guelph Public Library.

02.07.0260.t:
Dovercliffe Park/Old University, Guelph

This area lies in south-central Guelph between the Speed River and the University of Guelph campus, along the Gordon Street corridor known historically as College Hill. Growth here followed the founding of the Ontario Agricultural College in 1874, then in Guelph Township, and many homes were built for college staff. The city limits were extended south of Forbes Avenue in the 1950s. The colleges merged to form the University of Guelph in 1964.

Dovercliffe Park/Old University is generally bounded by the Speed River to the north, the Eramosa River and Victoria Road to the east and Stone Road to the south, and covers approximately 881 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 6, Dolime Quarry, a hydro transformer station (Cedar Transformer Station) and Edinburgh Well. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Dovercliffe Park/Old University includes The Arboretum, Centennial Park and Silver Creek Park, and the Speed River runs through or along the community. Cutten Fields Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools. Shopping is available at Stone Road Mall. University of Guelph is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include John McCrae Memorial Garden.

02.07.0250.t:
Clairfields/Hanlon Business Park, Guelph

This area is in Guelph's south end, near the Hanlon Expressway and Clair Road. In 1993 the city annexed land from Puslinch Township for future growth and employment, and part of these lands became the Hanlon Creek Business Park. Residential subdivisions in the south end were largely built from the 1990s onward. Guelph itself was founded in 1827 by John Galt of the Canada Company and became a city in 1879.

Clairfields/Hanlon Business Park is generally bounded by Gordon Street to the east, Maltby Road to the south and the Hanlon Expressway to the west, and covers approximately 905 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Hanlon Expressway, Alectra (industrial plant), a hydro transformer station (Arlen Transformer Station), a hydro transformer station (Guelph Hanlon Transformer Station) and industrial lands (approximately 23% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Clairfields/Hanlon Business Park includes Preservation Park, South End Community Park and Lewis Farm Park. Residents are served by one school.

02.07.0270.t:
Downtown, Guelph

Downtown Guelph is the original town site laid out by John Galt in 1827, with a radial and grid street plan around squares and broad main streets. The Canada Company sold its first residential lots near Farquhar and Freshfield streets, and the oldest remaining home in the core dates to approximately 1832. The Grand Trunk Railway arrived in 1856 and spurred growth. Guelph became a city in 1879.

Downtown is generally bounded by London Road to the north, the Speed River to the south and Edinburgh Road to the west, and covers approximately 227 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are the Goderich Subdivision rail line. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Downtown includes Silver Creek Park, Royal City Park and John Galt Park, and the Speed River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Main branch of the Guelph Public Library, and transit is provided by the Guelph Central Station GO Station.

02.04.0050.t:
Rural Centre Wellington East, Centre Wellington

This is the rural eastern part of the Township of Centre Wellington. Centre Wellington was formed on January 1, 1999, by merging Fergus, Elora, the townships of Nichol, Pilkington and West Garafraxa, and part of Eramosa Township. The rural area was settled from the 1830s and remains mostly farmland with small hamlets.

Rural Centre Wellington East is generally bounded by the Wellington North boundary and the Mapleton boundary to the north, Townline East Garafraxa West Garafraxa to the east and Wellington Road 22 to the south, and covers approximately 25,924 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a hydro transformer station and Belwood Transfer Station (landfill). Along or just beyond its edges are a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Centre Wellington East includes Belwood Conservation Area, Benham Tract and Camp Nokimis, and Irvine Creek and the Grand River run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Belwood.

02.08.0032.t:
Rural Puslinch East, Puslinch

Rural Puslinch East covers the eastern farmland of the Township of Puslinch, south of Guelph. The township was surveyed from 1828 to 1832 as Church Lands and named after Puslinch House in Devon, England, birthplace of Lady Colborne. Settlers, mostly Highland Scots, arrived in the 1830s, and the township was incorporated in 1850. The area includes the community of Arkell, named after John Arkell, who arrived in 1831.

Rural Puslinch East is generally bounded by Victoria Road to the north, Nassagaweya-Puslinch Townline to the east and Maltby Road and a hydro corridor to the west, and covers approximately 10,129 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Goderich Subdivision rail line, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), Highway 401, Highway 6, Aberfoyle Pit, Arkell Ridge Sand and Gravel Ltd. (quarry) and Crown Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Hanlon Expressway, Neubauer Pit, McNally Pit and a hydro transformer station. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Puslinch East includes Starkey Hill Conservation Area and Puslinch Community Park, and Aberfoyle Creek and Mountsberg Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Mountsberg Reservoir. Victoria Park Valley Golf Club and Victoria Park East Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by one school and the Puslinch branch of the Wellington County Library. Other notable landmarks include Arkell Springs.

07.01.1710.t:
Gilkson, Hamilton

Gilkson is a residential neighbourhood on Hamilton's West Mountain. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. Most of the neighbourhood was developed in approximately the 1970s and 1980s.

Gilkson is generally bounded by the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the north, Garth Street to the east, Stone Church Road to the south and Upper Paradise Road to the west, and covers approximately 77 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Gilkson includes Gilkson Park. Residents are served by one school.

02.02.0020.t:
Rural Wellington North, Wellington North

Rural Wellington North covers the countryside of the former Arthur Township and West Luther Township. The area was opened to settlement in the 1840s along the Garafraxa Colonization Road, with farms and mill hamlets such as Kenilworth, Damascus and Riverstown. On January 1, 1999 these townships merged with the Village of Arthur and the Town of Mount Forest to form the Township of Wellington North.

Rural Wellington North is generally bounded by the East Luther Grand Valley boundary and the Southgate boundary to the north and the Centre Wellington boundary to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 14,416 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Rural Wellington North is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

02.05.0030.t:
Erin, Erin

The village of Erin grew around mills built on the Credit River between 1826 and 1829 and was first known as McMillan's Mills. It was later called Erinsville and then Erin, after the township, whose name is a poetic name for Ireland. The Credit Valley Railway arrived in 1879, the same year Erin was incorporated as a village. In 1997 the village, Hillsburgh and Erin Township were combined into the Town of Erin.

Erin is generally bounded by Sideroad 17 to the north, Dundas Street to the east and Wellington Road 124 to the south, and covers approximately 811 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a landfill site, Erin Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 11% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Erin Pit. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Erin includes Erin Lion's Park and McMillan Park, and the Credit River (Erin Branch) runs through or along the community. Erin Heights Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Erin Village branch of the Wellington County Library.

02.05.0020.t:
Rural Erin, Erin

This is the rural part of the former Township of Erin, named with the poetic name for Ireland. Settlement began in the early 1820s, with early settlers at Ballinafad and Hillsburgh, and the first township meeting was held in 1824. Most early settlers were Scottish. In 1997 the township was amalgamated with the villages of Erin and Hillsburgh into the Town of Erin.

Rural Erin is generally bounded by Townline Erin Garafraxa to the north, Winston Churchill Boulevard to the east, Sideroad 32 to the south and Wellington Road 26 and Eramosa-Erin Townline to the west, and covers approximately 29,952 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a landfill site, Erin Pit, Erin Cemetery, Huxley Cemetery c. 1884-1984 and Churchill Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Erin includes Hillsburgh Park, Erin Lion's Park and McMillan Park, and the Eramosa River, the Credit River (Erin Branch) and the Speed River run through or along the community. Erin Heights Golf & Country Club and Calerin Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools, the Hillsburgh Public Library and the Erin Village branch of the Wellington County Library.

02.08.0033.t:
Crieff/Aikensville/Killean, Puslinch

Crieff, Aikensville and Killean are small rural hamlets in the Township of Puslinch, Wellington County. Puslinch was surveyed from 1828 to 1832 and was settled in the 1830s, largely by Highland Scots. Many early settlers reached Killean by the Stone Road from Dundas. Crieff shares its name with Crieff in Perthshire, Scotland. The township was incorporated in 1850.

Crieff/Aikensville/Killean is generally bounded by Wellington Road 34 to the north, a hydro corridor to the east, Gore Road to the south and Concession 1 and Ellis Road to the west, and covers approximately 6,454 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), Highway 401, Highway 6, the Hanlon Expressway, McMillan Pit, Lanci Pit, Mast Pit, Neubauer Pit, Mill Creek Pit, McNally Pit and a hydro transformer station. Along or just beyond its edges are Aberfoyle Pit and Killean Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Mill Creek, Aberfoyle Creek and Irish Creek run through or along the community.

02.08.0034.t:
Puslinch Lake Settlement Areas, Puslinch

Puslinch Lake is described as the largest kettle lake in North America and lies at the western edge of Puslinch, next to Cambridge. Settlers arrived in the 1830s, and by the late 1880s the lake was a summer resort for Wellington and Waterloo counties, with a hotel built by Guelph brewer George Sleeman in 1880. Cottage subdivisions were laid out in 1916 and the 1920s. Many cottages have since been replaced by year-round homes, and Barber's Beach became the Irish Creek Estates area after 2000.

Puslinch Lake Settlement Areas is generally bounded by Ellis Road to the north, Sideroad 10 to the east, Concession 1 to the south and Townline Road to the west, and covers approximately 1,247 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401 and Killean Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Puslinch Lake Settlement Areas includes Puslinch Lake Irish Creek Research Area and PLCA picnic area. The community includes or fronts onto Puslinch Lake and Little Lake. Puslinch Lake Golf Club is located in the area.

07.01.1650.t:
Thorner, Hamilton

Thorner is a residential neighbourhood on the south Hamilton Mountain, centred on a shopping plaza on Upper Wentworth Street. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most homes were built between 1961 and 1990.

Thorner is generally bounded by Mohawk Road to the north, Upper Sherman Avenue to the east, the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the south and Upper Wentworth Street to the west, and covers approximately 96 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and a hydro transformer station (Mohawk TS). Along or just beyond its edges are the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway, Anshe Sholom Cemetery and Burkholder United Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Thorner includes Thorner Park. Residents are served by one school. Shopping is available at CF Limeridge.

10.02.0120.t:
Bay Ridges, Pickering

Bay Ridges is on the Lake Ontario shore at Frenchman's Bay. In the mid-1800s a port village called Fairport grew up here around a grain elevator and wharf, and it declined once railways took over grain shipping. Summer cottages were built in the 1910s and 1920s, and many were converted to year-round homes after Highway 401 opened in the 1950s. Most of the present neighbourhood was built in the 1960s and 1970s, with the Nautical Village added in the early 2000s.

Bay Ridges is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, a hydro corridor to the east and Lake Ontario to the west, and covers approximately 427 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision), the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the CN rail line (York Subdivision), the CN rail line (CN Kingston Subdivision), Pickering Nuclear Generating Station, Fairport Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 8% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401 and a hydro transformer station (Pickering SS A). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bay Ridges includes Alex Robertson Park, Kinsmen Park and Douglas Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools, and transit is provided by the Pickering GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Frenchman's Bay.

09.02.0160.t:
Glen Shields, Vaughan

Glen Shields is a residential area in the Concord district of Vaughan, near Dufferin Street and Steeles Avenue. Concord began as a postal village in 1854 and remained rural for much of its history. The Glen Shields residential area was built in the 1970s and 1980s. It has been part of the Town, now City, of Vaughan since 1971.

Glen Shields is generally bounded by Highway 7 and Centre Street to the north, Dufferin Street to the east, the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 201 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 407 and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), the CN rail line (York Subdivision) and the CN rail line. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Glen Shields includes Marita Paine Park, Glen Shields Park and Riviera Park, and the Don River West Branch runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

04.02.0060.t:
Creemore, Clearview

Creemore is a village in the Mad River valley, founded by Irish settler Edward Webster, with settlement beginning in 1842. The name comes from the Irish "croí mór", meaning "big heart". Creemore was incorporated as a village in 1889. It became part of Clearview Township on January 1, 1994.

Creemore is generally bounded by the Mad River and Sideroad 6 & 7 Nottawasaga to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 400 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Creemore Union Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Creemore includes Gowan Memorial Park, Mad River Park and Creemore Green, and the Mad River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

07.01.1750.t:
Crerar, Hamilton

Crerar is a residential neighbourhood on the central Hamilton Mountain, near Upper James Street and the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway. It is named after General Harry Crerar, a leading Canadian field commander in the Second World War. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Crerar is generally bounded by the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the north, Upper Wentworth Street to the east, Stone Church Road to the south and Upper Wellington Street to the west, and covers approximately 77 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Crerar includes Crerar Neighbourhood Park.

01.E07.1050.t:
Agincourt North, City of Toronto (TRREB district E07)

Agincourt takes its name from a post office opened in 1858 by John Hill in his general store at today's Brimley Road and Sheppard Avenue, named after the 1415 Battle of Agincourt. The area was mostly farmland in Scarborough Township, with a Presbyterian congregation (now Knox United Church) from 1848 and a railway station on the Toronto and Nipissing line. The land north of Sheppard was largely converted to suburban housing in the last third of the 20th century. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Agincourt North is generally bounded by a hydro corridor to the north, Markham Road and Finch Avenue to the east, the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) and Brimley Road to the south and Midland Avenue and Huntingwood Drive to the west, and covers approximately 730 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), CPKC Toronto Yard and industrial lands (approximately 11% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Agincourt North includes Iroquois Park, Brimley Woods and Richmond Park. Residents are served by approximately 14 schools and the Woodside Square branch of the Toronto Public Library. Shopping is available at Woodside Square.

07.01.1800.t:
Albion Falls, Hamilton

Albion Falls is a neighbourhood on the east Hamilton Mountain, named after the nearby Albion Falls, a 19-metre waterfall on Red Hill Creek in the Red Hill Valley. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Albion Falls is generally bounded by Stone Church Road to the south and Escarpment Rail Trail to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 120 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the Red Hill Valley Parkway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Other notable landmarks include Red Hill Valley.

04.15.0320.t:
400 West, Barrie

This community lies along the west side of Highway 400 in Barrie. It grew mainly with the city's expansion in the 1980s and 1990s. Barrie began as a supply depot at the foot of the Nine Mile Portage during the War of 1812 and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a town in 1870 and a city in 1959, and its population roughly tripled during the 1980s and 1990s.

400 West is generally bounded by Highway 400 to the north, Salem Road to the south and Essa Road to the west, and covers approximately 604 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and industrial lands (approximately 8% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 400. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

04.15.0120.t:
Alliance, Barrie

Alliance is a residential community within the City of Barrie. Barrie began as a supply depot at the foot of the Nine Mile Portage during the War of 1812 and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a town in 1870 and a city in 1959, and its population roughly tripled during the 1980s and 1990s.

Alliance is generally bounded by Cundles Road to the north, Bell Farm Road and Duckworth Street to the east and Ottaway Avenue and Ferris Lane to the west, and covers approximately 94 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 400 and industrial lands (approximately 29% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school.

04.15.0310.t:
400 East, Barrie

This community lies in south-central Barrie, east of Highway 400 around Bayview Drive and Huronia Road. Much of south Barrie was developed during the city's rapid growth in the 1980s and 1990s. Barrie began as a supply depot at the foot of the Nine Mile Portage during the War of 1812 and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a town in 1870 and a city in 1959, and its population roughly tripled during the 1980s and 1990s.

400 East is generally bounded by Huronia Road to the north, Lovers Creek to the east, Lockhart Road to the south and Highway 400 to the west, and covers approximately 815 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 400 and industrial lands (approximately 47% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

400 East is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

04.15.0070.t:
400 North, Barrie

This community lies in north Barrie along Highway 400, near the Highway 400 and Highway 11 junction. It grew mainly with the city's expansion in the 1980s and 1990s. Barrie began as a supply depot at the foot of the Nine Mile Portage during the War of 1812 and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a town in 1870 and a city in 1959, and its population roughly tripled during the 1980s and 1990s.

400 North is generally bounded by Highway 400 to the south and the Meaford Subdivision rail line and Dunlop Street to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 517 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Meaford Subdivision rail line, Highway 400, a hydro transformer station (Barrie TS) and industrial lands (approximately 54% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

400 North is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

01.E07.1060.t:
Agincourt South-Malvern West, City of Toronto (TRREB district E07)

Agincourt takes its name from a post office opened in 1858 at today's Brimley Road and Sheppard Avenue, named after the 1415 Battle of Agincourt. The village grew around Knox Presbyterian Church (1848) and the Toronto and Nipissing railway station, now Agincourt GO Station. From the 1960s the area was built up with suburban housing and industry, and from the 1980s it became home to a large Chinese-Canadian community with Asian-themed shopping centres. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Agincourt South-Malvern West is generally bounded by the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line and Brimley Road to the north, the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) and Markham Road to the east, Highway 401 to the south and Kennedy Road to the west, and covers approximately 801 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line, Highway 401, a cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 24% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are CPKC Toronto Yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Agincourt South-Malvern West includes White Haven Park, Agincourt Park and McDairmid Woods Park. Residents are served by approximately 10 schools, and transit is provided by the Agincourt GO Station.

09.03.0060.t:
Aileen-Willowbrook, Markham

Aileen-Willowbrook is a residential area in the Thornhill part of Markham, near Bayview Avenue and John Street. Thornhill was founded in 1794 and named after Benjamin Thorne, who arrived in 1820. Growth in this part of Thornhill came mainly from the 1960s and 1970s, tied to the border with Toronto. Thornhill's police village ended in 1971 when York Region was created, and the east side passed to Markham.

Aileen-Willowbrook is generally bounded by German Mills Creek to the east, the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the south and Bayview Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 275 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision), the CN rail line (Bala Subdivision), the CN rail line and industrial lands (approximately 10% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (York Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision), Highway 407 and Holy Cross Catholic Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Aileen-Willowbrook includes Valley View Park, Bayview Reservoir Park and Johnsview Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Thornhill branch of the Markham Public Library.

09.03.0080.t:
Bayview Glen, Markham

Bayview Glen is a residential area in the Thornhill part of Markham, on the border with Toronto at Steeles Avenue. It was built on former farmland, including the Stone family farm, and was largely developed between 1960 and 1980. The east side of Thornhill became part of Markham in 1971 when York Region was created.

Bayview Glen is generally bounded by the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision) to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Bayview Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 141 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (York Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision), the CN rail line and the CN rail line (Bala Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bayview Glen includes Glencrest Park, Bayview Glen Park and Stonefarm Park, and the Don River East Branch runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

07.01.1230.t:
Ainslie Wood, Hamilton

Ainslie Wood takes its name from George Howlett Ainslie, who settled on a farm here in 1838; the wooded land owned by his family became a well-known recreation area. In 1908 the Burke Real Estate Company laid out streets and lots on former farmland. The area joined Hamilton from Ancaster Township in 1930, the same year McMaster University was established next door, and much of the housing followed through the mid-20th century.

Ainslie Wood is generally bounded by Cootes Drive to the north, Highway 403 and Main Street to the east and Coldwater Creek to the west, and covers approximately 388 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 403, a hydro transformer station (Newton TS) and White Chapel Memorial Gardens (cemetery). Along or just beyond its edges are a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Ainslie Wood includes Alexander Park and Stroud Road Park, and Coldwater Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. Other notable landmarks include Binkley farmhouse and Binkley Cemetery.

05.03.0290.t:
Airport Corporate, Mississauga

Airport Corporate is a business and employment area next to Toronto Pearson International Airport, in the former Toronto Township. The airport opened in 1937 as Malton Airport on land assembled from 13 farms. The surrounding farmland was developed for offices and industry as the airport grew, and the area became part of the Town of Mississauga in 1968 and the City in 1974.

Airport Corporate is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the east, Eglinton Avenue to the south and Etobicoke Creek to the west, and covers approximately 302 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401 and Highway 401 Collector. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and Toronto Pearson International Airport. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Airport Corporate includes Max Ward Park, and Etobicoke Creek runs through or along the community.

07.01.0170.t:
Airport Employment Area, Hamilton

This area surrounds John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport near Mount Hope, in the south of the city. The airport opened in 1940 as Mount Hope Airport, mainly a Royal Canadian Air Force base used for wartime flight training. The surrounding farmland has been planned by the City of Hamilton as the Airport Employment Growth District, a business park of over 555 hectares. The area became part of the City of Hamilton in the 2001 amalgamation.

Airport Employment Area is generally bounded by Garner Road and Twenty Road to the north, Upper James Street to the east, White Church Road to the south and Fiddlers Green Road to the west, and covers approximately 3,167 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 6, John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport and Bowman United Church Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Garners Corners Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Twenty Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Other notable landmarks include John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport and Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum.

05.02.0390.t:
Airport Road/ Highway 7 Business Centre, Brampton

This is an employment area in northeast Brampton around Airport Road and Queen Street East (formerly Highway 7), north of Toronto Pearson Airport. The land was farmland in Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships. Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships were merged with the Town of Brampton in 1974 to form the City of Brampton. The area was built up with industrial and business uses in the later 20th century, tied to the nearby airport and Bramalea's planned industrial lands.

Airport Road/ Highway 7 Business Centre is generally bounded by Auction Lane to the east and Mimico Creek and Airport Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 152 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include CN Brampton Intermodal Terminal and industrial lands (approximately 36% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Airport Road/ Highway 7 Business Centre is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

04.14.0050.t:
Alcona, Innisfil

Alcona is the largest community in Innisfil, on the west shore of Lake Simcoe along Innisfil Beach Road. Innisfil Township was surveyed in 1820 and its name comes from Inis Fáil, an ancient name for Ireland. The shoreline was first used for seasonal cottages, which gradually became year-round homes after paved roads made commuting to Toronto practical. The area became part of the Town of Innisfil on January 1, 1991, and has grown with suburban subdivisions since.

Alcona is generally bounded by Lake Simcoe to the east and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and Leslie Drive to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,242 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and a wastewater treatment plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.
