Green space in Alcona includes Innisfil Beach Bark, Previn Park and Webster Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Lakeshore branch of the Innisfil Public Library.

01.W06.0200.t:
Alderwood, City of Toronto (TRREB district W06)

The name Alderwood is linked to the meaning of 'Etobicoke', usually given as 'place where the alder trees grow'. The land was farmland in Etobicoke Township, bought by Archibald Cameron in 1850 and later by Daniel Horner, after whom Horner Avenue is named. It was laid out from approximately 1918 to 1920 as New Toronto Heights, with grid streets named after Greek letters, but most single-family homes were built after the Second World War through the 1960s. Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Alderwood is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and the Gardiner Expressway to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Canpa Subdivision) to the east, the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) to the south and Etobicoke Creek to the west, and covers approximately 500 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Canpa Subdivision), Highway 427 and industrial lands (approximately 31% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and the Gardiner Expressway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Alderwood includes Etobicoke Valley Park, Connorvale Park and Sir Adam Beck Park, and Etobicoke Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Alderwood branch of the Toronto Public Library.

04.15.0230.t:
Allandale, Barrie

This is the historic railway neighbourhood on the south shore of Kempenfelt Bay. A post office opened in 1859, and some houses date from the 1870s. Allandale grew around the railway after the Ontario, Simcoe and Huron line reached Kempenfelt Bay in 1853, and was named after Toronto businessman and railway promoter William Allan. It was incorporated as a village in 1891 and was annexed by Barrie as its South Ward in 1896.

Allandale is generally bounded by Burton Avenue to the east and Highway 400 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 116 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 400. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), the Meaford Subdivision rail line and a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Other notable landmarks include Historic Allandale railway station (1904).

04.15.0220.t:
Allandale Centre, Barrie

This community is part of the historic Allandale area in south Barrie. Allandale grew around the railway after the Ontario, Simcoe and Huron line reached Kempenfelt Bay in 1853, and was named after Toronto businessman and railway promoter William Allan. It was incorporated as a village in 1891 and was annexed by Barrie as its South Ward in 1896.

Allandale Centre is generally bounded by Lakeshore Drive to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and William Street to the east, Caroline Street to the south and the Meaford Subdivision rail line and Innisfil Street to the west, and covers approximately 34 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Meaford Subdivision rail line and a wastewater treatment plant. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school, and transit is provided by the Allandale Waterfront GO Station.

04.15.0240.t:
Allandale Heights, Barrie

This community is part of the Allandale area of south Barrie. Allandale grew around the railway after the Ontario, Simcoe and Huron line reached Kempenfelt Bay in 1853, and was named after Toronto businessman and railway promoter William Allan. It was incorporated as a village in 1891 and was annexed by Barrie as its South Ward in 1896.

Allandale Heights is generally bounded by Garden Drive to the east and Bayview Drive to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 200 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 400 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Allandale Heights includes Greenfield Park and Assikinack Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

04.09.0050.t:
Anten Mills, Springwater

Anten Mills is a community in the former Vespra Township, northwest of Barrie. Its name comes from a late 1800s mill owned by Charles Anderson and a Mr. Tennant, combining the first syllables of their names. On January 1, 1994 it became part of the Township of Springwater, formed from Flos and Vespra townships, the villages of Elmvale and Hillsdale, and part of Medonte. The area has since grown with rural residential subdivisions.

Anten Mills is generally bounded by Horseshoe Valley Road to the north, Wilson Drive to the south and North Simcoe Rail Trail to the west, and covers approximately 190 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Anten Mills.

Anten Mills is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

05.01.0010.t:
Alton, Caledon

Alton is a village in northwest Caledon, on Shaw's Creek, a tributary of the Credit River. It was first settled in 1816 by Martin Middaugh Jr., and grew as a mill hamlet. The name Alton was chosen in 1852, after Alton, Illinois, and the post office opened in 1854. Most of the village was built between the 1850s and the early 1900s, and it joined the Town of Caledon in 1974.

Alton is generally bounded by Main Street to the north and Mississauga Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 158 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Alton Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Alton includes Alton Park and Emeline Park. Residents are served by one school and the Alton branch of the Caledon Public Library.

13.05.0010.t:
Alderville First Nation, Alderville First Nation

Alderville First Nation is a Mississauga Anishinaabe community near the south shore of Rice Lake. Its people's ancestors lived around the Bay of Quinte, and a Methodist Mississauga community settled on Grape Island in the 1820s. The community has been at Alderville since the mid-1830s, on land set aside in 1835 in Alnwick Township. The reserve is made up of six separate parcels within Alnwick/Haldimand Township, approximately 30 km north of Cobourg.

Alderville First Nation is generally bounded by the Alnwick/Haldimand boundary to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 264 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Alderville First Nation.

Other notable landmarks include Rice Lake (south shore).

05.02.0370.t:
Vales of Castlemore, Brampton

The Vales of Castlemore is a residential area in northeast Brampton, named after the former hamlet of Castlemore in Toronto Gore Township. The remainder of the township was merged into the City of Brampton in 1974. The area was mainly farmland, with large-lot homes from the 1970s and 1980s. Suburban development has been active since the early 1990s and through the 2000s.

Vales of Castlemore is generally bounded by Countryside Drive to the north, Goreway Drive to the south and Airport Road to the west, and covers approximately 501 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Vales of Castlemore.

Green space in Vales of Castlemore includes Treeline Pond, Treeline Park and James and Margaret McGie Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

06.02.0130.t:
Alton, Burlington

Alton is a newer neighbourhood at the north end of Burlington, south of Highway 407. It is named after Thomas Alton, who came from Westmoreland, England, in 1819 and built up approximately 1,250 acres of farmland. The area stayed largely rural until it was built out with suburban housing from the 2000s. Burlington annexed most of Nelson Township and Aldershot on January 1, 1958, and became a city in 1974.

Alton is generally bounded by Bronte Creek to the east and Dundas Street and Highway 407 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 471 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 12% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407 and St. Paul’s Presbyterian Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Alton includes Norton Park, Palladium Park and Colin Alton Parkette, and Bronte Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Alton branch of the Burlington Public Library.

10.02.0060.t:
Amberlea, Pickering

Amberlea is a residential neighbourhood in Pickering, on land that was once farmland in Pickering Township. It was developed by Bramalea Consolidated Developments Limited, with the first homes built in 1975. Approximately 250 homes were completed in the first year. The area was largely built out in the late 1970s and 1980s.

Amberlea is generally bounded by a hydro corridor and the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) to the north, Parkside Drive to the east and the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the south, and covers approximately 432 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (York Subdivision) and the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Amberlea includes Amberlea Park, Shadybrook Park and McPherson Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools. Other notable landmarks include Altona Forest.

04.18.0060.t:
Bass Lake, Severn

Bass Lake is a rural and lakeside area in the Township of Severn, near Orillia, named after the nearby lake. It lies in the former Orillia Township, which was settled for farming in the 19th century and later saw cottage and residential development. The Township of Severn was formed on January 1, 1994 from the Village of Coldwater, the townships of Matchedash and Orillia, and parts of Medonte and Tay.

Bass Lake is generally bounded by Division Road to the north, Wainman Line to the east and Highway 12 to the south, and covers approximately 148 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 12. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Bass Lake is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

07.01.0100.t:
Ancaster, Hamilton

Ancaster began around mills built in 1791 and 1792 by James Wilson, and the area was first known as Wilson's Mills. The township was named Ancaster in 1793, reportedly after the Duke of Ancaster. It was Upper Canada's largest industrial and commercial centre in the 1820s but declined as Hamilton and Dundas grew. Suburban subdivisions began after 1946 and grew quickly from the 1970s. Ancaster became a town in 1974 and joined the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Ancaster is generally bounded by Highway 403 to the east, Garner Road to the south and a hydro corridor and Shaver Road to the west, and covers approximately 1,689 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 403, St. John's Anglican Church Cemetery, St. Andrew's Presbyterian Church Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 7% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 6 and Resurrection Catholic Cemetery. The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 2.5 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Ancaster includes Little League Park, James Smith Park and Golf Links Park, and Ancaster Creek runs through or along the community. Hamilton Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools and the Ancaster branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

04.11.0050.t:
Everett, Adjala-Tosorontio

Everett is a village in the former Tosorontio Township. It was incorporated as a police village in 1909. Everett became part of the Township of Adjala-Tosorontio when Adjala, Tosorontio and the police village merged on January 1, 1994. The village has seen newer residential growth in recent decades.

Everett is generally bounded by Main Street to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 237 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Everett is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

09.03.0170.t:
Angus Glen, Markham

Angus Glen is a planned community in north-central Markham built from the late 1990s. Its East Village was designed on New Urbanism principles, with rear-lane garages, and the West Village followed from the mid-2000s. It surrounds the Angus Glen Golf Club, which opened in 1995.

Angus Glen is generally bounded by Major MacKenzie Drive to the north, Kennedy Road to the east and Bruce Creek to the south, and covers approximately 193 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include St. Philip’s on-the-Hill Anglican Church Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Bethesda Lutheran Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Angus Glen includes Colty Corners and Angus Glen Village Green, and Bruce Creek runs through or along the community. Angus Glen Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by one school.

01.C02.0860.t:
Annex, City of Toronto (TRREB district C02)

The name comes from the 'Toronto Annex' subdivision created by developer Simeon Janes in 1886. The area was annexed to the City of Toronto in 1887; parts east of Brunswick Avenue had been in the Village of Yorkville and parts to the west in Seaton Village. Large Annex-style houses were built from the late 1800s to the early 1900s. Some houses were replaced with apartments in the 1950s and 1960s, but most original houses remain.

Annex is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision) to the north, Yonge Street to the east, Bloor Street to the south and Christie Street to the west, and covers approximately 280 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision) and a hydro transformer station (Bridgman TS) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Annex includes Ramsden Park, Vermont Square Park and Jesse Ketchum Park. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools, the Palmerston branch of the Toronto Public Library and the Spadina Road branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Christie, Bathurst, Spadina and St. George subway stations.

06.02.0210.t:
Appleby, Burlington

Appleby is in southeast Burlington, near Lake Ontario and the Oakville boundary. Many early settlers came from Appleby in Westmoreland, England, which gave the hamlet its name. The hamlet had saw and grist mills on its creeks and a post office by 1857. The present neighbourhood was developed in the 1950s and 1960s, after Burlington annexed Nelson Township in 1958.

Appleby is generally bounded by Fairview Street to the north, Burloak Drive to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Appleby Line to the west, and covers approximately 509 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Appleby.

Green space in Appleby includes Centennial Trail, Skyway Park and Fothergill Woods, and Appleby Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the New Appleby branch of the Burlington Public Library. Brock University Burlington Campus is also located in the community.

05.03.0310.t:
Applewood, Mississauga

Applewood is named for the apple orchards that covered the area before development. The early settlements were the villages of Dixie and Burnhamthorpe, which served the surrounding farms. The area stayed rural until 1955, when G.S. Shipp & Sons began the Applewood Heights subdivision; Applewood Acres was one of the first major planned developments after the Second World War. Most homes date from the 1950s and 1960s.

Applewood is generally bounded by Burnhamthorpe Road to the north, Etobicoke Creek and Little Etobicoke Creek to the east, Dundas Street to the south and Cawthra Road to the west, and covers approximately 714 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, St. John’s Dixie Cemetery and Burnhamthorpe Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Mount Peace Catholic Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Applewood includes Applewood Hills, Fleetwood Park and Bloor Athletic Field, and Little Etobicoke Creek and Etobicoke Creek run through or along the community. Markland Wood Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 13 schools and the Burnhamthorpe branch of the Mississauga Library.

04.15.0330.t:
Ardagh, Barrie

Ardagh is in southwest Barrie and takes its name from Ardagh Road. Much of it was developed during the city's growth in the 1980s and 1990s. The 1985 Barrie tornado touched down in this area. Barrie began as a supply depot at the foot of the Nine Mile Portage during the War of 1812 and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a town in 1870 and a city in 1959, and its population roughly tripled during the 1980s and 1990s.

Ardagh is generally bounded by the Meaford Subdivision rail line to the north, Essa Road to the east and County Road 27 to the west, and covers approximately 761 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the Meaford Subdivision rail line. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Ardagh includes Bear Creek Eco Park, Batteaux Park and Cumming Park, and Bear Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

04.18.0070.t:
Ardtrea, Severn

Ardtrea is a small rural hamlet in the Township of Severn, north of Orillia. The area was settled for farming in the 19th century as part of the former Orillia Township. The Township of Severn was formed on January 1, 1994 from the Village of Coldwater, the townships of Matchedash and Orillia, and parts of Medonte and Tay.

Ardtrea is generally bounded by Highway 11 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 124 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 11. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Ardtrea is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

09.07.0060.t:
Armitage, Newmarket

Armitage takes its name from a former hamlet on Yonge Street that was named for its first settler, Amos Armitage. The hamlet was later taken into Newmarket's town limits. The neighbourhood lies in south-central Newmarket, south of Mulock Drive, and its housing is mainly detached homes from the 1980s.

Armitage is generally bounded by Mulock Drive to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the east, the Aurora boundary to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 180 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Holland River East Branch runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

04.19.0010.t:
Atherley, Ramara

Atherley is a community at the Atherley Narrows, where Lake Simcoe meets Lake Couchiching, across from Orillia. The narrows are the site of ancient Indigenous fishing weirs, and in 1830 the government set up a village for the Chippewas here before their move to Rama in 1838. The Grand Trunk Railway built Atherley Junction station in 1897. Atherley was in Mara Township, which merged with Rama Township in 1994 to form the Township of Ramara.

Atherley is generally bounded by Highway 12 to the east, Orkney Beach Road to the south and Lake Simcoe to the west, and covers approximately 782 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 12. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Atherley includes Mara Provincial Park and Atherley Community Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. Residents are served by the Atherley branch of the Ramara Township Public Library.

09.06.0070.t:
Aurora Estates, Aurora

Aurora Estates is in south Aurora near the Richmond Hill and King borders, on the Oak Ridges Moraine. It is made up mainly of estate homes on large, often wooded lots. Aurora began as Machell's Corners, a hamlet at Yonge Street and Wellington Street where Richard Machell opened a store in 1804. The railway arrived in 1853, the village was incorporated in 1863 and it became a town in 1888.

Aurora Estates is generally bounded by Vandorf Sideroad to the north, Bayview Avenue to the east and Bloomington Road and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 660 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Aurora Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Aurora Estates includes Evans Park, and Tannery Creek runs through or along the community. Beacon Hall Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.06.0060.t:
Aurora Grove, Aurora

Aurora Grove lies east of downtown Aurora. It was mainly built from the 1970s to the 1990s, with newer subdivisions added later. Aurora began as Machell's Corners, a hamlet at Yonge Street and Wellington Street where Richard Machell opened a store in 1804. The railway arrived in 1853, the village was incorporated in 1863 and it became a town in 1888.

Aurora Grove is generally bounded by Wellington Street to the north, Bayview Avenue to the east, Vandorf Sideroad to the south and Industrial Parkway to the west, and covers approximately 227 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and industrial lands (approximately 28% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Aurora Grove includes Sheppard's Bush and James Lloyd Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.06.0020.t:
Aurora Heights, Aurora

Aurora Heights lies northwest of Yonge Street and Wellington Street. It was built mostly from the 1950s through the 1970s, during Aurora's post-war suburban growth. Aurora began as Machell's Corners, a hamlet at Yonge Street and Wellington Street where Richard Machell opened a store in 1804. The railway arrived in 1853, the village was incorporated in 1863 and it became a town in 1888.

Aurora Heights is generally bounded by Orchard Heights Boulevard to the north, Yonge Street to the east, Wellington Street to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 224 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Aurora Heights.

Green space in Aurora Heights includes Fleury Park, Machell Park and Copland Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

09.06.0030.t:
Aurora Highlands, Aurora

Aurora Highlands covers much of west Aurora between Yonge Street and Bathurst Street. Older sections such as Regency Acres date from the 1960s and 1970s, and the former Aurora Highlands golf course has been redeveloped as Highland Gate. Aurora began as Machell's Corners, a hamlet at Yonge Street and Wellington Street where Richard Machell opened a store in 1804. The railway arrived in 1853, the village was incorporated in 1863 and it became a town in 1888.

Aurora Highlands is generally bounded by Wellington Street and Murray Drive to the north, Yonge Street to the east, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 579 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Aurora Highlands includes Case Woodlot, Highland Gate Park and Confederation Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools.

07.01.1150.t:
Homeside, Hamilton

Homeside is a residential neighbourhood in Hamilton's east end, in the lower city. The area was farmland in the old townships east of Hamilton before it was annexed by the City of Hamilton in the twentieth century. Barton Township was fully absorbed by the city in 1960. Much of its housing was built in the first half of the twentieth century as the east end grew with nearby industry.

Homeside is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) to the north, Strathearne Avenue to the east, Main Street to the south and Kenilworth Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 113 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor and the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Homeside includes Andrew Warburton Memorial Park and Fairfield Park. Residents are served by one school.

09.06.0040.t:
Aurora Village, Aurora

Aurora Village is the town's historic core around Yonge Street and Wellington Street, the site of Machell's Corners. Richard Machell opened a store here in 1804, and the settlement was later renamed Aurora after the Roman goddess of dawn. The railway arrived in 1853, Aurora became a village in 1863 and a town in 1888. The area mixes 19th-century buildings with post-war and newer infill housing.

Aurora Village is generally bounded by Yonge Street to the north, Industrial Parkway to the south and Murray Drive and Wellington Street to the west, and covers approximately 468 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 19% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Aurora Village includes Sheppard's Bush, Craddock Park and Aurora Peace Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Aurora Public Library, and transit is provided by the Aurora GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Hillary House and Aurora Town Square.

09.03.0040.t:
Grandview, Markham

Grandview lies in the Thornhill area of Markham, south of the historic Thornhill village along John Street. Thornhill was founded in 1794 and named after Benjamin Thorne, who ran mills here from 1820. The area became part of the Town of Markham in 1971; its housing was largely built in the post-war decades, with later infill.

Grandview is generally bounded by the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the north, Bayview Avenue to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 158 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (York Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Grandview includes Grandview Park and Sir Robert Watson-Watt Parkette, and the Don River East Branch runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

05.02.0300.t:
Avondale, Brampton

Avondale is part of Bramalea, named after Avondale Boulevard, a street in Bramalea's first ('A') section. Bramalea was developed as a planned 'new town' in the former Chinguacousy Township by Bramalea Consolidated Developments (later Bramalea Limited), Canada's first satellite community. Development began with the A section in the 1960s and moved through the alphabet. Bramalea founder William Sheard built one of the first houses at Bramalea Road and Avondale Boulevard.

Avondale is generally bounded by Clark Boulevard to the north, Bramalea Road to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Dixie Road to the west, and covers approximately 323 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 20% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Avondale includes Clark Park, Victoria Park and Crawley Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools.

01.C06.0490.t:
Bathurst Manor, City of Toronto (TRREB district C06)

The area lies along Bathurst Street in what was York Township, which became part of North York in 1922. It was built as a suburban community between 1954 and the early 1960s. Its early population was largely Jewish. North York became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Bathurst Manor is generally bounded by the Don River West Branch and Dufferin Street to the north, Sheppard Avenue to the south and Allen Road to the west, and covers approximately 482 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and a hydro transformer station (Bathurst TS). Along or just beyond its edges are a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bathurst Manor includes G. Ross Lord Park, Hinder Area and Irving W Chapley Park, and the Don River West Branch runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto G. Ross Lord Park Reservoir. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

04.02.0040.t:
Batteaux, Clearview

Batteaux is a small rural community in the north part of Clearview Township, southwest of Collingwood. Clearview Township was formed on January 1, 1994, by merging the Town of Stayner, the Village of Creemore and the townships of Nottawasaga and Sunnidale. The surrounding area was settled for farming from the mid-1800s and remains largely rural.

Batteaux is generally bounded by 36+37 Nottawasaga Sideroad to the north, Concession 6 Nottawasaga Road to the east and Batteaux Creek to the south, and covers approximately 49 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Batteaux is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

07.01.1200.t:
Grayside, Hamilton

Grayside is a residential neighbourhood in the east end of the former City of Hamilton, near the Stoney Creek boundary. The area was farmland in the old townships east of Hamilton before it was annexed by the city and built up as suburban housing after the Second World War.

Grayside is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the north, Grays Road to the east, Barton Street to the south and Lake Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 105 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 73% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and Baycoat (industrial plant). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Grayside is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

09.09.0070.t:
Baldwin, Georgina

Baldwin is a small hamlet in south-east Georgina that grew around a mill on the Black River in the 1800s. The first two mills burned, and a third was moved to the site from Keswick in 1879 by owner William Heise. That mill stopped operating in 1968 but still stands. The hamlet was a stop on the Lake Simcoe Junction Railway in the late 1800s and became part of the Town of Georgina in 1971.

Baldwin is generally bounded by Highway 48 to the north, Weir's Sideroad to the east, Ravenshoe Road to the south and McCowan Road and Old Homestead Road to the west, and covers approximately 10,903 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (Brown Hill TS), Beamlight Solar Project, EarthLight Solar Farm, GoldLight Solar Project and Baldwin Airport. Along or just beyond its edges are a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Black River, Zephyr Creek and Pefferlaw Brook run through or along the community. Lyndhurst Golf Course is located in the area.

07.01.1520.t:
Balfour, Hamilton

Balfour is a neighbourhood on the Hamilton Mountain bounded by Fennell Avenue East, Mohawk Road East, Upper James Street and Upper Wellington Street. It is named after architect James Balfour (1854-1917), whose works included Hamilton's 1888 City Hall. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Balfour is generally bounded by Fennell Avenue to the north, Upper Wellington Street to the east, Mohawk Road to the south and Upper James Street to the west, and covers approximately 86 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Balfour.

Green space in Balfour includes Norwood Park. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Mountain Plaza Mall.

09.05.0020.t:
Ballantrae, Whitchurch-Stouffville

Ballantrae is named after Ballantrae in South Ayrshire, Scotland. The hamlet was settled in the early 1800s and had approximately 300 residents by 1895, and a railway spur from Stouffville to Lake Simcoe passed through it from 1877. Forest clearing left poor sandy soil, and reforestation began in the early 1900s. It joined the Town of Whitchurch-Stouffville in 1971, and a large new residential development was built from the late 1990s, tripling its population between 2001 and 2006.

Ballantrae is generally bounded by Ninth Line to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 572 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Ballantrae includes Clarke Tract and Ballantrae Community Centre and Sports Fields. Ballantrae Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by one school.

07.01.1100.t:
Beasley, Hamilton

Beasley is one of Hamilton's four original downtown neighbourhoods, bounded by the rail line north of Barton Street, James Street, Main Street and Wellington Street. It is named after Richard Beasley (1761-1842), one of Hamilton's first settlers. The area developed in the 19th century as part of the early town, which was laid out in Barton Township in 1815 and became a city in 1846.

Beasley is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) to the north, Wellington Street to the east, Main Street to the south and James Street to the west, and covers approximately 112 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transformer station (Hamilton Elgin TS) and Hamilton-Wentworth Detention Centre. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line and the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Beasley includes Beasley Park, John Rebecca Park and McLaren Park. Residents are served by one school. Hamilton General Hospital and St Joseph's Satellite Health Facility are also located in the community.

01.C13.0670.t:
Banbury-Don Mills, City of Toronto (TRREB district C13)

The area was first settled by Europeans in 1817, and the Don River powered several mills. It stayed rural until after the Second World War. Industrialist E.P. Taylor announced Don Mills as a planned new town in 1953, and it was built between 1952 and 1965 following garden city ideas. The area was part of North York until it joined the City of Toronto in 1998.

Banbury-Don Mills is generally bounded by York Mills Road to the north, the Don River East Branch to the east, Eglinton Avenue to the south and Wilket Creek to the west, and covers approximately 1,008 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision), the Don Valley Parkway, Milne Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 9% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Banbury-Don Mills includes Sunnybrook Park, Edwards Gardens and Bond Park, and the Don River East Branch and Wilket Creek run through or along the community. Donalda Golf and Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 14 schools and the Don Mills branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Sunnybrook Park, Wynford, Don Valley and Aga Khan Park & Museum LRT stations. Other notable landmarks include Shops at Don Mills (2009) and Aga Khan Museum.

07.01.1850.t:
Barnstown, Hamilton

Barnstown is a residential neighbourhood on the central Hamilton Mountain, between Stone Church Road East and Rymal Road East and between Upper Wellington and Upper Wentworth streets. Most homes were built in the 1990s, mainly as single detached houses. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Barnstown is generally bounded by Stone Church Road to the north, Upper Wentworth Street to the east, Rymal Road to the south and Upper Wellington Street to the west, and covers approximately 85 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Mount Hamilton Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Barnstown includes Elmar Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Other notable landmarks include Turner Park.

07.01.1350.t:
Greenford, Hamilton

Greenford is a residential neighbourhood in the east end of the former City of Hamilton. The area was farmland in the old townships east of Hamilton before it was annexed by the City of Hamilton in the twentieth century. Barton Township was fully absorbed by the city in 1960.

Greenford is generally bounded by Queenston Road to the north, Alpine Avenue and Cromwell Crescent to the east, King Street to the south and Nash Road to the west, and covers approximately 64 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Stoney Creek Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Greenford includes Sisters of St. Joseph Park. Residents are served by one school. St. Joseph's Healthcare Hamilton - King Campus is also located in the community.

07.01.1320.t:
Bartonville, Hamilton

Bartonville is in Hamilton's east end and takes its name from the former village of Bartonville in Barton Township. The east end was rural land in Barton and Saltfleet townships that Hamilton annexed in sections during the first half of the 20th century, after which it was built up as a residential area close to the city's industries.

Bartonville is generally bounded by Main Street to the north, Cochrane Road to the east, Lawrence Road to the south and Kenilworth Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 90 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Bartonville Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bartonville includes Montgomery Park. Brock University - Hamilton Campus is also located in the community.

01.C01.0900.t:
Bay Street Corridor, City of Toronto (TRREB district C01)

The area takes its name from Bay Street, first called Bear Street and renamed Bay Street in 1797 because it led to the bay on Toronto Harbour. North of Queen Street, the road was called Terauley Street until it was joined into Bay Street in the 1920s. The land was first laid out as park lots and estates in the early 1800s. The area has been rebuilt over time with office, institutional and retail uses, and a large condominium boom north of the financial district began in the 1990s.

Bay Street Corridor is generally bounded by Yonge Street to the north, Front Street and Simcoe Street to the south and University Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 179 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transformer station (Terauley TS). Along or just beyond its edges are the Union Station Rail Corridor rail line and a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bay Street Corridor includes Queen's Park, College Park and Trinity Square. Residents are served by one school, the Victoria University branch of the Emmanuel College Library and the St. Michael’s College branch of the John M. Kelly Library, and transit is provided by the Union, College, Queen's Park and Museum subway stations. Shopping is available at CF Toronto Eaton Centre. Toronto General Hospital, Hospital for Sick Children, University of Toronto St. George and University of St. Michael's College are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Old City Hall and Nathan Phillips Square and Toronto City Hall.

04.15.0080.t:
Bayfield, Barrie

This community lies along Bayfield Street (Highway 26) in north Barrie and is a mix of commercial and residential uses. Barrie annexed approximately 2,200 acres from Vespra Township in 1984, including the Bayfield Street strip north of Cundles Road. Barrie began as a supply depot at the foot of the Nine Mile Portage during the War of 1812 and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a town in 1870 and a city in 1959, and its population roughly tripled during the 1980s and 1990s.

The boundary of Bayfield follows local streets, lot lines and natural features rather than major roads, and the community covers approximately 98 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 400 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Shopping is available at Georgian Mall and Bayfield Mall.

04.15.0270.t:
Bayshore, Barrie

Bayshore is in southeast Barrie, near the south shore of Kempenfelt Bay on Lake Simcoe. It consists mainly of newer homes built during Barrie's growth from the 1980s onward. Barrie began as a supply depot at the foot of the Nine Mile Portage during the War of 1812 and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a town in 1870 and a city in 1959, and its population roughly tripled during the 1980s and 1990s.

Bayshore is generally bounded by Lake Simcoe and Dock Road to the north, Hewitt's Creek to the east and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the south, and covers approximately 234 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and a cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bayshore includes Golden Meadow Park Community Garden, Valleyview Park and Hurst Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. Residents are served by one school, and transit is provided by the Barrie South GO Station.

06.02.0030.t:
Bayview, Burlington

Bayview is in the Aldershot area of west Burlington, near Burlington Bay and the Royal Botanical Gardens. Aldershot was part of East Flamborough Township until Burlington annexed it in 1958. It was a leading fruit-growing area, and by the 1960s most farms had been sold for housing. Bayview Park on King Road, with views of the bay, is in North Aldershot.

Bayview is generally bounded by Highway 403 to the north, Waterdown Road and LaSalle Park Road to the east and Lake Ontario and Spring Gardens Road to the west, and covers approximately 471 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), Woodland Cemetery, Holy Sepulchre Cemetery, Beth Jacob Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 7% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision) and Highway 403. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bayview includes Royal Botanical Gardens and Hidden Valley Park, and Grindstone Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

09.03.0090.t:
Bayview Fairway-Bayview Country Club Estates, Markham

This area is in the Thornhill part of Markham, around the private Bayview Golf and Country Club in the Don River valley. The golf course, designed by C.E. Robbie Robinson, opened in 1960. The surrounding homes were largely built between 1960 and 1980, with many now replaced by larger custom homes. The east side of Thornhill became part of Markham in 1971 when York Region was created.

Bayview Fairway-Bayview Country Club Estates is generally bounded by the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the north, German Mills Creek to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 177 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Leslie Pumping Station. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (York Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision) and the CN rail line. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bayview Fairway-Bayview Country Club Estates includes German Mills Meadow and Natural Habitat, Duncan Park and Cottonwood Park, and German Mills Creek runs through or along the community. Bayview Golf and Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by one school.

09.04.0150.t:
Bayview Hill, Richmond Hill

Bayview Hill lies in the southeast part of Richmond Hill, around Bayview Avenue and 16th Avenue. The land was rural farmland outside the old village and became part of Richmond Hill when the town expanded under the creation of York Region in 1971. The subdivision was built in the early 1990s, mostly with large detached homes.

Bayview Hill is generally bounded by Major MacKenzie Drive to the north, Leslie Street to the east, 16th Avenue to the south and Bayview Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 405 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Bayview Hill.

Green space in Bayview Hill includes Artisian Park, Bayview Hill Park and Helmkay Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.06.0080.t:
Bayview Northeast, Aurora

Bayview Northeast lies northeast of Bayview Avenue and Wellington Street East, toward Leslie Street and Highway 404. It was largely developed from the 1990s onward on former farmland. Aurora began as Machell's Corners, a hamlet at Yonge Street and Wellington Street where Richard Machell opened a store in 1804. The railway arrived in 1853, the village was incorporated in 1863 and it became a town in 1888.

Bayview Northeast is generally bounded by Wellington Street to the south and Bayview Avenue to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 317 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 404 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bayview Northeast includes David Tomlinson Nature Reserve, Stewart Burnett Park and Thomas Coates Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. Other notable landmarks include Aurora Recreation Complex.

10.07.0210.t:
Beaton, Oshawa

Beaton is a residential community in the City of Oshawa. Oshawa was incorporated as a village in 1850, a town in 1879 and a city in 1924, and grew mainly as an automobile manufacturing centre after the McLaughlin company merged into General Motors of Canada in 1918. The city took its present boundaries in 1974, when it absorbed the rest of East Whitby Township.

Beaton is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north and Lake Ontario and McLaughlin Bay to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 217 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), Highway 401 and a wastewater treatment plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The community includes or fronts onto McLaughlin Bay.

09.06.0100.t:
Bayview Southeast, Aurora

Bayview Southeast is the southeast corner of Aurora near Bayview Avenue and Highway 404. It was largely developed from the mid-1990s onward on former farmland. Aurora began as Machell's Corners, a hamlet at Yonge Street and Wellington Street where Richard Machell opened a store in 1804. The railway arrived in 1853, the village was incorporated in 1863 and it became a town in 1888.

Bayview Southeast is generally bounded by Wellington Street to the north, Highway 404 to the east, Bloomington Road to the south and Bayview Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 1,424 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision) and the CN rail line. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 404. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Holland River East Branch runs through or along the community. Magna Golf Club and Westview Golf Club are located in the area. Transit is provided by the Bloomington GO Station.

01.C15.0570.t:
Bayview Village, City of Toronto (TRREB district C15)

Before development the land was used as a racehorse training stable and grounds, which is recalled in street names such as Citation Drive and Palomino Crescent. The community was planned in 1954 by a group of developers led by Farlinger Development Ltd., with town planner Dr. E. G. Faludi designing curving streets that follow the natural contours. Most homes were built between 1954 and 1964, and Bayview Village Shopping Centre opened in 1963. The area was in North York and joined the City of Toronto at amalgamation in 1998; high-rise condominiums have since been built along Sheppard Avenue.

Bayview Village is generally bounded by Finch Avenue to the north, Leslie Street and the Don River East Branch to the east, Highway 401 to the south and Bayview Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 525 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision) and Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bayview Village includes East Don Parkland, Bayview Village Park and Blue Ridge Park, and the Don River East Branch, Newtonbrook Creek and Blue Ridge Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools, and transit is provided by the Bayview, Bessarion and Leslie subway stations and the Oriole GO Station. Shopping is available at Bayview Village. North York General Hospital is also located in the community.

09.06.0050.t:
Bayview Wellington, Aurora

Bayview Wellington lies east of downtown Aurora around Bayview Avenue and Wellington Street East, with the East Holland River running through the area. It was developed as part of Aurora's eastward suburban growth in the late 20th century. Aurora began as Machell's Corners, a hamlet at Yonge Street and Wellington Street where Richard Machell opened a store in 1804. The railway arrived in 1853, the village was incorporated in 1863 and it became a town in 1888.

Bayview Wellington is generally bounded by the Newmarket boundary to the north, Bayview Avenue to the east, Wellington Street to the south and Industrial Parkway to the west, and covers approximately 310 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and industrial lands (approximately 10% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bayview Wellington includes Aurora Community Arboretum, Civic Square Park and Taylor Park. St. Andrews Valley Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. Other notable landmarks include Dr. G.W. Williams Secondary School.

01.C15.0530.t:
Bayview Woods-Steeles, City of Toronto (TRREB district C15)

Bayview Woods-Steeles is named for its location along Bayview Avenue at Steeles Avenue, on Toronto's northern boundary. The area was farmland in York Township, became part of North York in 1922 and joined the City of Toronto in 1998. It was built up as a postwar suburb with a mix of detached homes and apartment buildings, and is crossed by a Don River ravine network.

Bayview Woods-Steeles is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Leslie Street to the east, Finch Avenue to the south and Bayview Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 409 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bayview Woods-Steeles includes East Don Parkland, Cummer Park and Garnier Park, and the Don River East Branch and German Mills Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools, and transit is provided by the Old Cummer GO Station. Tyndale University is also located in the community.

10.03.0010.t:
Beaverton, Brock

Beaverton is on the east shore of Lake Simcoe at the mouth of the Beaver River. Settlement began in 1822, and it was first known as Calder's Mills; it was renamed Beaverton when the post office opened in 1835. It became the terminus of the Port Hope, Lindsay and Beaverton Railway in 1858 and was incorporated as a village in 1884. In 1974 it was merged with Thorah Township, Brock Township and Cannington to form the expanded Township of Brock.

Beaverton is generally bounded by White's Creek to the north, the Beaver River to the east, Township Concession 5 to the south and Lake Simcoe to the west, and covers approximately 690 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision) and a wastewater treatment plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Beaverton includes Beaverton Ball Park, Mill Gateway Park and King Street Park, and the Beaver River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Brock Libraries - Beaverton Branch.

04.05.0010.t:
Beausoleil First Nation, Christian Island 30

Christian Island 30 is the main reserve of the Beausoleil First Nation, an Ojibwe First Nation on Christian Island in southern Georgian Bay. The island was a Wendat refuge in 1649 and 1650, when the Jesuit Fort Sainte-Marie II stood there. The Assance Band, joined by Potawatomi and Odawa families, relocated to the island in the late 1850s. The island is reached by ferry from Cedar Point.

Beausoleil First Nation is generally bounded by Georgian Bay to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 2,974 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a quarry or aggregate pit and Christian Island United Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The community includes or fronts onto Jerry's Lake and Georgian Bay. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Sainte-Marie II site.

07.01.1780.t:
Quinndale, Hamilton

Quinndale is a residential neighbourhood on the south part of the Hamilton Mountain. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most homes were built between 1961 and 1980, with a further share added in the 1980s.

Quinndale is generally bounded by the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the north, Upper Ottawa Street to the east, Stone Church Road to the south and Upper Gage Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 75 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Quinndale includes Lions Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.04.0180.t:
Beaver Creek Business Park, Richmond Hill

Beaver Creek Business Park is an employment area in southeast Richmond Hill, along East and West Beaver Creek Roads, near Highway 7 and Highway 404. It takes its name from Beaver Creek, a local watercourse. The lands were rural until Richmond Hill was greatly enlarged in 1971 with the creation of York Region, after which they were developed for office and industrial uses. Richmond Hill's city hall is located on East Beaver Creek Road.

Beaver Creek Business Park is generally bounded by 16th Avenue to the north, Highway 404 to the east and Highway 7 to the south, and covers approximately 320 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 59% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 404. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Beaver Creek Business Park includes Beaver Greenway, and Beaver Creek runs through or along the community.

07.01.1670.t:
Berrisfield, Hamilton

Berrisfield is a residential neighbourhood on the east Hamilton Mountain, between Mohawk Road East and the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway and between Upper Ottawa Street and Upper Gage Avenue. Most homes were built between 1961 and 1980, mainly single detached houses. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Berrisfield is generally bounded by Mohawk Road to the north, Upper Ottawa Street to the east, the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the south and Upper Gage Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 96 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Berrisfield includes Bobby Kerr Park and Berrisfield Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

01.C04.0630.t:
Bedford Park-Nortown, City of Toronto (TRREB district C04)

Bedford Park was likely named after the Bedford Park Hotel, which opened in 1873 at Yonge Street near Fairlawn Avenue. The hamlet joined Davisville and Eglinton to form the Town of North Toronto in 1890, and North Toronto was annexed to the City of Toronto in 1912. Most of the original homes were built between approximately 1890 and 1940. The western part of the area was in North York before 1998.

Bedford Park-Nortown is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Yonge Street to the east and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 541 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 401 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bedford Park-Nortown includes Ledbury Park, Brookdale Park and Woburn Park, and the Don River West Branch runs through or along the community. Don Valley Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools and the Armour Heights branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the York Mills subway station. Other notable landmarks include Lawrence subway station and Avenue Road commercial strip.

01.W04.0340.t:
Beechborough-Greenbrook, City of Toronto (TRREB district W04)

Beechborough-Greenbrook is the area north of Eglinton Avenue West between Keele Street and the Barrie rail line, in what was York Township. The district is historically known as Silverthorn, after a former postal village that served the farming township. Eglinton Avenue developed as the main commercial street of the former City of York, and much of the housing north of Eglinton is low-rise rental apartments. It was part of the City of York until amalgamation into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Beechborough-Greenbrook is generally bounded by Greenbrook Drive to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the east, Eglinton Avenue to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 183 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include surface light rail transit (LRT) tracks, Eglinton Maintenance and Storage Facility and industrial lands (approximately 16% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Beechborough-Greenbrook includes Coronation Park, North Keelesdale Park and Woodborough Park, and Black Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools, and transit is provided by the Mount Dennis GO Station and the Mount Dennis, Caledonia and Keelesdale LRT stations.

04.12.0030.t:
Beeton, New Tecumseth

Beeton was first known as Clarksville, after early settler Robert Clark. It was renamed Beeton in 1878, a name tied to local beekeeping and postmaster D.A. Jones, known as the "Bee King of Canada". The village grew as a railway stop and was incorporated in 1884. It became part of the Town of New Tecumseth in 1991.

Beeton is generally bounded by Beeton Creek to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 227 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Trinity United Cemetery and St Andrew's Presbyterian Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the D. A. Jones branch of the New Tecumseth Public Library. Other notable landmarks include South Simcoe Railway (heritage line to Tottenham).

07.01.1630.t:
Greeningdon, Hamilton

Greeningdon is a residential neighbourhood on the Central Mountain, between Upper James Street and Garth Street. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. Much of the housing is detached bungalows and side-splits from the 1950s and 1960s.

Greeningdon is generally bounded by Mohawk Road to the north, Upper Wellington Street to the east, the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the south and Upper James Street to the west, and covers approximately 99 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 10% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.02.0180.t:
Beverley Glen, Vaughan

Beverley Glen is a residential community in the Thornhill area of Vaughan. The land was farmland in Vaughan Township until suburban development spread north from Toronto, largely from the 1970s and 1980s. Vaughan Township became the Town of Vaughan in 1971 and the City of Vaughan in 1990.

Beverley Glen is generally bounded by Highway 7 to the north, Bathurst Street to the east, Centre Street to the south and Dufferin Street to the west, and covers approximately 385 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 407 and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Beverley Glen includes Jean Augustine District Park, Beverley Glen Park and Thornhill Green Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

13.02.0010.t:
Bewdley, Hamilton Township

Bewdley is a hamlet at the western end of Rice Lake, approximately 15 km north of Port Hope. It began in the 1820s as Black's Landing, named after tavern owner William Black. It was renamed after Bewdley, England, the ancestral home of William Bancks, who arrived in 1833 and started a sawmill. Early sawmills drove its growth, and it lies within Hamilton Township, incorporated in 1850.

Bewdley is generally bounded by County Road 28 to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 8 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Bewdley.

Other notable landmarks include Rice Lake.

09.09.0040.t:
Belhaven, Georgina

Belhaven is a small hamlet in central Georgina, in the former Township of North Gwillimbury. It was first known as Plug Mount and adopted the name Belhaven in the 1860s. Its hotel and tavern was a stagecoach stop in the 1800s, and the hamlet hosted North Gwillimbury's annual town meetings. It became part of the Town of Georgina in 1971.

Belhaven is generally bounded by Baseline Road to the north, McCowan Road to the east, Ravenshoe Road to the south and Woodbine Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 5,788 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Maskinonge (Jersey) River runs through or along the community.

04.15.0150.t:
Grove East, Barrie

Grove East is a residential area in northeast Barrie along Grove Street East. Barrie grew from a supply depot at the end of the Nine Mile Portage and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a village in 1854, a town in 1871 and a city in 1959. The area was largely built up with suburban housing in the second half of the 20th century.

Grove East is generally bounded by Hickling Trail and College Crescent to the north, Penetanguishene Road to the east, Steel Street to the south and Duckworth Street to the west, and covers approximately 181 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Grove East.

Green space in Grove East includes Eastview Park, Hickling Park and Maitland Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

01.E09.1110.t:
Bendale, City of Toronto (TRREB district E09)

Bendale was originally called Benlomond, after Ben Lomond in Scotland, and the name was shortened in 1881. David and Mary Thomson, among Scarborough's first settlers, farmed land in the area. It was rural Scarborough Township until postwar growth, with schools opening in the late 1950s. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Bendale is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, McCowan Road to the east, Dorset Creek to the south and Midland Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 738 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 9% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision) and Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bendale includes Thomson Memorial Park, Birkdale Ravine and Amberdale Ravine, and Dorset Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools, the Bendale branch of the Toronto Public Library and the Scarborough Civic Centre branch of the Toronto Public Library. Shopping is available at Scarborough Town Centre. Scarborough Health Network - General Campus is also located in the community.

09.03.0210.t:
Berczy, Markham

Berczy Village is named after William Berczy, who led the first German settlers to Markham Township in 1794. The land was farmland, including the farm of Frederick and Emma Bagg. Construction began in the mid-1990s and most homes were complete by the early 2000s, with further building north of Madison Heights Boulevard and in the Upper Unionville extension (begun in 2011).

Berczy is generally bounded by Major MacKenzie Drive to the north, McCowan Road to the east, 16th Avenue to the south and Kennedy Road to the west, and covers approximately 437 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Bethesda Lutheran Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are St. Philip’s on-the-Hill Anglican Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Berczy includes Berczy Park North, Berczy Park South and Frederick Bagg Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools.

01.E06.1310.t:
Birchcliffe-Cliffside, City of Toronto (TRREB district E06)

Birch Cliff takes its name from a house built for John Stark and named after the birch trees on the Scarborough Bluffs, and the local post office adopted the name. The Toronto Hunt Club moved to the area in 1895, when it was mostly farms and woodland. In the 1920s Birch Cliff became the first part of Scarborough developed as a Toronto suburb, as a streetcar suburb along Kingston Road, while neighbouring Cliffside was built up as a large subdivision in the early 1950s. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Birchcliffe-Cliffside is generally bounded by the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) to the north, Midland Avenue to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Victoria Park Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 593 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the R.C. Harris Water Treatment Plant. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Transit Uxbridge Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Birchcliffe-Cliffside includes Birchmount Park, Scarborough Heights Park and Highview Park. The Toronto Hunt Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools and the Taylor Memorial branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Scarborough GO Station.

01.W05.0220.t:
Black Creek, City of Toronto (TRREB district W05)

Black Creek is the northern half of the Jane and Finch area, named after the creek that runs through it. The area was farmland in York Township, later North York, until it was developed as a planned suburb in the 1960s, with many high-rise and public housing buildings. The population grew from approximately 1,300 in 1961 to 33,000 in 1971 across the wider area. North York was amalgamated into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Black Creek is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Black Creek to the east, Finch Avenue to the south and Highway 400 to the west, and covers approximately 346 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, surface light rail transit (LRT) tracks and industrial lands (approximately 15% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 400. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Black Creek includes Remberto Navia Sports Field, Black Creek Parkland and Elm Park. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools, and transit is provided by the Norfinch Oakdale, Jane and Finch, Driftwood and Tobermory LRT stations. Shopping is available at Yorkgate Mall. Other notable landmarks include Line 6 Finch West and York Woods Branch, Toronto Public Library.

10.04.0030.t:
Blackstock, Scugog

Blackstock is a village in the former Cartwright Township, east of Port Perry. It was established in approximately 1851 as a farming service centre. Cartwright Township became part of the Township of Scugog on January 1, 1974, when Durham Region was created.

Blackstock is generally bounded by Old Scugog Road to the north and Regional Road 57 to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 86 hectares.
