Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Blackstock includes Blackstock Fairground exhibition ground.

01.E01.1360.t:
Blake-Jones, City of Toronto (TRREB district E01)

Blake-Jones takes its name from Blake Street and Jones Avenue and forms part of the wider Riverdale area east of the Don River. The district was annexed to the City of Toronto in 1884, along with Riverside, Don Mount and Leslieville. Most of its houses were built between the 1870s and the 1930s. The former City of Toronto joined the amalgamated City of Toronto in 1998.

Blake-Jones is generally bounded by Danforth Avenue to the north, Greenwood Avenue to the east, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) to the south and Pape Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 94 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include TTC Greenwood Yard and Jones Avenue Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Blake-Jones includes Oakvale Green, Kempton Howard Park and Phin Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Pape/Danforth branch of the Toronto Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Gerrard Street East.

07.01.1300.t:
Blakeley, Hamilton

Blakeley is a residential neighbourhood in Hamilton's lower east end. The east end was rural land in Barton and Saltfleet townships that Hamilton annexed in sections during the first half of the 20th century, and it was built up as housing for workers in the city's growing industries.

Blakeley is generally bounded by Main Street to the north, Gage Avenue to the east, Sherman Access to the south and Sherman Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 74 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Blakeley includes Cumberland Tot-Lot. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. St. Peter's Hospital is also located in the community.

10.06.0100.t:
Blue Grass Meadows, Whitby

Blue Grass Meadows is a residential area in the Town of Whitby. Whitby Township was surveyed in 1792 and named after Whitby in Yorkshire, England. The Town of Whitby was incorporated in 1855 and merged with Whitby Township in 1968. Most of the town's present residential areas were built as suburbs in the decades after that merger.

Blue Grass Meadows is generally bounded by Rossland Road to the north, the Oshawa boundary to the east, the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) to the south and Anderson Street to the west, and covers approximately 666 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Mount Lawn Memorial Garden (cemetery). Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Blue Grass Meadows includes Prince of Wales Park, Huron Park and Kirby Park, and Corbett Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools. Shopping is available at Whitby Mall.

01.W04.0330.t:
Briar Hill-Belgravia, City of Toronto (TRREB district W04)

Briar Hill-Belgravia lies around Eglinton Avenue West and Dufferin Street, next to the historic Fairbank postal village in the former York Township. The area was farmland until most of it was laid out in the 1920s and 1930s with small one-and-a-half and two-storey detached houses. Eglinton Avenue later developed as a commercial street. The area was part of the City of York until amalgamation into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Briar Hill-Belgravia is generally bounded by Briar Hill Avenue and Marlee Avenue to the east, Eglinton Avenue to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 188 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a hydro transformer station (Fairbank TS) and industrial lands (approximately 15% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), Allen Road and Prospect Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Briar Hill-Belgravia includes Walter Saunders Memorial Park, J.T.Watson Park and Dufferin Hill Park. Transit is provided by the Caledonia, Fairbank and Oakwood LRT stations.

05.01.0110.t:
Bolton East, Caledon

Bolton began as Bolton's Mills, where George Bolton and his uncle James Bolton built a grist mill on the Humber River in 1823. It was incorporated as a village in 1872 after the Toronto, Grey and Bruce Railway arrived. In 1974 it became part of the new Town of Caledon. The eastern part of Bolton is mostly residential subdivisions built from the 1960s and 1970s, with further growth in the 2000s.

Bolton East is generally bounded by King Street to the north, Albion-Vaughan Road and Highway 50 to the south and Queen Street to the west, and covers approximately 453 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 9% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bolton East includes R.J.A. Potts Memorial Park, Fountainbridge Park and Russel & Joan Robertson Park, and the Humber River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

05.01.0100.t:
Bolton North, Caledon

Bolton began as Bolton's Mills, where George Bolton and his uncle James Bolton built a grist mill on the Humber River in 1823. It was incorporated as a village in 1872 after the Toronto, Grey and Bruce Railway arrived. In 1974 it became part of the new Town of Caledon. The north part of Bolton is mostly residential subdivisions on the hills north of the river valley, built from the 1960s and 1970s, with further growth in the 2000s.

Bolton North is generally bounded by Columbia Way to the north, Caledon-King Townline to the east, King Street to the south and Queen Street and Highway 50 to the west, and covers approximately 408 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Laurel Hill Cemetery and Bolton Anglican/Methodist Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bolton North includes Albion-Bolton District Park, Ruth and Richard Hunt Park and Montrose Farm Park, and Cold Creek and the Humber River run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

05.01.0090.t:
Bolton West, Caledon

Bolton began as Bolton's Mills, where George Bolton and his uncle James Bolton built a grist mill on the Humber River in 1823. It was incorporated as a village in 1872 after the Toronto, Grey and Bruce Railway arrived. In 1974 it became part of the new Town of Caledon. The planned settlement of Glasgow, northwest of the village, was merged into Bolton in 1872. The western part of Bolton is mostly residential subdivisions built from the 1960s onward, with further growth in the 2000s.

Bolton West is generally bounded by Queen Street and King Street to the north and Coleraine Drive and Highway 50 to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,022 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), Laurel Hill Cemetery, Bolton Anglican/Methodist Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 46% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Albion Presbyterian Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bolton West includes Edelweiss Park, Albion-Bolton Fairgrounds and Adam Wallace Memorial Park, and the Humber River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Albion-Bolton branch of the Caledon Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Albion-Bolton Fairgrounds.

04.13.0010.t:
Bond Head, Bradford West Gwillimbury

Bond Head is a historic crossroads hamlet at Highway 27 and County Road 88 (the former 7th Line) in West Gwillimbury. It was first known as Wraggs Corners, after early settler Major Wraggs, and the area was surveyed in 1819. In 1837 postmaster Joel Robinson named it Bond Head after Sir Francis Bond Head, then lieutenant governor of Upper Canada. William Osler (born 1849) and William Mulock (born 1843) were both born in Bond Head.

The boundary of Bond Head follows local streets, lot lines and natural features rather than major roads, and the community covers approximately 172 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bond Head includes Audrey Wychopen Memorial Parkette.

07.01.1510.t:
Bonnington, Hamilton

Bonnington is a residential neighbourhood on the west Hamilton Mountain, generally between Fennell Avenue West, Mohawk Road West, Upper James Street and West 5th Street. Much of its housing was built before 1960, mostly single detached homes. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Bonnington is generally bounded by Fennell Avenue to the north, Upper James Street to the east, Mohawk Road to the south and West 5th Street to the west, and covers approximately 43 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Bonnington.

Green space in Bonnington includes Richwill Park.

06.02.0060.t:
Brant Hills, Burlington

Brant Hills is in north Burlington, on the slope of the Niagara Escarpment. The name honours Joseph Brant, and 'Hills' refers to the escarpment. Early settlers included the Ireland family, who came from Yorkshire in 1819 and founded Oakridge Farm; the City bought Ireland House in 1987 and made it a museum. The area was part of Nelson Township until Burlington annexed it in 1958, and it was built up with suburban housing in the later 20th century.

Brant Hills is generally bounded by Dundas Street to the north, Highway 407 to the east and Brant Street to the west, and covers approximately 362 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407 and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brant Hills includes Brant Hills Park, Cavendish Park and Duncaster Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Brant Hills branch of the Burlington Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Ireland House Museum.

10.08.0020.t:
Bowmanville, Clarington

Bowmanville began with settlement in 1794 and early mills on Barber's Creek, and was first called Darlington Mills. It was named after Charles Bowman, who bought the local store around 1824 and opened the post office. It became a village in 1852 and a town in 1858. In 1974 it merged with Darlington and Clarke townships to form the Town of Newcastle, later renamed Clarington. Subdivisions were added from the 1950s, with major growth from the 1980s onward.

Bowmanville is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision) to the east and Lake Ontario to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 3,606 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), Highway 401, a quarry or aggregate pit, a wastewater treatment plant, Bowmanville Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 5% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bowmanville includes Bowmanville Creek, Clarington Fields and Garnet B. Rickard Recreation Complex, and Bowmanville Creek and Soper Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Westside Marsh. Residents are served by approximately 18 schools and the Bowmanville branch of the Clarington Public Library. Lakeridge Health Bowmanville is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Historic King Street downtown.

09.03.0390.t:
Box Grove, Markham

Box Grove began as a 19th-century mill hamlet on the Rouge River; William Beebe was the first European settler in 1815. It was first known as Sparta and took the name Box Grove in approximately 1867, when it received a post office. The mills closed by the late 1800s after floods and fire, and the area stayed largely rural until residential development began in the late 1990s.

Box Grove is generally bounded by Highway 407 and Ninth Line to the north, Steeles Avenue to the south and the Rouge River to the west, and covers approximately 421 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision) and the CN rail line (York Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Box Grove includes Rouge National Urban Park, Bob Hunter Memorial Park and Box Grove Community Park, and the Rouge River runs through or along the community. Parkview Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by one school.

04.13.0030.t:
Bradford, Bradford West Gwillimbury

Bradford began after Irish settlers crossed the Holland River in 1819 and grew around William Milloy's tavern on the Penetanguishene Road (later Yonge Street). It was named Bradford in 1840 after Bradford in West Yorkshire, England. The railway arrived in 1853, Bradford became a village in 1857 and a town in 1960, and it merged with West Gwillimbury Township on January 1, 1991. The town has grown rapidly with new subdivisions since the 1990s, and GO Train service began in 1982.

Bradford is generally bounded by 9th Line to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the east, Line 6 and Canal Road to the south and 10th Sideroad to the west, and covers approximately 1,680 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 7% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a wastewater treatment plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bradford includes Fuller Heights Park, Alan Kuzmich Memorial Park and Bradford Lion's Park. Residents are served by approximately 13 schools and the Bradford West Gwillimbury Public Library, and transit is provided by the Bradford GO Station.

05.02.0440.t:
Bram East, Brampton

Bram East is in northeast Brampton and includes the former hamlets of Castlemore and Ebenezer in the former Toronto Gore Township. Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships were merged with the Town of Brampton in 1974 to form the City of Brampton. The area was mainly farmland until large-lot homes appeared in the 1970s and 1980s, and suburban subdivisions were built out from the 1990s and 2000s.

Bram East is generally bounded by Castlemore Road to the north, Highway 50 to the east, Queen Street to the south and Goreway Drive to the west, and covers approximately 1,521 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transformer station and St. Johns Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, CPKC Vaughan Intermodal Yard and Glenview Memorial Gardens (cemetery). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bram East includes Ebenezer Resource Management Tract, Duncan Foster Valley South and Castlemore Park, and the West Humber River runs through or along the community. Riverstone Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 13 schools and the Claireville branch of the Brampton Library. Other notable landmarks include Air Canada Flight 621 Memorial Garden.

05.02.0350.t:
Bramalea South Industrial, Brampton

Bramalea South Industrial is an employment area in the southern part of Bramalea. Bramalea was developed as a planned 'new town' in the former Chinguacousy Township by Bramalea Consolidated Developments (later Bramalea Limited), Canada's first satellite community. Bramalea was planned with its own industrial lands, which were built up mainly from the 1960s onward. Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships were merged with the Town of Brampton in 1974 to form the City of Brampton.

Bramalea South Industrial is generally bounded by Queen Street to the north, Airport Road to the east, Highway 407 to the south and Torbram Road to the west, and covers approximately 371 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Old Methodist Cemetery Grahamsville and industrial lands (approximately 92% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school.

05.02.0270.t:
Bramalea West Industrial, Brampton

Bramalea West Industrial is an employment area on the west side of Bramalea. Bramalea was developed as a planned 'new town' in the former Chinguacousy Township by Bramalea Consolidated Developments (later Bramalea Limited), Canada's first satellite community. Bramalea was planned with its own industrial lands, which were built up mainly from the 1960s onward. Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships were merged with the Town of Brampton in 1974 to form the City of Brampton.

Bramalea West Industrial is generally bounded by Clark Boulevard to the north, Dixie Road to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Highway 410 to the west, and covers approximately 305 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), Highway 410, surface light rail transit (LRT) tracks and industrial lands (approximately 63% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Beckett Sproule Pumping Station and Reservoir. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bramalea West Industrial includes Carleton Park.

07.01.1940.t:
Chappel, Hamilton

Chappel is a residential neighbourhood on the Hamilton Mountain, made up of the city's Chapel East and Chapel West planning areas. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Chappel is generally bounded by Rymal Road to the north, Upper Sherman Avenue to the east, a hydro corridor to the south and Upper Wellington Street to the west, and covers approximately 98 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Mount Hamilton Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 7% of the community area). The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 2.5 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Chappel includes Turner Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Turner Park branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

05.02.0030.t:
Bram West, Brampton

Bram West is in southwest Brampton along the Credit River. It includes the village of Churchville, founded in 1815 by Amaziah Church, who built a gristmill on the river, and part of Huttonville, which took its name from James Hutton after he bought the local mills in 1855. Churchville became part of Brampton in 1974 and was designated the city's only heritage conservation district in 1990. The surrounding farmland was developed with new subdivisions and business parks from the early 2000s.

Bram West is generally bounded by the Credit River to the north, Mavis Road to the east, a hydro corridor to the south and Winston Churchill Boulevard to the west, and covers approximately 2,464 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 407, a hydro transformer station (Jim Yarrow TS), a hydro transformer station (J), Meadowvale Cemetery & Crematorium, Churchville Cemetery, Page Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 8% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bram West includes Eldorado Park, Larande Park and Jimmie Mckerron Pond, and the Credit River and Levi Creek run through or along the community. Lionhead Golf & Country Club - Masters and Streetsville Glen Golf Course are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the South West branch of the Brampton Library. Other notable landmarks include Churchville Heritage Conservation District and Korean War Memorial Wall.

05.02.0340.t:
Bramalea North Industrial, Brampton

Bramalea North Industrial is an employment area in the northern part of Bramalea. Bramalea was developed as a planned 'new town' in the former Chinguacousy Township by Bramalea Consolidated Developments (later Bramalea Limited), Canada's first satellite community. Bramalea was planned with its own industrial lands alongside its housing, and these were built up mainly from the 1960s onward. Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships were merged with the Town of Brampton in 1974 to form the City of Brampton.

Bramalea North Industrial is generally bounded by Bovaird Drive to the north, Airport Road to the east, Mimico Creek to the south and Torbram Road to the west, and covers approximately 404 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 69% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Harrison's United Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bramalea North Industrial includes Trailside Park, and Mimico Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

05.02.0310.t:
Bramalea Road South Gateway, Brampton

Bramalea Road South Gateway is a small area at the south end of Bramalea Road near Steeles Avenue. Bramalea was developed as a planned 'new town' in the former Chinguacousy Township by Bramalea Consolidated Developments (later Bramalea Limited), Canada's first satellite community. The area includes Bramalea GO Station, which serves the Kitchener line at Steeles Avenue and Bramalea Road. Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships were merged with the Town of Brampton in 1974 to form the City of Brampton.

Bramalea Road South Gateway is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the east, Bramalea Road and the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the south and Orenda Road to the west, and covers approximately 33 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 46% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision). The community is also close to Toronto Pearson International Airport, approximately 2.7 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bramalea Road South Gateway includes Orenda Parkette.

09.07.0040.t:
Bristol-London, Newmarket

Bristol-London is a residential neighbourhood in north-central Newmarket, named after local streets. Newmarket was settled by Quakers led by Timothy Rogers between 1801 and 1803, was incorporated as a village in 1857 and as a town in 1880. The town's population grew from approximately 5,000 to 11,000 between 1950 and 1970, with further growth after York Region was formed in 1971.

Bristol-London is generally bounded by the East Gwillimbury boundary to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the east, Davis Drive to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 344 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Newmarket Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bristol-London includes Proctor Park, Rogers Park and Marilyn Powell Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools, and transit is provided by the Newmarket GO Station.

05.02.0220.t:
Brampton 407 Corridor, Brampton

The Brampton 407 Corridor is an employment area in south Brampton along Highway 407, which runs just north of the Mississauga boundary. The land was part of the former Chinguacousy Township. Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships were merged with the Town of Brampton in 1974 to form the City of Brampton. Industrial and business development here grew mainly from the later 20th century.

Brampton 407 Corridor is generally bounded by a hydro corridor and Highway 407 to the east and Etobicoke Creek to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 700 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), Highway 407, Highway 410, Emerald Energy from Waste, a hydro transformer station (Hurontario SS), a hydro transformer station (Bramalea TS) and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Malport Yard. The community is also close to Toronto Pearson International Airport, approximately 1.5 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brampton 407 Corridor includes Brampton Sports Park and Dixie-Highway 407 Park, and Etobicoke Creek runs through or along the community. Brampton Golf Club is located in the area.

05.02.0170.t:
Brampton East, Brampton

Brampton East covers areas southeast of downtown Brampton, including Peel Village. Peel Village was the first master-planned community in Brampton, then known as Flowertown, and the first to combine residential, commercial and industrial uses. Brampton was laid out in 1834 at Buffy's Corners and named after Brampton in Cumberland, England. It became a village in 1853, a town in 1873 and a city in 1974.

Brampton East is generally bounded by Etobicoke Creek and the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the north, Kennedy Road to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Main Street to the west, and covers approximately 330 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and St Mary's Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brampton East includes Centennial Park, Meadowland Park and Peel Village Park, and Etobicoke Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools.

05.02.0210.t:
Brampton East Industrial, Brampton

Brampton East Industrial is an employment area east of downtown Brampton, between the older town and Bramalea. Brampton was laid out in 1834 at Buffy's Corners and became a town in 1873. Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships were merged with the Town of Brampton in 1974 to form the City of Brampton. Industrial development in the area grew mainly in the second half of the 20th century.

Brampton East Industrial is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the north, Highway 410 to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Kennedy Road to the west, and covers approximately 267 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Beckett Sproule Pumping Station and Reservoir and industrial lands (approximately 74% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and Highway 410. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Shopping is available at Kennedy Square Mall.

05.02.0160.t:
Brampton North, Brampton

Brampton North covers established residential areas north of downtown Brampton. Brampton was laid out in 1834 at Buffy's Corners, around William Buffy's tavern, and named after Brampton in Cumberland, England. It became a village in 1853 and a town in 1873, and was known as the 'Flower Town of Canada' for its nursery industry. Much of the area was built up with housing in the decades after the Second World War.

Brampton North is generally bounded by Bovaird Drive to the north, Kennedy Road to the east, Church Street and Etobicoke Creek to the south and Main Street to the west, and covers approximately 350 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Old Brampton Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Brampton Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brampton North includes Valleybrook Park, Duggan Park and Calvert Park, and Etobicoke Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools.

04.19.0030.t:
Brechin, Ramara

Brechin is a village in the former Township of Mara, near the eastern shore of Lake Simcoe. Mara Township was named in 1820 and incorporated in 1850. The village grew as a local service centre for the surrounding farms and lakeshore cottage areas. In 1994 Mara and Rama townships were amalgamated to form the Township of Ramara, and Brechin is now one of its largest communities and home to its municipal office.

Brechin is generally bounded by County Road 47 to the east, Concession Road 3 to the south and the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 179 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision), Highway 12 and St. Andrew Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brechin includes Brechin Community Centre Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Brechin branch of the Ramara Township Public Library.

04.02.0090.t:
Brentwood, Clearview

Brentwood is a small rural community in Clearview Township, Simcoe County. Clearview Township was formed on January 1, 1994, by merging the Town of Stayner, the Village of Creemore and the townships of Nottawasaga and Sunnidale. The surrounding area was settled for farming and lumbering from the mid-1800s and remains largely rural.

Brentwood is generally bounded by Concession 2 Sunnidale to the north and Barrie-Collingwood Rail Trail to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 52 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Brentwood.

Brentwood is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

05.02.0130.t:
Brampton South, Brampton

Brampton South covers established residential areas south of downtown Brampton, near Steeles Avenue. Brampton was laid out in 1834 at Buffy's Corners and named after Brampton in Cumberland, England. It became a village in 1853 and a town in 1873. Much of the area was built up with housing in the decades after the Second World War.

Brampton South is generally bounded by Harold Street to the north, Main Street to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and McLaughlin Road to the west, and covers approximately 318 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Roy McMurtry Youth Centre and Ontario Correctional Institute lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brampton South includes Ridgehill Park, South Fletchers Creek Park and Peelton Park, and Etobicoke Creek and Fletchers Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Brampton Public Library. Shopping is available at Shoppers World Brampton.

05.02.0110.t:
Brampton West, Brampton

Brampton West covers established residential areas west of downtown Brampton. Brampton was laid out in 1834 at Buffy's Corners and named after Brampton in Cumberland, England. It became a village in 1853 and a town in 1873, and the Peel County seat in 1866. Much of the area was built up with housing in the decades after the Second World War.

Brampton West is generally bounded by Bovaird Drive to the north, Main Street to the east, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the south and McLaughlin Road to the west, and covers approximately 328 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are Old Brampton Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brampton West includes Fairglen Park, Chris Gibson Community Park and Fred Kee Park, and Fletchers Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

01.C12.0680.t:
Bridle Path-Sunnybrook-York Mills, City of Toronto (TRREB district C12)

York Mills is named for the saw and grist mills on the Don River; James Hogg ran a mill at Yonge Street from 1824, giving Hogg's Hollow its name. The Bridle Path area was farmland until the Bayview Bridge opened in 1929, after which developer Forsey Page laid out large estate lots. Most estate homes were built from the late 1940s to the 1960s. The area was part of York Township, then North York from 1922, and the City of Toronto from 1998.

Bridle Path-Sunnybrook-York Mills is generally bounded by York Mills Road to the north, Wilket Creek to the east and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 887 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Mount Hope Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Milne Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bridle Path-Sunnybrook-York Mills includes Sunnybrook Park, Edwards Gardens and Sherwood Park, and the Don River West Branch and Burke Brook run through or along the community. Rosedale Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools, and transit is provided by the York Mills subway station. Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre - Bayview Campus, Toronto Rehab - Lyndhurst Centre, York University Glendon Campus and Canadian Film Centre are also located in the community.

06.02.0090.t:
Brant, Burlington

Brant is a central Burlington area named after Brant Street, which honours Mohawk leader Joseph Brant, who settled on the Brant Tract around 1802. In 1810 James Gage cleared land fronting Brant Street, built a wharf and laid out the town site of Wellington Square. Burlington began as Wellington Square and Port Nelson, which merged into the Village of Burlington in 1873. The area has older housing near the downtown, with later residential growth through the 20th century.

Brant is generally bounded by Fairview Street to the north, Guelph Line to the east, Lake Ontario and a hydro corridor to the south and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the west, and covers approximately 740 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW), the Skyway Wastewater Treatment Plant and industrial lands (approximately 3% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brant includes Central Park, Maple Park and Spencer Smith Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Central branch of the Burlington Public Library. Shopping is available at Mapleview Centre. Joseph Brant Hospital is also located in the community.

01.E03.1260.t:
Broadview North, City of Toronto (TRREB district E03)

Broadview North lies east of the Don River valley along Broadview Avenue, north of Danforth Avenue. It grew near the old mill settlement of Todmorden, which began with a lumber mill granted in 1795 and took its name from Todmorden in England. The area was part of York Township until the Township of East York was formed in 1924. Its lots were largely built up after the Prince Edward Viaduct opened in 1918, and East York joined the City of Toronto in 1998.

Broadview North is generally bounded by the Don River to the north, Pape Avenue to the east, Fulton Avenue to the south and the Don Valley Parkway to the west, and covers approximately 170 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision), the Don Valley Parkway and a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the North Toronto Wastewater Treatment Plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Broadview North includes Todmorden Mills Park, Charles Sauriol Parkette and Livingstone Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Centennial College is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Todmorden Mills.

10.02.0160.t:
Brock Industrial, Pickering

Brock Industrial is an employment area in south Pickering, named after Brock Road, which runs through it. The land was originally farmland in Pickering Township, which was surveyed in 1791 and became a township in 1792. Industrial and business park development followed the post-war growth of the area and the opening of Highway 401. Pickering became a town in 1974 and a city in 2000.

Brock Industrial is generally bounded by Highway 401 and the Ajax boundary to the north, Church Street and Duffins Creek to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and a hydro corridor to the west, and covers approximately 771 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision), the CN rail line (York Subdivision), Pickering Nuclear Generating Station, the Duffins Creek Water Pollution Control Plant, a hydro transformer station (Pickering SS B), a hydro transformer station (Pickering SS A) and industrial lands (approximately 40% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401, Kennedy Detention Centre and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brock Industrial includes RESTRICTED AREA, and Duffins Creek runs through or along the community.

10.02.0140.t:
Brock Ridge, Pickering

Brock Ridge is a residential neighbourhood in north-central Pickering. Its name honours Sir Isaac Brock, the British general and administrator of Upper Canada during the War of 1812, and echoes nearby Brock Road. The land was farmland in Pickering Township before suburban development. The present neighbourhood was developed largely in the 1980s.

Brock Ridge is generally bounded by a hydro corridor to the north, the Ajax boundary and Duffins Creek to the east and Finch Avenue to the south, and covers approximately 320 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brock Ridge includes Brock Ridge Community Park, Major Oaks Park and Centennial Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

07.01.1500.t:
Buchanan, Hamilton

Buchanan is a neighbourhood on the west Hamilton Mountain, between Fennell Avenue and Mohawk Road and between Garth Street and West 5th Street. It is named after Isaac Buchanan, a businessman and political figure in Canada West. Most homes were built between the 1950s and 1970s. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Buchanan is generally bounded by Governors Boulevard and Delmar Drive to the north, West 5th Street to the east, Mohawk Road to the south and Garth Street to the west, and covers approximately 100 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Buchanan.

Green space in Buchanan includes Buchanan Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Terryberry branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

09.03.0380.t:
Cedarwood, Markham

Cedarwood is in south-east Markham, north of Steeles Avenue at the Toronto (Scarborough) border and east of Markham Road. The area lies near the former hamlet of Armadale, settled from approximately 1805, and was farmland of Markham Township until suburban growth. Most homes were built from approximately 1991 to 2010.

Cedarwood is generally bounded by Kirkham Drive to the north, the CN rail line (York Subdivision) and the Rouge River to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Markham Road to the west, and covers approximately 240 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and the CN rail line (York Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Cedarwood includes Rouge National Urban Park, Cedarwood Park and Unity Park, and Morningside Creek and the Rouge River run through or along the community. Parkview Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by one school.

06.02.0180.t:
Bronte Creek, Burlington

Bronte Creek is in east Burlington, next to Bronte Creek Provincial Park and the Oakville boundary. The park, established in the 1970s, keeps original apple orchards and farm buildings from the area's farming past. Burlington began as Wellington Square and Port Nelson, which merged into the Village of Burlington in 1873. Burlington annexed most of Nelson Township and Aldershot on January 1, 1958, and became a city in 1974. The area was mainly farmland until suburban growth in the later 20th century.

Bronte Creek is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, Tremaine Road to the east and Bronte Creek to the south, and covers approximately 247 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bronte Creek includes Bronte Creek Provincial Park, and Bronte Creek runs through or along the community.

01.W04.0310.t:
Brookhaven-Amesbury, City of Toronto (TRREB district W04)

Brookhaven-Amesbury lies along Lawrence Avenue West near Black Creek in the former York Township. The area became part of North York when it separated from York Township in 1922, and it was farmland before post-war suburban growth. Today more than half of its housing is in high-rise buildings. North York was amalgamated into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Brookhaven-Amesbury is generally bounded by Lawrence Avenue to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the east and the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 347 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 25% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brookhaven-Amesbury includes Amesbury Park, Westview Greenbelt and Olympia Park, and Black Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Amesbury Park branch of the Toronto Public Library.

10.06.0050.t:
Brooklin, Whitby

Brooklin grew after 1840 around a flour mill built by John and Robert Campbell on Lynde Creek. First called Winchester, it was renamed Brooklin in 1847 when a post office was opened. Larger residential growth began in the late 1950s, resumed in the mid-1990s, and continued through the 2000s. Downtown Brooklin was designated a Heritage Conservation District in 2008, and Highway 407 opened just south of the community in 2016.

Brooklin is generally bounded by Columbus Road to the north, Oshawa Creek to the east, Highway 407 ETR to the south and Ashburn Road to the west, and covers approximately 866 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 407 ETR. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brooklin includes Brooklin Memorial Park, Brooklin Optimist and Carson Park, and Lynde Creek runs through or along the community. Winchester Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools and the Brooklin branch of the Whitby Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Downtown Brooklin Heritage Conservation District.

07.01.1950.t:
Broughton, Hamilton

Broughton is a residential neighbourhood on the east Hamilton Mountain, made up of the city's Broughton East and Broughton West planning areas. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Broughton is generally bounded by Rymal Road to the north, a hydro corridor to the south and Upper Sherman Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 82 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Broughton includes Broughton West Park.

09.02.0190.t:
Brownridge, Vaughan

Brownridge is a residential community in the Thornhill area of Vaughan. Thornhill was settled in 1794 and was split between Vaughan and Markham townships along Yonge Street. The area was farmland until suburban growth extended north from Toronto, mainly from the 1970s onward. Vaughan became a town in 1971 and a city in 1990.

Brownridge is generally bounded by Centre Street to the north, Bathurst Street to the east, the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the south and Dufferin Street to the west, and covers approximately 335 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (York Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Brownridge includes Dufferin District Park, Wade Gate Park and Downham Green Park, and Westminster Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Vaughan Public Libraries - Dufferin Clark Branch. Shopping is available at Promenade Mall.

07.01.1640.t:
Bruleville, Hamilton

Bruleville is a residential neighbourhood on the central Hamilton Mountain, close to Lime Ridge Mall and the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Bruleville is generally bounded by Mohawk Road to the north, Upper Wentworth Street to the east, the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the south and Upper Wellington Street to the west, and covers approximately 100 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Anshe Sholom Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bruleville includes Bruleville Nature Park and Bruleville Park. Residents are served by one school.

09.03.0260.t:
Bullock, Markham

Bullock takes its name from Bullock Drive, its main road, and lies between historic Markham Village and the Markville area. The land was part of Markham Township, first settled in the 1790s and early 1800s. Much of the housing was built after the Second World War, with later infill and rebuilds; the area became part of the Town of Markham in 1971.

Bullock is generally bounded by the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision) to the north, Highway 407 to the south and McCowan Road to the west, and covers approximately 402 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 10% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision), Highway 407 and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bullock includes Milne Dam Conservation Park and Robinson Park, and the Rouge River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. Other notable landmarks include CF Markville (west edge) and Markham Centennial Community Centre.

07.01.1540.t:
Burkholme, Hamilton

Burkholme is a residential neighbourhood on the central Hamilton Mountain, bounded by Fennell Avenue East, Upper Sherman Avenue, Mohawk Road East and Upper Wentworth Street. Franklin Road School opened in 1953, and much of the remaining housing was added in the 1980s. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Burkholme is generally bounded by Fennell Avenue to the north, Upper Sherman Avenue to the east, Mohawk Road to the south and Upper Wentworth Street to the west, and covers approximately 86 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Burkholder United Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Burkholme includes Burkholder Park and Mohawk Gardens Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Other notable landmarks include Fenworth Place Mall.

07.01.1860.t:
Butler, Hamilton

Butler is a residential neighbourhood on the Hamilton Mountain. It is named after Richard Butler (1834-1925), a Hamilton editor, publisher and journalist. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Butler is generally bounded by Stone Church Road to the north, Upper Sherman Avenue to the east, Rymal Road to the south and Upper Wentworth Street to the west, and covers approximately 82 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Butler includes Billy Sherring Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.03.0180.t:
Buttonville, Markham

Buttonville is named after John Button, who bought land in Markham Township in 1808; the name first appeared in 1851 when a post office opened. By 1878 the village had a post office, gristmill, school and churches. Buttonville Municipal Airport opened in 1953, and surrounding farmland was developed for housing and business uses mainly from the 1980s to the mid-2000s. The airport closed in 2023.

Buttonville is generally bounded by 16th Avenue to the north, Rodick Road to the east, Highway 407 and a hydro corridor to the south and Highway 404 to the west, and covers approximately 613 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Buttonville Cemetery, St. John's Cemetery, Brown's Corners Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 19% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 404, Highway 407 and a hydro transformer station (Buttonville TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Buttonville includes John Button Park, and the Rouge River and Apple Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. Seneca College - Markham Campus is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Former Buttonville Municipal Airport site.

01.C08.0930.t:
Cabbagetown-South St. James Town, City of Toronto (TRREB district C08)

The Cabbagetown name is said to come from poor Irish immigrants of the late 1840s who grew cabbages in their front yards. The area was first known as Don Vale, mostly farmland outside the city before the 1850s, and it was later absorbed into Toronto. Most of its brick Victorian houses were built before the First World War. Gentrification and restoration of these houses began in the 1970s.

Cabbagetown-South St. James Town is generally bounded by Bloor Street and Parliament Street to the north, the Don River and the Don Valley Parkway to the east, Gerrard Street to the south and Wellesley Street and Carlton Street to the west, and covers approximately 144 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision), St. James Cemetery and Crematorium and Toronto Necropolis Cemetery & Crematorium. Along or just beyond its edges are the Don Valley Parkway and a hydro transformer station (Gerrard TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Cabbagetown-South St. James Town includes Riverdale Park West, Wellesley Park and Rekai Family Parkette, and the Don River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools, and transit is provided by the Castle Frank subway station. Other notable landmarks include Toronto Necropolis (1850).

07.01.1900.t:
Hannon, Hamilton

Hannon takes its name from the former rural hamlet of Hannon, near Rymal Road East on the southeast edge of the Mountain. The area remained farmland for most of its history. It has been built up with large residential subdivisions since approximately the 2000s.

Hannon is generally bounded by Stone Church Road to the north, Upper Red Hill Valley Parkway and Trinity Church Road to the east, a hydro corridor to the south and Rymal Road and Chippewa Trail to the west, and covers approximately 236 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Trinity United Church Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 28% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transformer station (Nebo TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Hannon is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

09.03.0150.t:
Cachet, Markham

Cachet is a residential neighbourhood in north-west Markham, between Highway 404 and Warden Avenue, built on former farmland of Markham Township. Very little was built before the 1990s; approximately 85% of its homes were built between 1991 and 2001. It consists mainly of large single-detached homes.

Cachet is generally bounded by Major MacKenzie Drive to the north, 16th Avenue to the east and Highway 404 to the west, and covers approximately 555 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 404 and a hydro transformer station (Buttonville TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Cachet includes Ashton Meadows Park, Calvert Park and Milton Fierheller Park, and the Rouge River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools. Other notable landmarks include King Square (Woodbine Avenue).

05.01.0070.t:
Caledon East, Caledon

Caledon East is a village in central Caledon, first settled in 1821. A station on the Northern Railway of Canada opened in 1877, and the former rail line is now the Caledon Trailway. The community became a police village in 1957 and was merged into the Town of Caledon in 1974. It has grown with newer subdivisions in recent decades.

Caledon East is generally bounded by Mountainview Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 493 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Saint James Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Caledon East includes Caledon East Park and Albert Spencer Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Caledon East branch of the Caledon Public Library.

05.01.0030.t:
Caledon Village, Caledon

Caledon Village is at Hurontario Street (Highway 10) and Charleston Sideroad. It was surveyed in 1820 and first known as Raeburn's Corners, then Charleston, where a post office opened in 1839. It grew after the railway arrived in the 1870s. The Caledon name comes from Caledonia, the Roman name for Scotland, and the community became Caledon Village in 1975 after the Town of Caledon was formed.

Caledon Village is generally bounded by Kennedy Road to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 263 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 10 and a quarry or aggregate pit. Along or just beyond its edges are Caledon Unitied Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Caledon Village includes John Alexander Park, Mistywood Park and Hawthorn Park. Residents are served by the Caledon Village branch of the Caledon Public Library.

01.W03.0380.t:
Caledonia-Fairbank, City of Toronto (TRREB district W03)

Fairbank takes its name from the Fairbank farm of English settler Matthew Parsons and the Fairbank postal village at Eglinton Avenue and Dufferin Street. The area began where Vaughan Road, an early route through farmland, met these roads, and a Methodist church stood there from 1844. Most of the neighbourhood was laid out in the 1920s and 1930s with small detached houses. It was part of York Township and later the City of York until amalgamation into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Caledonia-Fairbank is generally bounded by Eglinton Avenue to the north, Dufferin Street to the east, Morrison Avenue to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 155 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Prospect Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Caledonia-Fairbank includes Bert Robinson Park, Charles Caccia Park and Eglinton Gilbert Parkette. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools, and transit is provided by the Fairbank LRT station.

10.03.0040.t:
Cannington, Brock

Cannington was first called McCaskill's Mills, after a local family that owned mills. Settlement began in 1833, and it was renamed Cannington when the post office opened in 1849, after British prime minister George Canning. It was incorporated as a village in 1878. In 1974 it was merged with Brock Township, Thorah Township and Beaverton to form the expanded Township of Brock.

Cannington is generally bounded by the Beaver River to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 271 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Cannington.

The Beaver River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Brock Libraries - Cannington Branch.

07.01.0110.t:
Carlisle, Hamilton

Carlisle is a village in the former East Flamborough Township, north of Waterdown. George Baker began clearing land here in 1822, and the settlement was at first called Eatons and later Bakersville. The name Carlisle, after the English border town, came into use after a church was built in 1852. East Flamborough became part of the Town of Flamborough in 1974, which joined the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Carlisle is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision) to the east and Centre Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 367 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Carlisle includes Carlisle Recreation Centre, Carlisle Conservation Area and Carlisle Memorial Park, and Bronte Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by the Carlisle branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

07.01.1910.t:
Carpenter, Hamilton

Carpenter is a residential neighbourhood on the south-west Hamilton Mountain, north of John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport. Most homes are newer, built from approximately the early 1990s to the 2010s, on land that was formerly rural. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Carpenter is generally bounded by Rymal Road to the north, Garth Street to the east, Medici Lane and Hawkswood Trail to the south and a hydro corridor to the west, and covers approximately 63 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor lie along or just beyond its edges. The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 2.2 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Carpenter includes Carpenter Park. Residents are served by one school.

01.C02.0840.t:
Casa Loma, City of Toronto (TRREB district C02)

The area takes its name from Casa Loma, the castle built between 1911 and 1914 for financier Sir Henry Pellatt, designed by E. J. Lennox. It sits on the Davenport Hill escarpment, the former shoreline of glacial Lake Iroquois. The city took over the castle in 1924 for unpaid taxes, and it has operated as a museum since 1937. The surrounding streets were built up with large houses in the early 1900s.

Casa Loma is generally bounded by Lonsdale Road and Spadina Road to the north, Avenue Road to the east, the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision) to the south and Bathurst Street and St. Clair Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 188 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and a hydro transformer station (Bridgman TS). Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Casa Loma includes Sir Winston Churchill Park, Nordheimer Ravine and Roycroft Park Lands. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Wychwood branch of the Toronto Public Library. Hillcrest Grounds and George Brown College - Casa Loma Campus are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Toronto Archives and Casa Loma.

09.03.0130.t:
Cathedraltown, Markham

Cathedraltown is a planned neighbourhood named after the Slovak Catholic Cathedral of the Transfiguration, around which it was built on former farmland. It was designed with European cathedral towns and Regency and Georgian styles in mind. The first residents moved in in 2006.

Cathedraltown is generally bounded by Elgin Mills Road to the north, Victoria Square Boulevard to the east, Major MacKenzie Drive to the south and Highway 404 to the west, and covers approximately 197 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 404 and Elgin Mills Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Cathedraltown includes Frisby Park, Russell Dawson Park and Park Square. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Cathedral High Street.

09.03.0400.t:
Cedar Grove, Markham

Cedar Grove is a historic hamlet in east Markham settled by Pennsylvania Mennonites led by Peter Reesor from 1804. By 1878 it had four mills, a post office, a store, a tavern and a blacksmith shop. The surrounding land remains largely agricultural and lies within the area of Rouge National Urban Park, while newer housing to the west forms part of Box Grove.

Cedar Grove is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, York-Durham Line to the east and Steeles Avenue to the south, and covers approximately 1,099 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision) and Christ the King Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (York Subdivision) and Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Cedar Grove includes Rouge National Urban Park, Bob Hunter Memorial Park and Rouge National Urban Park (Bob Hunter Memorial), and Little Rouge Creek runs through or along the community.

10.07.0110.t:
Centennial, Oshawa

Centennial is a residential community in the City of Oshawa. Oshawa was incorporated as a village in 1850, a town in 1879 and a city in 1924, and grew mainly as an automobile manufacturing centre after the McLaughlin company merged into General Motors of Canada in 1918. The city took its present boundaries in 1974, when it absorbed the rest of East Whitby Township. Much of the city's housing was built during the post-war growth that followed.

Centennial is generally bounded by Taunton Road to the north, Wilson Road to the east, Rossland Road to the south and Oshawa Creek to the west, and covers approximately 524 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a hydro transformer station and a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Oshawa Executive Airport. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Centennial includes Northway Court Park, North Oshawa Park and Russett Park, and Oshawa Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Oshawa Public Libraries - John Aker Northview Branch. Other notable landmarks include NEB's Fun World.

01.E10.1150.t:
Centennial Scarborough, City of Toronto (TRREB district E10)

The area was first settled by Charles Annis in 1793 and Thomas Adams in 1808, and the village of Port Union grew up in the early to mid-1800s, with a post office by 1865. The original village was in Pickering Township, and the West Rouge area was annexed to Scarborough in 1974. It grew as a suburban community after the Second World War, and from the 1990s former industrial waterfront land became new subdivisions. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Centennial Scarborough is generally bounded by Kingston Road to the north, Port Union Road to the east, the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision) to the south and Highland Creek to the west, and covers approximately 532 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), Highway 2A and Asbestos Waste Site (John’s Manville Plant) (landfill). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401, Highland Creek Treatment Plant and Wesleyan Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Centennial Scarborough includes Highland Creek Ravine, Adams Park and Charlottetown Park, and Highland Creek and Centennial Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Port Union branch of the Toronto Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Lake Ontario waterfront trail.

07.01.1090.t:
Central, Hamilton

Central is Hamilton's downtown core, between Queen Street, the CN rail line, James Street North and Main Street. It is one of the city's four original neighbourhoods and grew from the town laid out by George Hamilton in 1815. The area once held an open-air farmers' market and early city hall buildings, many of which were cleared in the 1960s for downtown redevelopment.

Central is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) to the north, James Street to the east, Main Street to the south and Queen Street to the west, and covers approximately 109 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line and the CN rail line. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Central includes Central Park, Gary Hill Memorial Park and York Boulevard Parkette. Residents are served by one school and the Central branch of the Hamilton Public Library, and transit is provided by the West Harbour GO Station. Shopping is available at Jackson Square. Other notable landmarks include Art Gallery of Hamilton and Hess Village.

09.07.0050.t:
Central Newmarket, Newmarket

Central Newmarket is the historic core of the town. Quaker settlers led by Timothy Rogers arrived between 1801 and 1803, and Joseph Hill built a mill and dam on the Holland River that formed today's Fairy Lake. The name "New Market" set the settlement apart from York, the old market. The Northern Railway reached the downtown in 1853, and Newmarket became a village in 1857 and a town in 1880.

Central Newmarket is generally bounded by Davis Drive to the north, Prospect Street and Bayview Avenue to the east, Mulock Drive to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 435 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), Newmarket Well #2, Newmarket Well #1, a hydro transformer station (Armitage TS) and Pioneer Burying Ground. Along or just beyond its edges are Religious Society of Friends Burial Ground. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Central Newmarket includes Wesley Brooks Memorial Conservation Area, Haskett Park and Dennis Park, and the Holland River East Branch runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Newmarket Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Fairy Lake (Wesley Brooks Conservation Area).

10.05.0040.t:
Central, Ajax

This community is part of central Ajax, north of Highway 401. Ajax was named after the Royal Navy cruiser HMS Ajax, and grew from a Second World War munitions plant and its workers' village built on farmland in Pickering Township from 1939. It became a town in 1955 and joined the Regional Municipality of Durham in 1974, when its boundaries were expanded to include Pickering Village, Pickering Beach and Audley. Central Ajax saw much of its subdivision growth from the 1970s onward.

Central is generally bounded by Rossland Road to the north, Salem Road to the east, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision) to the south and Westney Road to the west, and covers approximately 620 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401 and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision) and the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Central includes Denis O'Connor Park, Lord Elgin Park and Cedar Park. Residents are served by approximately 10 schools and the McLean branch of the Ajax Public Library.

10.07.0130.t:
Central, Oshawa

Central Oshawa grew from the crossroads of Kingston Road and Simcoe Street, first known as Skae's Corners after Edward Skae's store. The name Oshawa, from an Ojibwa term often rendered as the crossing place, was adopted in 1842. The McLaughlin carriage works moved here in 1878, and the settlement became a town in 1879 and a city in 1924. Auto manufacturing drove rapid growth in the 1920s.

Central is generally bounded by King Street to the north, Wilson Road to the east, Highway 401 to the south and Oshawa Creek to the west, and covers approximately 377 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Central includes Chopin Park, Central Valley Park and Rotary Park, and Oshawa Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Oshawa Public Libraries - McLaughlin Branch. Other notable landmarks include Downtown Oshawa (King Street and Simcoe Street) and Canadian Automotive Museum.

10.05.0060.t:
Central East, Ajax

This community lies in the eastern part of central Ajax and includes the area of the historic Pickering Village. Pickering Village was the main settlement of Pickering Township in the first half of the 19th century, and Quaker settlers built mills on Duffins Creek from 1807. Ajax was named after the Royal Navy cruiser HMS Ajax, and grew from a Second World War munitions plant and its workers' village built on farmland in Pickering Township from 1939. It became a town in 1955 and joined the Regional Municipality of Durham in 1974, when its boundaries were expanded to include Pickering Village, Pickering Beach and Audley.

Central East is generally bounded by Rossland Road to the north, Lake Ridge Road to the east, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision) to the south and Salem Road to the west, and covers approximately 700 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401 and industrial lands (approximately 11% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision) and the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Central East includes Miles Park, Ajax Lexington Park and Ajax Turnerberry Parkette. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

05.03.0070.t:
Central Erin Mills, Mississauga

Central Erin Mills is part of Erin Mills, a planned "new town" on former farmland in the old Trafalgar and Toronto townships. The land was assembled by E. P.
