Taylor's Don Mills Development Corporation in the 1950s and taken over by Cadillac Fairview in 1968. Development of Erin Mills began in the early 1970s and moved north over the following decades, and this central part was built up mainly in the 1980s and 1990s.

Central Erin Mills is generally bounded by Britannia Road and Erin Mills Parkway to the north, the Credit River to the east, Highway 403 to the south and Winston Churchill Boulevard to the west, and covers approximately 966 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and Highway 403. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Central Erin Mills includes Erin Woods Park, Sugar Maple Woods and Quenippenon Meadows Community Park, and Mullet Creek, Sawmill Creek and the Credit River run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 10 schools and the Erin Meadows branch of the Mississauga Library. Shopping is available at Erin Mills Town Centre. Credit Valley Hospital is also located in the community.

10.07.0010.t:
Raglan, Oshawa

Raglan is a rural hamlet in the far north of Oshawa. It was first known as O'Boyle's Corners and then Newton. It was renamed Raglan when its post office opened in the 1850s, after Lord Raglan, a British commander in the Crimean War. Raglan was part of East Whitby Township until 1974, when the township was merged into the City of Oshawa.

Raglan is generally bounded by Simcoe Street to the south and Oshawa Creek to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 59 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Raglan includes Raglan Park.

04.15.0280.t:
Innis-Shore, Barrie

Innis-Shore is in southeast Barrie, between the Painswick area and the shore of Lake Simcoe. Its name refers to Innisfil Township, of which it was part, and to the nearby lakeshore. Much of Barrie's south end was part of Innisfil Township until January 1, 1982, when approximately 8,623 acres were annexed to the city. The area has been built out with newer subdivisions, mostly since the 2000s.

Innis-Shore is generally bounded by Lake Simcoe and the Innisfil boundary to the north, Big Bay Point Road to the east, Mapleview Drive to the south and Hewitt's Creek to the west, and covers approximately 372 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Barrie Surface Water Treatment Plant. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Innis-Shore includes Sandringham Park, Coronation Park and Queensway Park, and Hewitt's Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

05.02.0290.t:
Central Park, Brampton

Central Park is part of Bramalea and is named after Central Park Drive. Bramalea was developed as a planned 'new town' in the former Chinguacousy Township by Bramalea Consolidated Developments (later Bramalea Limited), Canada's first satellite community. Its G and H sections, known as 'The Villages of Central Park', were where zero-lot-line housing was first used. Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships were merged with the Town of Brampton in 1974 to form the City of Brampton.

Central Park is generally bounded by Bovaird Drive to the north, Bramalea Road to the east, Central Park Drive and Hanover Road to the south and Dixie Road to the west, and covers approximately 360 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Lundy Burial Ground Cemetery/Mount Olivet Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Central Park includes Manitou Park, Hilldale Park North and Crescent Hill Park. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools. Other notable landmarks include Chinguacousy Park (at the edge) and Brampton Library, Chinguacousy Branch.

10.05.0020.t:
Central West, Ajax

This community is part of central Ajax, near Duffins Creek on the west side of the town. Ajax was named after the Royal Navy cruiser HMS Ajax, and grew from a Second World War munitions plant and its workers' village built on farmland in Pickering Township from 1939. It became a town in 1955 and joined the Regional Municipality of Durham in 1974, when its boundaries were expanded to include Pickering Village, Pickering Beach and Audley. Central Ajax saw much of its subdivision growth from the 1970s onward.

Central West is generally bounded by Rossland Road and a hydro corridor to the north, Westney Road to the east, Highway 401 and Notion Road to the south and the Pickering boundary and Duffins Creek to the west, and covers approximately 719 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401, Pickering Quaker Cemetery, Elizabeth Street Pioneer Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision) and the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Central West includes Hermitage Park, St. Patrick Park and Mullen Park, and Duffins Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools, and transit is provided by the Ajax GO Station.

04.09.0080.t:
Centre Vespra, Springwater

Centre Vespra covers the central part of the former Vespra Township, northwest of Barrie. Vespra was settled for farming in the 19th century. On January 1, 1994 it became part of the Township of Springwater, formed from Flos and Vespra townships, the villages of Elmvale and Hillsdale, and part of Medonte.

Centre Vespra is generally bounded by a hydro corridor to the north, Dobson Road to the east and Barrie Hill Road to the west, and covers approximately 218 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Centre Vespra includes Oliver's Mill Park.

07.01.1400.t:
Centremount, Hamilton

Centremount is an established neighbourhood on the Hamilton Mountain near the brow of the Niagara Escarpment, next to Concession Street. Its housing is mainly brick bungalows and one-and-a-half-storey homes on tree-lined streets. The Mountain was largely rural land in the former Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages; the last of the township was annexed in 1960.

Centremount is generally bounded by Claremont Access to the north, Upper Wellington Street to the east, Fennell Avenue to the south and Upper James Street to the west, and covers approximately 85 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Centremount.

Green space in Centremount includes Bruce Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Other notable landmarks include Concession Street shopping district.

07.01.1240.t:
Chedoke Park, Hamilton

Chedoke Park is a neighbourhood in lower west Hamilton, named after the Chedoke area and Chedoke Creek. Chedoke Creek formed the western edge of the city around 1901, and the lands to the west were built up as Hamilton expanded during the 20th century.

Chedoke Park is generally bounded by Aberdeen Avenue to the north and Highway 403 and Scenic Drive to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 164 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a rail yard. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 403. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Chedoke Civic Golf Course is located in the area.

05.01.0020.t:
Cheltenham, Caledon

Cheltenham is a village on the Credit River in the former Chinguacousy Township, settled in approximately 1820. It is named after Cheltenham, England. Milling was its main industry until the local mill burned. It joined the Town of Caledon in 1974 and has the largest concentration of designated heritage properties among Caledon's villages.

Cheltenham is generally bounded by Creditview Road to the north, the Credit River to the east, Station Road to the south and Caledon Trailway and Mill Street to the west, and covers approximately 168 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Cheltenham Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Credit River runs through or along the community.

01.C08.0910.t:
Church-Yonge Corridor, City of Toronto (TRREB district C08)

The area lies between Yonge Street and Church Street in the old City of Toronto. Part of it was the estate of merchant Alexander Wood in the early 1800s. It was built up with Victorian houses and commercial buildings in the late 1800s and early 1900s. The Church and Wellesley area became the centre of Toronto's gay village from the 1980s, and many high-rise condominiums have been built since the 2000s.

Church-Yonge Corridor is generally bounded by Bloor Street to the north and Yonge Street and Jarvis Street to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 136 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Church-Yonge Corridor.

Green space in Church-Yonge Corridor includes St. James Park, Kerr Hall Quad and Barbara Hall Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools, and transit is provided by the College, Wellesley, Bloor-Yonge and King subway stations. St. Michael's Hospital and Toronto Metropolitan University are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Sankofa Square and The Omni King Edward Hotel.

04.14.0040.t:
Churchill, Innisfil

Churchill is a small rural hamlet in the south part of Innisfil, near Yonge Street (the former Penetanguishene Road, completed in 1825). Innisfil Township was surveyed in 1820 and settled mainly from the 1820s, with farm hamlets forming along the main roads. The township became the Town of Innisfil on January 1, 1991.

Churchill is generally bounded by Yonge Street to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 87 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Churchill is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

05.03.0020.t:
Churchill Meadows, Mississauga

Churchill Meadows was farmland in the former Trafalgar Township. It became part of Oakville in 1962 and part of Mississauga in 1974. Planning began in 1981, and most construction took place from 1997 to 2001, making it one of Mississauga's newest communities.

Churchill Meadows is generally bounded by Britannia Road to the north, Winston Churchill Boulevard to the east, Highway 403 to the south and Highway 407 to the west, and covers approximately 919 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 403 and a hydro transformer station. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Churchill Meadows includes Marco Muzzo Senior Memorial Woods and Park, Friendship Community Park and O'Connor Park. Residents are served by approximately 12 schools and the Churchill Meadows branch of the Mississauga Library.

05.03.0210.t:
City Centre, Mississauga

Mississauga City Centre was farmland until developer Bruce McLaughlin began buying land in the 1950s with plans for a new urban core. Square One Shopping Centre opened in 1973, and offices, hotels and condominium towers followed around the Hurontario Street and Burnhamthorpe Road intersection. Mississauga City Hall opened in 1987, and many high-rise towers were added from the 2000s onward.

City Centre is generally bounded by Highway 403 to the north and Confederation Parkway and Burnhamthorpe Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 225 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 403 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in City Centre includes Cleary Park, Kariya Park and Living Arts Park, and Cooksville Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school. Shopping is available at Square One Shopping Centre. Sheridan College - Hazel McCallion Campus is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Mississauga City Hall and Celebration Square.

04.18.0030.t:
Coldwater, Severn

Coldwater began in 1830 when Chief John Aisance and his Chippewa band settled on the Coldwater River, at a place they called Gissinausebing, meaning cold water. The band built a grist mill in 1833, a post office named Coldwater opened in 1835, and the area was opened to European settlement in 1836. Coldwater was incorporated as a village in 1908 and became part of the Township of Severn in 1994.

Coldwater is generally bounded by Uhthoff Trail and Upper Big Chute Road to the north, Anderson Line to the east, Southorn Road to the south and the Coldwater River and Sheridan Drive to the west, and covers approximately 324 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 12 and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Coldwater River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Severn Township Public Library.

04.11.0080.t:
Colgan, Adjala-Tosorontio

Colgan is a rural hamlet in the former Adjala Township, an area settled from the 1820s largely by Irish Catholic families who often named hamlets after places in Ireland or pioneer families. Its best-known building is St. James Catholic Church. Adjala Township was incorporated in 1850 and Tosorontio Township in 1855; the two merged to form the Township of Adjala-Tosorontio on January 1, 1994.

Colgan is generally bounded by Sparrow Way to the north and Adjala-Tecumseth Townline to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 192 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Keenansville Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include St. James Catholic Church.

04.15.0190.t:
City Centre, Barrie

This is downtown Barrie on the Kempenfelt Bay waterfront, the original settlement at the foot of the Nine Mile Portage. The settlement was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie and became the seat of Simcoe County. It became a town in 1870 and a city in 1959.

City Centre is generally bounded by Bayfield Street and Maple Avenue to the north, Simcoe Street and McDonald Street to the east and Lakeshore Drive and Bradford Street to the south, and covers approximately 103 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a wastewater treatment plant lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in City Centre includes Sam Cancilla Park and John Edwin Coupe Park. Residents are served by the Downtown branch of the Barrie Public Library. Shopping is available at Barrie By the Bay. Collège Boréal - Barrie Campus is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Dunlop Street, Heritage Park and Centennial Beach.

05.02.0450.t:
Claireville Conservation, Brampton

This area in east Brampton takes its name from the historic village of Claireville and the Claireville Conservation Area, one of the largest natural areas in the Greater Toronto Area. It was part of the former Toronto Gore Township until the 1974 merger that formed the City of Brampton. The area was mostly farmland, with small pockets of industrial and estate housing, until the early 2000s, when new subdivisions began north of Queen Street East.

Claireville Conservation is generally bounded by Queen Street to the north, The Gore Road to the east and Claireville Reservoir and Finch Avenue to the south, and covers approximately 637 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and Highway 407. Along or just beyond its edges are a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Claireville Conservation includes Claireville Conservation Area and Wet 'n' Wild Toronto, and the West Humber River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Claireville Reservoir.

01.E04.1230.t:
Clairlea-Birchmount, City of Toronto (TRREB district E04)

In the 19th century the corner of St. Clair Avenue and Victoria Park Avenue was a small village called Moffat's Corners, in a rural part of Scarborough Township (established 1850). Clairlea was one of the first parts of Scarborough developed as a Toronto suburb, transformed in the early 1950s. Scarborough joined Metropolitan Toronto in 1953 and became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Clairlea-Birchmount is generally bounded by Eglinton Avenue to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and Birchmount Road to the east, Taylor Massey Creek and Warden Avenue to the south and Victoria Park Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 743 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a hydro transformer station (Warden TS), Toronto East Detention Centre, The Dawes Road Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 24% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Transit Uxbridge Subdivision) and Pine Hills Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Clairlea-Birchmount includes Warden Woods Park, St. Clair Ravine and Clairlea Park, and Taylor Massey Creek runs through or along the community. Dentonia Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools, the Albert Campbell branch of the Toronto Public Library and the Eglinton Square branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Warden subway station, the Scarborough GO Station and the O'Connor and Pharmacy LRT stations. Shopping is available at Eglinton Square. Providence Healthcare is also located in the community.

01.C06.0610.t:
Clanton Park, City of Toronto (TRREB district C06)

The area is also known as Wilson Heights or Dublin Heights. The Dublin name comes from the farm of Irish linen merchant William Duncan, who settled near Sheppard Avenue and Dufferin Street in 1827, and the crossroads village that grew there. The area was part of York Township, then North York from 1922, and the City of Toronto from 1998. It was largely built up with bungalows in the 1950s, and former Downsview Airport lands were developed for housing in the 1990s.

Clanton Park is generally bounded by Sheppard Avenue and Wilson Heights Boulevard to the north, Bathurst Street to the east and Highway 401 to the south, and covers approximately 426 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401, Allen Road and Wilson Yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Clanton Park includes Elie Wiesel Park, Michael Mostyn Balmoral Park and Milton Berger Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools, and transit is provided by the Wilson subway station.

05.02.0020.t:
Huttonville, Brampton

Huttonville is a hamlet in the Credit River valley at Mississauga Road and Queen Street/Embleton Road in west Brampton. It was first settled in the 1820s and was known as Wolf's Den, Bully Hollow and Brown's Mills. James Hutton bought the mills in 1855, and the settlement became Hutton's Mills and later Huttonville. It became part of Brampton in 1974, and suburban development has grown around it since the 2000s.

Huttonville is generally bounded by Mississauga Road to the east and the Credit River to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 45 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Huttonville.

The Credit River runs through or along the community.

01.C10.0760.t:
Mount Pleasant West, City of Toronto (TRREB district C10)

The area lies between Yonge Street and Mount Pleasant Road and is part of Davisville Village. Davisville was founded by John Davis in 1840, who opened the first post office and the Davisville Pottery. Davis family land was sold for development in 1911, and many single-family homes were built in the 1920s and 1930s. Large apartment and condominium buildings were added from the 1970s to the 2000s.

Mount Pleasant West is generally bounded by Keewatin Avenue to the north, Mount Pleasant Road to the east, Kay Gardiner Beltline Trail to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 135 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Davisville Yard and Mount Pleasant Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Mount Pleasant West includes June Rowlands Park, Glebe Manor Square West and Al Green Sculpture Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools, and transit is provided by the Davisville and Eglinton subway stations and the Mount Pleasant LRT station.

05.03.0120.t:
Clarkson, Mississauga

Clarkson is named after Warren Clarkson, who arrived from New York State in 1808 and opened the first store on the stagecoach trail now called Clarkson Road. From the mid-1800s the area was known for strawberry and fruit farming. Suburban development followed in the 1950s, including the Park Royal subdivision opened in 1958. Clarkson became part of Mississauga in 1968.

Clarkson is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the north, Lake Ontario and Birchwood Creek to the east, Orr Road and Southdown Road to the south and the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) and Winston Churchill Boulevard to the west, and covers approximately 941 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), a rail yard and Spring Creek Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Clarkson includes Rattray Marsh Conservation Area, Jack Darling Memorial Park and Birchwood Park, and Sheridan Creek and Turtle Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 11 schools and the Clarkson branch of the Mississauga Library, and transit is provided by the Clarkson GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Bradley Museum and Benares House.

04.01.0010.t:
Collingwood, Collingwood

Collingwood is a town on Nottawasaga Bay, first known as Hens-and-Chickens Harbour. It grew after 1855, when the Ontario, Simcoe and Huron Railway reached the harbour. It is named after Admiral Cuthbert Collingwood and was incorporated as a town in 1858. Shipbuilding was a major industry from 1883 until the shipyards closed in 1986.

Collingwood is generally bounded by Georgian Bay to the north, Poplar Sideroad to the south and Sixth Street and Grey Road 21 to the west, and covers approximately 3,423 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 26, a quarry or aggregate pit, a wastewater treatment plant, Collingwood Dump (landfill), a cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Collingwood includes Fisher Fields, Optimist Harbourview Park and Central Park, and Silver Creek and the Pretty River run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Georgian Bay. Cranberry Golf Course and Blue Mountain Golf and Country Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools and the Collingwood Public Library. Collingwood General and Marine Hospital and Georgian College - South Georgian Bay Campus are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Blue Mountain Go Karts.

10.07.0030.t:
Columbus, Oshawa

Columbus was first called English Corners and took the name Columbus when its post office opened in 1847. The first settlers arrived in 1830, and by 1870 the village had more than 300 residents, a township hall, churches and mills. The first East Whitby Township council met in 1853. The village declined after a nearby mill dam washed out in 1890, and Columbus became part of Oshawa in 1974.

Columbus is generally bounded by Simcoe Street to the south and Columbus Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 102 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Columbus includes Columbus Park and Walter Beath Parkette.

04.10.0040.t:
Colwell, Essa

Colwell is a small hamlet in the Township of Essa, Simcoe County. Essa Township was incorporated in 1850 and developed mainly as a farming area. In 1991 the township merged with the Thornton Police Village to form the current Township of Essa.

Colwell is generally bounded by Bear Creek to the east, 9th Line to the south and the Meaford Subdivision rail line and 30th Sideroad to the west, and covers approximately 80 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the Meaford Subdivision rail line. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Colwell is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

01.E08.1200.t:
Cliffcrest, City of Toronto (TRREB district E08)

Cliffcrest takes its name from the Scarborough Bluffs, the sandy cliffs along Lake Ontario at its southern edge. The area was part of Scarborough Township from 1850, and Scarborough High School (now R. H. King Academy) opened there in 1922. It was largely built up as a postwar suburb of detached homes. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Cliffcrest is generally bounded by the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) to the north, Lake Ontario to the south and Midland Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 700 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Resthaven Memorial Gardens (cemetery), Holy Blossom Memorial Park (cemetery), Queen of The Clergy Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Transit Uxbridge Subdivision) and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Cliffcrest includes Bluffer's Park, Cudia Park and McCowan District Park. Residents are served by approximately 10 schools and the Cliffcrest branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Eglinton GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Scarborough Bluffs and R. H. King Academy.

07.01.1190.t:
Lakely, Hamilton

Lakely is a residential neighbourhood in the east end of the former City of Hamilton, near Lake Ontario. The area was farmland in the old townships east of Hamilton before it was annexed by the City of Hamilton in the twentieth century. Barton Township was fully absorbed by the city in 1960.

Lakely is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the north, Lake Avenue to the east, Barton Street to the south and Centennial Parkway to the west, and covers approximately 81 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (Hamilton Lake TS), Baycoat (industrial plant) and industrial lands (approximately 42% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Lakely is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

09.03.0050.t:
Commerce Valley, Markham

Commerce Valley lies in the Thornhill area of west Markham, near Highway 7, Leslie Street and Highway 407. It is mainly an office and business area, with newer condominium development, built on former Markham Township farmland. The wider Thornhill area was settled from 1794 and became part of the Town of Markham in 1971.

Commerce Valley is generally bounded by Highway 404 to the east and Highway 407 and Highway 7 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 202 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 407. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 404. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Commerce Valley includes Saddle Creek Park, Leitchcroft Park and Lotus Flower Park, and German Mills Creek runs through or along the community.

04.15.0160.t:
Codrington, Barrie

Codrington is an established residential area east of downtown Barrie, above the north shore of Kempenfelt Bay. It takes its name from Codrington Street, which runs through the area. Barrie grew from a supply depot at the end of the Nine Mile Portage and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a village in 1854, a town in 1871 and a city in 1959. The area includes some of the city's older residential streets, with later infill from the mid-20th century onward.

Codrington is generally bounded by Blake Street and Steel Street to the east and Wellington Street to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 215 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Codrington.

Green space in Codrington includes Archie Goodall Park and Lions Park. Residents are served by one school.

09.02.0150.t:
Concord, Vaughan

Concord likely takes its name from Hiram White, who came to Vaughan Township from Concord, Vermont, in 1818. A Northern Railway stop was renamed Concord in 1853, and it became a postal village in 1854. Suburban and industrial growth began in the 1950s after Highway 400 opened and CN built its MacMillan Yard. Industry grew along Highway 7 and Keele Street from the 1970s, and Glen Shields was built in the 1970s and 1980s.

Concord is generally bounded by Rutherford Road to the north, Dufferin Street to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Highway 400 to the west, and covers approximately 2,707 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), the CN rail line (York Subdivision), the York-Halton By-Pass Track rail line, the CN rail line, Highway 407, CN MacMillan Yard, a hydro transformer station (SR Greenwood Transformer Station), Beechwood Cemetery and Mausoleum, Edgeley Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 56% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 400 and Sherwood Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Concord includes Langstaff Park, Tudor District Park and Concord Community Park, and the Don River West Branch and Black Creek run through or along the community. Transit is provided by the Highway 407 subway station. Other notable landmarks include CN MacMillan Yard and The Village at Black Creek.

07.01.1060.t:
Cootes Paradise, Hamilton

This neighbourhood in west Hamilton takes its name from Cootes Paradise, the large marsh at the west end of Hamilton Harbour. The marsh was named after Thomas Coote, a British Army officer who hunted there in the 1780s. The marsh has been protected since 1927 and has been managed by the Royal Botanical Gardens since 1941. The nearby residential areas grew after McMaster University opened in Hamilton in 1930.

Cootes Paradise is generally bounded by Lake Ontario to the north, Forsyth Avenue and Main Street to the south and Cootes Drive to the west, and covers approximately 191 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Cootes Paradise includes Royal Botanical Gardens, Churchill Park and 10 Acre Field. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. McMaster University Medical Centre and McMaster University are also located in the community.

13.03.0010.t:
Cobourg, Cobourg

Cobourg was founded by United Empire Loyalists in 1798 as small villages including Amherst and Hardscrabble. It was named Cobourg in 1819 to honour the marriage of Princess Charlotte to Prince Leopold of Saxe-Coburg. It was incorporated as a town on July 1, 1837, and grew as a Lake Ontario harbour and railway town. Victoria College was located here until it moved to Toronto in 1892.

Cobourg is generally bounded by the Hamilton Township boundary to the north and Lake Ontario to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 2,213 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario.

04.16.0010.t:
Craighurst, Oro-Medonte

Craighurst is a hamlet on the Penetanguishene Road, which was surveyed after the War of 1812. It developed as a small community from the 1830s and had a post office from the 1850s. A Canadian Pacific Railway branch reached Craighurst in 1906. The townships of Oro and Medonte were incorporated in 1850 and were amalgamated, with the Hawkestone Police Village, to form the Township of Oro-Medonte on January 1, 1994.

Craighurst is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 76 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) and Knox Presbyterian Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Craighurst includes Railside Park.

07.01.1050.t:
Confederation Park, Hamilton

This neighbourhood in Hamilton's east end takes its name from Confederation Park, a large lakeshore park and tourist area on Lake Ontario. A full-sized amusement park operated in the park until 1978.

Confederation Park is generally bounded by Lake Ontario and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the east and Redhill Creek to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 162 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Along or just beyond its edges are a wastewater treatment plant and Baycoat (industrial plant). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Confederation Park includes Confederation Beach Park, and Redhill Creek runs through or along the community.

04.14.0010.t:
Cookstown, Innisfil

Cookstown began as Perry's Corners and was later called Dixon's Corners. It took the name Cooke's Town in 1847, linked to Thomas Cooke, whose house still stands on Highway 27. It was incorporated as a village in 1962 and merged into the Town of Innisfil on January 1, 1991. The historic core is a heritage conservation district.

Cookstown is generally bounded by Cookstown Creek to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 222 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Cookstown Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Cookstown branch of the Innisfil Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Tanger Outlets Cookstown and Trans Canada Trail (former rail line).

01.W03.0390.t:
Corso Italia-Davenport, City of Toronto (TRREB district W03)

Corso Italia occupies the eastern part of the area once known as Earlscourt, settled largely by British immigrants from approximately 1906 and annexed by the City of Toronto in 1910. Most houses were built in the early decades of the 20th century. By the 1970s, many Italian immigrants had moved north from the College Street area, and St. Clair Avenue West became known as Corso Italia. The Corso Italia business improvement area was created in 1984.

Corso Italia-Davenport is generally bounded by Morrison Avenue to the north, Dufferin Street and St. Clair Avenue to the east, Davenport Road and a hydro corridor to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 179 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Prospect Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and a hydro transformer station (Wiltshire TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Corso Italia-Davenport includes Earlscourt Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Dufferin/St. Clair branch of the Toronto Public Library.

05.03.0240.t:
Cooksville, Mississauga

Cooksville was first called Harrisville, after first settler Daniel Harris, and was renamed in 1836 after Jacob Cook, who ran stagecoach lines and held the mail contract on Dundas Street. Much of the village was destroyed by fire in 1852, and a large brickyard operated in the area from 1912 to 1995. It became a centre of early suburban and high-rise growth from the 1960s, and became part of Mississauga in 1968.

Cooksville is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) to the north, Tedlo Street and Cawthra Road to the east, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the south and Mavis Road to the west, and covers approximately 918 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a hydro transformer station (Cooksville TS) and St. Mary's Port Credit Catholic Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Cooksville includes Brickyard Park, Camilla Park and Richard Jones Park, and Cooksville Creek, Wolfedale Creek and Cawthra Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 13 schools and the Cooksville branch of the Mississauga Library, and transit is provided by the Cooksville GO Station. Mississauga Hospital is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Dundas Street and Hurontario Street intersection.

07.01.1270.t:
Corktown, Hamilton

Corktown is one of Hamilton's four original neighbourhoods, bounded by James Street South, Main Street, Wellington Street and the Niagara Escarpment. It takes its name from the Irish immigrants who settled near John and Hunter streets during the city's 19th-century industrial growth. Much of the housing dates from the 19th and early 20th centuries.

Corktown is generally bounded by Main Street to the north, Wellington Street to the east, Claremont Access to the south and James Street to the west, and covers approximately 90 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision) and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Corktown includes Corktown Park, Shamrock Park and Woolverton Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools, and transit is provided by Hamilton GO Centre. St. Joseph's Healthcare Hamilton - Charlton Campus is also located in the community.

07.01.1340.t:
Corman, Hamilton

Corman is a residential neighbourhood in Hamilton's east end, below the Niagara Escarpment. The east end was rural land in Barton and Saltfleet townships that Hamilton annexed in sections during the first half of the 20th century.

Corman is generally bounded by Queenston Road to the north, Nash Road to the east, King Street to the south and the Red Hill Valley Parkway to the west, and covers approximately 96 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Red Hill Valley Parkway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Corman includes Glendale Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

09.03.0320.t:
Cornell, Markham

Cornell is named after the Cornell family, led by William C. Cornell, who settled in Markham after arriving from Rhode Island in 1799; the name was chosen in 1999. The area was first farmed by the Reesor family. The Town of Markham planned Cornell in the early 1990s as a new urbanist community, designed in 1994, and construction began in 1997. Land south of Highway 7 began redevelopment in 2022.

Cornell is generally bounded by Donald Cousens Parkway to the north, Reesor Road to the east, Highway 407 to the south and Ninth Line to the west, and covers approximately 698 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Cornell includes Cornell Community Park, Benjamin Marr Park and Country Glen Park. The community includes or fronts onto Reesor Pond. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Cornell branch of the Markham Public Library. Markham Stouffville Hospital is also located in the community.

10.08.0010.t:
Courtice, Clarington

Courtice is in the former Darlington Township, next to the east boundary of Oshawa. It is named after the Courtice family, who arrived from Devonshire, England in the early 1830s. It remained a small rural village until housing developments began in the mid-1980s and brought rapid growth. It has been part of Clarington since 1974.

Courtice is generally bounded by Courtice Road to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Townline Road to the west, and covers approximately 2,426 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), Highway 401, the Courtice Water Pollution Control Plant, Durham York Energy Centre, St. Wolodymyr & St. Olha Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 418. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Courtice includes Darlington Provincial Park, Penfound Park and Roswell Park, and Black Creek and Farewell Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto McLaughlin Bay. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools and the Courtice branch of the Clarington Public Library.

05.02.0040.t:
Credit Valley, Brampton

Credit Valley is in west Brampton, north of the Credit River. Its earlier European history centres on the farming hamlet of Springbrook, settled in the 1800s, which stayed small until the land was developed. Most homes were built from the 2000s, and development is ongoing. Mount Pleasant GO Station opened on the Kitchener line in 2006.

Credit Valley is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and Bovaird Drive to the north, Chinguacousy Road to the east, the Credit River to the south and Mississauga Road to the west, and covers approximately 1,211 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Huttonville Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and a hydro transformer station (Mount Pleasant TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Credit Valley includes Eldorado Park, Andrew McCandless Park and Teramoto Park, and Huttonville Creek and the Credit River run through or along the community. Lionhead Golf & Country Club - Legends is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 11 schools. Other notable landmarks include Mount Pleasant GO Station.

05.03.0160.t:
Creditview, Mississauga

Creditview takes its name from the Credit River valley and Creditview Road. The area was farmland in the former Toronto Township, which became the Town of Mississauga in 1968 and the City in 1974. It was built out with suburban housing in the later decades of the 20th century; most of Mississauga was built out by 2005. Specific history for this community was not found.

Creditview is generally bounded by Confederation Parkway to the east, Burnhamthorpe Road to the south and Highway 403 to the west, and covers approximately 271 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and Highway 403. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Creditview includes Deer Run Park, Deer Wood Park and Ashgate Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

01.E03.1290.t:
Crescent Town, City of Toronto (TRREB district E03)

Crescent Town takes its name from Crescent School, which occupied the site after Susan Massey donated her mansion and 40 acres to the school in 1933. The land was part of Dentonia Park, the model farm Walter Massey assembled in the late 19th century. Crescent School left in 1969, and the property was sold to developers who built the present high-rise community, designed around Victoria Park subway station. The area was in East York, which joined the City of Toronto in 1998.

Crescent Town is generally bounded by Taylor Massey Creek and Dawes Road to the north, Victoria Park Avenue to the east, Balfour Avenue and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) to the south and Main Street to the west, and covers approximately 122 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Crescent Town includes Taylor Creek Park, Dentonia Park and Donora Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.02.0220.t:
Crestwood-Springfarm-Yorkhill, Vaughan

Crestwood-Springfarm-Yorkhill is part of the Vaughan side of Thornhill, west of Yonge Street. Thornhill was settled in 1794 and Yonge Street divided it between Vaughan and Markham. The area was largely built up from the 1960s and 1970s as Thornhill grew along its border with Toronto. In 1971 the Police Village of Thornhill ended and the area came under the new Town of Vaughan.

Crestwood-Springfarm-Yorkhill is generally bounded by Centre Street to the north, Yonge Street to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 440 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (York Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Crestwood-Springfarm-Yorkhill includes York Hill District Park, Bathurst Estates Park and Hefhill Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools.

09.03.0010.t:
Langstaff South, Markham

Langstaff South takes its name from Langstaff, a former hamlet near Yonge Street and Highway 7, likely named after settler John Langstaff, who arrived between 1803 and 1808. His farm later became the Langstaff Jail Farm. The area lies in the Thornhill part of Markham, which became part of the Town of Markham in 1971.

Langstaff South is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, Bayview Avenue and Jondan Crescent to the east and Yonge Street and Thornheights Road to the west, and covers approximately 111 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision), Holy Cross Catholic Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 30% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Langstaff South is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

09.04.0090.t:
Crosby, Richmond Hill

Crosby is part of Richmond Hill's older core along Yonge Street. The name relates to the Crosby family; Parker Crosby came from England in 1844 and ran a dry goods store at Yonge and Richmond Streets, and the family home, Crosby Hall, was built in 1863. The oldest homes near Centre Street date from the 1800s village period, with most housing built in the 1950s and 1960s.

Crosby is generally bounded by Elgin Mills Road to the north, Bayview Avenue to the east, Major MacKenzie Drive to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 370 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 18% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Richmond Hill Presbyterian Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Crosby includes Crosby Park, Town Park and Sussex Park, and German Mills Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools, and transit is provided by the Richmond Hill GO Station.

07.01.1140.t:
Crown Point, Hamilton

Crown Point is a neighbourhood in Hamilton's lower east end, centred on Ottawa Street. The east end was rural land in Barton and Saltfleet townships that Hamilton annexed in sections during the first half of the 20th century, and it was built up as housing for workers in the nearby steel and manufacturing plants. The first Tim Hortons store opened on Ottawa Street in 1964.

Crown Point is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) to the north, Kenilworth Avenue to the east, Main Street to the south and Gage Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 239 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 7% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Crown Point includes Belview Park, Crown Point Neighbourhood Park and R. T. Steele Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Kenilworth branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

04.15.0100.t:
Cundles East, Barrie

Cundles East is a residential area in north-central Barrie, east of Bayfield Street, named after Cundles Road. Cundles Road marked Barrie's northern limit until 1984, when the city annexed approximately 2,200 acres of Vespra Township land to the north. The area was largely built up with suburban housing in the later 20th century.

Cundles East is generally bounded by Cardinal Street and Farmingdale Crescent to the north, Ferris Lane and St. Vincent Street to the east and Highway 400 to the south, and covers approximately 131 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 400. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Cundles East includes Redpath Park and Robin Court Park. Residents are served by one school.

10.09.0010.t:
Scugog First Nations, Scugog

This area is the reserve of the Mississaugas of Scugog Island First Nation, on Scugog Island in Lake Scugog. The island was formed when a dam at Lindsay raised the lake level in 1834. The reserve consists of two tracts along Mississauga's Trail. The Great Blue Heron Casino is located on the reserve.

Scugog First Nations is generally bounded by Hood Drive to the north, Pogue Road to the south and Fralick's Beach Road to the west, and covers approximately 255 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Scugog First Nations is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

01.E03.1330.t:
Danforth, City of Toronto (TRREB district E03)

The area takes its name from Danforth Avenue, named after Asa Danforth Jr., an American contractor who built roads in Upper Canada in the 1790s. The district east of Greenwood Avenue was annexed to the City of Toronto in 1908 and 1909. It grew quickly as a streetcar suburb after the Prince Edward Viaduct opened in 1918, and most homes date from the 1910s to the 1930s. The Bloor-Danforth subway replaced the Danforth streetcar in 1966.

Danforth is generally bounded by Danforth Avenue and Milverton Boulevard to the east and Pape Avenue to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 114 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Danforth.

Green space in Danforth includes Langford Parkette and 24 Dewhurst Blvd Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools, and transit is provided by the Pape, Greenwood, Coxwell and Woodbine subway stations. Other notable landmarks include Monarch Park.

10.07.0180.t:
Eastdale, Oshawa

Eastdale is a residential community in east Oshawa. Oshawa was incorporated as a village in 1850, a town in 1879 and a city in 1924, and grew mainly as an automobile manufacturing centre after the McLaughlin company merged into General Motors of Canada in 1918. The city took its present boundaries in 1974, when it absorbed the rest of East Whitby Township. Much of the city's housing was built during the post-war growth that followed.

Eastdale is generally bounded by Rossland Road to the north, Townline Road to the east, King Street to the south and Wilson Road to the west, and covers approximately 514 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Farewell Memorial Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Eastdale includes Eastbourne Park, Easton Park and Galahad Park, and Harmony Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools.

01.E03.1270.t:
Danforth Village-East York, City of Toronto (TRREB district E03)

The area north of Danforth Avenue in East York was once church land, known as the Glebe, which is recalled in street names such as Glebemount and Glebeholme. It was part of York Township until the Township of East York was formed in 1924. Most of its houses were built before the Second World War, with growth driven by the Prince Edward Viaduct (1918) and streetcar service on the Danforth. East York joined the City of Toronto at amalgamation in 1998.

Danforth Village-East York is generally bounded by Milverton Boulevard and Woodbine Avenue to the east and Cosburn Avenue to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 216 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Danforth Village-East York.

Green space in Danforth Village-East York includes Dieppe Park, Cosburn Park and True Davidson Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the S. Walter Stewart branch of the Toronto Public Library. Michael Garron Hospital is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Coxwell subway station.

07.01.1310.t:
Delta, Hamilton

Delta is a neighbourhood in Hamilton's east end, named for the point where King Street and Main Street, which run parallel through the city, meet. The east end was rural land in Barton and Saltfleet townships that Hamilton annexed in sections during the first half of the 20th century.

Delta is generally bounded by Main Street to the north, Kenilworth Avenue to the east, Mountain Brow Boulevard to the south and Gage Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 204 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Delta includes Gage Park and Delta Parkette. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.03.0160.t:
Devil's Elbow, Markham

Devil's Elbow is an estate residential area in north-west Markham, near Woodbine Avenue, Major Mackenzie Drive and the Cachet area. It lies on former farmland of Markham Township, which was settled from the 1790s. It is made up mainly of custom homes on large lots, including the Cachet Country Club Estates and Glenridge Estates enclaves.

Devil's Elbow is generally bounded by Bruce Creek to the east and Major MacKenzie Drive to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 297 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Devil's Elbow includes Elanor Casely Park, Arthur Stollery Common and Joseph Reid Parkette, and Bruce Creek runs through or along the community. Angus Glen Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by one school.

04.02.0030.t:
Devil's Glen, Clearview

Devil's Glen is a rural area on the Niagara Escarpment in the southwest part of Clearview Township, near Singhampton. It takes its name from the Devil's Glen gorge, now protected as Devil's Glen Provincial Park. Clearview Township was formed on January 1, 1994, by merging the Town of Stayner, the Village of Creemore and the townships of Nottawasaga and Sunnidale. The area is mostly escarpment land, ski hills and rural properties.

Devil's Glen is generally bounded by Concession 10 Nottawasaga Road and the Mad River to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 263 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Devil's Glen.

The Mad River runs through or along the community.

09.04.0080.t:
Devonsleigh, Richmond Hill

Devonsleigh is in northeast Richmond Hill, east of Yonge Street around Elgin Mills Road. The area was farmland from the early 1800s, and an earlier First Nations village existed nearby between approximately 1300 and 1550 AD. Farm fields were turned into subdivisions in the 1990s and early 2000s. The origin of the name is not firmly recorded.

Devonsleigh is generally bounded by 19th Avenue to the north, Bayview Avenue to the east, Elgin Mills Road to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 364 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 9% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Devonsleigh includes New Berry Park and Harrington Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools. Other notable landmarks include Richmond Hill High School.

05.03.0320.t:
Dixie, Mississauga

Dixie was first called Sydenham and was renamed in 1865 after Beaumont Wilson Bowen Dixie, a local settler. Union Chapel was built in 1816 and rebuilt in 1837, and St. John's Dixie cemetery has been used since 1816. It is one of Mississauga's older areas, and today much of it is commercial or industrial, with a small residential area east of Dixie Road.

Dixie is generally bounded by Little Etobicoke Creek to the north, Etobicoke Creek to the east and Queensway and Dundas Street to the west, and covers approximately 528 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 49% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are St. John’s Dixie Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Dixie includes Coram Park, and Etobicoke Creek, Little Etobicoke Creek and Cawthra Creek run through or along the community. Markland Wood Golf Club is located in the area. Transit is provided by the Dixie GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Union Chapel and St. John's Dixie Cemetery.

01.C15.0560.t:
Don Valley Village, City of Toronto (TRREB district C15)

The area was a collection of farming hamlets in the early 19th century, and the Zion Schoolhouse and the Alexander Muirhead farmhouse survive from that period. It was part of York Township and became part of North York in 1922. It was built up as a suburb in the 1960s and 1970s, with much of it built by Consolidated Building Corporation from 1963. North York General Hospital opened in 1968 and Fairview Mall in 1970, and the area joined the City of Toronto in 1998.

Don Valley Village is generally bounded by Finch Avenue to the north, Highway 404 to the east, Sheppard Avenue to the south and Leslie Street to the west, and covers approximately 416 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision), Highway 404 and Zion Church and Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Don Valley Village includes Linus Park, Lescon Park and Bellbury Park. Residents are served by approximately 11 schools and the Fairview branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Don Mills subway station. Shopping is available at CF Fairview Mall.

09.04.0160.t:
Doncrest, Richmond Hill

Doncrest is a residential area in southeast Richmond Hill, north of Highway 7 and east of Bayview Avenue. The name refers to a tributary of the Don River and was likely chosen by town planners in the 1980s. Most homes are two-storey detached houses built in the 1980s and 1990s.

Doncrest is generally bounded by 16th Avenue to the north, Highway 7 to the south and Bayview Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 285 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Doncrest includes David Hamilton Park, King's College Park and Private Thomas Millar Armstrong Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

10.07.0190.t:
Donevan, Oshawa

Donevan is a residential community in east Oshawa. The east side of the city includes the area first settled by Moody Farewell in approximately 1801 near King Street East and Harmony Road. Oshawa was incorporated as a village in 1850, a town in 1879 and a city in 1924, and grew mainly as an automobile manufacturing centre after the McLaughlin company merged into General Motors of Canada in 1918. The city took its present boundaries in 1974, when it absorbed the rest of East Whitby Township.

Donevan is generally bounded by King Street to the north, Townline Road to the east, Highway 401 to the south and Wilson Road to the west, and covers approximately 572 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) and Farewell Memorial Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Donevan includes Knights of Columbus Park, Farewell Park and Kingside Park, and Farewell Creek and Harmony Creek run through or along the community. Harmony Creek Golf Centre Ltd is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

01.E04.1100.t:
Dorset Park, City of Toronto (TRREB district E04)

Dorset Park was formerly farmland in Scarborough Township, which was established in 1850, and a school section on the site dates from the 1840s. Most of its housing was built in the 1950s, and Kennedy Road developed as a business corridor between Highway 401 and Lawrence Avenue. Scarborough joined Metropolitan Toronto in 1953 and became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Dorset Park is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Midland Avenue to the east, a hydro corridor to the south and Birchmount Road to the west, and covers approximately 595 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (Scarboro TS) and industrial lands (approximately 31% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Dorset Park includes Dorset Park, Arsandco Park and Mondeo Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the McGregor Park branch of the Toronto Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Kennedy Commons and Winston Churchill Collegiate Institute.

01.W02.0460.t:
Dovercourt-Wallace Emerson-Junction, City of Toronto (TRREB district W02)

This City of Toronto planning neighbourhood combines Dovercourt, Wallace Emerson and the eastern Junction area. The Dovercourt name comes from the Denison family estate, and the Village of Dovercourt north of Dupont Street was founded in the 1870s. Wallace Emerson takes its name from the corner of Wallace Avenue and Emerson Avenue. The village was annexed by the City of Toronto in 1910, and most houses north of Bloor Street were built in the early 20th century, while former industrial land near Dupont Street has more recently been converted to lofts and townhouses.

Dovercourt-Wallace Emerson-Junction is generally bounded by Davenport Road to the north, the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision) and Christie Street to the east, Bloor Street to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 373 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Galt Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), a rail yard and a hydro transformer station (Wiltshire TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Dovercourt-Wallace Emerson-Junction includes Christie Pits Park, Dovercourt Park and Wallace Emerson Park. Residents are served by approximately 10 schools, and transit is provided by the Ossington, Lansdowne and Dufferin subway stations and the Bloor GO Station.

01.C01.0870.t:
Dufferin Grove, City of Toronto (TRREB district C01)

The area takes its name from Dufferin Grove Park, on Dufferin Street. The land was part of the estates of the Denison family, who settled in Toronto in the 1790s and farmed the area from the 1830s. By the 1880s the estates were being subdivided for housing. Most of the existing houses were built between approximately 1890 and 1930, mainly detached and semi-detached homes.

Dufferin Grove is generally bounded by Bloor Street to the north, Dovercourt Road to the east, College Street and Dundas Street to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 138 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 7% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Galt Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line and a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Dufferin Grove includes Dufferin Grove Park and MacGregor Playground. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools. Shopping is available at Dufferin Mall.

10.02.0130.t:
Duffin Heights, Pickering

Duffin Heights takes its name from Duffins Creek, which flows through this part of Pickering. The creek is named after Mike Duffin, one of the candidates for the first European settler in the area. The land was farmland in Pickering Township, which was surveyed in 1791. It is one of Pickering's newer neighbourhoods, built out mainly from the 2010s.

Duffin Heights is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) to the north, the Ajax boundary to the east and a hydro corridor to the south, and covers approximately 506 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Brock West Landfill (landfill) and Duffin Meadows Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Duffin Heights includes Canadian Green, and Urfé Creek runs through or along the community.

10.02.0090.t:
Dunbarton, Pickering

Dunbarton is named after William Dunbar, who came from Scotland in 1831 and settled in Pickering Township. The village of Dunbarton was established in 1849 along Dunbarton Creek and had a post office and a station on the Grand Trunk Railway. Its early settlers were mostly Scottish Presbyterians. Little remains of the original village, and the area was built up with suburban housing in the second half of the 20th century.

Dunbarton is generally bounded by Parkside Drive and Fairport Road to the north, Appleview Road to the east and Highway 401 to the south, and covers approximately 159 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (York Subdivision), Highway 401 and Erskine Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Metrolinx Kingston Subdivision) and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Dunbarton includes Bonita Park.

01.W05.0270.t:
Downsview-Roding-CFB, City of Toronto (TRREB district W05)

Downsview takes its name from the Downs View farm settled by John Perkins Bull in 1842 near Keele Street and Rustic Road. The area was farmland for over a century, and de Havilland Canada opened an aircraft plant here in 1929, which later became part of a Royal Canadian Air Force base. Most houses were built in large subdivisions just after the Second World War and into the 1960s. The base closed in the 1990s and much of its land is now Downsview Park, and North York was amalgamated into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Downsview-Roding-CFB is generally bounded by Sheppard Avenue to the north, Highway 401 to the south and the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) and Black Creek to the west, and covers approximately 1,524 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), Highway 401, Highway 400, Wilson Yard, Mt Sinai Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 11% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Downsview-Roding-CFB includes Downsview Park, Downsview Dells Park and Chalkfarm Park, and Black Creek runs through or along the community. Oakdale Golf & Country Club and Knudson 9 are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 15 schools, the Black Creek branch of the Toronto Public Library and the Downsview branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Sheppard West and Downsview Park subway stations and the Downsview Park GO Station. Shopping is available at North York Sheridan Mall. Hennick Humber Hospital and Centennial College Downsview Campus are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Wilson and Downsview Park subway stations.

05.02.0120.t:
Downtown Brampton, Brampton

Downtown Brampton grew from Buffy's Corners, the crossing of Main and Queen streets, named for William Buffy's tavern. In 1834 John Elliott laid out lots there and called the settlement Brampton, after Brampton in Cumberland, England. It became a village in 1853, the Peel County seat in 1866 and a town in 1873. Brampton became a city in 1974, and the current City Hall opened downtown in 1991.

Downtown Brampton is generally bounded by Vodden Street and the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the north, Etobicoke Creek to the east and Harold Street to the south, and covers approximately 304 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are St Mary's Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Downtown Brampton includes Centennial Park, Old Fairgrounds Park and Chris Gibson Community Park, and Etobicoke Creek runs through or along the community.
