Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Four Corners branch of the Brampton Library, and transit is provided by the Brampton Innovation District GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Gage Park (1902) and Peel Art Gallery, Museum and Archives.

10.06.0080.t:
Downtown Whitby, Whitby

Whitby takes its name from the town of Whitby in Yorkshire, England. Peter Perry set up a business centre here in 1836, which became the core of the present downtown. Whitby became the county seat of Ontario County in 1852 and was incorporated as a town in 1855. In 1968 the town merged with Whitby Township.

Downtown Whitby is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) to the north, Highway 401 to the south and Cochrane Street and Annes Street to the west, and covers approximately 495 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision) and the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Downtown Whitby includes Ash Park and Rotary Center Park, and Pringle Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Central branch of the Whitby Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Trafalgar Castle (1859 to 1862).

07.01.0140.t:
Dundas, Hamilton

Dundas grew around the head of the Desjardins Canal, in an area early known as Coote's Paradise. It was renamed in 1814 after Dundas Street, which was named for Scottish politician Henry Dundas. Dundas became a town in 1847 and the Great Western Railway arrived in 1853. After McMaster University opened nearby in 1930 it grew as a residential community, and it joined the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Dundas is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision) to the north, Coldwater Creek and York Road to the east and Sulphur Creek to the south, and covers approximately 1,206 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Dundas Wastewater Treatment Plant, Grove Cemetery, St. Augustine's Roman Catholic Cemetery and Parkside Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision) and a hydro transformer station (Dundas TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Dundas includes Dundas Driving Park, Warren Park and Veterans Memorial Park, and Spring Creek, Spencer Creek and Sulphur Creek run through or along the community. Dundas Valley Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools and the Dundas branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

07.01.1010.t:
Dundurn, Hamilton

Dundurn is a neighbourhood in lower west Hamilton named after Dundurn Castle, the home completed in 1835 by Sir Allan Napier MacNab, and Dundurn Street. The name comes from MacNab's ancestral home in Dundurn, Perthshire, Scotland. The area was later built up as Hamilton expanded westward.

Dundurn is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) and Lake Ontario to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 156 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the CN rail line, the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision), the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision), the CPKC rail line, Highway 403, Woodland Cemetery, Hamilton Cemetery and Section 14 (cemetery). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Dundurn includes Royal Botanical Gardens. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario.

07.01.1260.t:
Durand, Hamilton

Durand is one of Hamilton's four original neighbourhoods, bounded by Queen Street, Main Street, James Street South and the Niagara Escarpment. It is named after James Durand, an early landowner and legislator. The area developed from the 1840s and was fully built by the end of the 19th century, with many large homes for local industrialists.

Durand is generally bounded by Main Street to the north, James Street to the east, James Mountain Road to the south and Queen Street to the west, and covers approximately 110 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line and the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Durand includes Durand Park and Whitehern. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Hamilton City Hall and Central Public School.

04.15.0090.t:
East Bayfield, Barrie

East Bayfield is a residential area in north Barrie on the east side of Bayfield Street (formerly Highway 26). Barrie's northern limit was Cundles Road until 1984, when the city annexed approximately 2,200 acres from Vespra Township, including the Bayfield Street commercial strip. Most of the area was built up with suburban housing after that annexation.

East Bayfield is generally bounded by Nicklaus Drive and the Springwater boundary to the north, St. Vincent Street to the east and Cardinal Street and Farmingdale Crescent to the south, and covers approximately 116 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of East Bayfield.

Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

05.03.0150.t:
East Credit, Mississauga

East Credit lies on the east side of the Credit River, in the former Toronto Township. The township became the Town of Mississauga in 1968 and the City in 1974. The area was farmland until suburban subdivisions were built in the later decades of the 20th century; most of Mississauga was built out by 2005. Specific history for this community was not found.

East Credit is generally bounded by the Credit River to the north, Mavis Road to the east and Highway 403 to the south, and covers approximately 1,636 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), Highway 403, a hydro transformer station (Erindale TS) and Streetsville Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in East Credit includes Credit Meadows Park, Hewick Meadows Park and River Grove Park, and the Credit River, Carolyn Creek and Chappell/Wolfedale diversion run through or along the community. Braeben Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 15 schools.

07.01.1420.t:
Eastmount, Hamilton

Eastmount is a residential neighbourhood on the east-central part of Hamilton Mountain, above the escarpment. This part of Hamilton Mountain was farmland in Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the Mountain in stages, starting with the land north of Concession Street by 1891, and absorbed the last of Barton Township in 1960. A building boom on the Mountain began around 1910, and most of the remaining farmland was built over after the Second World War.

Eastmount is generally bounded by Sherman Access and Mountain Park Avenue to the north, Upper Sherman Avenue to the east, Fennell Avenue to the south and Upper Wentworth Street to the west, and covers approximately 105 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Eastmount.

Green space in Eastmount includes Eastmount Park and Concession / Upper Sherman. Residents are served by one school and the Concession branch of the Hamilton Public Library. Juravinski Cancer Centre and Juravinski Hospital are also located in the community.

01.E02.1320.t:
East End-Danforth, City of Toronto (TRREB district E02)

The area began in the 19th century as the postal village of Coleman, centred at Danforth Avenue and Dawes Road, and a railway station named East Toronto later served it. It was part of the Town of East Toronto, which was annexed to the City of Toronto in 1908. Most of its housing dates from the 1910s to the 1930s, when it grew as a streetcar suburb along Danforth Avenue. The Bloor-Danforth subway replaced the streetcar in 1966.

East End-Danforth is generally bounded by Balfour Avenue to the north, Victoria Park Avenue to the east, Kingston Road to the south and Woodbine Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 259 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and a hydro transformer station (Toronto Main TS). Along or just beyond its edges are St. John's Norway Cemetery & Crematorium. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in East End-Danforth includes East Toronto Athletic Field, Norwood Park and Cassels Avenue Playground. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Main Street branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Woodbine and Main Street subway stations and the Danforth GO Station.

09.02.0090.t:
East Woodbridge, Vaughan

Woodbridge grew from the village of Burwick, laid out by mill builder Rowland Burr after 1837. It was renamed Woodbridge before 1855 and became an incorporated village in 1882. Suburban growth began east of the Humber River in the 1950s, as many families moved out from Toronto. In 1971 the village was amalgamated into the Town of Vaughan, now the City of Vaughan.

East Woodbridge is generally bounded by Rutherford Road to the north, Highway 400 to the east, the Humber River and Highway 7 to the south and the East Humber River to the west, and covers approximately 1,582 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), Highway 407, Hillcrest Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 8% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 400. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in East Woodbridge includes Boyd Conservation Area, Maxey Park and Giovanni Caboto Park, and the East Humber River and the Humber River run through or along the community. The National Golf CLub of Canada is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools.

05.03.0220.t:
Fairview, Mississauga

Fairview lies in the central part of Mississauga, in the former Toronto Township. The township became the Town of Mississauga in 1968 and the City in 1974. The area was farmland until suburban housing was built in the later decades of the 20th century. Specific history for this community was not found.

Fairview is generally bounded by Hurontario Street to the east, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) to the south and Mavis Road to the west, and covers approximately 242 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Fairview includes Dr. Martin L. Dobkin Community Park, City View Park and Fairview Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools, and transit is provided by the Cooksville GO Station.

01.E03.1250.t:
East York, City of Toronto (TRREB district E03)

East York was the eastern part of York Township until residents voted to form their own municipality, and the Township of East York was incorporated on January 1, 1924. Rapid growth followed the opening of the Prince Edward Viaduct in 1918, and most of Old East York was built before the Second World War, with more modest homes added for returning veterans in the late 1940s. The township merged with the Town of Leaside in 1967 to form the Borough of East York, which became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

East York is generally bounded by Cosburn Avenue to the east and the Don River and Pape Avenue to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 234 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the Don Valley Parkway. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision) and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in East York includes Taylor Creek Park, Lower Don Parklands and Cullen Bryant Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Todmorden Room branch of the Toronto Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Former East York Civic Centre.

01.W08.0090.t:
Edenbridge-Humber Valley, City of Toronto (TRREB district W08)

Edenbridge takes its name from the home of developer Robert Home Smith, which was itself named after a village in southern England. The land was laid out as farm lots by 1805 but stayed largely undeveloped in Etobicoke Township. Home Smith's company subdivided the area as the Humber Valley Surveys, with construction from the mid-1930s through the 1960s, and apartments were added to the west in the 1960s. Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Edenbridge-Humber Valley is generally bounded by Eglinton Avenue to the north, the Humber River to the east, Dundas Street to the south and Islington Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 548 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), Lambton Cemetery and St. George’s on-the-Hill Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Edenbridge-Humber Valley includes James Gardens, Buttonwood Park and Humber Valley Park, and Silver Creek and the Humber River run through or along the community. St George's Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Other notable landmarks include Lambton Woods Park and Humbertown Shopping Centre.

04.16.0050.t:
Edgar, Oro-Medonte

Edgar is a rural community in the former Oro Township, which was surveyed around 1820 and incorporated in 1850. From 1952 to 1964 it was the site of a Cold War radar station. Oro Township joined Medonte Township and the Hawkestone Police Village to form Oro-Medonte in 1994.

Edgar is generally bounded by Lauder Road to the north, Old Barrie Road to the east and Oro-Medonte Line 4 to the west, and covers approximately 45 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Edgar United Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Other notable landmarks include Former Edgar Cold War radar station site.

04.15.0030.t:
Edgehill Drive, Barrie

Edgehill Drive is a residential area in west Barrie near Highway 400, named after Edgehill Drive, a local street. The land was originally part of the townships surveyed for settlement after the Lake Simcoe treaties of 1815 and 1818. Barrie grew from a supply depot at the end of the Nine Mile Portage and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a village in 1854, a town in 1871 and a city in 1959.

Edgehill Drive is generally bounded by Edgehill Drive to the north, Ferndale Drive and Ferndale Industrial Drive to the east, Dunlop Street to the south and the Springwater boundary and Miller Drive to the west, and covers approximately 128 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and industrial lands (approximately 10% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Edgehill Drive includes Pringle Park.

01.E08.1190.t:
Eglinton East, City of Toronto (TRREB district E08)

Eglinton East takes its name from Eglinton Avenue East and was historically known as Knob Hill. The land was part of Scarborough Township from 1850. It was built up after the Second World War, with most local schools opening in the 1950s and 1960s. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Eglinton East is generally bounded by Dorset Creek to the north, Bellamy Road to the east, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and Brimley Road to the south and Eglinton Avenue and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 324 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Eglinton East includes Glen Ravine Park, Lord Roberts Woods and Horton Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools, and transit is provided by the Kennedy and Eglinton GO stations. Other notable landmarks include John McCrae Public School.

01.W08.0110.t:
Eringate-Centennial-West Deane, City of Toronto (TRREB district W08)

This area in central Etobicoke was farmland in Etobicoke Township until the mid-20th century. West Deane Park was named by developer Edmund Peachey after his wife, Deane, and much of it was built in the 1960s, while the Vallengrove subdivision was developed in 1961. Centennial Park, which forms the western edge, gives part of the name. Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Eringate-Centennial-West Deane is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Rathburn Road and Martin Grove Road to the east, Renforth Drive to the south and Eglinton Avenue and Etobicoke Creek to the west, and covers approximately 867 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 427, Highway 27 and Richview Memorial Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401 and Toronto Pearson International Airport. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Eringate-Centennial-West Deane includes Centennial Park, West Deane Park and Eringate Park, and Mimico Creek, Etobicoke Creek and Elmcrest Creek run through or along the community. Centennial Park Golf Centre is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools and the Elmbrook Park branch of the Toronto Public Library.

09.02.0040.t:
Elder Mills, Vaughan

The community takes its name from Elder's Mills, one of the historic hamlets of Vaughan Township. The township was settled from the 1790s and incorporated in 1850. The area remained largely rural until suburban housing reached the north part of Woodbridge in the 2000s and 2010s. Since 1971 it has been part of the Town, now City, of Vaughan.

Elder Mills is generally bounded by the Humber River to the north, Robinson Creek to the south and the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) and Highway 27 to the west, and covers approximately 188 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Elder Mills includes McClure Meadows Park, and the Humber River and Robinson Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

07.01.1870.t:
Eleanor, Hamilton

Eleanor is a residential neighbourhood on the southern part of Hamilton Mountain, with Eleanor Park at its centre. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. Most of the housing here is detached homes built from approximately the late 1970s onward, as the city's suburban growth moved south on the Mountain.

Eleanor is generally bounded by Stone Church Road to the north, Upper Gage Avenue to the east, Rymal Road to the south and Upper Sherman Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 82 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Eleanor.

Green space in Eleanor includes Eleanor Park.

07.01.1810.t:
Falkirk, Hamilton

Falkirk is a residential neighbourhood on the West Mountain, near Garth Street and the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. The area was built up mainly as a suburban subdivision from approximately the 1970s to the 1990s, when the Mountain saw the city's fastest growth in new housing.

Falkirk is generally bounded by Stone Church Road to the north, Garth Street to the east and Rymal Road to the south, and covers approximately 132 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor lie along or just beyond its edges. The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 2.8 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Falkirk includes William Schwenger Park and Meadowbank Drive Parkette. Residents are served by one school.

01.W10.0050.t:
Elms-Old Rexdale, City of Toronto (TRREB district W10)

The Elms takes its name from The Elms golf course, named for the American elm trees once common in the area. The original Rexdale section was built in the 1950s by developer Rex Heslop on former farmland in Etobicoke Township, mostly as bungalows and semi-detached houses. Rexdale Plaza opened nearby in the late 1950s. The area became part of the amalgamated City of Toronto in 1998.

Elms-Old Rexdale is generally bounded by the West Humber River to the north, the Humber River to the east, Highway 401 to the south and Islington Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 299 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Elms-Old Rexdale includes Pine Point Park, West Humber Parkland and Summerlea Park, and the Humber River and Berry Creek run through or along the community. Humber Valley Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools. Other notable landmarks include Northern Elms Public Library.

04.09.0010.t:
Elmvale, Springwater

Elmvale lies near the site of Ossossane, a major Wendat settlement. The village was earlier known as Four Corners, Elm Flats and Saurin, and the name Elmvale came into use with its post office in 1859. It grew as a farm service village in Flos Township and was later incorporated as a village. On January 1, 1994 it became part of the Township of Springwater, formed from Flos and Vespra townships, the villages of Elmvale and Hillsdale, and part of Medonte.

The boundary of Elmvale follows local streets, lot lines and natural features rather than major roads, and the community covers approximately 292 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Elmvale Presbyterian Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Elmvale includes Homer Barrett Park, Bishop Park and Robinson Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Elmvale branch of the Springwater Public Library.

01.C04.0620.t:
Englemount-Lawrence, City of Toronto (TRREB district C04)

The area lies along Lawrence Avenue West and Bathurst Street. It was part of York Township and then North York, which joined the City of Toronto in 1998. Much of the area, including Lawrence Manor, was developed in the 1940s and 1950s, and Lawrence Plaza opened in 1953. Apartment buildings were later added along Bathurst Street and Lawrence Avenue.

Englemount-Lawrence is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Bathurst Street to the east, Briar Hill Avenue to the south and Allen Road to the west, and covers approximately 340 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Allen Road and Highway 401 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Englemount-Lawrence includes Baycrest Park, Viewmount Park and Former Baycrest Public School grounds. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Barbara Frum branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Glencairn, Lawrence West and Yorkdale subway stations. Baycrest Health Sciences is also located in the community.

05.03.0080.t:
Erin Mills, Mississauga

Erin Mills was named by E. P. Taylor's Don Mills Development Corporation, which bought the land in the 1950s; "Erin" refers to nearby Erindale and "Mills" to Don Mills or the mills on the Credit River. Cadillac Fairview took over the project in 1968 and developed it as a planned "new town" on more than 7,000 acres of farmland. Building began in the early 1970s, starting with the area between Dundas Street and Burnhamthorpe Road.

Erin Mills is generally bounded by Highway 403 to the north, the Credit River to the east, Dunwin Drive and Dundas Street to the south and Ridgeway Drive and Unity Drive to the west, and covers approximately 1,314 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include St. Peter's Anglican Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 403. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Erin Mills includes Tom Chater Memorial Park, Riverwood Park and South Common Park, and Glen Erin Brook, Sawmill Creek and Mullet Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 13 schools and the South Common branch of the Mississauga Library. Shopping is available at South Common Centre. University of Toronto Mississauga is also located in the community.

05.03.0180.t:
Erindale, Mississauga

Erindale was first known as Credit Village, then Springfield, and was later named after Erin, Ireland, the birthplace of its first rector, Rev. James Magrath. It grew in the early 1800s as a mill village and stagecoach stop on Dundas Street at the Credit River. A hydroelectric dam and lake operated from the early 1900s, and the site later became Erindale Park. Suburban growth followed from the 1960s, and the area became part of Mississauga in 1968.

Erindale is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) to the north, Mavis Road to the east and the Credit River to the west, and covers approximately 810 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), Highway 403, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and St. Peter's Anglican Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Erindale includes Riverwood Park, Erindale Park and Huron Park, and the Credit River and Wolfedale Creek run through or along the community. Mississaugua Golf & Country Club and Credit Valley Golf & Country Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 11 schools and the The Woodlands branch of the Mississauga Library. Shopping is available at Westdale Mall. Other notable landmarks include University of Toronto Mississauga.

05.02.0060.t:
Fletcher's Creek Village, Brampton

Fletcher's Creek Village is a residential area in west Brampton, close to downtown and Highway 410, with a railway line along its south side. The Fletcher family settled 100 acres of farmland in Chinguacousy Township in 1823 and farmed it for 117 years, until 1940. William Fletcher inherited the farm in 1870 and his son John took it over in 1913. Most homes were built in the late 1990s and early 2000s.

Fletcher's Creek Village is generally bounded by Bovaird Drive to the north, McLaughlin Road to the east, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and Williams Parkway to the south and Chinguacousy Road to the west, and covers approximately 178 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (Mount Pleasant TS) and Brampton Funeral Home & Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Fletcher's Creek Village includes Homestead Park, Whitewash Parkette and Pickard Park, and Fletchers Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

01.W08.0130.t:
Etobicoke West Mall, City of Toronto (TRREB district W08)

The area, also known as Eatonville, takes that name from Eatonville School, built on land donated by the Eaton family. In the late 19th century much of the land was a farm owned by Peter Shaver, which Eaton's bought in the 1890s to supply its stores until the 1950s. The farm was then subdivided, with most homes east of Highway 427 built in the 1950s and most homes to the west in the 1960s and 1970s. Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Etobicoke West Mall is generally bounded by Rathburn Road to the north, Highway 427 to the east and Renforth Drive to the south, and covers approximately 180 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 427. The community is also close to Toronto Pearson International Airport, approximately 2.2 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Etobicoke West Mall includes Broadacres Park, Dennis Flynn Park and West Mall Outdoor Artifical Ice Rink. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

07.01.1160.t:
Normanhurst, Hamilton

Normanhurst is a mainly residential neighbourhood in Hamilton's east end, just south of the industrial waterfront. It sits on land of the former Barton Township that was brought into Hamilton as the city grew east. Most of its homes were built before 1960, with some added between 1961 and 1980. Local shops are along Parkdale Avenue North and Barton Street East.

Normanhurst is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) to the north, Parkdale Avenue to the east, Queenston Road to the south and Strathearne Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 114 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 12% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Normanhurst includes Mahony Park and Parkdale Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

10.07.0200.t:
Farewell, Oshawa

Farewell takes its name from the Farewell family. Moody Farewell settled in approximately 1801 near King Street East and Harmony Road, an area once known as Farewell's Corners and later the Village of Harmony. Farewell Street runs through former Farewell property, and Farewell Creek is also named after the family. The area became part of the City of Oshawa as the city expanded east.

Farewell is generally bounded by Bloor Street and Highway 401 to the north, Farewell Creek to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Simcoe Street and Wentworth Street to the west, and covers approximately 372 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), a wastewater treatment plant, a cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 46% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Farewell includes Ed Broadbent Waterfront Park, Wellington Park and Veterans Tot Lot, and Harmony Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. Residents are served by one school.

07.01.1590.t:
Fessenden, Hamilton

The neighbourhood is named after Clementina Trenholme Fessenden (1844 to 1918), an author and social organizer who proposed Empire Day and was the first curator of Dundurn Castle. She was the mother of radio pioneer Reginald Fessenden, and the nearby Trenholme neighbourhood is also named after her. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960.

Fessenden is generally bounded by Mohawk Road to the north, Upper Paradise Road to the east, the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the south and a hydro corridor to the west, and covers approximately 89 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor and the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Fessenden includes Fonthill Park and Lions Gate Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

10.06.0030.t:
Lynde Creek, Whitby

Lynde Creek is a residential area in the west part of Whitby, named after the creek that crosses it. Whitby Township was surveyed in 1792, and the Town of Whitby was incorporated in 1855. The town and township merged in 1968. Suburban housing in the area was built in the decades after that merger.

Lynde Creek is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) and Barkerville Drive to the north, Cochrane Street to the east and Annes Street and Highway 401 to the south, and covers approximately 429 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision), the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lynde Creek includes D'Hillier Park, Jeffery Park and Otter Creek Park, and Otter Creek and Lynde Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

05.02.0050.t:
Fletcher's Meadow, Brampton

Fletcher's Meadow is in northwest Brampton, generally between McLaughlin Road and Creditview Road, north of Bovaird Drive. It is named after the farm of Robert and Elizabeth Fletcher, who settled 100 acres in Chinguacousy Township in 1823. Farming continued until the 1970s, and most of the neighbourhood was built during the late 1990s and early 2000s.

Fletcher's Meadow is generally bounded by Wanless Drive to the north, McLaughlin Road to the east, Bovaird Drive and the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the south and Creditview Road to the west, and covers approximately 930 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (Mount Pleasant TS) and Brampton Funeral Home & Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and Alloa Methodist Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Fletcher's Meadow includes Chinguacousy Sandalwood Community Park, Hartley Channel and Worthington Park. Residents are served by approximately 14 schools. Other notable landmarks include Cassie Campbell Community Centre.

05.02.0080.t:
Fletcher's West, Brampton

Fletcher's West is a residential area in west Brampton, west of the Fletcher's Creek neighbourhoods. The Fletcher family settled 100 acres of farmland in Chinguacousy Township in 1823 and farmed it for 117 years, until 1940. The land was farmland in Chinguacousy Township until 1974, when the township was merged with Toronto Gore Township and the Town of Brampton to form the City of Brampton. The area was built up with suburban housing from the late 20th century.

Fletcher's West is generally bounded by Queen Street to the north, McLaughlin Road to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Chinguacousy Road to the west, and covers approximately 422 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Roy McMurtry Youth Centre and Ontario Correctional Institute. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, a hydro transformer station (Jim Yarrow TS) and a hydro transformer station (J). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Fletcher's West includes Flower City Community Campus, Sheridan Woodlands Park and Drinkwater Community Park. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools.

01.C04.0710.t:
Forest Hill North, City of Toronto (TRREB district C04)

Forest Hill was named after the summer home of John Wickson. The Village of Forest Hill was incorporated in 1923 and joined the City of Toronto in 1967. The northern part, the 'Upper Village', was first occupied by the Belt Line Railway and industry. Most of its houses were built in the 1940s and 1950s.

Forest Hill North is generally bounded by Briar Hill Avenue to the north, Latimer Avenue to the east, Eglinton Avenue to the south and Marlee Avenue and Allen Road to the west, and covers approximately 153 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Allen Road and The Adath Israel Roselawn Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Forest Hill North includes Memorial Park - North York, Nicol MacNicol Parkette and Shallmar Parkette. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Forest Hill branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Cedarvale subway station and the Forest Hill and Chaplin LRT stations. Other notable landmarks include Beltline Trail.

04.18.0020.t:
Fesserton, Severn

Fesserton is a small hamlet in the western part of the Township of Severn, near Coldwater. It developed in the 19th century as a rural settlement in an area shaped by lumbering and farming. The Township of Severn was formed on January 1, 1994 from the Village of Coldwater, the townships of Matchedash and Orillia, and parts of Medonte and Tay.

Fesserton is generally bounded by Georgian Bay and Highway 400 to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 301 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 400 and a quarry or aggregate pit. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The community includes or fronts onto Georgian Bay.

01.C11.0800.t:
Flemingdon Park, City of Toronto (TRREB district C11)

The area is named after former Toronto mayor Robert John Fleming and his family, who owned Donlands Farm from 1922 until the late 1950s. It was part of York Township and then North York. Planning for a large apartment community began in 1958, the first apartments were occupied in 1961, and the community was completed in the early 1970s. North York became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Flemingdon Park is generally bounded by Eglinton Avenue to the north, the Don River East Branch and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision) to the east and the Don River West Branch to the west, and covers approximately 251 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the Don Valley Parkway. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision) and the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Flemingdon Park includes E. T. Seton Park, Flemingdon Park and Linkwood Lane Park, and the Don River East Branch runs through or along the community. Flemingdon Park Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Flemingdon Park branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Sunnybrook Park, Wynford, Don Valley and Aga Khan Park & Museum LRT stations. Other notable landmarks include Ontario Science Centre site (1969, closed 2024).

05.02.0090.t:
Fletcher's Creek South, Brampton

Fletcher's Creek South is a residential area in west Brampton named after Fletcher's Creek. The Fletcher family settled 100 acres of farmland in Chinguacousy Township in 1823 and farmed it for 117 years, until 1940. The land was farmland in Chinguacousy Township, which was merged into Brampton in 1974. The area was built up with suburban housing in the later 20th century.

Fletcher's Creek South is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Kennedy Road to the east, Highway 407 to the south and Mavis Road to the west, and covers approximately 621 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407, a hydro transformer station (Jim Yarrow TS) and Meadowvale Cemetery & Crematorium. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Fletcher's Creek South includes Fletcher's Green Community Park, County Court Park and Turtlecreek Park, and Fletchers Creek and Etobicoke Creek run through or along the community. Peel Village Golf Club and Brampton Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the South Fletcher's branch of the Brampton Library. Sheridan College - Davis Campus is also located in the community.

01.C03.0740.t:
Forest Hill South, City of Toronto (TRREB district C03)

Forest Hill was named after the summer home of John Wickson. The Village of Forest Hill was incorporated in 1923 and joined the City of Toronto in 1967. The southern part, the 'Lower Village', was built mainly in the 1920s and 1930s under bylaws that required architect-designed homes. It is known for large brick and stone houses.

Forest Hill South is generally bounded by Eglinton Avenue and Elmsthorpe Avenue to the north, Oriole Parkway to the east, Lonsdale Road and St. Clair Avenue to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 254 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Forest Hill South.

Green space in Forest Hill South includes Cedarvale Park, Forest Hill Road Park and Suydam Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools, and transit is provided by the St. Clair West subway station and the Forest Hill and Chaplin LRT stations. Other notable landmarks include Upper Canada College and Bishop Strachan School.

09.10.0010.t:
Fox Island, Georgina Islands

Fox Island is a small island in southern Lake Simcoe. In 1830 the government set aside Georgina, Snake and Fox islands as a reserve for the Chippewas of Lakes Huron and Simcoe. The island is now part of the reserve lands of the Chippewas of Georgina Island First Nation and has no roads.

Fox Island is generally bounded by Lake Simcoe to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 52 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Fox Island.

The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe.

07.01.0070.t:
Freelton, Hamilton

Freelton is named after Patrick Freel, an Irish immigrant who ran a tavern and hotel at the crossroads of the present Highway 6 and Brock Road. The village was founded in 1856, and Freel named its streets after members of his family. It was a village in West Flamborough Township, became part of the Town of Flamborough in 1974, and joined the City of Hamilton in 2001. In recent decades it has grown as a rural residential community.

Freelton is generally bounded by Highway 6 to the north and Regional Road 97 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 177 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 6 and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by the Freelton branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

06.02.0080.t:
Freeman, Burlington

Freeman is named after Joshua Freeman Sr., who settled in 1818 near today's Brant Street and Plains Road. The settlement grew as Freeman's Corners and then the Village of Freeman, with market gardens and a post office. A railway junction station, known locally as Freeman Station, brought industry from the 1850s. The Freeman postmark ended in 1952, and by the 1960s development had surrounded the old village.

Freeman is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and Fairview Street to the east and Highway 403 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 279 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the CN rail line (Metrolinx Oakville Subdivision), the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), the CN rail line (CN Oakville Subdivision), the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW), Highway 403 and industrial lands (approximately 19% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transformer station (Burlington Transformer Station). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Freeman includes Leighland Park. Transit is provided by the Burlington GO Station.

07.01.0250.t:
Fruitland, Hamilton

Fruitland takes its name from the fertile soil that supported the orchards and fruit farms of the area. It lies in the former Saltfleet Township, between Millen Road and Glover Road in the east end of Hamilton. Saltfleet became part of the Town (later City) of Stoney Creek in 1974, and Stoney Creek joined the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Fruitland is generally bounded by Barton Street and the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision) to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,034 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW), Mountainview Gardens Cemetery and Grimsby "The Fifty" Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision) and Fruitland Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Fruitland includes Winona Conservation Area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Stoney Creek branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

13.01.0010.t:
Garden Hill, Port Hope

Garden Hill is a rural hamlet in the north part of the Municipality of Port Hope. It lay in the former Hope Township, established in the early 1790s and named after Colonel Henry Hope, and was settled for farming in the 19th century. In 2001 Hope Township merged with the Town of Port Hope to form the present municipality.

Garden Hill is generally bounded by a hydro corridor and Mill Street to the north, County Road 10 to the east and Ganaraska Road to the west, and covers approximately 212 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Garden Hill includes Garden Hill Conservation Area and Alex Carruthers Memorial Park, and the North Ganaraska River runs through or along the community.

07.01.1120.t:
Gibson, Hamilton

The neighbourhood is named after Sir John Morison Gibson (1842 to 1929), a Hamiltonian who served as Lieutenant Governor of Ontario from 1908 to 1914. It is one of the older neighbourhoods of Hamilton's lower city, east of downtown. Much of its housing dates from the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when the city's east end grew with its factories.

Gibson is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) to the north, Sherman Avenue to the east, Main Street to the south and Wentworth Street to the west, and covers approximately 114 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a hydro transformer station (Stirton Transformer Station) and industrial lands (approximately 10% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Gibson includes Woodlands Park, Powell Park and Stirton Tot-Lot. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Barton branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

05.03.0190.t:
Gateway, Mississauga

Gateway is mainly a business and industrial area in the former Toronto Township. The township became the Town of Mississauga in 1968 and the City in 1974. The area was developed for employment uses in the later decades of the 20th century. Specific history for this community was not found.

Gateway is generally bounded by Fletchers Creek and a hydro corridor to the north, Highway 410 to the east, Matheson Boulevard to the south and Mavis Road to the west, and covers approximately 1,802 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 401, Highway 410, Britannia Cemetery, Derry West Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 55% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 403 and a hydro transformer station (Hurontario SS). The community is also close to Toronto Pearson International Airport, approximately 2.4 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Gateway includes Danville Park, Hershey Centre Sportszone North and Saigon Park, and Fletchers Creek runs through or along the community. Derrydale Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools, and transit is provided by the Courtneypark LRT station. Other notable landmarks include Paramount Fine Foods Centre.

04.15.0140.t:
Georgian Drive, Barrie

Georgian Drive is in northeast Barrie and takes its name from Georgian Drive, home to Georgian College. The college opened in 1967, and the Royal Victoria Regional Health Centre moved to its current Georgian Drive site in 1997. Residential development in the area grew around these two institutions from the late 20th century onward.

Georgian Drive is generally bounded by Highway 400 and the Springwater boundary to the north, Penetanguishene Road to the east, Hickling Trail to the south and Georgian Drive to the west, and covers approximately 159 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 400 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Georgian Drive includes Georgian Fields, Cheltenham Park and Dunsmore Park. Royal Victoria Regional Health Centre and Georgian College are also located in the community.

09.10.0030.t:
Georgina Island, Georgina Islands

Georgina Island, in southern Lake Simcoe, is home to the Chippewas of Georgina Island First Nation, an Ojibwa band. The island was set aside as a reserve in 1830, together with Snake and Fox islands. Before the Trent-Severn Waterway raised lake levels, residents could cross to the mainland at Virginia Beach on foot. Access is now by ferry in summer and by airboat or ice road in winter.

Georgina Island is generally bounded by Lake Simcoe to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 2,326 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe.

09.03.0100.t:
German Mills, Markham

German Mills is named for the German settlers that William Berczy brought to Markham Township in 1794, who built a sawmill and grist mill on the Don River. The mill complex declined within approximately six years, and the settlement later became a ghost town. Today the area is mainly residential, with many single-family homes built in the 1970s and 1980s.

German Mills is generally bounded by the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the north, Highway 404 to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and German Mills Creek to the west, and covers approximately 190 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (York Subdivision), Highway 404 and Leslie Pumping Station lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in German Mills includes German Mills Meadow and Natural Habitat, Simonston Park and Bishops Cross Park, and German Mills Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools. Shopping is available at The Shops on Steeles and 404.

07.01.1490.t:
Gershome, Hamilton

Gershome is a residential neighbourhood in the east end of the former City of Hamilton. The area was farmland in the old townships east of Hamilton before it was annexed by the City of Hamilton in the twentieth century. Barton Township was fully absorbed by the city in 1960. The neighbourhood was built up mainly as a post-war suburb.

Gershome is generally bounded by King Street to the north, Centennial Parkway to the east, Glover Mountain Road to the south and Marcella Crescent to the west, and covers approximately 110 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision) and Stoney Creek Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Gershome is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

07.01.1600.t:
Gilbert, Hamilton

Gilbert is a residential neighbourhood in the former City of Hamilton. The land was farmland in the old townships around the city before it was annexed and built up as suburban housing, mainly from approximately the 1970s.

Gilbert is generally bounded by Mohawk Road to the north, Garth Street to the east, the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the south and Upper Paradise Road to the west, and covers approximately 74 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway and St. Peter's Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Gilbert includes William McCulloch Park.

04.11.0010.t:
Glencairn, Adjala-Tosorontio

Glencairn is a small rural hamlet in the former Tosorontio Township. Tosorontio is a Huron word meaning "Beautiful Mountain", and settlement of the area began in the 19th century. Adjala Township was incorporated in 1850 and Tosorontio Township in 1855; the two merged to form the Township of Adjala-Tosorontio on January 1, 1994.

Glencairn is generally bounded by the Mad River to the north and Webster Road and Walker's Creek to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 86 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Glencairn Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Glencairn includes Glencairn Conservation Area, and Walker's Creek runs through or along the community.

05.02.0400.t:
Gore Industrial South, Brampton

Gore Industrial South is an employment area in southeast Brampton, in the former Toronto Gore Township. Toronto Gore was separated from Chinguacousy Township in 1819, and its name refers to a wedge-shaped tract of land. The remainder of the township was merged into the City of Brampton in 1974. Industrial and business development in the area grew mainly from the later 20th century.

Gore Industrial South is generally bounded by Auction Lane to the north, Intermodal Drive to the east, Highway 407 and a hydro corridor to the south and Airport Road to the west, and covers approximately 406 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, CN Brampton Intermodal Terminal, a hydro transformer station (Goreway TS), Goreway Power Station and industrial lands (approximately 60% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Mimico Creek runs through or along the community.

01.W05.0240.t:
Glenfield-Jane Heights, City of Toronto (TRREB district W05)

Glenfield-Jane Heights is the southern half of the Jane and Finch area, between Finch Avenue and Sheppard Avenue. The area was farmland in York Township, later North York, until it was developed in the 1960s as a planned suburb with a mix of houses and high-rise apartments. The population of the wider Jane and Finch area grew from approximately 1,300 in 1961 to 33,000 in 1971. North York was amalgamated into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Glenfield-Jane Heights is generally bounded by Finch Avenue to the north, Black Creek to the east, Jane Street to the south and Highway 400 and Sheppard Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 518 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 10% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 400. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Glenfield-Jane Heights includes Downsview Dells Park, Derrydowns Park and Spenvalley Park, and Black Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 11 schools, the Jane/Sheppard branch of the Toronto Public Library and the York Woods branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Norfinch Oakdale, Jane and Finch, Driftwood and Tobermory LRT stations. Shopping is available at Jane-Finch Mall. Other notable landmarks include Line 6 Finch West.

07.01.1330.t:
Glenview, Hamilton

Glenview is a residential neighbourhood in the east end of the lower city, near the Red Hill Valley. The area was farmland in the old townships east of Hamilton before it was annexed by the City of Hamilton in the twentieth century. Barton Township was fully absorbed by the city in 1960.

Glenview is generally bounded by Queenston Road to the north, the Red Hill Valley Parkway to the east, Lawrence Road to the south and Cochrane Road to the west, and covers approximately 102 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Red Hill Valley Parkway. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor and Bartonville Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Glenview includes Red Hill Bowl, and Redhill Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.07.0020.t:
Glenway Estates, Newmarket

Glenway Estates is a residential neighbourhood in west Newmarket, west of Yonge Street between Davis Drive and Mulock Drive. It takes its name from the former Glenway Country Club, a private golf club in the area. Its homes are mainly detached houses from the 1980s. The golf club closed before the 2012 season and its lands have since been redeveloped for housing.

Glenway Estates is generally bounded by Davis Drive to the north, Yonge Street to the east, McCaffrey Road to the south and Bathurst Street and Keith Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 252 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are Newmarket Well #2 and Newmarket Well #1. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Glenway Estates includes Joe Perschini Park, Kirby Crescent Park and McGregor Farm Park. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Upper Canada Mall (at the edge, Yonge Street and Davis Drive).

05.02.0380.t:
Gore Industrial North, Brampton

Gore Industrial North is an employment area in east Brampton, in the former Toronto Gore Township. Toronto Gore was separated from Chinguacousy Township in 1819, and its name refers to a wedge-shaped tract of land. The remainder of the township was merged into the City of Brampton in 1974. Industrial and business development in the area grew mainly from the later 20th century.

Gore Industrial North is generally bounded by Humberwest Parkway to the east and Airport Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 243 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 70% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Gore Industrial North includes Bottomwood Park.

05.02.0430.t:
Goreway Drive Corridor, Brampton

The Goreway Drive Corridor follows Goreway Drive in east Brampton, through land that was part of Toronto Gore Township. Toronto Gore was formed in 1819 and was mainly farmland with small hamlets such as Castlemore and Claireville. The remainder of the township was merged into the City of Brampton in 1974. The corridor was built up with housing and business uses mainly from the later 20th century onward.

Goreway Drive Corridor is generally bounded by Humberwest Parkway and Goreway Drive to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 63 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transformer station lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Goreway Drive Corridor is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

09.07.0080.t:
Gorham-College Manor, Newmarket

Gorham-College Manor is a residential neighbourhood east of downtown Newmarket, named after Gorham Street and College Manor Drive. It includes some century homes along with later housing. Newmarket was settled by Quakers between 1801 and 1803 and was incorporated as a town in 1880.

Gorham-College Manor is generally bounded by Davis Drive to the north, Leslie Street to the east, Mulock Drive to the south and Prospect Street and Bayview Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 409 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Gorham-College Manor includes Fairgrounds Park, College Manor Park and Sunnyhill Park, and Bogart Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools. Southlake Regional Health Centre is also located in the community.

07.01.1720.t:
Gourley, Hamilton

The neighbourhood takes its name from Colonel William Gourlay (1794 to 1867), a local farmer and part-time soldier who served during the Rebellion of 1837; the neighbourhood name is spelled with an "e". It lies on the West Mountain, west of Garth Street and north of Stone Church Road West. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. Gourley Park became city land in 1975.

Gourley is generally bounded by the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the north, West 5th Street to the east, Stone Church Road to the south and Garth Street to the west, and covers approximately 111 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Gourley includes Gourley Park. Residents are served by one school.

03.04.0020.t:
Grand Valley, East Luther Grand Valley

Grand Valley began as a hamlet called Luther Village, with the first log house built in 1855. Railway access arrived in 1871, and the community was renamed Grand Valley in 1886. It was incorporated as the Village of Grand Valley in 1897. In 1995 it merged with East Luther Township, and the combined municipality was renamed the Town of Grand Valley in 2012.

Grand Valley is generally bounded by Luther Road to the north, the Grand River to the east, Emma Street to the south and Leeson Street to the west, and covers approximately 90 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Grand Valley Union (cemetery). Along or just beyond its edges are Saint Alban's Anglican Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Grand River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by the Grand Valley Public Library.

09.03.0290.t:
Greensborough, Markham

Greensborough was mostly farmland north of Markham Village and next to the historic hamlet of Mount Joy. Most development began after Donald Cousens Parkway was completed in 2005, following a Smart Growth plan with mixed housing types, commercial space and parkland. Parts of the north end were still being built in 2025.

Greensborough is generally bounded by Major MacKenzie Drive to the north, Ninth Line to the east, 16th Avenue to the south and Markham Road to the west, and covers approximately 413 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Greensborough includes Mount Joy Park, Swan Lake Park and Greensborough Pond, and Little Rouge Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Swan Lake. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools, and transit is provided by the Mount Joy GO Station.

07.01.0090.t:
Greensville, Hamilton

Greensville is a village in the former West Flamborough Township, on Spencer Creek above the Niagara Escarpment. In the nineteenth century, mills grew up along the creek in the Greensville and Bullock's Corners area; William Bullock built a grist and sawmill there in 1850, and the Clark brothers ran a blanket factory on the site from 1866 until 1938. West Flamborough became part of the Town of Flamborough in 1974, which joined the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Greensville is generally bounded by Cramer Road to the north and the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision) to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 682 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision) and a quarry or aggregate pit. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Greensville includes Spencer Gorge Conservation Area and Bullock's Corners Park, and Spencer Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Greensville Branch.

01.E01.1370.t:
Greenwood-Coxwell, City of Toronto (TRREB district E01)

Greenwood-Coxwell takes its name from Greenwood Avenue and Coxwell Avenue, its western and eastern limits. The area lies east of Riverdale and Leslieville in the former City of Toronto. Greenwood Avenue was the city limit after the 1884 annexation, and the land to the east was annexed in 1909. Most of its housing is early 20th century semi-detached and detached homes, and Gerrard Street East is home to the Gerrard India Bazaar.

Greenwood-Coxwell is generally bounded by Greenwood Avenue and Danforth Avenue to the north, Coxwell Avenue to the east and Eastern Avenue and Queen Street to the south, and covers approximately 167 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are TTC Greenwood Yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Greenwood-Coxwell includes Monarch Park, Felstead Park and Jonathan Ashbridge Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Gerrard/Ashdale branch of the Toronto Public Library.

06.02.0020.t:
Grindstone, Burlington

Grindstone is in the Aldershot area of west Burlington and is named after Grindstone Creek, which flows to Burlington Bay. The Grindstone Creek watershed was an early fruit-growing area, and the first peaches grown in Canada were cultivated there. Aldershot was part of East Flamborough Township until Burlington annexed it in 1958. It was a leading fruit-growing area, and by the 1960s most farms had been sold for housing.

Grindstone is generally bounded by the Hamilton boundary to the east, Highway 403 to the south and Highway 6 to the west, and covers approximately 1,509 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision), a quarry or aggregate pit, Gate of Heaven Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 3% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), Highway 403, Highway 6, a hydro transformer station (Burlington Transformer Station) and Beth Jacob Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Grindstone includes Bayview Park and Kerncliff Park, and Grindstone Creek runs through or along the community. Wedgewood Golf Centre is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

01.E08.1170.t:
Guildwood, City of Toronto (TRREB district E08)

Guildwood takes its name from the Guild Inn, the arts colony and inn run by Rosa and Spencer Clark, which opened in 1914 as a private residence. After Metropolitan Toronto was formed, the Clarks sold approximately 450 acres, which became the Guildwood Village subdivision. Development began in 1957 with winding roads, cul-de-sacs and underground utilities. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Guildwood is generally bounded by the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) to the north, Lake Ontario to the east and Scarborough Golf Club Road to the west, and covers approximately 375 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Washington Methodist Church Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Guildwood includes Guild Park and Gardens, South Marine Park and East Point Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Guildwood branch of the Toronto Public Library.

07.01.1700.t:
Gurnett, Hamilton

Gurnett is a residential neighbourhood on Hamilton Mountain. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. It was built up as suburban housing in the second half of the twentieth century.

Gurnett is generally bounded by the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the north, Upper Paradise Road to the east, Stone Church Road to the south and a hydro corridor to the west, and covers approximately 98 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor and the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Gurnett includes Shawinigan Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

04.16.0070.t:
Guthrie, Oro-Medonte

Guthrie is a rural community in the former Oro Township, which was surveyed around 1820 along the road to Penetanguishene. The area was settled for farming in the 19th century. The townships of Oro and Medonte were incorporated in 1850 and were amalgamated, with the Hawkestone Police Village, to form the Township of Oro-Medonte on January 1, 1994.

Guthrie is generally bounded by Melville Court to the north, Oro-Medonte Line 5 Overpass to the east and Highway 11 to the west, and covers approximately 65 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 11 and Guthrie United Church & Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Midhurst 4. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school.

09.04.0100.t:
Harding, Richmond Hill

Harding lies between Yonge Street and Bayview Avenue, south of Major Mackenzie Drive. It is named after William Harding, who acquired land here in 1875. From the 1910s to the 1930s the area was home to large rose-growing greenhouses, part of Richmond Hill's history as a centre of the rose industry. Most of the housing was built in the 1970s.

Harding is generally bounded by Major MacKenzie Drive to the north, Bayview Avenue to the east, Weldrick Road to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 161 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Harding includes Harding Park, Lennox Park and Glenbrae Park. Residents are served by one school.

05.01.0040.t:
Inglewood, Caledon

Inglewood is a village on the Credit River in west Caledon. It grew as a railway junction after the Hamilton and North-Western and Credit Valley railways arrived in 1877 and 1879. It was earlier known as Sligo South and Riverdale, and the name Inglewood, after a forest in Cumberland, England, became official in 1886. Rail service ended by 1970, and the old lines are now recreational trails.

Inglewood is generally bounded by McLaughlin Road and North Riverdale Drive to the north and Olde Baseline Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 175 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 10 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Inglewood includes Inglewood Park. Other notable landmarks include Caledon Trailway.

07.01.1000.t:
Hamilton Beach, Hamilton

Hamilton Beach lies on the sand bar that separates Hamilton Harbour from Lake Ontario. The Burlington Canal was cut through the bar in 1832, a beach train began running in 1877, and an amusement park operated there from 1903 to 1978. The strip was run by a provincially appointed Beach Commission from 1907 until 1957, when Hamilton annexed the part south of the canal. Many of the homes began as summer cottages and were later converted to year-round use.

Hamilton Beach is generally bounded by a hydro corridor and Lake Ontario to the north and Eastport Drive to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 194 hectares.
