Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and industrial lands (approximately 21% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Hamilton Beach includes Jimmy Lomax Park, Kinsmen Playground and Dieppe Veterans Memorial Park. Ontario Correctional Services College is also located in the community.

07.01.1560.t:
Hampton Heights, Hamilton

Hampton Heights is a residential neighbourhood on the east part of Hamilton Mountain. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. It was built up mainly as post-war suburban housing.

Hampton Heights is generally bounded by Fennell Avenue to the north, Upper Ottawa Street to the east, Mohawk Road to the south and Upper Gage Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 86 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Hampton Heights.

Green space in Hampton Heights includes Ferwood Park and Hampton Park.

04.16.0110.t:
Hawkestone, Oro-Medonte

Hawkestone began in the 1830s as Hodges' Landing, a settler landing on Lake Simcoe established by Richard Hodges. It was renamed Hawkestone in 1856 after a new wharf was built. The railway arrived in 1871, and Hawkestone was incorporated as a police village in 1922. It became part of the Township of Oro-Medonte in 1994.

Hawkestone is generally bounded by Hawkestone Creek and Highway 11 to the north, Lake Simcoe to the south and Oro-Medonte Rail Trail to the west, and covers approximately 209 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 11 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Hawkestone Creek runs through or along the community.

09.04.0170.t:
Headford Business Park, Richmond Hill

Headford was a postal village established in 1856 near Leslie Street and Major Mackenzie Drive. It declined by the early 20th century. The area is now mainly a business park bounded by Major Mackenzie Drive, Leslie Street, Highway 404 and 16th Avenue, developed after the lands became part of Richmond Hill in 1971.

Headford Business Park is generally bounded by Major MacKenzie Drive to the north, Highway 404 to the east, 16th Avenue to the south and Leslie Street to the west, and covers approximately 198 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 28% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 404. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Rouge River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

06.02.0100.t:
Headon, Burlington

Headon is in north Burlington, below the Niagara Escarpment. It is named after Thomas Headon, who set up a homestead in this heavily forested area in the 1840s. The area was part of Nelson Township until Burlington annexed it in 1958. The present Headon Forest neighbourhood was developed in the 1980s.

Headon is generally bounded by Highway 407 and Dundas Street to the north, Walkers Line to the east, Upper Middle Road to the south and Guelph Line to the west, and covers approximately 383 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and St. Paul’s Presbyterian Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Headon includes Ireland Park, Pinemeadow Park and Newport Park, and Tuck Creek and Shoreacres Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. Other notable landmarks include M.M. Robinson High School and Notre Dame Catholic Secondary School.

05.02.0180.t:
Heart Lake, Brampton

Heart Lake takes its name from the heart-shaped kettle lake at the centre of Heart Lake Conservation Area. The lake, then called Snell's Lake, was chosen in 1878 as a water source for the Town of Brampton, and the conservation area opened in 1957. The first housing, the master-planned Villages of Heart Lake near Kennedy Road and Sandalwood Parkway, was built in the 1970s, with later phases in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Heart Lake became part of the City of Brampton in 1974.

Heart Lake is generally bounded by Mayfield Road and Conservation Drive to the north and Heart Lake Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 177 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Heart Lake.

Green space in Heart Lake includes Heart Lake Conservation Area. The community includes or fronts onto Heart Lake.

05.02.0190.t:
Heart Lake East, Brampton

Heart Lake East is the eastern part of the Heart Lake area of north Brampton. The area takes its name from the heart-shaped kettle lake in Heart Lake Conservation Area, which opened in 1957. Heart Lake became part of the City of Brampton in 1974. Housing was first built in the 1970s, with further phases in the late 1990s and early 2000s.

Heart Lake East is generally bounded by Conservation Drive to the north, Heart Lake Road to the east, Bovaird Drive to the south and Kennedy Road to the west, and covers approximately 328 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 410 and a cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Heart Lake East includes White Spruce Park, Richvale Park and Donnelly East Park. Turnberry Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools.

05.02.0140.t:
Snelgrove, Brampton

Snelgrove is a former hamlet centred on Hurontario Street and Mayfield Road at the north edge of Brampton. It was first called Edmonton and was renamed in the 1880s, when the Canadian Pacific Railway wanted to avoid confusion with Edmonton, Alberta. The name is linked to the Snell family, who settled in Chinguacousy Township in 1838. When the township was split in 1974, the boundary was set so the whole community fell within Brampton.

Snelgrove is generally bounded by Conservation Drive and Mayfield Road to the east and the Caledon boundary and Wanless Drive to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 430 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Snelgrove.

Green space in Snelgrove includes Conservation Drive Park, Ken Park and Chinguacousy Lions Club Water Tower Park, and Etobicoke Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

05.02.0150.t:
Heart Lake West, Brampton

Heart Lake West is the western part of the Heart Lake area of north Brampton. The area takes its name from the heart-shaped kettle lake in Heart Lake Conservation Area, which opened in 1957. Heart Lake became part of the City of Brampton in 1974. Housing was first built in the 1970s, with further phases in the late 1990s and early 2000s.

Heart Lake West is generally bounded by Conservation Drive to the north, Kennedy Road to the east, Bovaird Drive to the south and Hurontario Street to the west, and covers approximately 426 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Heart Lake West includes Loafer's Lake Park, Morris Kerbel Park and Stafford Woods, and Etobicoke Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Cyril Clark branch of the Brampton Library.

01.C15.0650.t:
Henry Farm, City of Toronto (TRREB district C15)

Henry Farm is named after George Stewart Henry, Premier of Ontario from 1930 to 1934, whose family farm occupied the land. The land was first settled by Henry Mulholland in 1806 and was reacquired by George S. Henry in 1898. In 1958 Henry sold the farm to developers, and it was built up as a housing subdivision between approximately 1964 and 1972. The area was part of North York, which joined the City of Toronto in 1998.

Henry Farm is generally bounded by Victoria Park Avenue to the east and Sheppard Avenue and Highway 401 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 275 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401, Highway 404 and the Don Valley Parkway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Henry Farm includes East Don Parkland, Parkway Forest Park and Havenbrook Park, and the Don River East Branch runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools, and transit is provided by the Don Mills subway station.

01.W02.0440.t:
High Park North, City of Toronto (TRREB district W02)

High Park North takes its name from High Park, which forms its southern edge. The land was part of the Keele estate farm and racetrack, bought and subdivided by Daniel Clendenan in 1882 and 1883 as part of the growing town of West Toronto Junction. The town was annexed by the City of Toronto in 1909. Most surviving houses date from the late 1800s to the 1920s, and high-rise apartments were built in the 1960s and 1970s after the Bloor-Danforth subway opened.

High Park North is generally bounded by Humberside Avenue and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) to the east, Bloor Street to the south and Runnymede Road and Annette Street to the west, and covers approximately 188 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Galt Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line and a rail yard lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in High Park North includes Lithuania Park, Ravina Gardens Park and Kennedy-Margdon Parkette. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Runnymede branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the High Park, Keele, Runnymede and Dundas West subway stations.

01.W01.0450.t:
High Park-Swansea, City of Toronto (TRREB district W01)

This community combines Swansea, west of High Park, with the park itself. Swansea was first subdivided in the 1880s as Windermere, and took its later name from the Swansea Works factory, whose owner came from the Swansea area of Wales. Swansea separated from York Township as a village in 1926 and joined the City of Toronto in 1967. Most houses date from approximately 1905 to 1935, with apartment buildings and newer townhomes and condominiums added after the 1960s.

High Park-Swansea is generally bounded by Bloor Street to the north, Roncesvalles Avenue to the east, the Gardiner Expressway to the south and the Humber River to the west, and covers approximately 556 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Gardiner Expressway and a rail yard. Along or just beyond its edges are the Humber Wastewater Treatment Plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in High Park-Swansea includes High Park, Humber Marshes and Rennie Park, and the Humber River and Spring Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Grenadier Pond. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools, the High Park branch of the Toronto Public Library and the Swansea Memorial branch of the Toronto Public Library. St. Joseph's Health Centre is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include High Park Zoo.

10.02.0030.t:
Highbush, Pickering

Highbush is a residential neighbourhood in west Pickering; its name likely refers to the dense forest that once covered the area. Early housing was small cottages from the early 1900s. New subdivisions were added in the 1980s and 1990s. Many street names, such as Pine Grove and Forestview, reflect the wooded setting.

Highbush is generally bounded by a hydro corridor to the north, the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the south and the City of Toronto boundary to the west, and covers approximately 216 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (York Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Highbush includes Rouge National Urban Park. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Altona Forest.

01.E10.1140.t:
Highland Creek, City of Toronto (TRREB district E10)

Highland Creek is named after the creek that runs through it and was one of the first parts of Scarborough Township settled by Europeans. The village grew along Old Kingston Road among farmland. The University of Toronto bought land in the area in 1963 and Scarborough College opened in 1965, after which the area developed mainly as residential neighbourhoods. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Highland Creek is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Kingston Road to the east, Highland Creek and Old Kingston Road to the south and Morningside Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 508 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Wesleyan Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Highland Creek includes Highland Creek Community Park and Bramber Woods Park, and Highland Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Highland Creek branch of the Toronto Public Library. University of Toronto Scarborough is also located in the community.

05.02.0460.t:
Highway 427, Brampton

The Highway 427 community is at the eastern edge of Brampton, next to the City of Vaughan, and takes its name from the nearby highway. The land was part of Toronto Gore Township, which included the hamlets of Claireville and Castlemore. The remainder of the township was merged into the City of Brampton in 1974. The area was mainly farmland until development began from the late 20th century.

Highway 427 is generally bounded by Mayfield Road to the north, Highway 50 to the east, Castlemore Road to the south and The Gore Road to the west, and covers approximately 1,250 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are CPKC Vaughan Intermodal Yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

West Rainbow Creek runs through or along the community.

07.01.1530.t:
Hill Park, Hamilton

Hill Park is a residential neighbourhood on Hamilton Mountain. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. It was built up mainly as post-war suburban housing.

Hill Park is generally bounded by Fennell Avenue to the north, Upper Wentworth Street to the east, Mohawk Road to the south and Upper Wellington Street to the west, and covers approximately 90 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Hill Park.

Green space in Hill Park includes Sackville Hill Memorial Park. Residents are served by one school.

01.C15.0540.t:
Hillcrest Village, City of Toronto (TRREB district C15)

Hillcrest Village lies in the northeast corner of the former City of North York, west of the Don Valley and south of Steeles Avenue. The land was farmland in York Township, became part of North York in 1922 and joined the City of Toronto in 1998. It was built up as a suburban residential area in the second half of the 20th century.

Hillcrest Village is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Victoria Park Avenue and a hydro corridor to the east, Finch Avenue to the south and Leslie Street to the west, and covers approximately 540 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 404, a hydro transformer station (Leslie Transmission Station), Highland Memory Gardens Cemetery, Zion Church and Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 10% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Hillcrest Village includes Leslie Greenbelt, Duncan Creek Park and McNicoll Park, and Duncan Woods Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Hillcrest branch of the Toronto Public Library. Seneca Polytechnic and Loyalist College in Toronto are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include A. Y. Jackson Secondary School.

09.06.0010.t:
Hills of St Andrew, Aurora

Hills of St Andrew lies in north Aurora near the Newmarket border and takes its name from nearby St. Andrew's College on Yonge Street. It is a residential area of mainly detached homes built during Aurora's suburban growth. Aurora began as Machell's Corners, a hamlet at Yonge Street and Wellington Street where Richard Machell opened a store in 1804. The railway arrived in 1853, the village was incorporated in 1863 and it became a town in 1888.

Hills of St Andrew is generally bounded by the Newmarket boundary to the north, Yonge Street to the east, Orchard Heights Boulevard to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 329 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Hills of St Andrew.

Residents are served by one school.

04.09.0020.t:
Hillsdale, Springwater

Hillsdale was founded as a stopping point roughly halfway between Lake Simcoe and Georgian Bay. It grew as a small village serving the surrounding farms. On January 1, 1994 it became part of the Township of Springwater, formed from Flos and Vespra townships, the villages of Elmvale and Hillsdale, and part of Medonte.

Hillsdale is generally bounded by Highway 400 to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 418 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 400, a cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 9% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Sturgeon River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

09.09.0010.t:
Historic Lakeshore Communities, Georgina

This area covers the Lake Simcoe shoreline settlements east of Keswick, including Roches Point, Eastbourne, Orchard Beach and Balfour Beach, in the former Township of North Gwillimbury. Roches Point is named after early landowner James Roche, who held land there in the early 1800s. Cottage building grew after the Eastbourne Golf Club opened in 1914, and Balfour Beach was founded as a cottage community in 1926. The area became part of the Town of Georgina in 1971 and is now a mix of cottages and year-round homes.

Historic Lakeshore Communities is generally bounded by Lake Simcoe to the east and Baseline Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 29,184 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Georgina Water Treatment Plant and Keswick Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Historic Lakeshore Communities includes Metro Road Tract, Georgina Pioneer Village and Willow Beach Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. Orchard Beach Golf Club and Willow Greens Golf Centre are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Other notable landmarks include Christ Church Roches Point (1862).

04.11.0030.t:
Hockley, Adjala-Tosorontio

Hockley is a rural hamlet near the Hockley Valley, at the border of Adjala-Tosorontio and the Town of Mono. Its historic community hall was built in 1894 by the local Orange Lodge, and its former Primitive Methodist church dates from 1869. The surrounding area was settled from the 1820s and remains largely rural.

Hockley is generally bounded by Mono-Adjala Townline to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 501 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Hockley.

The Nottawasaga River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

09.08.0010.t:
Holland Landing, East Gwillimbury

Holland Landing is at the north end of the original Yonge Street, where the Holland River is navigable to Lake Simcoe. It is named after Samuel Holland, the first Surveyor General of British North America. Quaker settlers arrived in the early 1800s, and it served as an inland port, with steamboats from approximately 1833 to 1853. It is now an unincorporated community in the Town of East Gwillimbury, York Region.

Holland Landing is generally bounded by 2nd Concession Road to the east and Highway 11 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,356 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), Holland Landing Well and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Holland Landing includes Holland Landing Prairie Provincial Park, Holland Landing Conservation Area and Ridge View Park, and the East Holland River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Holland Landing branch of the East Gwillimbury Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Anchor Park (Holland Landing anchor).

04.15.0340.t:
Holly, Barrie

Holly takes its name from Holly, one of the early settlements of Innisfil Township, which was first surveyed in 1820. The area was transferred to Barrie through annexation of Innisfil lands; the largest transfer, of approximately 8,623 acres, took effect on January 1, 1982. Holly has been largely built out with suburban housing in recent decades.

Holly is generally bounded by Essa Road to the east and County Road 27 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 544 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Holly includes Marsellus Park, Mapleton Park and Harvie Park, and Bear Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools.

04.16.0030.t:
Horseshoe Valley, Oro-Medonte

Horseshoe Valley is named after a horseshoe-shaped ring of hills on the Oro Moraine; locals earlier called the area Hungry Hollow. A ski club opened there in 1962, started by Toronto-area home builder Bill Lohuaru, and later became Horseshoe Resort. Condominiums were completed in the late 1970s, and building lots and homes were developed around the resort in later decades. The area became part of Oro-Medonte in 1994.

Horseshoe Valley is generally bounded by Oro-Medonte Line 4 to the east and Oro-Medonte Line 3 to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 620 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Horseshoe Valley.

Green space in Horseshoe Valley includes Copeland Forest Resource Management Area. Horseshoe Valley Club is located in the area.

01.W09.0080.t:
Humber Heights, City of Toronto (TRREB district W09)

Humber Heights was originally the Etobicoke side of the Weston community, centred on St. Philip's Anglican Church, one of Etobicoke's first churches. In the 19th century the Scarlett family owned most of the farm lots along the Humber River between Lambton and Weston. Much of the housing was built on former farmland in the 1960s, and some higher-density buildings have since been added along Eglinton Avenue. Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Humber Heights is generally bounded by St Phillips Road to the north, the Humber River to the east, Eglinton Avenue to the south and Royal York Road to the west, and covers approximately 276 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Riverside Cemetery and St. Philip's Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Sanctuary Park Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Humber Heights includes La Rose Park, Westmount Park and Douglas Ford Park, and the Humber Creek and the Humber River run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. Other notable landmarks include Weston Golf and Country Club and Riverside Cemetery.

01.W05.0210.t:
Humber Summit, City of Toronto (TRREB district W05)

Humber Summit lies along the east branch of the Humber River in the northwest corner of the former York Township. It began in the 1840s as a small pioneer community around grist and saw mills, and later became a cottage and resort area known as Riverbend Park. Many riverside cottages were swept away by Hurricane Hazel in 1954, and most of the present suburban housing was built in the 1960s. The area became part of North York in 1922 and of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Humber Summit is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Highway 400 to the east, Finch Avenue to the south and the Humber River to the west, and covers approximately 795 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (Finch TS), Pine Ridge Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 52% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 400. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Humber Summit includes Rowntree Mills Park, Apted Park and Islington Park, and the Humber River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Humber Summit branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Duncanwoods, Milvan Rumike, Emery and Signet Arrow LRT stations.

01.W04.0262.t:
Humberlea-Pelmo Park W4, City of Toronto (TRREB district W04)

Pelmo Park-Humberlea is in the former North York, which separated from York Township in 1922. Pelmo Park lies north of Woodward Avenue near Jane Street, and Humberlea is centred on Weston Road along the Humber River, with Highway 401 dividing the two. The area was rural farmland before suburban housing was built after the Second World War. North York was amalgamated into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Humberlea-Pelmo Park W4 is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Woodward Avenue and Jane Street to the east and the Humber River to the west, and covers approximately 214 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), Highway 400 and industrial lands (approximately 11% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) and Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Humberlea-Pelmo Park W4 includes Mallaby Park, Pelmo Park and Pellatt Parkette, and Black Creek and the Humber River run through or along the community. Residents are served by one school. Reactivation Care Center is also located in the community.

01.W05.0261.t:
Humberlea-Pelmo Park W5, City of Toronto (TRREB district W05)

Pelmo Park-Humberlea is in the former North York, which separated from York Township in 1922. Humberlea is centred on Weston Road along the Humber River between Sheppard Avenue and Oak Street, while Pelmo Park lies to the south near Jane Street, with Highway 401 dividing the two. The area was rural farmland before suburban housing was built after the Second World War. North York was amalgamated into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Humberlea-Pelmo Park W5 is generally bounded by the Humber River to the north, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) to the east and Highway 401 to the south, and covers approximately 207 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Humberlea-Pelmo Park W5 includes West Humber Parkland, Louise Russo Park and Strathburn Park, and the Humber River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

01.W05.0250.t:
Humbermede, City of Toronto (TRREB district W05)

Humbermede takes its name from the Humber River, which forms its western edge, and is often called Emery after a former rural hamlet. A farming hamlet first named Dayton grew up by approximately 1870 at Finch Avenue and Weston Road, with a railway station and post office, and was later renamed Emery. The area was part of York Township, then North York from 1922, and began converting to suburban use around 1960. North York was amalgamated into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Humbermede is generally bounded by Finch Avenue to the north, Highway 400 to the east, Sheppard Avenue to the south and the Humber River to the west, and covers approximately 441 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 24% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 400 and a hydro transformer station (Finch TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Humbermede includes West Humber Parkland, Humber Sheppard Park and Lindy Lou Park, and the Humber River and Emery Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Woodview Park branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Duncanwoods, Milvan Rumike, Emery and Signet Arrow LRT stations. Other notable landmarks include Line 6 Finch West.

01.C03.0020.t:
Humewood-Cedarvale, City of Toronto (TRREB district C03)

Humewood is named after William Hume Blake, whose estate included what is now Humewood Park. The area was part of York Township and later the City of York, which joined the new City of Toronto in 1998. Single-family homes were built in Humewood in the 1920s and in Cedarvale in the 1940s. Mid-rise and high-rise apartments were added later.

Humewood-Cedarvale is generally bounded by Eglinton Avenue to the north, Bathurst Street to the east, St. Clair Avenue and Arlington Avenue to the south and Winnett Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 191 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Humewood-Cedarvale.

Green space in Humewood-Cedarvale includes Cedarvale Park, Humewood Park and Glen Cedar Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools, and transit is provided by the Forest Hill LRT station.

07.01.1570.t:
Huntington, Hamilton

Huntington is a residential neighbourhood on the east part of Hamilton Mountain. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. It was built up mainly as post-war suburban housing.

Huntington is generally bounded by Fennell Avenue to the north, Mountain Brow Boulevard to the east, Mohawk Road to the south and Upper Ottawa Street to the west, and covers approximately 132 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Huntington.

Green space in Huntington includes Fay Park, Fay Avenue Park and Huntington Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.07.0070.t:
Huron Heights-Leslie Valley, Newmarket

Huron Heights-Leslie Valley is a residential neighbourhood in eastern Newmarket, near Leslie Street and Davis Drive. Its housing was built mostly from the 1970s through the 1990s. This followed the formation of York Region in 1971, when development in Newmarket began to move east toward Highway 404.

Huron Heights-Leslie Valley is generally bounded by the East Gwillimbury boundary to the north, Leslie Street to the east, Davis Drive to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 344 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Huron Heights-Leslie Valley includes George Richardson Park, Bayview Parkway Soccer fields and George Richardson Park Trail, and the Holland River East Branch and the East Holland River run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools, and transit is provided by the Newmarket GO Station.

05.03.0200.t:
Hurontario, Mississauga

Hurontario is named after Hurontario Street, the historic road that ran north from Port Credit. The area includes the site of the former village of Britannia, which grew around Britannia Road and Hurontario Street in the 1800s with a church, school, general store and blacksmith. The farmland was developed with suburban housing in the later decades of the 20th century, after the township became the Town of Mississauga in 1968 and the City in 1974.

Hurontario is generally bounded by Matheson Boulevard to the east, Highway 403 to the south and Mavis Road to the west, and covers approximately 1,177 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 403. The community is also close to Toronto Pearson International Airport, approximately 2.8 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Hurontario includes Parkway Belt Park, Britannia Woods Community Forest and Huron Heights Park, and Cooksville Creek runs through or along the community. Andy Bathgate Golf Driving Range is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 13 schools.

07.01.1410.t:
Inch Park, Hamilton

The neighbourhood is named after Adam Inch (1857 to 1933), a dairy farmer and local politician, and his wife Jacqueline. When the city limits were extended in the early 1930s, part of the Inch farm was taken, and land was set aside in 1939 for an athletic field. The park was developed in 1944, and a swimming pool and outdoor rink followed in 1953.

Inch Park is generally bounded by Mountain Park Avenue to the north, Upper Wentworth Street to the east, Fennell Avenue to the south and Upper Wellington Street to the west, and covers approximately 108 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Inch Park.

Green space in Inch Park includes Inch Park and Sam Lawrence Park. Residents are served by one school.

06.02.0160.t:
Industrial Burlington, Burlington

Industrial Burlington covers employment lands in central Burlington, mainly along the Queen Elizabeth Way and the railway corridor. The opening of the QEW after 1939, along with rail access, drew industry to Burlington. Burlington began as Wellington Square and Port Nelson, which merged into the Village of Burlington in 1873. Burlington annexed most of Nelson Township and Aldershot on January 1, 1958, and became a city in 1974. Industrial growth here took place mainly from the 1950s onward.

Industrial Burlington is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and Upper Middle Road to the north, Burloak Drive and Mainway to the east, Fairview Street to the south and the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) and Guelph Line to the west, and covers approximately 1,418 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW), a hydro transformer station (Cumberland TS), a cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 52% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Industrial Burlington includes Sherwood Forest Park and Centennial Trail, and Sheldon Creek, Shoreacres Creek and Appleby Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by one school, and transit is provided by the Appleby GO Station. McMaster University - DeGroote School of Business is also located in the community.

01.E04.1220.t:
Ionview, City of Toronto (TRREB district E04)

Ionview lies in the former Scarborough Township, near the old villages of Wexford (1840s) and Scarborough Junction (1873). The area stayed largely rural until the postwar housing boom of the 1940s and 1950s, when it was built up with homes and apartment towers. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Ionview is generally bounded by a hydro corridor to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision) to the east and Birchmount Road to the west, and covers approximately 195 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and surface light rail transit (LRT) tracks. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision) and Bethel Pioneer Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Ionview includes Jack Goodlad Park, Maidavale Park and Eglinton Ravine Park. Residents are served by one school and the Kennedy/Eglinton branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Birchmount and Ionview LRT stations, the Kennedy subway station and the Kennedy GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Taylor-Massey Creek.

07.01.0150.t:
Iroquoia Heights, Hamilton

Iroquoia Heights is a residential area in the east part of Ancaster, near the Iroquoia Heights Conservation Area and Highway 403. Ancaster Township was settled in the 1790s, and housing subdivisions began around the village from 1946. The township became the Town of Ancaster in 1974, and the town joined the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Iroquoia Heights is generally bounded by Highway 403 to the north, a hydro corridor to the east and the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the south, and covers approximately 230 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 403, the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway and White Chapel Memorial Gardens (cemetery). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Iroquoia Heights includes Scenic Woods Park and Conny Park.

07.01.1920.t:
Kennedy, Hamilton

Kennedy is a residential neighbourhood on Hamilton Mountain, made up of Kennedy East and Kennedy West in the city's planning maps. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960.

Kennedy is generally bounded by Rymal Road to the north, a hydro corridor and Upper James Street to the east and Garth Street to the west, and covers approximately 101 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor lie along or just beyond its edges. The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 2.1 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Kennedy includes St. Elizabeth. Residents are served by one school.

01.E04.1210.t:
Kennedy Park, City of Toronto (TRREB district E04)

Kennedy Park takes its name from Kennedy Road and was historically known as Scarborough Junction, where the Grand Trunk Railway (1856) and the Toronto and Nipissing Railway (1873) met. The local economy shifted from farming to serving travellers and the railways, and by 1896 it was the most populated area of Scarborough Township. After the Second World War it was one of the first parts of Scarborough built up as a modern suburb. Scarborough joined the City of Toronto in 1998.

Kennedy Park is generally bounded by Eglinton Avenue to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and Brimley Road to the east, St Clair Avenue to the south and a hydro corridor and Birchmount Road to the west, and covers approximately 358 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision), Pine Hills Cemetery and Bethel Pioneer Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Transit Uxbridge Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Kennedy Park includes Corvette Park, Farlinger Ravine and Greystone Park, and Taylor-Massey Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools, and transit is provided by the Kennedy subway station and the Kennedy GO Station.

06.02.0150.t:
Tansley, Burlington

Tansley is in north-central Burlington and takes its name from a former rural crossroads community. The settlement was first known as St. Ann's and was renamed Tansley when its post office opened in 1885. It was part of Nelson Township, annexed by Burlington in 1958. The area stayed largely agricultural until the 1990s and was mostly built out in the 2000s.

Tansley is generally bounded by Upper Middle Road to the north, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the east, Mainway to the south and Walkers Line to the west, and covers approximately 131 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor and the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Tansley includes Tansley Woods Park, and Shoreacres Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Tansley Woods branch of the Burlington Public Library.

07.01.1030.t:
Industrial Sector, Hamilton

The Industrial Sector covers the heavy industrial lands along the south shore of Hamilton Harbour, in the north and east of the lower city. The area was developed for industry from the late nineteenth century, and large steel works grew there in the early twentieth century. It contains little housing.

Industrial Sector is generally bounded by Lake Ontario to the north and the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,330 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line, Nikola Tesla Boulevard, ArcelorMittal Long Products Canada Hamilton East (industrial plant), a landfill site, ArcelorMittal Dofasco (industrial plant), a hydro transformer station (Beach TS), a hydro transformer station (Birmingham Transmission Station) and industrial lands (approximately 83% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Industrial Sector includes St. Christopher's Park, North Central Community Park and Dofasco Property Park, and Redhill Creek runs through or along the community.

09.02.0050.t:
Islington Woods, Vaughan

Islington Woods is a residential area in Woodbridge, named after Islington Avenue. Woodbridge began as the mill village of Burwick after 1837 and was incorporated as a village in 1882. Suburban growth spread outward from the old village from the 1950s through the 1990s. In 1971 Woodbridge was amalgamated into the Town of Vaughan, now the City of Vaughan.

Islington Woods is generally bounded by Rutherford Road to the north, the East Humber River to the east and the Humber River to the west, and covers approximately 671 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Islington Woods includes Boyd Conservation Area, Thompson Creek Park and Kiloran Park, and the Humber River and the East Humber River run through or along the community. Board of Trade Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

10.07.0150.t:
Kedron, Oshawa

Kedron is named after a former hamlet in East Whitby Township, north of the original town of Oshawa. The area was rural farmland for most of its history. Kedron, together with Columbus and Raglan, became part of the City of Oshawa in 1974, when the Regional Municipality of Durham was created. Residential development in the area is recent.

Kedron is generally bounded by Winchester Road to the north, the Clarington boundary to the east, Conlin Road to the south and East Oshawa Creek to the west, and covers approximately 845 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 407 ETR. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Kedron includes Kedron Park, and East Oshawa Creek runs through or along the community. Kedron Dells Golf Course is located in the area.

01.W03.0370.t:
Keelesdale-Eglinton West, City of Toronto (TRREB district W03)

Keelesdale takes its name from Keele Street, and the community lies south of Eglinton Avenue West in what was York Township. The area was originally farmland served by small postal villages, and Eglinton Avenue later became the main commercial street of the former City of York. Most houses south of Eglinton are modest detached homes from the first half of the 20th century. The area was part of the City of York until amalgamation into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Keelesdale-Eglinton West is generally bounded by Eglinton Avenue to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the east, Rowntree Avenue and Lavender Road to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 171 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), a rail yard and Eglinton Maintenance and Storage Facility. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Keelesdale-Eglinton West includes Haverson Park and Silverthorn Parkette, and Black Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Evelyn Gregory branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Mount Dennis, Caledonia and Keelesdale LRT stations. Other notable landmarks include York Civic Centre (former).

01.W08.0140.t:
Islington-City Centre West, City of Toronto (TRREB district W08)

The community grew around Montgomery's Inn, built in 1832 at Dundas Street West and Islington Avenue, and took the name Islington in 1860 when it gained its own post office. Etobicoke Township's first council meetings were held at the inn after 1850. Residential areas grew in the 1950s, and the Bloor-Danforth subway reached Islington in 1968 and Kipling in 1980, followed by high-density office and residential building. Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Islington-City Centre West is generally bounded by Highway 427 and Rathburn Road to the north, Islington Avenue and Mimico Creek to the east, the Gardiner Expressway and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the south and Etobicoke Creek to the west, and covers approximately 1,630 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Canpa Subdivision), the CPKC rail line, Highway 427, the Gardiner Expressway, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW), a hydro transformer station (A.W Manby TS), Islington Burying Grounds and industrial lands (approximately 28% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Lakeshore Psychiatric Hospital Cemetery. The community is also close to Toronto Pearson International Airport, approximately 2.6 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Islington-City Centre West includes Hampshire Heights Park, Echo Valley Park and Tom Riley Park, and Mimico Creek and Etobicoke Creek run through or along the community. Islington Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools and the Eatonville branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Kipling and Islington subway stations. Shopping is available at CF Sherway Gardens and Cloverdale Mall. Queensway Health Centre is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Montgomery's Inn.

09.04.0020.t:
Jefferson, Richmond Hill

Jefferson is in north Richmond Hill, near Yonge Street and Jefferson Side Road, at the edge of the Oak Ridges Moraine. The name comes from the Jefferson family, who settled on Lot 59 and ran a store and post office from approximately 1840. French Royalist settlers, the Windham settlement, had earlier arrived nearby in 1799. The rural area was developed with new subdivisions, with homes first occupied in 2007.

Jefferson is generally bounded by Yonge Street to the north, 19th Avenue and Bayview Avenue to the east, Gamble Road to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 696 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are Pardes Chaim Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Jefferson includes Laurentian Park, Oak Ridges Corridor Conservation Reserve and Monticello Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools. Other notable landmarks include French Royalist Park.

07.01.1740.t:
Jerome, Hamilton

Jerome is a residential neighbourhood on Hamilton Mountain. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. It was built up as suburban housing in the second half of the twentieth century.

Jerome is generally bounded by the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the north, Upper Wellington Street to the east, Stone Church Road to the south and Upper James Street to the west, and covers approximately 76 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway, Ohev Zedeck Cemetery and Barton Stone United Church Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Jerome is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

07.01.0030.t:
Jerseyville, Hamilton

Jerseyville was settled in the late 1790s by Loyalists from New Jersey and was first called Jersey Settlement. It took its present name in 1852, when a post office opened. It is a small rural community in the former Ancaster Township, which became the Town of Ancaster in 1974 and joined the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Jerseyville is generally bounded by Hamilton-Brantford Rail Trail to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 53 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 403 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Jerseyville includes Jerseyville Park.

01.W02.0410.t:
Junction Area, City of Toronto (TRREB district W02)

The Junction takes its name from the nearby meeting of several railway lines, now known as the West Toronto Diamond. The area was largely rural until railways arrived in the 1880s, when the former Carlton Race Course lands were subdivided. West Toronto Junction was incorporated as a village in 1887 and as a town in 1889, and it grew quickly as a railway and meat-packing centre. It was annexed by the City of Toronto in 1909.

Junction Area is generally bounded by the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) to the east, Humberside Avenue and Annette Street to the south and Runnymede Road to the west, and covers approximately 263 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Galt Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 12% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), the CPKC rail line, the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision) and a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Junction Area includes Runnymede Park, Maple Claire Park and Baird Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Annette Street branch of the Toronto Public Library. Runnymede Healthcare Centre is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Dundas Street West main street.

01.C01.0960.t:
Kensington-Chinatown, City of Toronto (TRREB district C01)

Much of the area was part of the estate of George Taylor Denison, who bought the land in 1815. The estate was subdivided in the 1850s, and small houses were built for Irish and Scottish labourers in the 1880s. In the early 1900s Jewish and Italian immigrants moved in, and Kensington became known as the Jewish Market. Chinatown grew along Spadina Avenue in the 1950s and 1960s, after the original Chinatown near Bay and Dundas was cleared for the new City Hall.

Kensington-Chinatown is generally bounded by College Street to the north, University Avenue to the east, Queen Street to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 155 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Kensington-Chinatown.

Green space in Kensington-Chinatown includes Alexandra Park, Grange Park and Bellevue Square Park. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools and the Sanderson branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Queen's Park, Osgoode and St. Patrick subway stations. Toronto Western Hospital and Mount Sinai Hospital are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Spadina Avenue and Dundas Street West (Chinatown).

07.01.1210.t:
Kentley, Hamilton

Kentley is a residential neighbourhood in the east end of the former City of Hamilton. The area was farmland in the old townships east of Hamilton before it was annexed by the City of Hamilton in the twentieth century. Barton Township was fully absorbed by the city in 1960.

Kentley is generally bounded by Barton Street to the north, Centennial Parkway to the east, Queenston Road to the south and the Red Hill Valley Parkway to the west, and covers approximately 139 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Red Hill Valley Parkway and Eastlawn Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Kentley includes Sam Manson Park. Residents are served by the Red Hill branch of the Hamilton Public Library. Shopping is available at Eastgate Square.

07.01.1730.t:
Kernighan, Hamilton

The neighbourhood is named after Robert Kirkland Kernighan (died 1926), a poet and journalist from the Hamilton area. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. It was built up as suburban housing in the later twentieth century.

Kernighan is generally bounded by the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the north, Upper James Street to the east, Stone Church Road to the south and West 5th Street to the west, and covers approximately 35 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Ohev Zedeck Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway and Barton Stone United Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Kernighan includes Kernighan Neighbourhood Park.

09.09.0020.t:
Keswick North, Georgina

Keswick began as a settlement called Medina in the 1820s, in the former Township of North Gwillimbury. When its post office opened in 1836 it was named Keswick, and the name stayed. Keswick became part of the Town of Georgina in 1971. For many years it was mainly a cottage community for Toronto residents, and major suburban development began in the late 1980s.

Keswick North is generally bounded by Old Homestead Road to the north, Woodbine Avenue to the east and Lake Simcoe to the west, and covers approximately 1,065 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a wastewater treatment plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Keswick North includes Richmond Park, Claredon Beach Park and Keswick Beach Association, and the Maskinonge River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Keswick branch of the Georgina Public Library.

09.09.0030.t:
Keswick South, Georgina

Keswick began as a settlement called Medina in the 1820s, in the former Township of North Gwillimbury. When its post office opened in 1836 it was named Keswick, and it became part of the Town of Georgina in 1971. The area was mainly cottages and farmland until the late 1980s. Large subdivisions such as Simcoe Landing were built from the 2000s, with growth continuing after Highway 404 was extended to Woodbine Avenue in 2014.

Keswick South is generally bounded by Woodbine Avenue to the east, Ravenshoe Road to the south and Lake Simcoe and the Holland River to the west, and covers approximately 2,165 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Keswick South.

Green space in Keswick South includes West Park, Oakmeadow Park and Vista Park, and the Holland River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Discovery Branch Library.

04.15.0200.t:
Lakeshore, Barrie

Lakeshore covers the waterfront area at the west end of Kempenfelt Bay, next to Allandale and downtown Barrie. Allandale grew around the railway after the first train from Toronto arrived on October 11, 1853, and was annexed by Barrie in 1896. The historic Allandale railway station opened in 1905, and the Spirit Catcher sculpture was installed on the waterfront in 1987.

Lakeshore is generally bounded by Simcoe Street to the north, Lake Simcoe to the east, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and Gowan Street to the south and Lakeshore Drive to the west, and covers approximately 222 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and a rail yard. Along or just beyond its edges are a wastewater treatment plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lakeshore includes Allandale Station Park, Centennial Park and Heritage Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. Transit is provided by the Allandale Waterfront GO Station.

09.01.0050.t:
King City, King

King City began as the hamlet of Springhill, established in 1836. Growth started after the Ontario, Simcoe and Huron Railway arrived in 1853, and the name King City was adopted for the merged hamlets in 1890. It is the largest community in King Township, named after John King, a British Under-Secretary. Residential growth increased after a sanitary sewer system was built from 2005.

King City is generally bounded by 15th Sideroad to the north, Dufferin Street to the east, the Vaughan boundary to the south and Jane Street to the west, and covers approximately 1,510 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and King City Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in King City includes King City Lions Park, Rafferty's Corners Park and Salamander Park, and the East Humber River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the King City branch of the King Township Public Library, and transit is provided by the King City GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Seneca College King Campus (Eaton Hall) and King Township Museum grounds.

01.E05.1070.t:
L'Amoreaux, City of Toronto (TRREB district E05)

L'Amoreaux is named after Josue L'Amoreaux (1738 to 1834), a French Huguenot Loyalist who settled in the area in 1816 with his family. The land was farmland in Scarborough Township for over a century. Much of the area was built up from the late 1950s onward, mainly with detached homes and townhouses, plus some apartment and condominium buildings. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

L'Amoreaux is generally bounded by a hydro corridor to the north, Kennedy Road and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line to the east, Huntingwood Drive to the south and Victoria Park Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 702 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include St Paul's L'Amoreaux (cemetery). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in L'Amoreaux includes L'Amoureaux Park, Fairglen Park and Timberbank Park. Residents are served by approximately 15 schools and the Bridlewood branch of the Toronto Public Library. Shopping is available at Bridlewood Mall. Scarborough Health Network - Birchmount Hospital is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Sir John A. Macdonald Collegiate Institute.

07.01.1580.t:
King's Forest Lower, Hamilton

King's Forest Lower is in Hamilton's east end, below the escarpment and near King's Forest Park in the Red Hill Valley. The area was farmland in the old townships east of Hamilton before it was annexed by the City of Hamilton in the twentieth century. Barton Township was fully absorbed by the city in 1960. The Red Hill Valley Parkway through the valley was completed in 2007.

King's Forest Lower is generally bounded by Greenhill Avenue to the north, a hydro corridor and Mount Albion Road to the east and Mountain Brow Boulevard to the west, and covers approximately 280 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the Red Hill Valley Parkway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in King's Forest Lower includes Rosedale Park, and Redhill Creek runs through or along the community. King's Forest Golf Club and Glendale Golf and Country Club are located in the area. Other notable landmarks include Red Hill Valley.

07.01.1690.t:
King's Forest Upper, Hamilton

King's Forest Upper is on the east part of Hamilton Mountain, above King's Forest Park and the Red Hill Valley. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. Mohawk Sports Park, on Mountain Brow Boulevard, was first known as Upper King's Forest Sports Park and became Mohawk Sports Park in 1971.

King's Forest Upper is generally bounded by Mohawk Road to the north, Mountain Brow Boulevard to the east, Limeridge Road to the south and Upper Kenilworth Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 71 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of King's Forest Upper.

Green space in King's Forest Upper includes Mohawk Sports Park and Oak Knoll Park.

01.W09.0060.t:
Kingsview Village-The Westway, City of Toronto (TRREB district W09)

The name Kingsview was given in the 1950s to housing built north of Dixon Road on land owned by Ernest Byworth, and refers to its position on high ground. The area was farmland in Etobicoke Township, settled mainly by people from the British Isles. Most single-family homes were built in the 1950s and 1960s, and Kingsview Village Junior School opened in 1956. Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Kingsview Village-The Westway is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, the Humber River to the east, The Westway to the south and Kipling Avenue and Dixon Road to the west, and covers approximately 489 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) and Sanctuary Park Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401, Riverside Cemetery and St. Philip's Cemetery. The community is also close to Toronto Pearson International Airport, approximately 2.4 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Kingsview Village-The Westway includes Alex Marchetti Park, Wincott Park and Mallaby Park, and the Humber Creek runs through or along the community. Weston Golf and Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools.

07.01.1110.t:
Landsdale, Hamilton

Landsdale is an older neighbourhood in Hamilton's lower city, east of downtown. Much of its housing was built in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, as the city expanded east.

Landsdale is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) to the north, Wentworth Street to the east, Main Street to the south and Wellington Street to the west, and covers approximately 114 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Landsdale includes Jack C. Beemer Park, Birge Park and Wellington Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

01.W08.0150.t:
Kingsway South, City of Toronto (TRREB district W08)

The Kingsway takes its name from The Kingsway road, which starts beside the site of the King's Mill built on the Humber River in the 1790s. Developer Robert Home Smith assembled land along the Humber from 1906 to 1912 and subdivided it as part of the Humber Valley Surveys in 1912. The first houses were built in 1924, and 665 homes were built between 1924 and 1947, mainly in English and Arts and Crafts styles. Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Kingsway South is generally bounded by Dundas Street to the north, the Humber River to the east, Bloor Street to the south and Mimico Creek to the west, and covers approximately 259 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are Park Lawn Cemetery and St. George’s on-the-Hill Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Kingsway South includes Home Smith Park, Tom Riley Park and Lambton - Kingsway Park, and Mimico Creek and the Humber River run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Brentwood branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Old Mill and Royal York subway stations.

07.01.1250.t:
Kirkendall, Hamilton

Kirkendall is an older neighbourhood in Hamilton's lower west end, centred on Locke Street. Locke Street South began to grow around 1885, after a brick sewer and gas lines were installed, and the Hamilton Street Railway built a terminus at Locke and Herkimer in 1890. Most of its houses date from the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Kirkendall is generally bounded by Main Street to the north, Queen Street to the east, Beckett Drive to the south and Highway 403 and Aberdeen Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 263 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 10% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 403 and a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Kirkendall includes Hamilton AAA Grounds, Highland Gardens Park and Hill Street Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Locke branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

09.02.0020.t:
Kleinburg, Vaughan

Kleinburg is named after John Nicholas Klein, a German settler who built a flour mill on the west branch of the Humber River in approximately 1848. The Toronto, Grey and Bruce Railway opened a station nearby in 1870, around which the hamlet of Nashville grew. Suburban housing began at the south end of the village in the 1960s, and the Nashville Heights area has been built out since the early 2010s. Kleinburg became part of the Town of Vaughan in 1971.

Kleinburg is generally bounded by the King boundary to the north, Highway 400 and Teston Road to the east, Major MacKenzie Drive to the south and Albion-Vaughan Road and Highway 50 to the west, and covers approximately 6,963 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), a wastewater treatment plant, a hydro transformer station (Kleinburg TS), Nashville Cemetery and Photo added by SD Cowan St. Paul's Presbyterian Church Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 400 and CPKC Vaughan Intermodal Yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Kleinburg includes Bindertwine Park, William T. Foster Woods and Summit Park, and the Humber River, the East Humber River and West Robinson Creek run through or along the community. Copper Creek Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Vaughan Public Libraries - Kleinburg Branch. Other notable landmarks include McMichael Canadian Art Collection.

10.07.0160.t:
Taunton, Oshawa

Taunton takes its name from Taunton Road, the main east-west road across this part of Durham Region; the name comes from Taunton in Somerset, England. A small village called Taunton existed near the Whitby-Oshawa boundary in the 1800s. The area was farmland in East Whitby Township and became part of the City of Oshawa in 1974. The neighbourhood in northeast Oshawa was largely built in the 2010s.

Taunton is generally bounded by Conlin Road to the north, Townline Road to the east, Taunton Road to the south and Wilson Road to the west, and covers approximately 498 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Taunton.

Green space in Taunton includes Greenhill Park, Coldstream Park and Mackie Park. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Oshawa Public Libraries - Delpark Centre Branch.

04.04.0010.t:
Lafontaine, Tiny

Lafontaine is a village in the Township of Tiny that was settled by French-Canadian families from Quebec in the mid-1800s. It was originally called Sainte-Croix. It was renamed to honour Louis-Hippolyte Lafontaine, an early joint premier of the Province of Canada. The village still holds Le Festival du Loup, a francophone festival, each July.

Lafontaine is generally bounded by Lafontaine Road to the east, Rue Eric to the south and Cedar Point Road to the west, and covers approximately 63 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lafontaine includes Lafontaine Park. Residents are served by one school.

07.01.0280.t:
Lakeshore, Hamilton

Lakeshore is the area along the Lake Ontario shore in the former Saltfleet Township, below the escarpment in Stoney Creek. It was mainly farmland and orchards for most of its history. Saltfleet became part of the Town (later City) of Stoney Creek in 1974, and Stoney Creek joined the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Lakeshore is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the east and Lake Ontario to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 251 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lakeshore includes Lawrence P. Sayers Park and Frederick Parkette.

05.03.0330.t:
Lakeview, Mississauga

Lakeview lies on Lake Ontario in the former Toronto Township. The area was home to the Long Branch Aerodrome from 1915, a small arms factory from 1940 to 1976, and the Lakeview Generating Station from 1962 to 2005. Residential areas grew through the 20th century, and the former generating station site is being redeveloped as Lakeview Village.

Lakeview is generally bounded by Queensway to the north, Etobicoke Creek to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Cawthra Road and the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 1,066 hectares.
