Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW), the Lakeview Wastewater Treatment Plant, Lakeview Water Treatment Facility, a hydro transformer station (Applewood Junction) and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transformer station (Cooksville TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lakeview includes Cawthra Park, Lakeview Park and Lakefront Promenade Park, and Applewood Creek, Serson Creek and Etobicoke Creek run through or along the community. Toronto Golf Course and Lakeview Golf Course are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 11 schools and the Lakeview branch of the Mississauga Library. Shopping is available at Dixie Outlet Mall.

07.01.1440.t:
Sunninghill, Hamilton

Sunninghill is a residential neighbourhood on the East Mountain, with shops along Fennell Avenue East. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. The East Mountain grew quickly after the Second World War, and most homes in Sunninghill were built before 1960.

Sunninghill is generally bounded by Mountain Brow Boulevard and Sherman Access to the north, Upper Ottawa Street to the east, Fennell Avenue to the south and Upper Gage Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 82 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Sunninghill.

Green space in Sunninghill includes Highview Park and Mountain Drive Park. Residents are served by one school.

10.07.0140.t:
Lakeview, Oshawa

Lakeview lies along Lake Ontario in south Oshawa, near Oshawa Harbour, which was built from 1840. Much of the lakefront was the Henry family farm, which Thomas Henry acquired in 1830. In 1920 Sam and George McLaughlin bought the lakefront land through General Motors of Canada and deeded it to the town as Lakeview Park. Oshawa annexed the area to the south, including the harbour, in 1924.

Lakeview is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Simcoe Street to the east and Lake Ontario to the south, and covers approximately 609 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), a wastewater treatment plant and industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lakeview includes Lakeview Park, Cordova Valley Park and Lakefront West Park, and Oshawa Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Oshawa Public Libraries - Jess Hann Branch.

09.02.0200.t:
Lakeview Estates, Vaughan

Lakeview Estates is a residential area in the Thornhill part of Vaughan. Thornhill was founded in 1794 and takes its name from Benjamin Thorne, who ran mills there from 1820. The old village was split between Vaughan and Markham townships. In 1971 the Vaughan side became part of the Town, now City, of Vaughan, and most surrounding land was developed for housing in the following decades.

Lakeview Estates is generally bounded by Bathurst Street to the east and the CN rail line (York Subdivision) and Steeles Avenue to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 87 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (York Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lakeview Estates includes Lakehurst Park, Conley Park South and Conley Park North, and the Don River West Branch runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

01.W02.0430.t:
Lambton Baby Point, City of Toronto (TRREB district W02)

Lambton grew from Cooper's Mills, a mill site on the Humber River, which was renamed Lambton Mills in 1838 after John Lambton, Earl of Durham. Baby Point is named after James Baby, who settled on the site of the former Seneca village of Teiaiagon in 1816. Developer Home Smith began the Baby Point subdivision in 1912, and most homes there were built in the 1920s and 1930s, while the Warren Park area was built out from the 1950s to the 1970s. The area was part of York Township and later the City of York until amalgamation into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Lambton Baby Point is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and Gooch Avenue to the north, Jane Street to the east, Home Smith Park Road to the south and the Humber River to the west, and covers approximately 184 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and a rail yard lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lambton Baby Point includes Étienne Brûlé Park, Lambton Park and Lessard Park, and the Humber River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

09.04.0120.t:
Langstaff, Richmond Hill

Langstaff is in south Richmond Hill, between Yonge Street and Bayview Avenue, from Highway 7 to 16th Avenue. It is named after John Langstaff, who came from New Jersey in 1808, and the crossroads became known as Langstaff Corners; a post office opened in 1870. The area was annexed to Richmond Hill in 1971. It is now being redeveloped as an urban centre with many condominiums along Yonge Street.

Langstaff is generally bounded by 16th Avenue to the north, Bayview Avenue to the east, Highway 407 to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 373 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision), Highway 407 and a hydro transformer station (William C. Lazenby TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Langstaff includes Russell Farm Park, Dr. James Langstaff Comunity Park and Springbrook Park, and German Mills Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Other notable landmarks include Holmwood (Langstaff family home).

01.C07.0600.t:
Lansing-Westgate, City of Toronto (TRREB district C07)

Lansing began as a small settlement and postal village at Yonge Street and Sheppard Avenue, with a store and a post office. It was part of York Township and became part of North York in 1922. The area developed with mostly single-family homes from approximately 1910 to the 1950s. North York became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Lansing-Westgate is generally bounded by the Don River West Branch to the north, Yonge Street to the east, Highway 401 to the south and Bathurst Street and Sheppard Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 512 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401 and York Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lansing-Westgate includes Earl Bales Park, Hinder Area and Burnett Park, and the Don River West Branch runs through or along the community. Don Valley Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools, and transit is provided by the Sheppard-Yonge subway station.

06.02.0040.t:
LaSalle, Burlington

LaSalle is in the Aldershot area of west Burlington on Burlington Bay. It is named after LaSalle Park, renamed in 1923 after French explorer René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, who is said to have landed there in 1669. The park, owned by the City of Hamilton and leased to Burlington, has a pavilion first built in 1917. Aldershot was part of East Flamborough Township until Burlington annexed it in 1958. It was a leading fruit-growing area, and by the 1960s most farms had been sold for housing.

LaSalle is generally bounded by Highway 403 to the north, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and LaSalle Park Road and Waterdown Road to the west, and covers approximately 786 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (Burlington Transformer Station), East Plains Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 403 and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in LaSalle includes LaSalle Park, Francis Road Trail and Kiwanis Park, and Indian Creek and Falcon Creek run through or along the community. Burlington Golf and Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Aldershot branch of the Burlington Public Library, and transit is provided by the Aldershot GO Station.

07.01.1660.t:
Lawfield, Hamilton

Lawfield is a neighbourhood on the east-central Mountain, bounded by Upper Gage Avenue, Upper Sherman Avenue, Mohawk Road East and the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. Most of its homes were built between approximately 1961 and 1980.

Lawfield is generally bounded by Mohawk Road to the north, Upper Gage Avenue to the east, the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the south and Upper Sherman Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 91 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lawfield includes Lawfield Park and Austin Park. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Bill Friday Lawfield Arena.

01.C04.0690.t:
Lawrence Park North, City of Toronto (TRREB district C04)

The name comes from Lawrence Park, developed from 1907 by the Dovercourt Land Building and Saving Company on land bought from John Lawrence. The area was part of the Town of North Toronto, formed in 1890, which was annexed to the City of Toronto in 1912. Most homes were built between 1910 and the late 1940s, and the area was largely complete by the 1950s.

Lawrence Park North is generally bounded by Lawrence Avenue to the south and Roe Avenue to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 228 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Lawrence Park North.

Green space in Lawrence Park North includes Wanless Park, Ranleigh Park and Woburn Park. Rosedale Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools, and transit is provided by the Lawrence subway station. Other notable landmarks include Yonge Street commercial strip.

01.C04.0700.t:
Lawrence Park South, City of Toronto (TRREB district C04)

The area was part of the Town of North Toronto, formed in 1890 and annexed to the City of Toronto in 1912. Streetcar service on Yonge Street from 1886 led to a residential boom in the Lytton Park area from 1888. Most homes were built between approximately 1890 and 1930. The Lawrence Park name comes from the nearby suburb developed from 1907 on land bought from John Lawrence.

Lawrence Park South is generally bounded by Lawrence Avenue to the north, Blythwood Road to the east and Briar Hill Avenue and Avenue Road to the south, and covers approximately 323 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but The Adath Israel Roselawn Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lawrence Park South includes Alexander Muir Memorial Gardens, Chatsworth Ravine and Blythwood Ravine Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools, and transit is provided by the Avenue LRT station. Other notable landmarks include Lytton Park and Yonge Street commercial strip.

01.C11.0780.t:
Leaside, City of Toronto (TRREB district C11)

The name comes from the Lea family, who settled the area in 1820; William Lea built an octagonal house called 'Leaside' in 1854. The Canadian Northern Railway planned a town around its rail yards, and the Town of Leaside was incorporated in 1913. Growth was slow until the Leaside Viaduct opened in 1927, and most homes were built from the late 1920s to the 1950s. Leaside merged with East York in 1967 and became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Leaside is generally bounded by Laird Drive and Eglinton Avenue to the north, Millwood Road to the east, the Don River and Ravine Beltline Trail to the south and Bayview Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 480 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision) and the North Toronto Wastewater Treatment Plant. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), the Don Valley Parkway, a hydro transformer station (Leaside Transformer Station), Mount Pleasant Cemetery and Mount Hope Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Leaside includes Sunnybrook Park, Don Valley Brick Works Park and Moore Park Ravine, and the Don River and the Don River West Branch run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Leaside branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Leaside and Laird LRT stations. Other notable landmarks include Evergreen Brick Works.

04.14.0060.t:
Lefroy, Innisfil

Lefroy is named after Sir John Henry Lefroy, known for his magnetic survey work. The village was founded in 1853 when the Ontario, Simcoe and Huron Union Railway opened a station there to serve the lumber and ice trade at nearby Belle Ewart. It soon had a general store, bank, post office and hotels, and much of its early commercial area survives. It became part of the Town of Innisfil on January 1, 1991.

Lefroy is generally bounded by Belle Aire Beach Road to the north, Pine Avenue to the south and Sideroad 20 to the west, and covers approximately 250 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lefroy includes LSAMI Park and Church Street Park.

09.03.0360.t:
Legacy, Markham

Legacy was built on part of a golf course established in 1950 on the Tomlinson property in Box Grove, which IBM bought in 1967. In 1997 IBM sold part of the course to Minto, which built the Legacy neighbourhood, and the valley portion became the city-owned Markham Green Golf Club. The area is part of the historic Box Grove district.

Legacy is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, Ninth Line to the east and the Rouge River to the west, and covers approximately 132 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 407 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Legacy includes Legacy Park, Fairview Vista Park and Old Mill Pond Park, and the Rouge River runs through or along the community. Markham Green is located in the area. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Box Grove Church (Legacy Drive).

04.15.0060.t:
Letitia Heights, Barrie

Letitia Heights is a residential area in west Barrie, named after Letitia Street. The area mixes some older homes with subdivisions built built mainly in the later 20th century. Barrie grew from a supply depot at the end of the Nine Mile Portage and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a village in 1854, a town in 1871 and a city in 1959.

Letitia Heights is generally bounded by Burns Circle to the north, Anne Street to the east, Edgehill Drive to the south and Ferndale Drive to the west, and covers approximately 247 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Barrie Union Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 400 and Barrie Landfill (landfill). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Letitia Heights includes Lampman Park and Oates Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. Other notable landmarks include Barrie Union Cemetery.

07.01.1680.t:
Lisgar, Hamilton

Lisgar is a residential neighbourhood on Hamilton Mountain, shown with Berrisfield in the city's neighbourhood planning maps. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. It was built up as suburban housing in the second half of the twentieth century.

Lisgar is generally bounded by Mohawk Road to the north, Upper Kenilworth Avenue to the east, Limeridge Road to the south and Upper Ottawa Street to the west, and covers approximately 94 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Lisgar.

Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

05.03.0010.t:
Lisgar, Mississauga

Lisgar takes its name from a nearby hamlet first called Switzer's Corners, renamed in honour of Lord Lisgar, Governor General from 1869 to 1872. The area was farmland in Trafalgar Township, became part of Oakville in 1962 and part of Mississauga in 1974. Housing development began in 1986 and the area was largely built out in the 1990s.

Lisgar is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) to the north, Tenth Line to the east, Britannia Road to the south and Highway 407 to the west, and covers approximately 749 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lisgar includes Lisgar Fields, Trelawny Woods and Tobias Mason Park. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools, and transit is provided by the Lisgar GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Osprey Marsh.

04.15.0110.t:
Little Lake, Barrie

Little Lake is in north Barrie and shares its name with Little Lake, a small lake just to the north that has been a local recreation spot since the 1890s. Barrie's northern limit was Cundles Road until 1984, when the city annexed approximately 2,200 acres from Vespra Township, including the Bayfield Street commercial strip. Much of the area was built up with housing after that annexation.

Little Lake is generally bounded by the Springwater boundary to the north, Little Lake and Georgian Drive to the east and St. Vincent Street and Cundles Road to the west, and covers approximately 175 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 400. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Little Lake includes Little Lake Park, Osprey Ridge Park and Stollar Park.

01.C01.0980.t:
Little Portugal, City of Toronto (TRREB district C01)

The name comes from the many Portuguese residents and businesses that settled along Dundas Street West and College Street from the 1950s and 1960s. The part west of Dufferin Street was once in the Village of Brockton, which was annexed to the City of Toronto in 1884. The sub-area around Beaconsfield Avenue is known as Beaconsfield Village. Most of the housing dates from the late 1800s and early 1900s.

Little Portugal is generally bounded by College Street to the north, Dovercourt Road to the east, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Galt Subdivision) to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) and Dundas Street to the west, and covers approximately 121 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a rail yard. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Galt Subdivision) and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Little Portugal includes McCormick Park, Lisgar Park and Pessoa Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

04.16.0090.t:
Warminister, Oro-Medonte

Warminster is a rural community in the former Medonte Township. The area is close to the site of Cahiague, a large Huron village where Samuel de Champlain spent the winter of 1615. The townships of Oro and Medonte were incorporated in 1850 and were amalgamated, with the Hawkestone Police Village, to form the Township of Oro-Medonte on January 1, 1994.

Warminister is generally bounded by Cheslock Crescent to the north, Town Line to the east, Highway 12 to the south and Warminster Sideroad to the west, and covers approximately 147 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 12. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school.

10.02.0100.t:
Liverpool, Pickering

Liverpool began as a crossroads hamlet, originally called Liverpool Market, on Kingston Road at Liverpool Road. Its focal point was the Liverpool Arms Inn, built in 1827, which served travellers between Kingston and Toronto. The area was farmland in Pickering Township for most of the 1800s. Most of the neighbourhood's houses were built in the 1970s and 1980s.

Liverpool is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) to the north and a hydro corridor to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 719 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a hydro transformer station (Cherrywood TS) and Erskine Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Liverpool includes Dixie Park, David Farr Park and Glengrove Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools. Other notable landmarks include Former Liverpool Arms Inn (Kingston Road at Liverpool Road).

01.W06.0190.t:
Long Branch, City of Toronto (TRREB district W06)

Long Branch is named after Long Branch Park, a lakeside resort named in 1886 after Long Branch, New Jersey. The land was part of a 1797 grant to Loyalist Colonel Samuel Smith, and summer resort subdivisions were laid out from 1884 into the 1890s, with more housing from the 1910s and 1920s. Long Branch was incorporated as a village in 1930 and joined the Borough of Etobicoke in 1967. Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Long Branch is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) to the north, Twenty Second Street and Twenty Third Street to the east, Lake Promenade to the south and Lake Ontario and Etobicoke Creek to the west, and covers approximately 229 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Canpa Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Lakeview Wastewater Treatment Plant and the R. L. Clark Water Treatment Plant lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Long Branch includes Marie Curtis Park, Birch Park and Laburnham Park, and Etobicoke Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Long branch of the Toronto Public Library.

04.11.0070.t:
Loretto, Adjala-Tosorontio

Loretto is one of the oldest communities in the former Adjala Township, which was settled from the 1820s largely by Irish Catholic families. It was named after Loreto in the Marche region of Italy. Highway 50 runs through the hamlet. Adjala Township was incorporated in 1850 and Tosorontio Township in 1855; the two merged to form the Township of Adjala-Tosorontio on January 1, 1994.

The boundary of Loretto follows local streets, lot lines and natural features rather than major roads, and the community covers approximately 161 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Loretto.

Loretto is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

05.03.0270.t:
Malton, Mississauga

Malton was settled in approximately 1819 and named by blacksmith and innkeeper Richard Halliday after his former home in Malton, England. The Grand Trunk Railway arrived in 1854, and Malton Airport, now Toronto Pearson, opened in 1937. Wartime housing known as Victory Village was built in 1942, followed by new subdivisions in the 1950s and 1960s. Malton became part of Mississauga in 1968.

Malton is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the north, Highway 427 to the east, Derry Road to the south and Airport Road to the west, and covers approximately 695 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), Highway 427, Toronto Pearson International Airport and Malport Yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Malton includes Derry Greenway, Victory Park and Northwood Park, and West Mimico Creek and Mimico Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 14 schools and the Malton branch of the Mississauga Library. Shopping is available at Westwood Square.

05.03.0130.t:
Lorne Park, Mississauga

Lorne Park began as a lakeside resort park opened in 1879 by the Toronto Park Association, with visitors arriving by steamer. The name is often linked to the Marquess of Lorne, but its origin is not certain. After the wharf collapsed in 1903 it became a summer retreat for Torontonians, and the surrounding lands were built up as suburbs after the Second World War. It became part of Mississauga in 1968.

Lorne Park is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the north, the Credit River and the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) to the east and Lake Ontario and Birchwood Creek to the south, and covers approximately 780 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), a rail yard and a hydro transformer station (Lorne Park TS). Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and Spring Creek Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Lorne Park includes Whiteoaks Park, Richard's Memorial Park and Jack Darling Memorial Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Lorne Park branch of the Mississauga Library. Other notable landmarks include Benares Historic House.

07.01.0010.t:
Lynden, Hamilton

Lynden was first called VanSickle in 1843, after local miller Benony VanSickle. In 1853 it was renamed by Jeremiah Bishop after Lyndon, Vermont. It is a small rural village in the western part of the city and became part of the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Lynden is generally bounded by Lynden Road and the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision) to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 63 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision) and Lynden Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by the Lynden branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

07.01.1550.t:
Macassa, Hamilton

The neighbourhood is named after Macassa, an Indigenous name for Hamilton Harbour meaning "beautiful water". The city bought land here in 1952, and Macassa Park, on Upper Sherman Avenue between Fennell Avenue and Mohawk Road, was developed in 1959 and 1960. The surrounding Mountain land was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed and built up after the Second World War.

Macassa is generally bounded by Fennell Avenue to the north, Upper Gage Avenue to the east, Mohawk Road to the south and Upper Sherman Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 80 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Macassa.

Green space in Macassa includes Macassa Park and Vincent Massey Park. Residents are served by one school.

05.02.0200.t:
Madoc, Brampton

Madoc is an established residential area east of downtown Brampton, north of Queen Street and west of Highway 410, around Madoc Drive. Brampton was laid out in 1834 at Buffy's Corners and named after Brampton in Cumberland, England. It became a village in 1853 and a town in 1873. The area is one of Brampton's older residential pockets, with a mix of detached, semi-detached, townhouse and apartment housing.

Madoc is generally bounded by Bovaird Drive to the north, Highway 410 to the east, Archdekin Drive to the south and Kennedy Road to the west, and covers approximately 406 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 410 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Madoc includes Lakelands Park, Century Gardens and Major Oaks Park. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools.

07.01.1830.t:
Mewburn, Hamilton

Mewburn is a neighbourhood on the south part of Hamilton Mountain, including the area between Upper James Street and West 5th Street near Stone Church Road and Rymal Road. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960. Much of the southern part of the neighbourhood has been developed since approximately the 2000s.

Mewburn is generally bounded by Stone Church Road to the north, Upper James Street to the east, Rymal Road to the south and West 5th Street to the west, and covers approximately 38 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Barton Stone United Church Cemetery. The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 2.7 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Mewburn is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

06.01.1034.t:
Milton North, Milton

Milton North is a TRREB community in the northern part of the Town of Milton. The Town of Milton grew from a grist mill settlement founded by Jasper Martin on Sixteen Mile Creek in approximately 1820, and was incorporated as a town in 1857. The present town was formed in 1974, when it absorbed Nassagaweya Township and parts of Trafalgar, Esquesing and Nelson townships. Specific history for this community was not found.

Milton North is generally bounded by 5 Side Road to the north, Esquesing Line to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Tremaine Road to the west, and covers approximately 1,643 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), Highway 401, Maplehurst Correctional Complex, Milton Pioneer Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 35% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Mansewood United Presbyterian Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Milton North includes Chris Hadfield Park and Dirt bike park, and Sixteen Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Conestoga College Parkhill/Milton Campus (Temporary) and Wilfrid Laurier University Milton Campus (Temporary) are also located in the community.

01.E11.1040.t:
Malvern, City of Toronto (TRREB district E11)

Malvern began as a postal village in Scarborough Township, where a post office named after the English town of Malvern opened in 1856 at Finch Avenue and Markham Road. It remained a farming community for over a century. In the late 1950s the federal housing agency (CMHC) assembled the farmland to build a planned community, and the first residents moved in in 1972. The area was part of the City of Scarborough until amalgamation into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Malvern is generally bounded by Finch Avenue to the north, Morningside Avenue to the east, Highway 401 to the south and Markham Road to the west, and covers approximately 896 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), Highway 401 and industrial lands (approximately 13% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line and CPKC Toronto Yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Malvern includes Neilson Park, Major Abbas Ali Park and Burrows Hall Park, and Malvern Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 17 schools, the Burrows Hall branch of the Toronto Public Library and the Malvern branch of the Toronto Public Library. Shopping is available at Malvern Town Centre.

09.02.0140.t:
Maple, Vaughan

Maple was first called Noble's Corner, after first postmaster Joseph Noble, and later Rupertsville; settlement dates from approximately 1852. The railway arrived in the early 1850s, and the present Maple station was built by the Grand Trunk Railway in 1903. Larger subdivisions began in the 1980s, the former Maple Airport lands were built on from 1993, and development reached Highway 400 and Teston Road by approximately 2000. Maple became part of the Town of Vaughan in 1971.

Maple is generally bounded by Jane Street and Teston Road to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the east, Rutherford Road to the south and Highway 400 and Major MacKenzie Drive to the west, and covers approximately 1,179 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include St. Andrew's Presbyterian Cemetery and Sherwood Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), Highway 400 and Maple United Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Maple includes Mackenzie Glen Park, Frank Robson Park and Maple Reservoir Park. Residents are served by approximately 12 schools and the Vaughan Public Libraries - Maple Branch, and transit is provided by the Maple GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Canada's Wonderland.

01.W04.0280.t:
Maple Leaf, City of Toronto (TRREB district W04)

Maple Leaf lies between Lawrence Avenue West and Highway 401, east of Culford Road, in what was York Township. The area became part of North York in 1922 and remained largely rural until suburban housing was built after the Second World War. North York was amalgamated into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Maple Leaf is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the east, Lawrence Avenue to the south and Culford Road to the west, and covers approximately 246 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and Highway 401 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Maple Leaf includes North Park, Queens GreenBelt Park and Ernie Lustig - Rainbow Park, and Maple Leaf Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

04.18.0050.t:
Marchmont, Severn

Marchmont is a small community just north of the City of Orillia, in the former Orillia Township. The area was settled for farming in the 19th century and has seen rural residential growth since. The Township of Severn was formed on January 1, 1994 from the Village of Coldwater, the townships of Matchedash and Orillia, and parts of Medonte and Tay.

Marchmont is generally bounded by Division Road to the south and Town Line and Highway 12 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 393 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 12. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Marchmont includes Marchmont Community Park, and the North River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

09.03.0310.t:
Markham Village, Markham

Markham Village grew around the Reesor family's mills on the Rouge River; the settlement was first known as Reesorville and took the name Markham in 1825. It was incorporated as a village in 1872 and became part of the Town of Markham in 1971. Housing beyond the historic core was added through the 20th century, including post-war and later subdivisions.

Markham Village is generally bounded by 16th Avenue to the north, Ninth Line to the east, Highway 7 to the south and Mount Joy Creek to the west, and covers approximately 378 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Elmwood Cemetery and St. Andrew's Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Markham Village includes Rouge Valley Park, Mintleaf Park and Reesor Park, and the Rouge River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Markham Village branch of the Markham Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Main Street Markham.

06.01.1035.t:
Old Milton, Milton

Old Milton is the historic core of the town. It grew around the grist mill and mill pond that Jasper Martin built on Sixteen Mile Creek in approximately 1820, and the town was named after the poet John Milton. Milton became the county town of Halton in 1853 and was incorporated in 1857. Much of the older housing and the Main Street commercial buildings date from approximately 1850 to 1890.

Old Milton is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Ontario Street to the east, Bronte Street and Derry Road to the south and the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 366 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), a wastewater treatment plant and Evergreen Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Old Milton includes Milton Fairgrounds, Brian Best Park and Rotary Park, and Sixteen Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools. Other notable landmarks include Main Street heritage district, Mill Pond and Victoria Park and Milton Town Hall.

01.W08.0120.t:
Markland Wood, City of Toronto (TRREB district W08)

The name Markland Wood is said to come from 'Mark's Land', after Mark Cavotti, who bought the land from the Silverthorn family in 1958. Development began in 1960, after flood levels were set following Hurricane Hazel. Most single-family houses were completed by 1967, with tract housing and two condominium apartment buildings added in the 1970s. Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Markland Wood is generally bounded by Old Burnhamthorpe Road to the north, Renforth Drive and Highway 427 to the east, Dundas Street to the south and Etobicoke Creek to the west, and covers approximately 300 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 427. The community is also close to Toronto Pearson International Airport, approximately 3.0 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Markland Wood includes Neilson Park, Bloordale Park and Millwood Park, and Elmcrest Creek and Etobicoke Creek run through or along the community. Markland Wood Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

09.03.0230.t:
Markville, Markham

Markville takes its name from CF Markville shopping centre, which opened in 1982 at Highway 7 and McCowan Road and was named for its location between the historic villages of Markham and Unionville. The site was once a nursery garden and part of the Eckhart estate. Surrounding housing was built mainly from the 1980s onward.

Markville is generally bounded by 16th Avenue to the north, McCowan Road to the east and Highway 7 to the south, and covers approximately 236 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision) and Quantztown Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Markville includes Centennial Park, Austin Drive Park and Lincoln Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools, and transit is provided by the Centennial GO Station. Shopping is available at CF Markville.

05.03.0170.t:
Mavis-Erindale, Mississauga

Mavis-Erindale lies north of the historic village of Erindale, along Mavis Road, in the former Toronto Township. The township became the Town of Mississauga in 1968 and the City in 1974. The area was farmland until suburban housing was built in the later decades of the 20th century. Specific history for this community was not found.

Mavis-Erindale is generally bounded by Burnhamthorpe Road to the north, Mavis Road to the east, Wolfedale Road to the south and the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 198 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 71% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Wolfedale Creek runs through or along the community.

10.07.0070.t:
McLaughlin, Oshawa

McLaughlin is a residential community in the City of Oshawa, and it shares its name with the McLaughlin family. Robert McLaughlin moved his carriage works to Oshawa in 1878, and his son R.S. McLaughlin founded the McLaughlin Motor Car Company in 1907, which became General Motors of Canada in 1918. Oshawa annexed part of East Whitby Township west of Park Road in 1950 and absorbed the rest in 1974.

McLaughlin is generally bounded by Rossland Road to the north, Oshawa Creek to the east, King Street to the south and Corbett Creek to the west, and covers approximately 467 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Union Cemetery and Pioneer Memorial Garden (cemetery). Along or just beyond its edges are Mount Lawn Memorial Garden (cemetery). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in McLaughlin includes Dundee Park, McLaughlin Park and Fernhill Park, and Goodman Creek runs through or along the community. Oshawa Golf & Curling Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools.

07.01.1170.t:
McQuesten, Hamilton

The neighbourhood is named after Thomas Baker McQuesten (1882 to 1948), a Hamilton lawyer, alderman and Ontario cabinet minister who led the city's parks board and helped bring McMaster University to Hamilton. It is in the east end of the lower city. The area was farmland in the old townships east of Hamilton before it was annexed by the City of Hamilton in the twentieth century. Barton Township was fully absorbed by the city in 1960.

McQuesten is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) to the north, the Red Hill Valley Parkway and Redhill Creek to the east, Queenston Road to the south and Parkdale Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 187 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 12% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) and the Red Hill Valley Parkway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in McQuesten includes Hillcrest Park and Roxborough Park, and Redhill Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Parkdale branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

07.01.0160.t:
Meadowlands, Hamilton

Meadowlands is a suburban neighbourhood in the east part of Ancaster, bounded by the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway and Highway 403 to the north and Garner Road to the south. The developer took the name from the Meadowlands sports complex in New Jersey. The area was farmland until it was built up as part of Ancaster's recent growth east of Highway 403. Ancaster became part of the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Meadowlands is generally bounded by the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the north, a hydro corridor to the east, Garner Road to the south and Highway 403 to the west, and covers approximately 726 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a hydro transformer station (Horning TS) and Garners Corners Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 403, the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway, Highway 6 and Bowman United Church Cemetery. The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 2.5 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Meadowlands includes Meadowlands Park, Biba Park and Kitty Murray Lane Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools. Redeemer University is also located in the community.

05.03.0040.t:
Meadowvale, Mississauga

Meadowvale takes its name from the historic village of Meadowvale, named for the meadows of the Credit River valley. The farmland west of the village was developed as a planned "new town", started in 1969, with most subdivisions built in the 1970s and 1980s. The area includes two largely man-made lakes, Lake Aquitaine and Lake Wabukayne, linked by parks and trails.

Meadowvale is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) to the north, Britannia Road and Erin Mills Parkway to the south and Tenth Line to the west, and covers approximately 816 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Eden (Switzers) Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Meadowvale includes Lake Aquitaine Park, Lake Wabukayne Park and Eden Woods Park. Residents are served by approximately 13 schools and the Meadowvale branch of the Mississauga Library. LifeLabs Medical Laboratory Services is also located in the community.

09.04.0040.t:
Mill Pond, Richmond Hill

Mill Pond is a residential area just west of Yonge Street in central Richmond Hill. It is named after the pond, a kettle lake that powered a sawmill and other mills in the 1800s. Heritage homes surround the pond, with later housing in the Heritage Estates area toward Bathurst Street.

Mill Pond is generally bounded by Elgin Mills Road to the north, Yonge Street to the east, Major MacKenzie Drive to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 442 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Richmond Hill Presbyterian Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Mill Pond includes Mill Pond Park, Pioneer Park and Rumble Pond Park South. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools. MacKenzie Health - Richmond Hill is also located in the community.

05.03.0050.t:
Meadowvale Business Park, Mississauga

Meadowvale Business Park is the employment area of the Meadowvale planned community, which was started in 1969 on farmland in the former Toronto Township. It is the largest business park along the Highway 401 corridor in Mississauga. The park was built up with offices and industrial buildings from the 1970s onward.

Meadowvale Business Park is generally bounded by a hydro corridor to the north and the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and Highway 401 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,350 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), Highway 401, a hydro transformer station (Meadowvale TS) and industrial lands (approximately 41% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Meadowvale Business Park includes Meadowvale Sports Park, and Mullet Creek and Wabukayne Creek run through or along the community. Ninth Line Family Golf is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools, and transit is provided by the Lisgar and Meadowvale GO stations.

05.03.0140.t:
Meadowvale Village, Mississauga

Meadowvale Village is a historic mill village on the Credit River, settled in the early 1800s by Irish immigrants from New York State led by John Beatty. Milling was the main industry, and Gooderham and Worts ran the Silverthorne grist mill in the 1860s and 1870s. In 1980 it became Ontario's first Heritage Conservation District. It became part of Mississauga in 1968 and the newer Meadowvale district took its name.

Meadowvale Village is generally bounded by the Brampton boundary to the north, Fletchers Creek to the east, Highway 401 to the south and a hydro corridor and Meadowvale Boulevard to the west, and covers approximately 995 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Meadowvale Village includes Meadowvale Conservation Area, Courtneypark Athletic Fields and Horseshoe Park, and the Credit River, Fletchers Creek and Levi Creek run through or along the community. Derrydale Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 11 schools and the Courtneypark branch of the Mississauga Library. Other notable landmarks include Gooderham Estate (Old Derry Road).

09.03.0280.t:
Middlefield, Markham

Middlefield is in south-east Markham, north of Steeles Avenue at the Toronto (Scarborough) border. The area was farmland of Markham Township near the former hamlet of Armadale, settled from approximately 1805. It was developed for housing mainly in the 1980s and 1990s, with newer homes added into the 2000s.

Middlefield is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, Markham Road to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and McCowan Road to the west, and covers approximately 586 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (York Subdivision), a hydro transformer station and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407 and Eckardt Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Middlefield includes Elson Park, James Edward Park and Beaupre Park. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Aaniin branch of the Markham Public Library.

05.02.0100.t:
Northwest Sandalwood Parkway, Brampton

Northwest Sandalwood Parkway is a residential area in north Brampton around Sandalwood Parkway and Hurontario Street, near Mayfield Road. The land was farmland in Chinguacousy Township, close to the former hamlet of Snelgrove. Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships were merged with the Town of Brampton in 1974 to form the City of Brampton. The area is made up mainly of newer subdivisions built in recent decades.

Northwest Sandalwood Parkway is generally bounded by McLaughlin Road to the north, Hurontario Street to the east and Bovaird Drive to the south, and covers approximately 518 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 33% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Northwest Sandalwood Parkway includes Burnt Elm Park, Van Scott Parkette and Iceland Parkette. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

04.09.0090.t:
Midhurst, Springwater

Midhurst is named after the town of Midhurst in England, and is the largest community in Springwater. A grist mill and power house on Willow Creek operated in the 1800s, and a provincial tree nursery was later based here. It lies in the former Vespra Township and has grown with residential subdivisions in recent decades. On January 1, 1994 it became part of the Township of Springwater, formed from Flos and Vespra townships, the villages of Elmvale and Hillsdale, and part of Medonte.

Midhurst is generally bounded by Craig Road to the north, Old Second to the east and Wilson Drive to the west, and covers approximately 2,711 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (Midhurst TS), a quarry or aggregate pit and Midhurst Union Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Midhurst includes Springwater Provincial Park, Glenhuron Park and Cherry Park, and Willow Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Midhurst branch of the Springwater Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Simcoe County Museum.

01.E07.1020.t:
Milliken, City of Toronto (TRREB district E07)

Milliken is named after Norman Milliken, who settled in the area around 1807, and its post office of 1858 carried the family name. The rural hamlet of Milliken Corners grew around the family's lumber business. In 1954 the area south of Steeles Avenue went to Metropolitan Toronto as part of Scarborough, while Milliken Mills to the north stayed in York County. Farming ended in the early 1980s, and residential development ran from the 1970s to the late 1980s.

Milliken is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Markham Road to the east, Middlefield Road to the south and Kennedy Road and a hydro corridor to the west, and covers approximately 947 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line, the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (Cavanagh TS), a hydro transformer station (Agincourt TS), Armadale Free Methodist Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 35% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are CPKC Toronto Yard and Ebenezer Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Milliken includes Milliken Park, Muirlands Park and Audrelane Park. Residents are served by approximately 11 schools and the Goldhawk Park branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Milliken GO Station.

09.03.0270.t:
Milliken Mills East, Markham

Milliken Mills takes its name from Norman Milliken, who settled in the area in approximately 1807 and ran a lumber business at what was called Milliken Corners; a post office named Milliken opened in 1858. When Steeles Avenue became the Toronto boundary in 1954, the northern part stayed in York County. Residential development began in the 1970s and was largely complete by the late 1980s.

Milliken Mills East is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, McCowan Road to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Kennedy Road to the west, and covers approximately 656 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (York Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision), Ebenezer Cemetery and Eckardt Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Milliken Mills East includes Armadale Park, Randall Park and Aldergrove Park. Markham Executive Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools. Shopping is available at Pacific Mall.

09.03.0200.t:
Milliken Mills West, Markham

Milliken Mills takes its name from Norman Milliken, who settled in the area in approximately 1807 and ran a lumber business at what was called Milliken Corners; a post office named Milliken opened in 1858. When Steeles Avenue became the Toronto boundary in 1954, the northern part stayed in York County. Residential development began in the 1970s and was largely complete by the late 1980s.

Milliken Mills West is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, Kennedy Road to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Highway 404 to the west, and covers approximately 1,396 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (York Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (D. H. Cockburn Transformer Station), a hydro transformer station (Parkway TS), St. John's Warden Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 44% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407 and Highway 404. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Milliken Mills West includes Milliken Mills, Highgate Park and Risebrough Park, and Cummer Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Milliken Mills branch of the Markham Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Benjamin Milliken House (7710 Kennedy Road).

04.15.0250.t:
Painswick North, Barrie

Painswick North is part of the Painswick area in south Barrie, named after the early settlement of Painswick in Innisfil Township. The Warnica family settled in the area in 1823. Much of Barrie's south end was part of Innisfil Township until January 1, 1982, when approximately 8,623 acres were annexed to the city. Painswick was built up with suburban housing mainly from the 1980s onward.

Painswick North is generally bounded by the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the north, Big Bay Point Road to the south and Huronia Road to the west, and covers approximately 278 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and a rail yard lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Painswick North includes Huronia Park, Willoughby Park and Cudia Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

07.01.1430.t:
Raleigh, Hamilton

Raleigh is a residential neighbourhood on the East Mountain, around the numbered East streets such as East 32nd and East 33rd. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. The East Mountain grew quickly after the Second World War. In 1949 the city issued a record 61 building permits at once for homes on East 27th and 28th Streets.

Raleigh is generally bounded by Sherman Access to the north, Upper Gage Avenue to the east, Fennell Avenue to the south and Upper Sherman Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 92 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Raleigh.

Green space in Raleigh includes Peace Memorial Park and Concession / Upper Sherman.

01.W10.0730.t:
Mount Olive-Silverstone-Jamestown, City of Toronto (TRREB district W10)

The area grew from Smithfield, a postal village founded in 1870 at Albion Road and Martin Grove Road to serve the surrounding farms of Etobicoke Township. The neighbourhood name comes from three local streets: Mount Olive, Silverstone and Jamestown. It was urbanized as part of the Rexdale district, mainly from the late 1950s through the 1970s. Etobicoke became part of the amalgamated City of Toronto in 1998.

Mount Olive-Silverstone-Jamestown is generally bounded by the Humber River and the Vaughan boundary to the north, Finch Avenue to the east, the West Humber River and Kipling Avenue to the south and Martin Grove Road to the west, and covers approximately 462 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include surface light rail transit (LRT) tracks. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Mount Olive-Silverstone-Jamestown includes Rowntree Mills Park, West Humber Parkland and Thackeray Park, and the Humber River and the West Humber River run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 10 schools and the Albion branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Martin Grove, Albion, Stevenson and Rowntree Mills LRT stations. Shopping is available at The Albion Centre. Other notable landmarks include Smithfield Park.

05.03.0250.t:
Mineola, Mississauga

Mineola lies between Port Credit and Cooksville in the southern part of the former Toronto Township. The township became the Town of Mississauga in 1968 and the City in 1974. The area was rural until suburban homes were built through the 20th century. Specific history for this community was not found.

Mineola is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the north, Cawthra Road to the east, the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) to the south and the Credit River to the west, and covers approximately 539 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Mineola includes Dellwood Park, Spruce Park and Lyndwood Park, and the Credit River and Cooksville Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools, and transit is provided by the Port Credit GO Station.

04.07.0010.t:
Midland, Midland

Midland lies on Georgian Bay in the historic Huronia (Wendat) region. Before the railway it was a small settlement called Mundy's Bay. In 1871 the Midland Railway chose the site as its new terminus; the town site was surveyed in 1872-73 and the line arrived by 1879. Midland was incorporated as a village in 1878 and as a town in 1890, growing on shipping, lumber and the grain trade.

Midland is generally bounded by Georgian Bay and the Penetanguishene boundary to the north, the Tay boundary to the south and the Tiny boundary to the west, and covers approximately 3,175 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a quarry or aggregate pit, a wastewater treatment plant, a water treatment plant, Lakeview Cemetery, St. Margaret's Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a landfill site. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Midland includes Little Lake Park, Wye Marsh Provincial Wildlife Area and Sainte-Marie Park. The community includes or fronts onto Little Lake and Georgian Bay. Midland Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools and the Midland Public Library. Georgian Bay General Hospital - Midland and Georgian College - Midland Campus are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Huronia Museum and The Castle Village and Enchanted Kindgom Park.

01.W06.0170.t:
Mimico, City of Toronto (TRREB district W06)

Mimico comes from an Ojibwe word meaning roughly 'abundant with wild pigeons', referring to the passenger pigeon. A railway station opened in 1855 and a town plan was filed in 1856, but the area stayed largely rural until the early 20th century. Mimico became a village in 1911 and a town in 1917, with houses built mainly from the 1920s to the 1940s and apartment buildings added in the 1950s and 1960s. It merged into the Borough of Etobicoke in 1967, and Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Mimico is generally bounded by Lake Ontario and the Gardiner Expressway to the east and the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Canpa Subdivision) to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 658 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Oakville Subdivision), Toronto South Detention Centre, a hydro transformer station (Horner TS), VIA Toronto Maintenance Centre, GO Willowbrook Rail Maintenance Facility, a correctional facility, Lakeshore Psychiatric Hospital Cemetery, Christ Church Mimico Memorial Gardens (cemetery) and industrial lands (approximately 30% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Canpa Subdivision) and the Gardiner Expressway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Mimico includes Humber Bay Park East, Humber Bay Park West and Palace Pier Park, and Mimico Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Mimico Centennial branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Mimico GO Station.

04.09.0060.t:
Minesing, Springwater

Minesing is a village in the former Vespra Township, west of Barrie, beside the Minesing Wetlands along the Nottawasaga River. Former settlements such as Josephine and McKinnon once existed in the Minesing Swamp. On January 1, 1994 it became part of the Township of Springwater, formed from Flos and Vespra townships, the villages of Elmvale and Hillsdale, and part of Medonte.

Minesing is generally bounded by Highway 26 to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 93 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Minesing Union Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Minesing branch of the Springwater Public Library.

05.03.0230.t:
Mississauga Valleys, Mississauga

Mississauga Valleys lies in central Mississauga, in the former Toronto Township. The township became the Town of Mississauga in 1968 and the City in 1974. The area was farmland until suburban development in the later decades of the 20th century. Specific history for this community was not found.

Mississauga Valleys is generally bounded by Burnhamthorpe Road to the north, Cawthra Road to the east, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) to the south and Hurontario Street to the west, and covers approximately 359 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Mount Peace Catholic Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and St. John’s Dixie Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Mississauga Valleys includes Mississauga Valley, Stonebrook Park and McKenzie Park, and Cooksville Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Mississauga Valley branch of the Mississauga Library.

07.01.1380.t:
Mohawk, Hamilton

Mohawk is a residential neighbourhood on Hamilton Mountain. The name follows Mohawk Road, which follows an old Indigenous trail across the Mountain. The Mountain was farmland in Barton Township before it was annexed by Hamilton in stages; the last of the township was absorbed in 1960.

Mohawk is generally bounded by Beckett Drive to the north, West 5th Street to the east, Delmar Drive and Governors Boulevard to the south and Garth Street to the west, and covers approximately 94 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Mohawk.

Residents are served by one school. St. Joseph's Healthcare Hamilton and Mohawk College are also located in the community.

05.01.0060.t:
Mono Mills, Caledon

Mono Mills is a hamlet in north Caledon, just south of the Town of Mono boundary. It began in the 1820s, and its post office opened in 1839. The name combines its location partly in Mono Township with the grist mill that once operated there. By the 1870s the mill supported a wagon works, stores and hotels, and the hamlet became part of Caledon in 1974.

Mono Mills is generally bounded by Highway 9 to the north and Airport Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 101 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Mono Mills.

Green space in Mono Mills includes Lions Park, Victoria Park and John W. Nichols Community Park.

04.16.0020.t:
Moonstone, Oro-Medonte

Moonstone is an unincorporated rural community in the former Medonte Township, which was incorporated in 1850. The townships of Oro and Medonte were incorporated in 1850 and were amalgamated, with the Hawkestone Police Village, to form the Township of Oro-Medonte on January 1, 1994. The community is known for the nearby Mount St. Louis Moonstone ski resort.

Moonstone is generally bounded by Moonstone Road to the east and Oro-Medonte Line 7 and Valleyview Drive to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 115 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Moonstone.

Other notable landmarks include Mount St. Louis Moonstone.

04.02.0080.t:
New Lowell, Clearview

New Lowell is a village in the former Sunnidale Township, in the east part of Clearview Township. A timber plant owned by Jacques and Hay operated there in the 19th century. Clearview Township was formed on January 1, 1994, by merging the Town of Stayner, the Village of Creemore and the townships of Nottawasaga and Sunnidale. New Lowell remains a small village surrounded by farmland and forest.

New Lowell is generally bounded by County Road 10 to the east and Coates Creek and Concession 5 Sunnidale Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 545 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and New Lowell United Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in New Lowell includes New Lowell Recreation Park and New Lowell Conservation Area, and Coates Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Sunnidale branch of the Clearview Public Library.

07.01.1610.t:
Rolston, Hamilton

Rolston is a residential neighbourhood on the west Hamilton Mountain. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most homes were built between 1961 and 1980, with some added in the 1980s and 1990s.

Rolston is generally bounded by Mohawk Road to the north, West 5th Street to the east, the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the south and Garth Street to the west, and covers approximately 129 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rolston includes Captain Cornelius Park, Newlands Park and King's Mead Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

01.C10.0770.t:
Mount Pleasant East, City of Toronto (TRREB district C10)

The area lies east of Mount Pleasant Road and is part of the Davisville area. Davisville was founded by John Davis in 1840, who opened the first post office and the Davisville Pottery. Davisville joined the Town of North Toronto in 1890, which was annexed to the City of Toronto in 1912. Many single-family homes were built in the 1920s and 1930s.

Mount Pleasant East is generally bounded by Mount Pleasant Road and Blythwood Road to the north, Bayview Avenue to the east, Moore Avenue to the south and Kay Gardiner Beltline Trail to the west, and covers approximately 309 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Mount Pleasant Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Davisville Yard and Mount Hope Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Mount Pleasant East includes Sherwood Park, Glebe Manor Square East and Charlotte Maher Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Mount Pleasant branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Leaside and Mount Pleasant LRT stations.

01.E09.1130.t:
Morningside, City of Toronto (TRREB district E09)

Morningside takes its name from Morningside Avenue and is also known as Seven Oaks. The land was farmland in Scarborough Township, established in 1850. It was built up as part of Scarborough's suburban growth in the second half of the 20th century. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Morningside is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Morningside Avenue to the east, West Highland Creek and Orton Park Road to the south and Highland Creek and Scarborough Golf Club Road to the west, and covers approximately 561 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and a hydro transformer station (Ellesmere TS). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Morningside includes Morningside Park, Ellesmere Greenspace and Seven Oaks Park, and Highland Creek, Ellesmere Creek and West Highland Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools. Scarborough Health Network - Centenary Hospital is also located in the community.

01.C08.0950.t:
Moss Park, City of Toronto (TRREB district C08)
