The area is named after the Moss Park estate of the Allan family, including William Allan, whose mansion stood on Sherbourne Street between Queen and Shuter Streets. Much of the area was built to house workers in the industrial district to the south. In the 1960s, urban renewal cleared older housing, and the Moss Park public housing towers were built on the former estate.

Moss Park is generally bounded by Parliament Street and Carlton Street to the north, Queen Street to the east, Eastern Avenue and Front Street to the south and Jarvis Street to the west, and covers approximately 145 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision) and the Don Valley Parkway lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Moss Park includes Allan Gardens, Moss Park and Underpass Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools, the Parliament Street branch of the Toronto Public Library and the St. Lawrence branch of the Toronto Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Toronto Police - 51 Division and Allan Gardens Conservatory.

01.W04.0350.t:
Mount Dennis, City of Toronto (TRREB district W04)

Mount Dennis is named after the Dennis family, Loyalist shipbuilders led by John Dennis, who owned land and a boatyard on the Humber River around 1800. The area, in York Township, stayed largely rural with orchards and gravel and clay pits until Kodak Canada moved its plant to Eglinton Avenue and Weston Road in 1913. Workers then built their own modest houses, and the area urbanized further in the 1950s. It was part of the City of York until amalgamation into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Mount Dennis is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) and Sidney Belsey Crescent to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) to the east, Lambton Avenue to the south and the Humber River and Eglinton Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 207 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), St. John's on the Humber Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) and Eglinton Maintenance and Storage Facility. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Mount Dennis includes Eglinton Flats and Fergy Brown Park, and the Humber River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Mount Dennis branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Mount Dennis GO Station. West Park Healthcare Centre is also located in the community.

07.01.0180.t:
Mount Hope, Hamilton

Mount Hope is a village in the former Glanford Township, founded in the 1800s. An air force airfield opened beside it in 1940 and became a civilian airport in 1963; it is now John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport. Glanford merged with Binbrook to form the Township of Glanbrook in 1974, which joined the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Mount Hope is generally bounded by Airport Road to the north and Chippewa Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 662 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 6. Along or just beyond its edges are John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Mount Hope includes Mount Hope Park and Southampton Estates Park, and the Welland River runs through or along the community. Southern Pines Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Mount Hope branch of the Hamilton Public Library. Other notable landmarks include John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport and Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum.

06.02.0070.t:
Mountainside, Burlington

Mountainside is in north-central Burlington, north of the Queen Elizabeth Way, with the Niagara Escarpment as its backdrop. It was first called Mountain Gardens; 'Mountain' refers to the escarpment. The neighbourhood was developed in the 1950s, around the time Burlington annexed Nelson Township in 1958.

Mountainside is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, Guelph Line to the east and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the south, and covers approximately 447 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW), Highway 403 and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Mountainside includes Mountainside Park, Roly Bird Park and Clarksdale Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools. Other notable landmarks include Mountain Gardens Public School and M.M. Robinson High School.

07.01.1360.t:
Mountview, Hamilton

Mountview is a residential neighbourhood on the west side of the Hamilton Mountain. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most homes were built between 1961 and 1980, with some newer housing added in the 1990s and early 2000s.

Mountview is generally bounded by Scenic Drive to the north, Sanatorium Road to the east, Mohawk Road to the south and a hydro corridor to the west, and covers approximately 161 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Mountview includes Scenic Drive Park and Mountview Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.08.0050.t:
Mt Albert, East Gwillimbury

Mount Albert began in 1821, when Quaker settlers Samuel and Rufus Birchard bought land in the area. The settlement was first called Birchardville and was later renamed Mount Albert after the 1860 royal visit to Upper Canada. By 1850 a village had formed, with grist, flour, woollen and lumber mills on Mount Albert Creek. Suburban growth began in the 1970s, with newer subdivisions added from the mid-1990s onward.

Mt Albert is generally bounded by Ninth Line to the east and Highway 48 and the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision) to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 371 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Mt Albert includes Ross Family Complex and Library, Cupples Farm Park and Millenium Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Mount Albert branch of the East Gwillimbury Public Library.

07.01.1180.t:
Nashdale, Hamilton

Nashdale is a residential area in the east end of Hamilton, near Nash Road. It lies on land that was once part of Barton Township, which Hamilton annexed in stages until the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Specific records on the naming and build-out of the neighbourhood were not found.

Nashdale is generally bounded by Redhill Creek and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the north, Centennial Parkway to the east, Barton Street to the south and the Red Hill Valley Parkway to the west, and covers approximately 125 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), the Red Hill Valley Parkway and industrial lands (approximately 53% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and Eastlawn Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Redhill Creek runs through or along the community. Transit is provided by the Confederation GO Station.

01.C14.0520.t:
Newtonbrook East, City of Toronto (TRREB district C14)

Newtonbrook takes its name from the Newton Brook Wesleyan Methodist church, named after Reverend Robert Newton. European settlement began in the early 1800s, with saw and grist mills on the branches of the Don River. The area was farmland in York Township and became part of North York in 1922. It was subdivided for large-scale housing in the 1950s and joined the City of Toronto at amalgamation in 1998.

Newtonbrook East is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Bayview Avenue to the east, Finch Avenue to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 408 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Newtonbrook East includes Lillian Park, Silverview Park and Bayview Arena Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools, and transit is provided by the Finch subway station. Sunnybrook - St. John's Rehab Hospital is also located in the community.

07.01.1470.t:
Red Hill, Hamilton

Red Hill is a mainly residential neighbourhood in east Hamilton, named for the Red Hill Creek valley. Red Hill Creek runs approximately 7 km from Albion Falls on the Escarpment to Windermere Basin on Hamilton Harbour. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most homes were built between 1961 and 1980.

Red Hill is generally bounded by King Street and Redhill Creek to the north, a hydro corridor and Mount Albion Road to the south and the Red Hill Valley Parkway to the west, and covers approximately 121 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision) and the Red Hill Valley Parkway. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Red Hill includes Glen Castle Park and Hixon Road Park, and Redhill Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

01.W06.0180.t:
New Toronto, City of Toronto (TRREB district W06)

New Toronto was planned in 1890 as an industrial town on farmland along the Lake Ontario shore in Etobicoke Township. The Grand Trunk Railway's Mimico Yard opened in 1906 and drew more industry, but little housing was built until after the First World War. New Toronto was incorporated as a village in 1913 and a town in 1920, and grew steadily through the 1920s to 1950s. It joined the Borough of Etobicoke in 1967, and Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

New Toronto is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) to the north, Dwight Avenue to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Twenty Second Street and Twenty Third Street to the west, and covers approximately 334 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the R. L. Clark Water Treatment Plant, VIA Toronto Maintenance Centre and industrial lands (approximately 17% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) and GO Willowbrook Rail Maintenance Facility. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in New Toronto includes Colonel Samuel Smith Park, Don Russell Memorial Park and Prince of Wales Park. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the New Toronto branch of the Toronto Public Library. Humber Polytechnic - Lakeshore Campus and Humber Polytechnic - Lakeshore Campus West are also located in the community.

10.08.0050.t:
Newcastle, Clarington

Newcastle is a community in the former Clarke Township, near the Lake Ontario shore. Its post office opened in 1845, and it was incorporated in 1856. It became part of the Town of Newcastle in 1974, and the municipality was renamed Clarington in the early 1990s partly to avoid confusion with the village. Newcastle stayed small until the 1990s, when new residential development brought rapid growth.

Newcastle is generally bounded by Highway 35 and Arthur Street to the north, the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) to the east and Lake Ontario and Graham Creek to the south, and covers approximately 862 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), Highway 401 and the Newcastle Water Pollution Control Plant. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 35. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Newcastle includes Samuel Wilmot Nature Area, Newcastle Community Park and Port of Newcastle Park, and Wilmot Creek, Graham Creek and Foster Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Newcastle branch of the Clarington Public Library.

09.07.0100.t:
Newmarket Industrial Park, Newmarket

Newmarket Industrial Park is an employment area of the Town of Newmarket. Newmarket was settled by Quakers between 1801 and 1803 and grew as a mill and market town on the Holland River. It became a town in 1880 and has grown considerably since York Region was formed in 1971.

Newmarket Industrial Park is generally bounded by the East Gwillimbury boundary to the north, Davis Drive to the east and Highway 404 and Leslie Street to the south, and covers approximately 364 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 404 and industrial lands (approximately 52% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Newmarket Industrial Park is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

01.C07.0510.t:
Newtonbrook West, City of Toronto (TRREB district C07)

Newtonbrook takes its name from the Newton Brook Wesleyan church, named after Reverend Robert Newton. The area was settled in the early 1800s, with saw and grist mills on branches of the Don River. It was part of York Township, then North York from 1922. The area was subdivided for large residential developments in the 1950s and joined the City of Toronto in 1998.

Newtonbrook West is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Yonge Street to the east, Finch Avenue to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 470 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a hydro transformer station (Fairchild TS) and Bathurst Lawn Memorial Park (cemetery). Along or just beyond its edges are Beth Tzedec Memorial Park (cemetery). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Newtonbrook West includes Goulding Park, Hendon Park and Lissom Park. Residents are served by approximately 10 schools, and transit is provided by the Finch subway station. Shopping is available at Centerpoint Mall.

01.C01.0990.t:
Niagara, City of Toronto (TRREB district C01)

The area takes its name from Niagara Street, laid out along the banks of the now-buried Garrison Creek. In the late 1700s it was part of the Fort York military reserve. Railways crossed the area from the 1850s, and it became an industrial district through the late 1800s and early 1900s. Since the 2000s, former factory lands such as Liberty Village have been redeveloped with condominiums, offices and shops.

Niagara is generally bounded by Queen Street to the north, Bathurst Street to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and the Gardiner Expressway to the west, and covers approximately 302 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Union Station Rail Corridor rail line, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Galt Subdivision), the Gardiner Expressway, a rail yard, a hydro transformer station (Strachan TS) and Strachan Avenue Burying Ground. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Niagara includes Coronation Park, Garrison Common and Stanley Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools, and transit is provided by the Exhibition GO Station. Centre For Addiction and Mental Health - Queen Street Site is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Fort York National Historic Site and Liberty Village.

09.01.0020.t:
Nobleton, King

Nobleton is named after Joseph Noble, an early settler and tavern keeper. It was first settled in 1812 at a crossroads between King City and Bolton. Slow urban growth began in the 1950s and 1960s, with housing added in the north in the 1990s and 2000s. Growth increased after a new wastewater system was built.

Nobleton is generally bounded by Sideroad 15 to the north, 8th Concession to the east, the Vaughan boundary to the south and 10th Concession to the west, and covers approximately 1,470 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Nobleton Community Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Nobleton includes Tasca Park, Sports Park and Hill Farm Meadow, and the East Humber River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Nobleton branch of the King Township Public Library.

01.C08.0920.t:
North St. James Town, City of Toronto (TRREB district C08)

The area grew in the 1800s as a middle-class district of houses. In the 1950s it was rezoned, and many older homes were replaced with apartment towers following the 'towers in the park' idea. Towers were built from 1959 to the late 1960s, and the population rose from 862 in 1961 to 11,462 in 1971. A planned expansion south of Wellesley Street was stopped in the late 1960s.

North St. James Town is generally bounded by Bloor Street to the north, Parliament Street to the east, Wellesley Street to the south and Jarvis Street and Ted Rogers Way to the west, and covers approximately 42 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but St. James Cemetery and Crematorium lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in North St. James Town includes Wellesley - Magill Park and Dr. Gordon Chong park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the St. James Town branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Sherbourne subway station.

04.16.0100.t:
Prices Corners, Oro-Medonte

Prices Corners is a rural crossroads community in the Township of Oro-Medonte. The townships of Oro and Medonte were incorporated in 1850 and were amalgamated, with the Hawkestone Police Village, to form the Township of Oro-Medonte on January 1, 1994. The area was settled for farming in the 19th century.

Prices Corners is generally bounded by Price Drive to the north, Highway 12 to the east and Broadview Avenue to the south, and covers approximately 62 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 12. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Prices Corners is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

07.01.1020.t:
North End, Hamilton

The North End is one of the oldest parts of Hamilton, lying between the CN rail line and Hamilton Harbour, west of Wellington Street. It grew in the 1800s with the port and the James Street North corridor and became a working-class area settled by Irish, Italian and later Portuguese immigrants. The city built low-income family housing here in the 1960s. West Harbour GO Station opened at its southern edge in 2015, and waterfront redevelopment plans followed in 2018.

North End is generally bounded by Wellington Street to the east, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) to the south and Lake Ontario to the west, and covers approximately 160 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 7% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line, the CN rail line and Hamilton-Wentworth Detention Centre. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in North End includes Bayfront Park, Eastwood Park and Waterfront Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the West Harbour branch of the Hamilton Public Library, and transit is provided by the West Harbour GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Pier 4 Park.

09.04.0050.t:
North Richvale, Richmond Hill

North Richvale is part of Richvale, a residential area in southwest Richmond Hill, lying north of Carrville Road. The land was farmland outside the old village and became part of Richmond Hill with the 1971 municipal expansion. It was developed mostly with detached homes in the later 20th century.

North Richvale is generally bounded by Major MacKenzie Drive to the north, Yonge Street to the east, Carrville Road to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 434 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of North Richvale.

Green space in North Richvale includes Richvale Athletic Park, Richvale Greenway North and Mt. Pleasant Park, and Patterson Creek and East Patterson Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Central branch of the Richmond Hill Public Library. Shopping is available at Hillcrest Mall.

01.E01.1350.t:
North Riverdale, City of Toronto (TRREB district E01)

Riverdale is named for its position on the east bank of the Don River valley. The area, then called Riverside and Don Mount, was annexed to the City of Toronto in 1884. North Riverdale, between Danforth Avenue and Gerrard Street, was largely built up with Victorian and Edwardian homes in the late 1800s and early 1900s. The opening of the Prince Edward Viaduct in 1918 further encouraged growth along the Danforth.

North Riverdale is generally bounded by Danforth Avenue to the north, Pape Avenue to the east, Gerrard Street to the south and the Don River and the Don Valley Parkway to the west, and covers approximately 176 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the Don Valley Parkway. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (Gerrard TS), a hydro transformer station (Carlaw TS) and Toronto Necropolis Cemetery & Crematorium. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in North Riverdale includes Riverdale Park East, Withrow Park and Hubbard Park. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Riverdale branch of the Toronto Public Library. Hennick Bridgepoint Hospital is also located in the community.

04.15.0170.t:
North Shore, Barrie

North Shore runs along the north side of Kempenfelt Bay, east of downtown Barrie. Barrie grew from a supply depot at the end of the Nine Mile Portage and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a village in 1854, a town in 1871 and a city in 1959. The area includes older homes near downtown and newer housing further east along the shoreline.

North Shore is generally bounded by Blake Street to the north, Penetanguishene Road to the east and Lake Simcoe to the south, and covers approximately 254 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of North Shore.

Green space in North Shore includes Shoreview Park, St Vincent Park and Kempenfelt Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe.

04.02.0020.t:
Nottawa, Clearview

Nottawa is a small village in the former Nottawasaga Township, south of Collingwood. Nottawasaga Township was incorporated in 1851 and was settled mostly for farming. Clearview Township was formed on January 1, 1994, by merging the Town of Stayner, the Village of Creemore and the townships of Nottawasaga and Sunnidale. Nottawa remains a small village surrounded by farmland.

The boundary of Nottawa follows local streets, lot lines and natural features rather than major roads, and the community covers approximately 349 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Nottawa includes McKean Memorial Park, and the Pretty River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

05.03.0280.t:
Northeast, Mississauga

Northeast is mainly an industrial and business area in the northeast part of the former Toronto Township, near Toronto Pearson International Airport. The township became the Town of Mississauga in 1968 and the City in 1974. Farmland and small crossroads hamlets, such as Mount Charles at Derry and Dixie roads, gave way to industry as the airport area grew. Specific history for this community was limited.

Northeast is generally bounded by a hydro corridor to the north, Highway 427 and Derry Road to the east, Highway 401 and Etobicoke Creek to the south and Highway 410 and Highway 403 to the west, and covers approximately 5,337 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Pearson Subdivision), Highway 401, Highway 403, a hydro transformer station (Tomken TS), Toronto Pearson International Airport, Malport Yard, Assumption Catholic Cemetery and Crematorium, Moore's Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 44% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and Highway 427. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Northeast includes Paul Coffey Park, Edward Scarlett Park and King Park, and Etobicoke Creek, Little Etobicoke Creek and Mimico Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools, and transit is provided by the Malton GO Station. Fire and Emergency Services Training Institute is also located in the community.

10.05.0050.t:
Northeast Ajax, Ajax

This community covers northeastern Ajax, formerly farmland in Pickering Township, including the area around the old hamlet of Audley, which was a stopover in the mid-19th century. Ajax was named after the Royal Navy cruiser HMS Ajax, and grew from a Second World War munitions plant and its workers' village built on farmland in Pickering Township from 1939. It became a town in 1955 and joined the Regional Municipality of Durham in 1974, when its boundaries were expanded to include Pickering Village, Pickering Beach and Audley. Most housing in north Ajax was built from the 1990s onward.

Northeast Ajax is generally bounded by a hydro corridor and 5th Concession Road to the north, Lake Ridge Road to the east, Rossland Road to the south and Harwood Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 1,325 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Northeast Ajax includes Pan Am Games Ajax Ballpark. Deer Creek Golf Course - North and Deer Creek Golf Course - South are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Audley branch of the Ajax Public Library.

05.02.0320.t:
Northgate, Brampton

Northgate is a residential area in the northern part of Bramalea in east Brampton. Bramalea was developed from the late 1950s and 1960s as a planned satellite town in the former Chinguacousy Township by Bramalea Limited, with streets named in alphabetical phases. Bramalea was part of Chinguacousy Township until it became part of the City of Brampton in 1974. Housing in the area was built from the 1960s onward.

Northgate is generally bounded by Bovaird Drive to the north, Torbram Road to the east, Queen Street to the south and Bramalea Road to the west, and covers approximately 425 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Harrison's United Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Northgate includes Professor's Lake Park, Jefferson Park and Greenbriar Park South. The community includes or fronts onto Professors Lake. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools.

10.07.0060.t:
Northglen, Oshawa

Northglen is in the north end of Oshawa and takes its name from its northern, ravine-like setting. The land was part of Whitby Township from the 1790s and later East Whitby Township, and was farmland and woodlots for most of its history. Scattered rural homes appeared on roads such as Thornton Road North and Conlin Road from the mid-1950s. The area became part of the City of Oshawa when East Whitby Township was merged into the city in 1974.

Northglen is generally bounded by Taunton Road to the north, Oshawa Creek to the east and Rossland Road to the south, and covers approximately 421 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Oshawa Executive Airport and Thornton Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Northglen includes Rose Valley Park, Brookside Park and Deer Valley Park, and Goodman Creek runs through or along the community. Oshawa Airport Golf Club and Durham Golf are located in the area. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Ontario Regiment Museum (Oshawa Executive Airport).

04.15.0010.t:
Northwest, Barrie

Northwest is an area in northwest Barrie, west of the older city core near Highway 400. Barrie grew from a supply depot at the end of the Nine Mile Portage and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a village in 1854, a town in 1871 and a city in 1959. The area was developed mainly in the later 20th century.

Northwest is generally bounded by Livingstone Street to the north, Burns Circle and Irwin Drive to the east and the Springwater boundary and Benson Drive to the west, and covers approximately 105 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Barrie Landfill Borrows Area (landfill) and Barrie Union Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Northwest includes Cloughley Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

10.05.0010.t:
Northwest Ajax, Ajax

This community covers northwestern Ajax, formerly farmland in Pickering Township near the Duffins Creek valley. Ajax was named after the Royal Navy cruiser HMS Ajax, and grew from a Second World War munitions plant and its workers' village built on farmland in Pickering Township from 1939. It became a town in 1955 and joined the Regional Municipality of Durham in 1974, when its boundaries were expanded to include Pickering Village, Pickering Beach and Audley. Most housing in north Ajax was built from the 1990s onward.

Northwest Ajax is generally bounded by 5th Concession Road to the north, Harwood Avenue to the east, Rossland Road to the south and a hydro corridor and the Pickering boundary to the west, and covers approximately 1,309 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), Brock South Landfill (landfill) and Pine Ridge Memorial Gardens (cemetery). Along or just beyond its edges are Brock North Landfill (landfill) and Duffin Meadows Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Northwest Ajax includes Greenwood Conservation Area, and Duffins Creek runs through or along the community. Fox Run Golf Centre is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

01.E03.1240.t:
O'Connor-Parkview, City of Toronto (TRREB district E03)

O'Connor-Parkview takes its name from O'Connor Drive and the Parkview Hills area, and includes the smaller communities of Topham Park, Woodbine Gardens and Parkview Hills. The land was part of York Township and became part of East York in 1924. It was largely built up in the 1940s and 1950s, including housing built for returning veterans around Topham Park. East York joined the City of Toronto in 1998.

O'Connor-Parkview is generally bounded by the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision) to the north, Victoria Park Avenue to the east, Taylor Massey Creek to the south and Taylor-Massey Creek and the Don River West Branch to the west, and covers approximately 461 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision), the Don Valley Parkway and industrial lands (approximately 12% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in O'Connor-Parkview includes Taylor Creek Park, E. T. Seton Park and Topham Park, and Taylor-Massey Creek, the Don River East Branch and Taylor Massey Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Dawes Road branch of the Toronto Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Don Valley (northwest edge).

05.02.0010.t:
Northwest Brampton, Brampton

Northwest Brampton includes Mount Pleasant, which began as the farming hamlet of Pleasant around Bovaird Drive and Creditview Road in Chinguacousy Township. It became part of Brampton in 1974, and the name Mount Pleasant came into use in the 1990s. Much of the area stayed farmland until the mid-2000s, when Mount Pleasant GO Station opened in 2005 and a transit-oriented community was built around it.

Northwest Brampton is generally bounded by Mayfield Road to the north, Wanless Drive and Creditview Road to the east, the Credit River and Mississauga Road to the south and Winston Churchill Boulevard to the west, and covers approximately 2,608 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), Cemetery of Saint Elias Church and Alloa Methodist Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Huttonville Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Northwest Brampton includes Creditview Sandalwood Park, Robert Post Park and Jim Irons Park, and the Credit River runs through or along the community. Golf Academy is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Mount Pleasant Village branch of the Brampton Library, and transit is provided by the Mount Pleasant GO Station.

10.07.0050.t:
Northwood, Oshawa

Northwood is in the north end of Oshawa, and its name refers to its northern, wooded ravine setting. The land was part of Whitby Township from the 1790s and later East Whitby Township, and was used for farms and woodlots. Rural homes were built from the mid-1950s, followed by the Bickle subdivision in the mid-1960s. The area joined the City of Oshawa in 1974, and the Durham College campus (opened 1967) covers much of its northern part.

Northwood is generally bounded by Oshawa Creek and the Whitby boundary to the north and Taunton Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 482 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and industrial lands (approximately 10% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407 ETR and Oshawa Executive Airport. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Other notable landmarks include Durham College and Ontario Tech University (north campus).

05.02.0070.t:
Northwood Park, Brampton

Northwood Park is an established residential area in west Brampton, north of Queen Street West near McLaughlin Road and Chinguacousy Road. Brampton was laid out in 1834 at Buffy's Corners and named after Brampton in Cumberland, England. It became a village in 1853 and a town in 1873. Most homes in the area were built from the 1960s onward, largely bungalows and two-storey houses on larger lots.

Northwood Park is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and Williams Parkway to the north, McLaughlin Road to the east, Queen Street to the south and Chinguacousy Road to the west, and covers approximately 250 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 12% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transformer station (Mount Pleasant TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Northwood Park includes Major William Sharpe Park, Cowton Family Meadow and Castlehill Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

10.07.0120.t:
O'Neill, Oshawa

O'Neill is named after Albert O'Neill, a long-serving principal of O'Neill Collegiate and Vocational Institute on Simcoe Street North. The school was founded in 1909 as Oshawa High School. The neighbourhood lies just north of downtown and is one of Oshawa's oldest residential areas, with many homes from the early 1900s and pockets of mid-century bungalows and split-levels. Its growth followed the expansion of the McLaughlin carriage and automobile works and General Motors in the early 20th century.

O'Neill is generally bounded by Rossland Road to the north, Wilson Road to the east, King Street to the south and Oshawa Creek to the west, and covers approximately 463 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in O'Neill includes Alexandra Park, Centennial Park and Woodview Park, and Oshawa Creek runs through or along the community. Oshawa Golf & Curling Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools. Lakeridge Health Oshawa is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Parkwood Estate (National Historic Site).

09.04.0010.t:
Oak Ridges, Richmond Hill

Oak Ridges began in 1799 as the Windham settlement of French Royalists along Yonge Street. By 1840 the area was known as Oak Ridges, and from 1896 to 1927 it had a station on the Schomberg and Aurora Railway. It was annexed to Richmond Hill from King and Whitchurch townships in 1971. Housing grew from the 1950s, with large subdivisions built in the 1990s.

Oak Ridges is generally bounded by Bloomington Road to the north, Yonge Street to the east and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 652 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Oak Ridges.

Green space in Oak Ridges includes Oak Ridges Corridor Conservation Reserve, Russell Tilt Park and Oak Ridges Meadows. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Oak Ridges branch of the Richmond Hill Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Bond Lake.

09.04.0070.t:
Oak Ridges Lake Wilcox, Richmond Hill

This area surrounds Lake Wilcox, the largest kettle lake in the Oak Ridges area and its original centre of settlement. Cottage and housing development began around the lake in the 1950s. It was annexed to Richmond Hill from King and Whitchurch townships in 1971, with further subdivisions added from the 1990s.

Oak Ridges Lake Wilcox is generally bounded by Bloomington Road to the north, Bayview Avenue to the east and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 676 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Oak Ridges Lake Wilcox.

Green space in Oak Ridges Lake Wilcox includes Oak Ridges Corridor Conservation Reserve, Lake Wilcox Park and William Bond Park, and the East Humber River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Wilcox Lake. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

01.E06.1300.t:
Oakridge, City of Toronto (TRREB district E06)

Oakridge lies in the southwest corner of the former Scarborough Township (established 1850), along Danforth Road and Danforth Avenue east of Victoria Park. Most of its homes were built between the two world wars and after the Second World War. Scarborough joined Metropolitan Toronto in 1953 and the City of Toronto in 1998.

Oakridge is generally bounded by Taylor Massey Creek and Warden Avenue to the north, Mack Avenue to the east, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) to the south and Victoria Park Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 183 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and a hydro transformer station (Warden TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Oakridge includes Warden Woods Park, Cataraqui Park and Fir Valley Woods Park, and Taylor Massey Creek runs through or along the community. Dentonia Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools, and transit is provided by the Victoria Park subway station. Other notable landmarks include Danforth Avenue.

07.01.0040.t:
Orkney, Hamilton

Orkney is a small rural community in the Flamborough area of Hamilton. The surrounding land was surveyed after Treaty No. 3 in 1792 and organized into the townships of Beverly, East Flamborough and West Flamborough. These townships merged with Waterdown to form the Township of Flamborough in 1974, which became a town in 1985 and was amalgamated into the City of Hamilton in 2001. The area remains largely agricultural.

Orkney is generally bounded by Orkney Road to the north, Concession 2 to the east and Beverlyglen Drive to the west, and covers approximately 44 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Orkney.

Orkney is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

09.09.0080.t:
Pefferlaw, Georgina

Pefferlaw was founded in the late 1820s by Captain William Johnson, a former Royal Navy officer. By 1832 he had built a sawmill, a woollen mill and a gristmill on the river, and the first store opened in 1833. The name was suggested by Johnson's brother, after a field on their old family homestead. The Canadian Northern railway arrived in approximately 1906, and the village became part of the Town of Georgina in 1971.

Pefferlaw is generally bounded by Lake Simcoe to the north, Lake Ridge Road to the east and Weir's Sideroad to the west, and covers approximately 3,231 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Pefferlaw includes Pefferlaw Tract, Duclos Point Provincial Park and Cronsberry Tract, and the Pefferlaw River and Pefferlaw Brook run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. Pines of Georgina Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by the Pefferlaw branch of the Georgina Public Library.

01.C03.0720.t:
Oakwood Village, City of Toronto (TRREB district C03)

The area takes its name from Oakwood Avenue and was formerly known as Oakwood-Vaughan. It was part of York Township and later the City of York. Stephen Rogers built one of the first houses at what is now Rogers Road and Oakwood Avenue. The area grew as a streetcar suburb in the early 1900s and became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Oakwood Village is generally bounded by Eglinton Avenue to the north, Winnett Avenue and Arlington Avenue to the east, St. Clair Avenue to the south and Dufferin Street to the west, and covers approximately 235 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Oakwood Village.

Green space in Oakwood Village includes Fairbank Memorial Park, Graham Park and Roseneath Park. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools and the Oakwood Village branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Fairbank and Oakwood LRT stations. Other notable landmarks include Five Points (Oakwood, Vaughan and Belvidere intersection).

09.04.0110.t:
Observatory, Richmond Hill

Observatory is named after the David Dunlap Observatory. Alexander Marsh farmed the land from 1815, and in 1932 Jessie Donalda Dunlap donated it to the University of Toronto in memory of her husband David Dunlap. The observatory opened in 1935 and closed as a university facility in 2007. Most housing dates from the 1980s and 1990s, with newer development on part of the former observatory lands.

Observatory is generally bounded by Weldrick Road to the north, Bayview Avenue to the east, 16th Avenue to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 213 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Observatory includes David Dunlop Observatory Park, Bridgeview Park and Gapper Park, and German Mills Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.03.0300.t:
Old Markham Village, Markham

Old Markham Village is the historic core of Markham, founded by Mennonite settlers after 1804 and first known as Reesorville after the Reesor family. It took the name Markham in 1825 and grew around saw, grist and woollen mills on the Rouge River. It was incorporated as a village in 1872 and joined the Town of Markham in 1971; Main Street keeps many 19th- and early 20th-century buildings.

Old Markham Village is generally bounded by the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision) and 16th Avenue to the north, Mount Joy Creek to the east and Highway 7 to the south, and covers approximately 126 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are Elmwood Cemetery and St. Andrew's Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Old Markham Village includes Morgan Park and Tannery Pond Park. Residents are served by one school, and transit is provided by the Markham GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Main Street Markham.

10.08.0040.t:
Orono, Clarington

Orono is a village in the former Clarke Township, north of Highway 401. It was founded in 1832, and its post office opened in 1852. It was named after Orono, Maine, because the landscape seemed similar. Orono was the seat of Clarke Township government before the township became part of Clarington in 1974.

Orono is generally bounded by Taunton Road to the north and Highway 35 to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 207 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 35. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Orono includes Orono Park and Peters Pike Parkette. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Jungle Cat World.

03.08.0010.t:
Orangeville, Orangeville

Orangeville is named after Orange Lawrence, a Connecticut-born businessman who settled there in 1844 and owned several mills. The first land patent in the area was issued in 1820, and a post office opened in 1851. Orangeville became a village in 1863 and a town in 1874. It is the seat of Dufferin County.

Orangeville is generally bounded by the Mono boundary and County Road 16 to the north, the Caledon boundary and Hurontario Street to the east, Caledon East Garafraxa Road and Town Line to the south and County Road 23 to the west, and covers approximately 1,565 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 10, the Orangeville Water Pollution Control Plant and industrial lands (approximately 9% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Orangeville Greenwood Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Orangeville includes Orangeville Lions Sports Park, Princess of Wales Park and EveryKidsPark, and Mill Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Island Lake. Residents are served by approximately 13 schools, the Alder Street branch of the Orangeville Public Library and the Mill Street branch of the Orangeville Public Library. Shopping is available at Orangeville Mall. Headwaters Health Care Centre - Dufferin is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Broadway historic main street.

06.02.0190.t:
Orchard, Burlington

Orchard is in east Burlington, entered from Appleby Line, with Bronte Creek Provincial Park on its eastern edge. As the name suggests, it was a fruit orchard farm run by the Dryden family, and the main street, Dryden, is named after them. The family farmed the land until the 1990s, when the present neighbourhood was built.

Orchard is generally bounded by Dundas Street to the north, Bronte Creek to the east, Upper Middle Road to the south and Appleby Line to the west, and covers approximately 301 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Orchard includes Bronte Creek Provincial Park, Orchard Community Park and Pathfinder Park, and Sheldon Creek and Bronte Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools.

04.17.0010.t:
Orillia, Orillia

The name Orillia is most often linked to the Spanish word orilla, meaning shore, and was first recorded in 1820. The site at the Narrows between Lake Simcoe and Lake Couchiching was a Huron-Wendat and later Ojibwe settlement, and Samuel de Champlain visited the area in 1615. The town site was laid out in 1840, and Orillia became a village in 1867, a town in 1875 and a city in 1969. It grew as a commercial centre, manufacturing town and summer resort.

Orillia is generally bounded by Lake Couchiching and Oro-Medonte Line 15 to the north and Lake Simcoe to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 7,963 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 11, Highway 12, Waste Diversion Site (landfill), Wastewater Treatment Centre, a hydro transformer station, Saint Andrew's - Saint James Cemetery, Saint Michael's Roman Catholic Cemetery and Huronia Regional Centre Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Orillia includes Scout Valley, Tudhope Park and Kitchener Park, and Trent-Severn Waterway runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe and Lake Couchiching. Couchiching Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 12 schools and the Orillia Public Library. Orillia Soldiers' Memorial Hospital, Lakehead University - Orillia Campus and Georgian College - Orillia Campus are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Stephen Leacock Museum.

04.15.0300.t:
Painswick South, Barrie

Painswick South is the southern part of the Painswick area in south Barrie, named after the early settlement of Painswick in Innisfil Township, where the Warnica family settled in 1823. Much of Barrie's south end was part of Innisfil Township until January 1, 1982, when approximately 8,623 acres were annexed to the city. The area was built up with suburban housing mainly from the 1990s onward. Barrie South GO Station opened on Yonge Street in 2007.

Painswick South is generally bounded by Big Bay Point Road to the north, Mapleview Drive and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the east and Lovers Creek to the west, and covers approximately 409 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Painswick South includes Lennox Park, Shalom Park and J. Gibbons Park, and Lovers Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Painswick branch of the Barrie Public Library, and transit is provided by the Barrie South GO Station.

05.01.0080.t:
Palgrave, Caledon

Palgrave is a village in northeast Caledon, near the Humber River. It was first called Buckstown, after the manager of the Western Hotel built in 1846, and was renamed Palgrave in 1869. The Hamilton and North-Western Railway ran through the village from 1877. It became part of the Town of Caledon in 1974.

Palgrave is generally bounded by Highway 9 to the north, the King boundary and Caledon King Town Line to the east and Highway 50 to the west, and covers approximately 3,950 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) and Morningside Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Churchill Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Palgrave includes Caledon Equestrian Park, Palgrave Park and Caledon Trailway, and the Humber River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Gibson Lake. Glen Eagles Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by one school.

06.02.0110.t:
Palmer, Burlington

Palmer is a residential area in central Burlington, north of the QEW. It takes its name from Palmer Drive, named after Charles Palmer, a local farmer who later served in municipal politics. The land was part of Nelson Township, which Burlington annexed in 1958. The neighbourhood was largely developed in the 1970s and 1980s.

Palmer is generally bounded by Upper Middle Road to the north, Walkers Line to the east, Hannibal Road to the south and Guelph Line to the west, and covers approximately 211 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Palmer includes Palmer Park, Lansdown Park and Brittany Park, and Tuck Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

01.C01.0880.t:
Palmerston-Little Italy, City of Toronto (TRREB district C01)

The area is named after Palmerston Boulevard and the Little Italy district on College Street. College Street was laid out through the area by 1900, and most buildings date from the early 1900s. Italian immigrants moved here from The Ward, and by the 1920s the College-Clinton area was the city's main Little Italy. Many Italian families later moved north, and Portuguese and Latin American communities also settled in the area.

Palmerston-Little Italy is generally bounded by Bloor Street to the north, Bathurst Street to the east, College Street to the south and Dovercourt Road to the west, and covers approximately 143 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Palmerston-Little Italy includes Bickford Park, Art Eggleton Park and Healey Willan Park. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the College/Shaw branch of the Toronto Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Harbord Collegiate Institute.

07.01.1040.t:
Parkview, Hamilton

Parkview is a neighbourhood in Hamilton's east end with a mix of industrial and residential land, near Parkdale Avenue North. It sits on land of the former Barton Township that was brought into Hamilton as the city grew east. Most of its homes were built before 1960, with further housing added between 1961 and 1980.

Parkview is generally bounded by Nikola Tesla Boulevard to the north, Redhill Creek to the east, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) to the south and Parkdale Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 194 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a wastewater treatment plant and industrial lands (approximately 32% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), Nikola Tesla Boulevard, the Red Hill Valley Parkway and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Parkview includes Globe Park, Leaside Park and Woodward Park, and Redhill Creek runs through or along the community.

05.02.0410.t:
Parkway Belt Industrial Area, Brampton

The Parkway Belt Industrial Area is an employment area in south Brampton near Highway 407. Its name comes from the provincial Parkway Belt West Plan of 1978, which set aside land for highway and utility corridors and open space across the western GTA. The land was part of Chinguacousy Township until 1974, when the township was merged with Toronto Gore Township and the Town of Brampton to form the City of Brampton. The province revoked the Parkway Belt West Plan effective July 1, 2026.

Parkway Belt Industrial Area is generally bounded by a hydro corridor to the north, Intermodal Drive and Finch Avenue to the east and the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and Highway 407 to the west, and covers approximately 564 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), Highway 407, Malport Yard, a cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 33% of the community area). The community is also close to Toronto Pearson International Airport, approximately 2.1 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Mimico Creek and West Mimico Creek run through or along the community. Parkshore Golf Club is located in the area.

01.C13.0660.t:
Parkwoods-Donalda, City of Toronto (TRREB district C13)

The area has a long Indigenous history, with archaeological finds along Deerlick Creek dating back thousands of years. It was part of York Township, then North York from 1922. Much of the housing south of York Mills Road was bought new between 1957 and 1962, and the area was largely built up in the late 1950s and 1960s. North York became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Parkwoods-Donalda is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Victoria Park Avenue to the east, Lawrence Avenue to the south and the Don River East Branch to the west, and covers approximately 724 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) and the Don Valley Parkway. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision) and Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Parkwoods-Donalda includes Moatfield Farm Park, Brookbanks Park and Graydon Hall Park, and the Don River East Branch and Deerlick Creek run through or along the community. Donalda Golf and Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 17 schools and the Brookbanks branch of the Toronto Public Library.

09.02.0170.t:
Patterson, Vaughan

Patterson is a residential area in the northeast part of Vaughan, near the community of Maple. The area was farmland in Vaughan Township, which was settled from the 1790s and incorporated in 1850. Like much of north Vaughan, it was converted to suburban housing after the township became the Town of Vaughan in 1971, during the city's rapid growth from the 1990s onward.

Patterson is generally bounded by Dufferin Street and Teston Road to the north, Bathurst Street to the east, Highway 7 and Confederation Parkway to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and Major MacKenzie Drive to the west, and covers approximately 1,714 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Baker-Cober Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), Highway 407 and Maple United Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Patterson includes MacMillan Nature Preserve, Maple Nature Reserve and Cook Woodlot, and the Don River East Branch, Patterson Creek and Carrville Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 17 schools and the Vaughan Public Libraries - Pleasant Ridge Branch.

06.01.1036.t:
Scott, Milton

Scott is named after William Scott, an early landowner who came to Milton in 1821 and farmed in the area. The neighbourhood was planned under the Sherwood Survey Secondary Plan in 2004, Milton's first round of new urban neighbourhoods. It was built out mainly from the mid-2000s.

Scott is generally bounded by Bronte Street and Steeles Avenue to the north, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the east, Derry Road to the south and Tremaine Road to the west, and covers approximately 359 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are Milton Pioneer Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Scott includes Sherwood District Park, Scott Neighbourhood Park East and Scott Neighbourhood Park West. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Sherwood branch of the Milton Public Library.

04.06.0010.t:
Penetanguishene, Penetanguishene

The name Penetanguishene is believed to come from an Indigenous word meaning 'land of the white rolling sands'. The Royal Navy built a naval yard here in 1813, and the naval base operated until 1834, with a military post remaining until 1856. French-speaking families from Drummond Island and Canada East settled here in the 1820s to 1840s, giving the town its bilingual character. Penetanguishene was incorporated as a town in 1875, when it separated from Tiny Township, and later grew with logging and rail service.

Penetanguishene is generally bounded by the Midland boundary to the south and Georgian Bay and the Tiny boundary to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 2,460 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, tank, Central North Correctional Centre, St. Anne's Cemetery and Asylum Point / Mental Health Centre Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a quarry or aggregate pit. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Penetanguishene includes Penetanguishene Rotary Park, Martin Valley Park and Gendron Park, and Sucker Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto St. Andrews Lake and Georgian Bay. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools and the Penetanguishene Public Library. Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care and Georgian Bay General Hospital - Penetanguishene are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Discovery Harbour and Administration Building.

04.04.0030.t:
Perkinsfield, Tiny

Perkinsfield is a community in the Township of Tiny. In the mid-1800s, families from Quebec settled in the township for its inexpensive and fertile farmland. The Township of Tiny was named in 1822 after a pet dog of Lady Sarah Maitland, wife of Lieutenant Governor Sir Peregrine Maitland. It was part of the United Townships of Tiny and Tay from 1851 and became a separate township in 1869.

Perkinsfield is generally bounded by Asselin Drive and Balm Beach Road to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 97 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Perkinsfield is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

04.09.0030.t:
Phelpston, Springwater

Phelpston is a small hamlet in the former Flos Township, north of Barrie. It developed in the 19th century as a rural farm settlement. On January 1, 1994 it became part of the Township of Springwater, formed from Flos and Vespra townships, the villages of Elmvale and Hillsdale, and part of Medonte.

Phelpston is generally bounded by Flos Road 4 to the north and Marl Creek to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 95 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Saint Patrick's Roman Catholic Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Phelpston is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

09.02.0100.t:
Pine Valley Business Park, Vaughan

Pine Valley Business Park is an employment area on the east side of Woodbridge, named after Pine Valley Drive. The land was farmland in Vaughan Township until industrial growth reached the Woodbridge area from the 1970s onward. Industrial development along Steeles Avenue east of the Humber River was largely built in the 1980s. The area has been part of the Town, now City, of Vaughan since 1971.

Pine Valley Business Park is generally bounded by Highway 7 to the north, Weston Road to the east, Highway 407 to the south and Pine Valley Drive to the west, and covers approximately 208 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 407 and industrial lands (approximately 66% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Pine Valley Business Park is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

10.07.0170.t:
Pinecrest, Oshawa

Pinecrest is in east Oshawa, on a hillside above the Harmony Creek valley. The land was originally farmland in East Whitby Township. It became part of the City of Oshawa in 1974, when the township was merged into the city. Most of the neighbourhood was developed in the 1990s and early 2000s.

Pinecrest is generally bounded by Taunton Road to the north, Townline Road to the east, Rossland Road to the south and Wilson Road to the west, and covers approximately 522 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transformer station. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Pinecrest includes Harmony Valley Park, The Nathan and Marvin Goldman Woodlot and Attersley Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

09.03.0350.t:
Rouge River Estates, Markham

Rouge River Estates is a residential area in east Markham near the Rouge River valley. It lies on former farmland of Markham Township, which was settled from the 1790s and early 1800s. Like much of east Markham, it was built up during the town's suburban growth from the 1980s onward.

Rouge River Estates is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, the Rouge River to the east, 14th Avenue to the south and Markham Road to the west, and covers approximately 81 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 407 and a hydro transformer station lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rouge River Estates includes Roxbury Park. Residents are served by one school.

01.E03.1340.t:
Playter Estates-Danforth, City of Toronto (TRREB district E03)

Playter Estates takes its name from the Playter family; George Henry Playter received land in York Township after moving to the Toronto area in 1793. The farm lands around the family farmhouse were subdivided by 1912 to form Playter Estates. The area grew along with the Danforth after the Prince Edward Viaduct opened in 1918, and it lies within the former City of Toronto.

Playter Estates-Danforth is generally bounded by Fulton Avenue to the north, Pape Avenue to the east, Danforth Avenue to the south and the Don River and Chester Hill Road to the west, and covers approximately 89 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the Don Valley Parkway. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Playter Estates-Danforth includes Playter Gardens Park, Logan Avenue Parkette and Carlaw Avenue Parkette. Residents are served by one school, and transit is provided by the Broadview, Chester and Pape subway stations.

07.01.0130.t:
Pleasant View, Hamilton

Pleasant View (also written Pleasantview) is a rural area at the edge of the Niagara Escarpment in the former Town of Dundas, now part of the City of Hamilton. Its land use has long been limited to protect the Escarpment. A 1990s Ontario Municipal Board decision set a minimum lot size of 10 hectares for new single detached homes. The city began a Pleasantview Land Use Study in 2021, and the area was proposed for the Niagara Escarpment Commission's Area of Development Control.

Pleasant View is generally bounded by Highway 6 to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and York Road and the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 1,013 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision), Highway 403 and a hydro transformer station (Dundas TS). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 6. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Pleasant View includes Royal Botanical Gardens, and Spencer Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario and Marshall Pond.

01.C15.0550.t:
Pleasant View, City of Toronto (TRREB district C15)

Pleasant View lies in the former City of North York, north of Sheppard Avenue and east of Don Mills Road. The land was farmland in York Township, became part of North York in 1922 and joined the City of Toronto in 1998. It was built up as a postwar suburb, with detached homes and a number of high-rise apartment and condominium buildings.

Pleasant View is generally bounded by Victoria Park Avenue to the north, Sheppard Avenue to the south and Highway 404 to the west, and covers approximately 301 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 404 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Pleasant View includes Shawnee Park, Clydesdale Park and Pinto Park. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Pleasant View branch of the Toronto Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Van Horne Park.

05.03.0260.t:
Port Credit, Mississauga

Port Credit grew at the mouth of the Credit River, where a trading post was set up in 1720; the name refers to goods traded on credit there. A village plan was laid out in 1834, and the harbour served as a fishing port and grain shipping centre. Port Credit became a police village in 1909 and a town in the early 1960s, and joined the City of Mississauga in 1974.

Port Credit is generally bounded by Cumberland Drive to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 277 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Trinity Anglican Church Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) and a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Port Credit includes J.C. Saddington Park, Port Credit Memorial Park and J.J. Plaus Park, and the Credit River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Port Credit branch of the Mississauga Library, and transit is provided by the Port Credit GO Station.

13.04.0010.t:
Rural Alnwick/Haldimand, Alnwick/Haldimand

This community covers the rural parts of Alnwick/Haldimand Township in Northumberland County. Haldimand Township was formed in 1791 and named after Governor Sir Frederick Haldimand; Alnwick Township was surveyed in 1795, named after Alnwick in England, and first settled by United Empire Loyalists. The two townships merged on January 1, 2001. The area remains largely agricultural, between Lake Ontario and Rice Lake, with hamlets such as Grafton, Roseneath, Centreton and Vernonville.

Rural Alnwick/Haldimand is generally bounded by Rice Lake to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 6,442 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The community includes or fronts onto Rice Lake.

06.01.1037.t:
Timberlea, Milton

Timberlea is thought to take its name from the forests and sawmill industry the Milton area was known for in the 1800s. The area was approved for development in 1978 and was built up mainly in the late 1970s and 1980s. It lies south of Main Street and north of Derry Road.

Timberlea is generally bounded by Main Street to the north, Thompson Road to the east, Derry Road to the south and Ontario Street to the west, and covers approximately 252 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 9% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Evergreen Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.
