Green space in Timberlea includes Laurier Park and Coulson Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools, and transit is provided by the Milton GO Station. Shopping is available at Milton Mall. Other notable landmarks include E.C. Drury School for the Deaf.

01.C08.0940.t:
Regent Park, City of Toronto (TRREB district C08)

The area was once a large part of Cabbagetown, a working-class district of the old City of Toronto. The original houses were cleared to build Regent Park, one of Canada's first large public housing projects. Regent Park North was approved in 1947 and first occupied in 1949, and Regent Park South was completed in 1960. A phased mixed-income redevelopment began in 2005.

Regent Park is generally bounded by Gerrard Street to the north, the Don Valley Parkway to the east, Queen Street to the south and Parliament Street to the west, and covers approximately 66 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are the Don Valley Parkway and a hydro transformer station (Gerrard TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Regent Park includes Regent Park, Regent Park Athletic Grounds and Louis March Park, and the Don River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Nelson Mandela Park Public School.

13.01.0030.t:
Port Hope, Port Hope

Port Hope began as a fur trade post in 1778, known as Smith's Creek, and Loyalists settled here from 1793. It took the name Port Hope in 1819, after Hope Township, which honours Colonel Henry Hope. The town was incorporated in 1834 and was largely built in the 19th century; slow growth from 1881 to 1951 helped preserve its downtown, considered one of Ontario's best-preserved 19th-century streetscapes. In 2001 the town merged with Hope Township to form the present Municipality of Port Hope.

Port Hope is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Hamilton Road to the east and Lake Ontario to the south, and covers approximately 1,292 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), the Port Hope Water Treatment Plant, Union Cemetery, United Church Cemetery, Saint Mark's Anglican Church Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 8% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Port Hope includes Port Hope Agricultural Park, Wladyka Park and Optimist Park, and the Ganaraska River and Gage Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. Port Hope Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Port Hope Public Library, and transit is provided by the Port Hope VIA Rail station. Other notable landmarks include Historic downtown Port Hope and Trinity College School.

06.01.1038.t:
Willmott, Milton

Willmott is one of the neighbourhoods planned under Milton's Sherwood Survey, the town's first major expansion of new urban neighbourhoods in the 2000s. Home construction began in approximately 2010. The source of the name was not confirmed.

Willmott is generally bounded by Derry Road to the north, Regional Road 25 to the east, Louis St. Laurent Avenue to the south and the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 265 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Willmott includes Milton Community Park, Sunny Mount Park and Wilmott Neighbourhood Park, and Sixteen Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Milton District Hospital is also located in the community.

10.06.0040.t:
Port Whitby, Whitby

Port Whitby grew around Whitby Harbour on Lake Ontario. Grain from northern farms was shipped from the harbour from 1833, and the Port Whitby and Port Perry Railway was built from the harbour in the 1870s. The harbour is now a recreational marina. The area has been part of the Town of Whitby, incorporated in 1855 and merged with the township in 1968.

Port Whitby is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Water Street to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Lynde Creek to the west, and covers approximately 499 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision), the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), a cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 7% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Port Whitby includes Kiwanis Heydenshore Park, Portage Park and Rotary Sunrise Lake Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. Residents are served by one school, and transit is provided by the Whitby GO Station. Ontario Shores Centre for Mental Health Sciences and Lakeridge Health Whitby are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Iroquois Park Sports Centre.

09.01.0030.t:
Pottageville, King

Pottageville is a small community in King Township named after early settler Edward Pottage. Land in the area was drained for farming in the 1920s. It lies on the Oak Ridges Moraine and is surrounded by provincially significant wetlands and forest. King Township has been part of the Regional Municipality of York since 1971.

Pottageville is generally bounded by Highway 400 to the east, 18th Sideroad to the south and 8th Concession to the west, and covers approximately 1,522 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 400 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Carrying Place Golf & Country Club is located in the area.

01.W08.0100.t:
Princess-Rosethorn, City of Toronto (TRREB district W08)

Princess Gardens is named after Princess Anne and Princess Margaret, with Princess Anne Manor in the east and Princess Margaret Gardens in the west. The area was a post-war subdivision in Etobicoke Township, built from the late 1940s along an extension of The Kingsway north of Dundas Street, with curved streets and cul-de-sacs. Rosethorn Junior School opened in 1952. Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Princess-Rosethorn is generally bounded by Eglinton Avenue to the north, Islington Avenue to the east, Mimico Creek and Rathburn Road to the south and Martin Grove Road to the west, and covers approximately 516 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. The community is also close to Toronto Pearson International Airport, approximately 2.2 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Princess-Rosethorn includes Ravenscrest Park, Princess Margaret Park and Princess Anne Park, and Mimico Creek runs through or along the community. Islington Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools. Other notable landmarks include St. George's Golf and Country Club.

10.06.0070.t:
Pringle Creek, Whitby

Pringle Creek is a residential area in Whitby, named after the creek that runs through it. Whitby Township was surveyed in 1792, and the Town of Whitby was incorporated in 1855. The town and township merged in 1968. Suburban housing in the area was built in the decades after that merger.

Pringle Creek is generally bounded by Taunton Road to the north, Anderson Street to the east, the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) to the south and Brock Street to the west, and covers approximately 610 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Resurrection Catholic Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Pringle Creek includes Fallingbrook Open Space, Wyndfield Park and Pringle Creek Park, and Pringle Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools and the Rossland branch of the Whitby Public Library.

06.01.0030.t:
Campbellville, Milton

Campbellville is named after John Campbell, who settled there in 1832. A saw mill, a tavern (1847) and a store and post office (1849) followed, and the community became a police village in 1914. It was the main centre of Nassagaweya Township until the township became part of the Town of Milton in 1974.

Campbellville is generally bounded by Reid Sideroad to the north, Highway 401 to the east and McLaren Road to the south, and covers approximately 204 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Campbellville includes Campbellville Old Ball Park.

04.08.0030.t:
Port McNicoll, Tay

Port McNicoll was established in 1908 as a Great Lakes port on Georgian Bay. It was named after Canadian Pacific Railway executive David McNicoll and became the home port of the CPR's Great Lakes steamship service. It separated from Tay Township as a village in 1917. It was amalgamated back into the Township of Tay on January 1, 1994.

Port McNicoll is generally bounded by Georgian Bay to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 466 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a wastewater treatment plant and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The community includes or fronts onto Georgian Bay. Residents are served by the J & M Young branch of the Tay Township Public Library.

10.04.0010.t:
Port Perry, Scugog

Port Perry was laid out in 1848 by Peter Perry on the shore of Lake Scugog, and was named after him in 1852. The arrival of the Port Whitby and Port Perry Railway in 1872 helped it grow, and it was incorporated as a village in 1871. In 1974 it was amalgamated with Reach, Cartwright and Scugog townships to form the Township of Scugog.

Port Perry is generally bounded by Scugog Line 8 to the north, Lake Scugog to the east and Reach Street and Scugog Line 6 to the west, and covers approximately 1,671 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a landfill site, Prince Albert Cemetery and Immaculate Conception Borelia Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Port Perry includes Port Perry Fair Ground, Port Perry Waterfront and Palmer Park, and Port Perry Lagoons and Cawkers Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Scugog. Canterbury Common Residents' Association is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Scugog Public Library. Lakeridge Health - Port Perry is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Queen Street historic downtown.

05.02.0260.t:
Queen Street Corridor, Brampton

The Queen Street Corridor follows Queen Street East, Brampton's main east-west street, between the downtown and Bramalea. Brampton was laid out in 1834 at Buffy's Corners and named after Brampton in Cumberland, England. It became a village in 1853 and a town in 1873. Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships were merged with the Town of Brampton in 1974 to form the City of Brampton. The corridor developed with commercial and mixed uses through the second half of the 20th century.

Queen Street Corridor is generally bounded by Clark Boulevard and Bramalea Road to the east, Highway 410 to the south and the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and Church Street to the west, and covers approximately 521 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 410, Brampton Cemetery, St Mary's Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 26% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Queen Street Corridor includes Donald M. Gordon Chinguacousy Park, Norton Place Park and Knightsbridge Park, and Etobicoke Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by the Chinguacousy branch of the Brampton Library. Shopping is available at Bramalea City Centre. Peel Memorial Centre for Integrated Health and Wellness is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Petting Zoo.

04.15.0180.t:
Queen's Park, Barrie

Queen's Park is an older residential area just north of downtown Barrie. It is named after Queen's Park, the site of the city's Armoury. Barrie grew from a supply depot at the end of the Nine Mile Portage and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a village in 1854, a town in 1871 and a city in 1959.

Queen's Park is generally bounded by Highway 400 to the north, Maple Avenue and Bayfield Street to the east and Dunlop Street to the west, and covers approximately 122 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 400 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Queen's Park includes Donald Street Park. Residents are served by one school. RVH Dialysis is also located in the community.

09.08.0020.t:
Queensville, East Gwillimbury

Queensville began as a crossroads village known as Four Corners and later Hackett's Corners, after storekeeper William Hackett. It was renamed Queensville in 1843 in honour of Queen Victoria. It was part of East Gwillimbury Township, incorporated in 1850, and has been part of the Town of East Gwillimbury since 1971. The village stayed small for most of its history, with large new subdivisions planned and built from the 2010s onward.

Queensville is generally bounded by Woodbine Avenue to the east and 2nd Concession Road and Queensville Sideroad to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,209 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 404. Along or just beyond its edges are Queensville Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Queensville includes Queensville Community Centre, Valleyview Park and Milne Park. Residents are served by one school and the Queensville branch of the East Gwillimbury Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Health and Active Living Plaza.

09.03.0240.t:
Raymerville, Markham

Raymerville takes its name from Raymerville Drive, named after the Raymer family, the first family to settle and farm the area. It lies between 16th Avenue and Bullock Drive, east of McCowan Road. The neighbourhood was built mainly in the 1980s; Ramer Wood Public School opened in 1986.

Raymerville is generally bounded by 16th Avenue to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision) to the south and McCowan Road to the west, and covers approximately 229 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision) and Quantztown Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Raymerville includes Raybeck Park, Cedar Valley Park and Stargell Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Other notable landmarks include Ramer Wood Public School.

01.W10.0040.t:
Rexdale-Kipling, City of Toronto (TRREB district W10)

Rexdale is named after developer Rex Heslop, who bought farmland in Etobicoke Township in 1955 and built streets, services and houses. By 1956 the area had approximately 3,600 homes and Rexdale Plaza had opened. The area was largely built out in the 1950s and 1960s as part of suburban Etobicoke. Etobicoke became part of the amalgamated City of Toronto in 1998.

Rexdale-Kipling is generally bounded by the West Humber River to the north, Islington Avenue to the east, Rexdale Boulevard to the south and Kipling Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 249 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rexdale-Kipling includes West Humber Parkland, Rexlington Park and Rexdale Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Rexdale branch of the Toronto Public Library.

04.20.0010.t:
Rama First Nation, Rama First Nation 32

The Chippewas of Rama First Nation are an Anishinaabe community whose ancestors lived around Lake Simcoe. In 1830 the government settled them in a village at the Atherley Narrows, and after the 1836 land surrender they moved in 1838 to Rama, buying approximately 1,600 acres with their own funds. The reserve, Mnjikaning First Nation 32, lies on the eastern shore of Lake Couchiching near Orillia. The name Mnjikaning refers to the ancient fishing weirs at the Atherley Narrows.

Rama First Nation is generally bounded by the Ramara boundary to the east, Willison Sideroad to the south and Lake Couchiching to the west, and covers approximately 1,316 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision) and a quarry or aggregate pit lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Black River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Couchiching and Lake St. John. Residents are served by the Chippewas of Rama First Nation Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Casino Rama.

07.01.1770.t:
Randall, Hamilton

Randall is a residential neighbourhood on the south Hamilton Mountain. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most of its homes were built in the 1980s, with the rest mainly from the 1960s, 1970s and 1990s.

Randall is generally bounded by the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the north, Upper Gage Avenue to the east, Stone Church Road to the south and Upper Sherman Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 72 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

05.03.0300.t:
Rathwood, Mississauga

Rathwood lies in the eastern part of the former Toronto Township, near the site of the old hamlet of Burnhamthorpe at Dixie and Burnhamthorpe roads. Burnhamthorpe, first called Sand Hill, was named after the birthplace of Lord Horatio Nelson and had a school, church, store and mill in the 1800s. The area was farmland until suburban development in the later decades of the 20th century.

Rathwood is generally bounded by Eastgate Parkway to the north, Etobicoke Creek and a hydro corridor to the east and Burnhamthorpe Road to the west, and covers approximately 717 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 403 and Burnhamthorpe Cemetery. The community is also close to Toronto Pearson International Airport, approximately 2.2 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rathwood includes Garnetwood Park, Applewood Hills and Rathwood District Park, and Cooksville Creek East Branch and Etobicoke Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools. Shopping is available at Rockwood Mall.

07.01.1220.t:
Riverdale, Hamilton

Riverdale is a residential neighbourhood in Hamilton's lower east end, near Centennial Parkway North and Barton Street East. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most homes were built between 1961 and 1980, with a smaller share from the 1980s and 1990s.

Riverdale is generally bounded by Barton Street to the north, Gray Road and Berkindale Drive to the east, Queenston Road to the south and Centennial Parkway to the west, and covers approximately 163 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor and a hydro transformer station (Hamilton Lake TS) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Riverdale includes Lake Avenue Park and Oaklands Park, and Stoney Creek and Battlefield Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

01.W03.0360.t:
Rockcliffe-Smythe, City of Toronto (TRREB district W03)

The Smythe part of the name comes from the gravel pit Conn Smythe opened here in the 1920s. The area was part of York Township and was mostly farmland through the 1800s. After the Second World War, once the gravel pit was exhausted, the surrounding land was developed for housing, much of it for returning servicemen and their families. It was part of the City of York until amalgamation into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Rockcliffe-Smythe is generally bounded by Lambton Avenue and Eglinton Avenue to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) to the east, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) to the south and the Humber River to the west, and covers approximately 509 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a rail yard, a hydro transformer station (Runnymede TS) and industrial lands (approximately 7% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) and the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rockcliffe-Smythe includes Smythe Park, Black Creek Park West and Black Creek Site East, and Black Creek, the Humber River and Lavender Creek run through or along the community. Lambton Golf & Country Club and Scarlett Woods Golf Club (City of Toronto) are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools.

07.01.0020.t:
Rockton, Hamilton

Rockton is a rural village in the former Beverly Township, now part of the Flamborough area of Hamilton. The Beverly Agricultural Society held its first meeting at the Rockton township hall in 1853, and its fall fair has been held in Rockton since the mid-1850s. The fair has been known as the Rockton World's Fair since 1878. Beverly joined the Township of Flamborough in 1974, which was amalgamated into the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Rockton is generally bounded by Highway 8 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 90 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rockton includes Beverly Community Park and Rockton World's Fairgrounds.

10.06.0090.t:
Rolling Acres, Whitby

Rolling Acres is a residential area in Whitby. Whitby Township was surveyed in 1792 and named after Whitby in Yorkshire, England. The Town of Whitby was incorporated in 1855 and merged with Whitby Township in 1968. The area was developed as suburban housing in the decades after that merger.

Rolling Acres is generally bounded by Taunton Road to the north, Rossland Road to the south and Anderson Street to the west, and covers approximately 422 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are Thornton Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rolling Acres includes Darren Park, Eric Clarke Park and Divine Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

01.W01.0470.t:
Roncesvalles, City of Toronto (TRREB district W01)

Roncesvalles takes its name from Roncesvalles Avenue, named by Colonel Walter O'Hara after the 1813 Battle of Roncesvalles in Spain, in which he fought. O'Hara's land north of Queen Street was subdivided after his death in 1874, and the area was annexed to the City of Toronto in the 1880s. Most of the neighbourhood was built between approximately 1900 and the First World War, with larger homes on High Park Boulevard and High Park Gardens from 1910 to 1930.

Roncesvalles is generally bounded by the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Galt Subdivision) to the east, Queen Street to the south and Roncesvalles Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 152 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Galt Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line and a rail yard lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Roncesvalles includes Sorauren Avenue Park, West Lodge Park and Charles G. Williams Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools. Other notable landmarks include St. Joseph's Health Centre.

06.02.0140.t:
Rose, Burlington

Rose is a residential community in the City of Burlington. Burlington was formed in 1873 when the lakeside villages of Wellington Square and Port Nelson merged, and it became a town in 1914. Most of the surrounding farmland of Nelson Township was annexed in 1958. The city grew rapidly after the Second World War and became a city in 1974.

Rose is generally bounded by Dundas Street to the north, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and Appleby Line to the east, Upper Middle Road to the south and Walkers Line to the west, and covers approximately 389 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rose includes Millcroft Park, Taywood Park and Berton Park, and Shoreacres Creek runs through or along the community. Millcroft Golf and Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

10.02.0020.t:
Rouge Park, Pickering

Rouge Park is a neighbourhood in west Pickering named after Rouge National Urban Park, which forms its western edge. The Rouge valley was used by First Nations for hunting, fishing and travel long before European settlers arrived in the 1790s. The area was farmland in Pickering Township until suburban development in the late 20th century. Finch Avenue is its main road.

Rouge Park is generally bounded by a hydro corridor and the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) to the east and the City of Toronto boundary and Scarborough-Pickering Townline Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 167 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rouge Park includes Rouge National Urban Park.

10.02.0050.t:
Rosebank, Pickering

Rosebank is a residential neighbourhood in southwest Pickering, near the Rouge River and Lake Ontario. In the early 1900s the area had many small cottages, often used seasonally. The first subdivisions were built in the 1970s. Infill housing has been added in recent decades.

Rosebank is generally bounded by Highway 401 and Petticoat Creek to the north, Lake Ontario to the east, the City of Toronto boundary to the south and the Rouge River to the west, and covers approximately 202 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rosebank includes Petticoat Creek Conservation Area and Rouge National Urban Park, and the Rouge River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

07.01.1460.t:
Rosedale, Hamilton

Rosedale is a residential neighbourhood in east Hamilton, bounded by the Escarpment, Lawrence Road, the Red Hill Valley Parkway and Kenilworth Avenue. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most homes were built before 1960, with further housing added between 1961 and 1980.

Rosedale is generally bounded by Lawrence Road to the north, Redhill Creek and the Red Hill Valley Parkway to the east, Greenhill Avenue to the south and Mountain Brow Boulevard to the west, and covers approximately 153 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are the Red Hill Valley Parkway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rosedale includes Rosedale Park, and Redhill Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

01.C09.0820.t:
Rosedale-Moore Park, City of Toronto (TRREB district C09)

Rosedale was the estate of Sheriff William Botsford Jarvis; his wife Mary named it for the wild roses that grew there. The estate was subdivided from 1854 as Toronto's first 'garden suburb'. Moore Park was developed by John Thomas Moore from 1891 and was annexed to the City of Toronto in 1912. Both areas were largely built up with large houses in the late 1800s and early 1900s.

Rosedale-Moore Park is generally bounded by Moore Avenue to the north, Ravine Beltline Trail and Mud Creek to the east, Bloor Street to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 467 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision) and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are Mount Pleasant Cemetery, St. James Cemetery and Crematorium and St. Michael's Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rosedale-Moore Park includes David A. Balfour Park, Don Valley Brick Works Park and Moore Park Ravine, and Yellow Creek and the Don River run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools, the Deer Park branch of the Toronto Public Library and the Toronto Reference Library branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Bloor-Yonge, Sherbourne, Castle Frank and Rosedale subway stations. Other notable landmarks include Chorley Park and Mount Pleasant Cemetery (north edge).

06.02.0120.t:
Roseland, Burlington

Roseland is an older residential area on the Lake Ontario shore, east of downtown Burlington. It began with the Roseland Park survey of 1923, laid out by developer Hughes Cleaver with tree-lined boulevards in the English garden-suburb style. The adjoining Hillcrest survey followed in 1925, and many houses date from the 1930s and 1940s. Later infill and replacement housing has been added since.

Roseland is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) to the north, Walkers Line to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Guelph Line to the west, and covers approximately 489 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the Burlington Water Purification Plant. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) and a hydro transformer station (Cumberland TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Roseland includes Sweetgrass Park, Cumberland Park and Centennial Trail. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools. Shopping is available at Burlington Centre. Other notable landmarks include Lakeshore Road waterfront.

04.11.0020.t:
Rosemont, Adjala-Tosorontio

Rosemont is a small hamlet on Highway 89 near the boundaries with Mono and Mulmur. It grew as a rural crossroads community serving surrounding farms in the 19th century. The Adjala-Tosorontio portion became part of the amalgamated township on January 1, 1994.

Rosemont is generally bounded by Mulmur-Tosorontio Townline and Highway 89 to the north, 30 Adjala Sideroad to the south and Mono-Adjala Townline to the west, and covers approximately 88 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Rosemont is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

01.E10.1032.t:
Rouge E10, City of Toronto (TRREB district E10)

The area takes its name from the Rouge River on its eastern edge. The river valley was part of the Toronto Carrying-Place Trail, and the Seneca village of Ganatsekwyagon (now the Bead Hill National Historic Site) stood here until the late 17th century. The land was farmland in Scarborough Township, and the part north of Sheppard Avenue was built up as a suburb in the late 20th century. Much of the area remains undeveloped parkland, and Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Rouge E10 is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, the Rouge River to the east, the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision) to the south and Port Union Road to the west, and covers approximately 364 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rouge E10 includes Rouge National Urban Park, West Rouge Park and Fanfare Park, and the Rouge River and Adam's Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools, and transit is provided by the Rouge Hill GO Station.

01.E11.1031.t:
Rouge E11, City of Toronto (TRREB district E11)

The Rouge community takes its name from the Rouge River, which forms its eastern edge in the northeast corner of the former Scarborough Township. The river valley was part of the Toronto Carrying-Place Trail, and the Seneca village of Ganatsekwyagon (now the Bead Hill National Historic Site) stood here in the late 17th century. The area remained largely agricultural for most of its history, with suburban housing built mainly north of Sheppard Avenue in later decades. It was part of the City of Scarborough until amalgamation into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Rouge E11 is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Scarborough-Pickering Townline Road and the Pickering boundary to the east, Highway 401 to the south and Morningside Avenue and Markham Road to the west, and covers approximately 3,419 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (York Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), the CPKC rail line, Highway 401, a hydro transformer station (Sheppard TS), a hydro transformer station (Malvern TS) and industrial lands (approximately 8% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Christ the King Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rouge E11 includes Rouge National Urban Park, Beare Hill Park and Bob Hunter Greenspace, and the Rouge River, Little Rouge Creek and Morningside Creek run through or along the community. Cedar Brae Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 13 schools. Other notable landmarks include Toronto Zoo and African Savanna.

04.15.0350.t:
Rural Barrie Southwest, Barrie

Rural Barrie Southwest covers lands in the southwest of the city that were part of the Town of Innisfil until January 1, 2010, when Barrie annexed approximately 2,293 hectares south and southeast of its boundary. Innisfil Township was first surveyed in 1820. The annexed lands in this area fall within the city's Salem Secondary Plan, a greenfield growth area.

Rural Barrie Southwest is generally bounded by Huronia Road and Lockhart Road to the east, the Innisfil boundary to the south and County Road 27 to the west, and covers approximately 1,474 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 400. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Innisbrook Golf Course is located in the area.

09.03.0370.t:
Rouge Fairways, Markham

Rouge Fairways lies in the historic Box Grove area of south-east Markham. It was built on former golf course lands: a course was established in 1950 on the Tomlinson property and later owned by IBM (1967), which sold part of it for housing in 1997. Development took place from the late 1990s.

Rouge Fairways is generally bounded by the Rouge River to the east, the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the south and 14th Avenue and Kirkham Drive to the west, and covers approximately 139 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (York Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rouge Fairways includes Tomlinson Park, and the Rouge River runs through or along the community. Parkview Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Markham Green Golf Club.

09.04.0140.t:
Rouge Woods, Richmond Hill

Rouge Woods is in east Richmond Hill and takes its name from the Rouge River, which crosses the area. One of the earliest settlers was David Eyer, a Mennonite farmer from Pennsylvania, whose 1828 home survives as the Eyer Wideman Centre. The area was farmland until houses were built in the 1990s and early 2000s.

Rouge Woods is generally bounded by Elgin Mills Road to the north, Leslie Street to the east, Major MacKenzie Drive to the south and Bayview Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 404 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Elgin Mills Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rouge Woods includes Headwaters Community Park, John Tipp Park and Heron Pond. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools.

10.02.0040.t:
Rougemount, Pickering

Rougemount is in west Pickering on high ground near the Rouge River valley. The first European settlers arrived in the early 1800s and used the Rouge River to power grist, saw and flour mills. The original housing dates from the early 1900s. The present neighbourhood took shape in the 1970s as new subdivisions were added.

Rougemount is generally bounded by the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the north, Petticoat Creek to the east, Highway 401 to the south and Little Rouge Creek and the City of Toronto boundary to the west, and covers approximately 185 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (York Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rougemount includes Rouge National Urban Park, and Little Rouge Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

04.13.0020.t:
Rural Bradford West Gwillimbury, Bradford West Gwillimbury

Rural Bradford West Gwillimbury covers the farmland and hamlets of the former West Gwillimbury Township, which takes its name from the family of Elizabeth Simcoe (née Gwillim). Settlers, mostly of Irish origin, arrived from 1807, and Scottish families founded the Scotch Settlement west of Bradford in 1819. The township was incorporated in 1850 and merged with the Town of Bradford on January 1, 1991. Part of the area lies in the Holland Marsh, drained for farming from 1923.

Rural Bradford West Gwillimbury is generally bounded by the Innisfil boundary to the north, the West Holland River and the Holland River to the east, the West Holland River (old) to the south and the New Tecumseth boundary to the west, and covers approximately 20,324 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), Highway 400, a quarry or aggregate pit, a wastewater treatment plant, Mount Pleasant Cemetery, Holy Martyrs Catholic Cemetery and Wilson Hill Pioneer Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Bradford West Gwillimbury includes Scanlon Creek Conservation Area, Sinclair Tract and Hodgson Tract, and the Holland River and the West Holland River (old) run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. The Club at Bond Head - North and The Club at Bond Head - South are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 15 schools and the Bradford West Gwillimbury Public Library, and transit is provided by the Bradford GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Auld Kirk (Scotch Settlement).

10.03.0020.t:
Rural Brock, Brock

Rural Brock covers the countryside of the Township of Brock in north Durham Region, including hamlets such as Gamebridge, Port Bolster, Wilfrid and Vroomanton. The original Brock Township was surveyed in 1817 and named after Major General Sir Isaac Brock. It became part of Ontario County in 1852. In 1974 it was merged with Thorah Township, Beaverton and Cannington to form the current Township of Brock.

Rural Brock is generally bounded by Lake Simcoe to the north, Simcoe Street to the east, Brock-Scugog Townline Road to the south and Lake Ridge Road to the west, and covers approximately 47,151 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision), Highway 12, Highway 7, a wastewater treatment plant, a landfill site, Sunderland Solar Farm, a hydro transformer station (Beaverton TS), DiscoveryLight, SparkleLight Solar Farm, Old Stone Church Cemetery, Cedar Vale Cemetery and Sunderland Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Brock includes Beaverton Ball Park, Mill Gateway Park and Thorah Centennial Park, and the Beaver River and Vrooman Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. Cedarhurst Golf Club and Fair Havens Ministries are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools, the Brock Libraries - Beaverton Branch and the Brock Libraries - Cannington Branch. Other notable landmarks include Trent-Severn Waterway and Forget me Not Alpacas.

09.03.0020.t:
Royal Orchard, Markham

Royal Orchard is in the Thornhill area of Markham, north of the historic Thornhill village between Yonge Street and Bayview Avenue. Thornhill was founded in 1794 and named after Benjamin Thorne, who ran mills here from 1820. Most homes are single-detached houses built in the 1970s and 1980s; the area joined the Town of Markham in 1971.

Royal Orchard is generally bounded by Bayview Avenue to the east, the Don River East Branch to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 305 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are Holy Cross Catholic Cemetery and Saint Luke’s Roman Catholic Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Royal Orchard includes Royal Orchard Park, Bayview Lane Park and Romfield Park, and the Don River East Branch and Pomona Creek run through or along the community. Ladies Golf Club of Toronto is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools. Shouldice Hospital is also located in the community.

01.W02.0420.t:
Runnymede-Bloor West Village, City of Toronto (TRREB district W02)

This community is centred on the Bloor West Village shopping street, which developed in the early to mid-20th century after the Bloor streetcar line opened in the 1920s. The name Runnymede comes from the 1838 estate of John Scarlett, an early landowner in the area. The Bloor-Danforth subway opened through the area in 1966, and in 1970 local merchants formed the first business improvement area in the world. Most houses are early 20th-century detached and semi-detached homes.

Runnymede-Bloor West Village is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and Gooch Avenue to the north, Runnymede Road to the east, Jane Street and Bloor Street to the south and St Mark's Road to the west, and covers approximately 163 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) and a rail yard lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Runnymede-Bloor West Village includes Beresford Park, Neil McLellan Park and George Chater Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Daniel G. Hill branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Jane and Runnymede subway stations.

04.11.0060.t:
Rural Adjala-Tosorontio, Adjala-Tosorontio

This community covers the rural areas of the township outside its hamlets. Adjala Township was settled from the 1820s, largely by Irish Catholic families, and was named after a son of Chief Tecumseh; Tosorontio is a Huron word meaning "Beautiful Mountain". The two townships merged on January 1, 1994. The area remains mainly agricultural, with the Nottawasaga River crossing it and the Niagara Escarpment to the west.

Rural Adjala-Tosorontio is generally bounded by Mulmur-Tosorontio Townline and the Essa boundary to the north and Adjala-Tecumseth Townline and Mono-Adjala Townline to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 36,440 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a hydro transformer station, a quarry or aggregate pit, a landfill site and Sloan's Presbyterian Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Glencairn Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Adjala-Tosorontio includes Earl Rowe Provincial Park and Wardens' Park, and the Mad River and the Pine River run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Earl Rowe Lake. Silver Brooke Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Nottawasaga River.

03.05.0010.t:
Rural Amaranth, Amaranth

This community covers the rural parts of Amaranth Township in Dufferin County. The township is named after the amaranth plant, which grows widely in the area, and it was incorporated in 1854. The area remains largely agricultural, with small hamlets such as Waldemar, Laurel and Amaranth Station.

Rural Amaranth is generally bounded by Highway 89 to the north, Mono Amaranth Townline to the east, County Road 109 to the south and Townline Amaranth East Luther to the west, and covers approximately 26,578 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a quarry or aggregate pit, a landfill site, a hydro transformer station (Orangeville TS), Orangeville Greenwood Cemetery and Laurel Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 10. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Amaranth includes Waldemar Park and Country Meadows Park, and the Grand River and Willow Brook run through or along the community. Lynbrook Golf and Meadow Land Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

07.01.0060.t:
Rural Ancaster, Hamilton

Rural Ancaster covers the countryside of the former Ancaster Township, named by Lieutenant Governor John Graves Simcoe in 1793. The township's settlement began around the mills built by James Wilson in 1791 and 1792. In 1974 the Town of Ancaster absorbed the township, including hamlets such as Jerseyville and Alberton. Ancaster was amalgamated into the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Rural Ancaster is generally bounded by Governors Road to the north and Fiddlers Green Road to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 13,275 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision), Highway 403, White Chapel Memorial Gardens (cemetery), Resurrection Catholic Cemetery and Jerseyville Cemetery. The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 1.3 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Ancaster includes Ancaster Community Center, Copetown Bog and Jerseyville Park, and Sulphur Creek and Big Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Dunmark Lake. Mystic Golf Club and Knollwood Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Dundas Valley Conservation Area.

04.15.0290.t:
Rural Barrie Southeast, Barrie

Rural Barrie Southeast covers lands in the southeast of the city that were part of the Town of Innisfil until January 1, 2010, when Barrie annexed approximately 2,293 hectares south and southeast of its boundary. Innisfil Township was first surveyed in 1820. The annexed lands are planned for new growth under the city's Hewitt's Secondary Plan.

Rural Barrie Southeast is generally bounded by Big Bay Point Road to the north, 20th Sideroad to the east and Lockhart Road and Mapleview Drive to the west, and covers approximately 866 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school.

10.07.0100.t:
Samac, Oshawa

Samac is named after Camp Samac, a Scouts Canada camp that opened in 1946 on land donated by Colonel R. S. (Sam) McLaughlin, president of General Motors of Canada. The land was part of East Whitby Township and joined the City of Oshawa in 1974. The neighbourhood was largely built in stages through the 2000s and 2010s.

Samac is generally bounded by Conlin Road to the north, Wilson Road to the east, Taunton Road to the south and Oshawa Creek to the west, and covers approximately 581 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Oshawa Waste Management Facility (landfill). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Samac includes Cedar Valley Park, Ritson Fields and Conlin Meadows Park, and Oshawa Creek and East Oshawa Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. Durham College and Ontario Tech University are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Camp Samac.

12.08.0010.t:
Rural Asphodel-Norwood, Asphodel-Norwood

This community covers the rural parts of Asphodel-Norwood Township in Peterborough County. Surveyor Richard Birdsall named the township in 1820, as its trilliums reminded him of asphodel flowers. Settlement began in the 1820s along the Ouse River, where Major Joseph Keeler built a mill at what became Norwood. The Village of Norwood and Asphodel Township merged on January 1, 1998.

Rural Asphodel-Norwood is generally bounded by the Otonabee-South Monaghan boundary to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 71 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Rural Asphodel-Norwood.

Rural Asphodel-Norwood is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

09.06.0090.t:
Rural Aurora, Aurora

This community covers the remaining rural and estate lands of Aurora, much of it on the Oak Ridges Moraine. Aurora began as Machell's Corners, a hamlet at Yonge Street and Wellington Street where Richard Machell opened a store in 1804. The railway arrived in 1853, the village was incorporated in 1863 and it became a town in 1888. The town's built-up area expanded greatly after the Second World War.

Rural Aurora is generally bounded by the Newmarket boundary to the north and Highway 404 to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 417 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 16% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 404. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Aurora includes David Tomlinson Nature Reserve, Edward Coltham Park and Trent Park. Residents are served by one school.

07.01.1450.t:
Sherwood, Hamilton

Sherwood is a residential neighbourhood on the East Mountain, with local shops and a library on Fennell Avenue East. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. The East Mountain grew quickly after the Second World War, and most homes in Sherwood were built between the post-war years and 1980.

Sherwood is generally bounded by Kenilworth Access to the north, Mountain Brow Boulevard to the east, Fennell Avenue to the south and Upper Ottawa Street to the west, and covers approximately 79 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Sherwood.

Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Sherwood branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

06.02.0010.t:
Rural Burlington, Burlington

Rural Burlington is the countryside north of Highway 407 and Dundas Street, much of it on and below the Niagara Escarpment. It was settled from the early 1800s as part of Nelson Township, with mills powered by escarpment streams. Hamlets such as Kilbride, Lowville, Cumminsville and Highville had formed by the mid-1800s. The township was annexed by Burlington in 1958, and the area remains largely rural.

Rural Burlington is generally bounded by Derry Road to the north, Tremaine Road to the east, Highway 407 and Dundas Street to the south and Milburough Town Line and the Hamilton boundary to the west, and covers approximately 9,549 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (Tremaine TS), Nelson Quarry, Burlington Memorial Gardens (cemetery) and Canadian Wesleyan New Connexion Methodist Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407 and DeForest Pioneer Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Burlington includes City View Park, Kerncliff Park and Lowville Park, and Bronte Creek and Limestone Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Medad. Hidden Lake Golf Club and Crosswinds Golf & Country Club are located in the area. Residents are served by one school and the Kilbride branch of the Burlington Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Mount Nemo Conservation Area.

05.01.0050.t:
Rural Caledon, Caledon

Rural Caledon covers the farmland, hamlets and conservation lands of the Town of Caledon outside its villages. It was settled from the 1820s, mostly by families from Scotland, Ireland and England, with mills along the Credit and Humber rivers. The railway arrived in the 1870s. In 1974 Caledon Township merged with Albion Township, the northern part of Chinguacousy Township and the villages of Bolton and Caledon East to form the Town of Caledon.

Rural Caledon is generally bounded by Highway 9 to the north, Highway 50 to the east, Mayfield Road to the south and Winston Churchill Boulevard to the west, and covers approximately 63,510 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), Highway 10, Highway 410, Brampton-Caledon Airport, a quarry or aggregate pit, Caledon East Public Cemetery, Boston-Mills Cemetery and Providence Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Orangeville Water Pollution Control Plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Caledon includes Albion Hills Conservation Area, Palgrave Forest and Wildlife Area and Forks of the Credit Provincial Park, and the Credit River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Caledon Lake and Green Lake. TPC Toronto at Osprey Valley and Devil's Pulpit are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 20 schools, the Alton branch of the Caledon Public Library and the Caledon East branch of the Caledon Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Belfountain, Downey's Farm and Great War Flying Museum.

10.08.0030.t:
Rural Clarington, Clarington

Rural Clarington covers the farmland and hamlets of the former Darlington and Clarke townships outside the urban areas. These townships were joined with Bowmanville and Newcastle in 1974 to form the Town of Newcastle, later renamed Clarington. Hamlets include Enniskillen, Hampton, Newtonville, Kendal, Burketon and Tyrone. The area remains largely agricultural.

Rural Clarington is generally bounded by Boundary Road and the Scugog boundary to the north, Lake Ontario to the south and Townline Road to the west, and covers approximately 54,294 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), Highway 407 ETR, Highway 35, Highway 401, Darlington Nuclear Generating Station, Hybridyne Solar Project, a quarry or aggregate pit, a landfill site, a hydro transformer station (Bowmanville SS), a hydro transformer station (Clarington TS), Bond Head Cemetery, Eldad United Church Cemetery and Providence Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Clarington includes Ganaraska Forest 2, Darlington Hydro Fields and Hampton Conservation Area, and Wilmot Creek and the Ganaraska River run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. Bowmanville Golf and Country Club and Stonehenge Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools. Other notable landmarks include Canadian Tire Motorsport Park and Jungle Cat World.

04.02.0050.t:
Rural Clearview, Clearview

Rural Clearview covers the farmland, hamlets and escarpment lands of Clearview Township outside its villages. The area was part of the former Nottawasaga Township, incorporated in 1851, and Sunnidale Township, incorporated in 1858. Railway construction in the 1850s helped open the area for settlement. Clearview Township was formed on January 1, 1994, by merging the Town of Stayner, the Village of Creemore and the townships of Nottawasaga and Sunnidale.

Rural Clearview is generally bounded by the Wasaga Beach boundary to the north, the Springwater boundary to the east, Mulmur-Nottawasaga Townline to the south and County Road 124/124 to the west, and covers approximately 55,705 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 26, a quarry or aggregate pit, Collingwood Regional Airport, a landfill site, a hydro transformer station (Stayner TS), Edenvale Aerodrome, Creemore Union Cemetery, St. Patrick's Cemetery and New Lowell United Church Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a wastewater treatment plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Clearview includes Minesing Wetlands Conservation Area, Noisy River Provincial Park and Nottawasaga Lookout Provincial Nature Reserve, and the Mad River and Batteaux Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Edward Lake. Osler Brook Golf and Country Club and Mad River Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools, the Clearview Public Library and the Sunnidale branch of the Clearview Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Devil's Glen Provincial Park and Great Northern Exhibition Grounds.

07.01.0080.t:
Rural Dundas, Hamilton

Rural Dundas covers the rural and escarpment lands of the former Town of Dundas. Dundas was renamed in 1814 after Dundas Street and was incorporated as a town in 1847 from parts of West Flamborough and Ancaster townships. Much of the surrounding land is protected as the Dundas Valley Conservation Area, which has limited growth. Dundas became part of the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Rural Dundas is generally bounded by Governors Road to the east and the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision) to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 272 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Rural Dundas is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

03.07.0010.t:
Rural East Garafraxa, East Garafraxa

East Garafraxa is a rural township in Dufferin County, west of Orangeville. The origin of the name Garafraxa is uncertain, with several theories offered. Garafraxa Township was incorporated in 1850, and East Garafraxa became a separate township in 1869. The area is mainly farmland with small hamlets such as Marsville, Reading and Orton.

Rural East Garafraxa is generally bounded by County Road 109 to the north, Caledon East Garafraxa Townline to the east, Townline Erin Garafraxa to the south and Townline East Garafraxa West Garafraxa to the west, and covers approximately 16,547 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a quarry or aggregate pit and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural East Garafraxa includes Brookhaven Park, and the Grand River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Belwood. Residents are served by one school.

09.08.0040.t:
Rural East Gwillimbury, East Gwillimbury

This is the rural part of the former Township of East Gwillimbury, named after Elizabeth Simcoe, whose maiden name was Gwillim. Settlement followed the building of Yonge Street north to Holland Landing in the 1790s. The township was incorporated in 1850 and became the Town of East Gwillimbury in 1971. Approximately 75% of the town's land is protected under the Greenbelt and the Oak Ridges Moraine, and the rural area remains mostly farmland, woodlots and hamlets such as Holt and Brown Hill.

Rural East Gwillimbury is generally bounded by Ravenshoe Road to the north, York Durham Line to the east, Davis Drive to the south and Bathurst Street and the Newmarket boundary to the west, and covers approximately 23,280 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), Highway 404, a landfill site, Rice Group Queensville Yard (quarry), Queensville Cemetery, Mount Albert Cemetery and Selby Burying Ground. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural East Gwillimbury includes Bendor and Graves Tract, Brown Hill Tract and Zephyr North Tract, and the East Holland River and the Black River run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Franklin Pond. Pheasant Run Golf Club and Silver Lakes Golf & Country Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools, the Mount Albert branch of the East Gwillimbury Public Library and the Queensville branch of the East Gwillimbury Public Library, and transit is provided by the East Gwillimbury GO Station.

03.04.0010.t:
Rural East Luther Grand Valley, East Luther Grand Valley

This is the rural part of the former East Luther Township. East Luther was separated from Wellington County's Township of Luther when Dufferin County was formed in 1881. In 1995 the township merged with the Village of Grand Valley, and the municipality was renamed the Town of Grand Valley in 2012. The area is mainly farmland and includes part of the Luther Marsh.

Rural East Luther Grand Valley is generally bounded by the Wellington North boundary and the Southgate boundary to the north, Townline Amaranth East Luther to the east and County Road 109 to the south, and covers approximately 16,251 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a wastewater treatment plant, a hydro transformer station, Grand Valley Union (cemetery) and Saint Alban's Anglican Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Grand River and Boyne Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Grand Valley Public Library.

05.03.0090.t:
Sheridan Park, Mississauga

Sheridan Park is a research and employment area named after the former village of Sheridan, which grew around Winston Churchill Boulevard and the Queen Elizabeth Way. The village was renamed Sheridan in 1857 after the playwright Richard Brinsley Sheridan. The area became part of the Town of Mississauga in 1968 and the City in 1974.

Sheridan Park is generally bounded by Sheridan Park Drive to the north, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the south and Winston Churchill Boulevard to the west, and covers approximately 145 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 66% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school.

07.01.0050.t:
Rural Flamborough, Hamilton

Rural Flamborough covers the countryside of the former Beverly, East Flamborough and West Flamborough townships, surveyed after Treaty No. 3 in 1792. Farming, especially corn and strawberries, shaped the area, which includes hamlets such as Carlisle, Freelton, Greensville, Millgrove and Troy. The townships merged with Waterdown in 1974 to form Flamborough, which became a town in 1985 and joined the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Rural Flamborough is generally bounded by Gore Road to the north, Milburough Line to the east and Governors Road to the south, and covers approximately 47,443 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Dundas Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), Highway 6, a quarry or aggregate pit, a hydro transformer station, Rockton Aerodrome, a landfill site, Mount Zion Cemetery, Millgrove Cemetery and Beverly Troy Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Flamborough includes Valens Lake Conservation Area, Courtcliffe Park and Joe Sam's Leisure Park, and Fairchild Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Mountsberg Reservoir and Valens Reservoir. Flamborough Hills Golf & Country Club and Beverly Golf & Country Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools, the Carlisle branch of the Hamilton Public Library and the Freelton branch of the Hamilton Public Library. Other notable landmarks include African Lion Safari, Westfield Heritage Village and The Apple Orchard.

07.01.0190.t:
Rural Glanbrook, Hamilton

Rural Glanbrook covers the farmland of the former Glanford and Binbrook townships, surveyed in the 1790s. Binbrook was renamed in 1792 after a town in Lincolnshire, England. The two townships merged in 1974 to form the Township of Glanbrook, which was amalgamated into the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Rural Glanbrook is generally bounded by Regional Road 20 to the north, Westbrook Road to the east, Haldibrook Road to the south and a hydro corridor to the west, and covers approximately 18,053 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a quarry or aggregate pit, a hydro transformer station (Nebo TS), a landfill site, Chapel Hill Memorial Gardens (cemetery) and Glanbrook Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Mount Hamilton Cemetery. The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 0.4 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Glanbrook includes Binbrook Conservation Area, Turner Park and Binbrook Tract Conservation Area, and the Welland River and Twenty Mile Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Niapenco. Scenic Woods Golf Club and Chippawa  Creek Golf Course are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools and the Binbrook branch of the Hamilton Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Cameron Speedway & Amusements.

13.02.0020.t:
Rural Hamilton, Hamilton Township

Rural Hamilton covers the countryside of Hamilton Township in Northumberland County, outside its hamlets. The township was named after Henry Hamilton, Lieutenant-Governor of Quebec from 1782 to 1785, and was surveyed in 1791. United Empire Loyalists and other settlers followed, and the township was incorporated in 1850. It remained predominantly agricultural through the 19th and 20th centuries, with hamlets such as Baltimore, Camborne, Gores Landing and Harwood serving the farm area.

Rural Hamilton is generally bounded by the Cobourg boundary to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 100 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), Highway 401 and Providence Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Other notable landmarks include Rice Lake.

10.07.0020.t:
Rural Oshawa, Oshawa

Rural Oshawa covers the agricultural lands in the north part of the city, formerly in East Whitby Township. The township was settled for farming from the late 1700s and early 1800s and included small villages such as Columbus, Raglan and Kedron. In 1974, when the Regional Municipality of Durham was created, the remaining parts of East Whitby Township were merged into the City of Oshawa. Much of the area remains farmland.

Rural Oshawa is generally bounded by Coates Road to the north, Townline Road and the Clarington boundary to the east, Winchester Road to the south and the Whitby boundary to the west, and covers approximately 5,536 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), Highway 407 ETR, a quarry or aggregate pit and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Oshawa includes Purple Woods, Columbus Park and Raglan Park, and East Oshawa Creek and Oshawa Creek run through or along the community. Columbus Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Other notable landmarks include Oshawa Zoo & Fun Farm.

04.14.0020.t:
Rural Innisfil, Innisfil

Rural Innisfil covers the farmland and small hamlets of Innisfil outside its main villages. The township was surveyed in 1820, with the Hewson and Soules families among the first settlers, and its name comes from Inis Fáil, an ancient name for Ireland. It formed its first elected council in 1850 and remained largely agricultural. On January 1, 1991, the township, the Village of Cookstown and part of West Gwillimbury were combined into the Town of Innisfil.

Rural Innisfil is generally bounded by Lockhart Road to the north, Lake Simcoe to the east, the Bradford West Gwillimbury boundary to the south and County Road 27 and the Barrie boundary to the west, and covers approximately 32,550 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), Highway 400, a landfill site and Innisfil Wastewater Treatment. Along or just beyond its edges are Cookstown United Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Innisfil includes Friday Harbour Nature Preserve, Innisfil Beach Bark and Previn Park, and Innisfil Creek and Lovers Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. National Pines Golf Club and The Nest Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 10 schools, the Cookstown branch of the Innisfil Public Library and the Lakeshore branch of the Innisfil Public Library. Shopping is available at Tanger Outlets Cookstown.

09.01.0040.t:
Rural King, King

Rural King covers the farmland, estates and small hamlets of King Township outside its main villages. The township was named by John Graves Simcoe after John King, a British Under-Secretary of State. It was surveyed in 1800, settled from 1802 and incorporated in 1850. Its population peaked near 8,000 in 1875, and the township has been part of the Regional Municipality of York since 1971.

Rural King is generally bounded by the West Holland River (old) to the north, Bathurst Street to the east, the Vaughan boundary to the south and Highway 9 to the west, and covers approximately 30,295 hectares.
