Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), Highway 400, Nobleton Water Resource Recovery Facility, a landfill site, York Energy Centre, a hydro transformer station (Holland TS), a hydro transformer station (York Energy Centre), Kettleby Cemetery, St. Paul's Presbyterian Cemetery and Eleventh Line Old Presbyterian (cemetery). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural King includes Cold Creek Conservation Area, Cawthra Mulock Nature Reserve and Happy Valley Tract, and the East Humber River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Mary Lake and Lake Seneca. Cardinal Golf Complex and Nobleton Lakes Country Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Ansnorveldt branch of the King Township Public Library. Seneca College - King Campus is also located in the community.

01.W04.0290.t:
Rustic, City of Toronto (TRREB district W04)

Rustic lies between Lawrence Avenue West and Highway 401, east of Jane Street. The area was part of York Township and became part of North York in 1922. It was farmland until suburban housing was built in the decades after the Second World War. North York was amalgamated into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Rustic is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Culford Road to the east, Lawrence Avenue to the south and Jane Street to the west, and covers approximately 200 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Black Creek Drive and Highway 400. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rustic includes Maple Leaf Park, Gracefield Park and Rustic Park, and Black Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

09.02.0130.t:
Rural Vaughan, Vaughan

Rural Vaughan covers the remaining farmland and countryside of the former Vaughan Township. The township was named after Benjamin Vaughan, a British commissioner in the 1783 peace talks with the United States. It was settled from 1792, incorporated in 1850, and contained hamlets such as Teston, Purpleville and Vellore. In 1971 it merged with the Village of Woodbridge to form the Town of Vaughan, which became a city in 1991.

Rural Vaughan is generally bounded by the King boundary to the north, Bathurst Street to the east, Teston Road and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the south and Highway 400 to the west, and covers approximately 3,597 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), Pardes Chaim Cemetery, Pardes Shalom Cemetery, Maple United Church Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 3% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 400. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Vaughan includes North Maple Regional Park, Peak Point Park and Nevada Park, and East Patterson Creek and Patterson Creek run through or along the community. Eagles Nest Golf Club and Maple Downs Golf & Country Club are located in the area. Residents are served by one school, and transit is provided by the Maple GO Station.

09.03.0120.t:
Rural Markham, Markham

Rural Markham covers the remaining agricultural and hamlet lands of the former Markham Township, mainly in the north and east of the city. The township was surveyed in 1793 and named by John Graves Simcoe after William Markham, Archbishop of York; settlers arrived from 1794. By 1857 most of the township was cleared and farmed. Much of the eastern rural area is now within Rouge National Urban Park.

Rural Markham is generally bounded by the Whitchurch-Stouffville boundary to the north, York-Durham Line to the east and Major MacKenzie Drive to the west, and covers approximately 6,657 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), Highway 407, Dickson Hill Cemetery, First Baptist Church Cemetery and Peach's United Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Markham includes Rouge National Urban Park, Gordon Stollery Park and Winterberry Parkette, and the Little Rouge River, Little Rouge Creek and Katabokokonk Creek run through or along the community. Angus Glen Golf Club and Upper Unionville Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by one school and the Angus Glen branch of the Markham Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Markham Fairgrounds.

03.01.0010.t:
Rural Melancthon, Melancthon

Melancthon is a rural township in the north-west corner of Dufferin County, north and west of Shelburne. Its name is linked to the Protestant reformer Philip Melanchthon, as the surveyor named several townships in the area after Reformation figures. The township was incorporated in 1853 as part of Grey County and transferred to Dufferin County in 1881. It remains mainly agricultural, with hamlets such as Horning's Mills, Corbetton and Riverview.

Rural Melancthon is generally bounded by the Grey Highlands boundary to the north, Mulmur-Melancthon Townline to the east, Highway 89 to the south and the Southgate boundary to the west, and covers approximately 31,228 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 10, a landfill site, a quarry or aggregate pit, a hydro transformer station and Shelburne Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Noisy River runs through or along the community. Shelburne Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Other notable landmarks include Horning's Mills hamlet.

07.01.1840.t:
Ryckmans, Hamilton

Ryckmans takes its name from Samuel Ryckman (1777-1846), a farmer and surveyor who built a log house and barn at what is now Ryckman's Corners. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Housing here was built from the 1980s through the 2010s, with commercial development along Rymal Road and Upper James Street.

Ryckmans is generally bounded by Stone Church Road to the north, Upper Wellington Street to the east, Rymal Road to the south and Upper James Street to the west, and covers approximately 85 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Mount Hamilton Cemetery and Barton Stone United Church Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 2.8 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Ryckmans includes Dr William Bethune Park.

03.06.0010.t:
Rural Mono, Mono

Rural Mono covers the countryside of the Town of Mono in Dufferin County. Mono was incorporated as a township in Simcoe County on January 1, 1850, and was moved to the new Dufferin County in 1881. Its historic hamlets include Camilla, Mono Centre, Hockley, Relessey and Glen Cross. The township reorganized as the Town of Mono on June 1, 1999.

Rural Mono is generally bounded by Highway 89 to the north, Mono-Adjala Townline to the east, Highway 9 to the south and Mono Amaranth Townline to the west, and covers approximately 28,045 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 10, a quarry or aggregate pit, Forest Lawn Cemetery, St. John's Cemetery and Mono East Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Mono includes Mono Cliffs Provincial Park, Hockley Valley Provincial Park and Mono Tract Forest, and the Nottawasaga River and Sheldon Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Island Lake. The Iron and The Eagle Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Other notable landmarks include Turda Farms.

04.09.0070.t:
Snow Valley, Springwater

Snow Valley is a community in the former Vespra Township, west of Barrie, known for the Snow Valley ski area. The land was farmland and woodland until rural residential development in recent decades. On January 1, 1994 it became part of the Township of Springwater, formed from Flos and Vespra townships, the villages of Elmvale and Hillsdale, and part of Medonte.

Snow Valley is generally bounded by Wilson Drive to the east and Seadon Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 728 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are a quarry or aggregate pit. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Snow Valley includes Snow Valley Highlands Park, Snow Valley Park and Helen Coutts Memorial Park.

03.03.0010.t:
Rural Mulmur, Mulmur

Rural Mulmur covers the countryside of the Township of Mulmur in Dufferin County. The township was incorporated on January 1, 1851, and is made up of farmland and approximately 30 small communities. These include the hamlets of Mansfield, Honeywood, Rosemont, Stanton, Terra Nova and Whitfield.

Rural Mulmur is generally bounded by Mulmur-Nottawasaga Townline to the north, Mulmur-Tosorontio Townline to the east, Highway 89 to the south and Mulmur-Melancthon Townline to the west, and covers approximately 28,758 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 10, a landfill site, Honeywood Cemetery and Primrose Presbyterian Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Lavender Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Mulmur includes Boyne Valley Provincial Park, and the Pine River, the Boyne River and Mud Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

05.02.0240.t:
Sandringham-Wellington, Brampton

Sandringham-Wellington is a residential neighbourhood in the western part of Springdale in north Brampton, east of Heart Lake Conservation Area. Springdale was planned in the 1980s on farmland in Chinguacousy Township, and construction began in 1991. It was planned as a 'town within a city' for approximately 75,000 people. Most homes were built in the 1990s and 2000s.

Sandringham-Wellington is generally bounded by Countryside Drive to the north, Airport Road to the east, Bovaird Drive to the south and Heart Lake Road to the west, and covers approximately 1,682 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 410. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Sandringham-Wellington includes Dixie Sandalwood Park, Batsman Park and Odlum Valley. Rosedale Village Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 25 schools and the Springdale branch of the Brampton Library. Brampton Civic Hospital is also located in the community.

05.02.0230.t:
Sandringham-Wellington North, Brampton

Sandringham-Wellington North is the northern part of the Sandringham-Wellington neighbourhood in Springdale, north Brampton. Springdale was planned in the 1980s on farmland in Chinguacousy Township, and construction began in 1991. It was planned as a 'town within a city' for approximately 75,000 people. Most homes were built from the 1990s and 2000s.

Sandringham-Wellington North is generally bounded by Countryside Drive to the east and Mayfield Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 656 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 410. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Sandringham-Wellington North includes Sesquicentennial Park and Dr. José P. Rizal Park. Residents are served by one school.

04.02.0070.t:
Stayner, Clearview

Stayner grew up during construction of the Toronto, Simcoe and Huron Railway between 1851 and 1855. It was first called Nottawasaga Station and became an agricultural and lumbering centre. Stayner was incorporated as a village in 1872 and a town in 1888. Since January 1, 1994, it has been the administrative centre of Clearview Township.

Stayner is generally bounded by 27+28 Nottawasaga Sideroad to the north and County Road 7 to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,111 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a landfill site, a hydro transformer station (Stayner TS) and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Stayner includes Ives Park, Centennial Park and Station Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Clearview Public Library.

04.12.0040.t:
Rural New Tecumseth, New Tecumseth

Rural New Tecumseth covers the farmland of the former Tecumseth Township in southern Simcoe County. The area was settled from approximately 1820, and the township was incorporated on January 1, 1850. In 1991 the township was amalgamated with Alliston, Beeton and Tottenham to form the Town of New Tecumseth.

Rural New Tecumseth is generally bounded by Highway 89 and the Essa boundary to the north, the Bradford West Gwillimbury boundary to the east, Highway 9 to the south and Adjala-Tecumseth Townline to the west, and covers approximately 26,215 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), a wastewater treatment plant, a landfill site, CPKC Spence Yard, Trinity United Cemetery, Mount Tegart Cemetery and Fraser Presbyterian Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural New Tecumseth includes Beattie Pinery Provincial Park, Tottenham Conservation Area and Treetop's Park, and the Nottawasaga River and Beeton Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Tottenham Pond. Woodington Lake Golf Club - Legacy and The Club at Bond Head - South are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools, the D. A. Jones branch of the New Tecumseth Public Library and the Pam Kirkpatrick branch of the New Tecumseth Public Library.

04.16.0080.t:
Rural Oro-Medonte, Oro-Medonte

Rural Oro-Medonte covers the farmland and countryside of the former Oro and Medonte townships. Oro was surveyed around 1820 along the road to Penetanguishene, and in 1819 land there was granted to Black militiamen, forming the Oro Black Settlement. The townships were incorporated in 1850 and amalgamated with the Hawkestone Police Village in 1994. The former Toronto, Simcoe and Muskoka Junction Railway line, opened in 1871, is now the Oro-Medonte Rail Trail.

Rural Oro-Medonte is generally bounded by the Severn boundary to the north, Lake Simcoe to the south and Penetanguishene Road and Highway 400 to the west, and covers approximately 73,201 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), Highway 11, Highway 400, Highway 12, Orillia 2, Orillia 3, Midhurst 4, Midhurst 3, Oro-Medonte Solar Farm, a landfill site, a quarry or aggregate pit, Guthrie United Church & Cemetery and Hobart Memorial Church Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Vasey United Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Oro-Medonte includes Copeland Forest Resource Management Area, Hardwood Ski and Bike and Bass Lake Provincial Park, and the Sturgeon River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe and Bass Lake. Settlers' Ghost Golf Club and Horseshoe Valley Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools. Other notable landmarks include Oro African Methodist Episcopal Church (national historic site) and Oro Fair Grounds.

10.02.0010.t:
Rural Pickering, Pickering

Rural Pickering covers the agricultural north part of the city, originally Pickering Township, which was surveyed in 1791 and became a township in 1792. The area has historic hamlets such as Brougham, Claremont, Greenwood and Whitevale, several of them now heritage districts. Large areas were expropriated for a proposed airport in 1972; the airport was cancelled in 2025 and most of the lands are being transferred to Rouge National Urban Park. Pickering became a town in 1974 and a city in 2000.

Rural Pickering is generally bounded by Uxbridge-Pickering Townline Road to the north, Lake Ridge Road to the east, the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) and Scarborough-Pickering Townline Road to the south and York-Durham Line to the west, and covers approximately 18,327 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), Highway 407, Highway 407 ETR, Brock North Landfill (landfill), Claremont Union Cemetery, Sharrard Cemetery and Bethel Cemetery c. 1852. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), Brock West Landfill (landfill), Brock South Landfill (landfill) and a hydro transformer station (Cherrywood TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Pickering includes Rouge National Urban Park, Pickering Museum Village and Greenwood Park, and Ganatsekiagon Creek, Michell Creek and West Duffins Creek run through or along the community. Cherry Downs Golf & Country Club and Watson's Glen Golf Course are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Claremont branch of the Pickering Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Whitevale Heritage Conservation District.

13.01.0020.t:
Rural Port Hope, Port Hope

Rural Port Hope covers the farmland and hamlets of the former Hope Township, established in the early 1790s and named after Colonel Henry Hope. The township was settled by Loyalists and later immigrants from the 1790s onward. Its hamlets include Campbellcroft, Dale, Garden Hill and Knoxville. In 2001 Hope Township merged with the Town of Port Hope to form the Municipality of Port Hope.

Rural Port Hope is generally bounded by the Cavan Monaghan boundary and Eagleson Line to the north, County Road 28 to the east, Lake Ontario and Highway 401 to the south and the Clarington boundary and East Townline Road to the west, and covers approximately 26,576 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), Highway 401, Penn Energy - Van Dorp Solar Projects, a quarry or aggregate pit and a landfill site. Along or just beyond its edges are United Church Cemetery and Providence Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Port Hope includes Garden Hill Conservation Area, Richardson's Lookout Conservation Area and Alex Carruthers Memorial Park, and the Ganaraska River and the North Ganaraska River run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. Residents are served by one school and the Canton branch of the Port Hope Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Ganaraska Forest Centre.

04.19.0020.t:
Rural Ramara, Ramara

Rural Ramara covers the countryside and lakeshore areas of the former Rama and Mara townships, between Lake Simcoe and Lake Couchiching. The two townships were named in 1820, combined from 1852 to 1869, and transferred from Ontario County to Simcoe County in 1974. They were amalgamated on January 1, 1994 to form the Township of Ramara. The area includes farmland and many small lakeshore communities, such as Atherley, Longford Mills, Uptergrove and Lagoon City.

Rural Ramara is generally bounded by Lake Couchiching to the north and Lake Simcoe to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 56,640 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision), Highway 12, Pumphouse and St. Andrew Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a quarry or aggregate pit. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Ramara includes McRae Point Provincial Park, Mara Provincial Park and Brechin Community Centre Park, and the Black River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe and Lake Couchiching. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools, the Chippewas of Rama First Nation Public Library and the Brechin branch of the Ramara Township Public Library.

04.15.0020.t:
Sandy Hollow, Barrie

Sandy Hollow is a residential area in west Barrie, west of the older city core. Barrie grew from a supply depot at the end of the Nine Mile Portage and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a village in 1854, a town in 1871 and a city in 1959. The area was developed mainly in the later 20th century.

Sandy Hollow is generally bounded by Benson Drive to the north, Ferndale Drive to the east, Edgehill Drive to the south and the Springwater boundary and Miller Drive to the west, and covers approximately 151 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Barrie Landfill (landfill) and Barrie Landfill Borrows Area (landfill). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Sandy Hollow is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

04.15.0210.t:
Sanford, Barrie

Sanford is a small residential pocket on the south side of central Barrie, near Allandale and the downtown waterfront. Allandale grew around the railway from 1853 and was annexed by Barrie in 1896. Barrie grew from a supply depot at the end of the Nine Mile Portage and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a village in 1854, a town in 1871 and a city in 1959.

Sanford is generally bounded by Dufferin Street to the north, Bradford Street to the east and Innisfil Street and Sanford Street to the south, and covers approximately 25 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a wastewater treatment plant lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Sanford includes Brock Park.

07.01.1390.t:
Southam, Hamilton

Southam is named after William Southam (1843-1932), a Hamilton publisher and philanthropist. It is a residential neighbourhood on the Mountain next to Mohawk College. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most of its homes were built before 1960.

Southam is generally bounded by James Mountain Road and Claremont Drive to the north, Upper James Street to the east, Fennell Avenue to the south and West 5th Street to the west, and covers approximately 33 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Southam.

Green space in Southam includes Auchmar Estate, Southam Park and T. Melville Bailey Park. Other notable landmarks include Mohawk College (edge).

01.E08.1180.t:
Scarborough Village, City of Toronto (TRREB district E08)

Scarborough Village began in the 1800s as a crossroads village on Markham Road between Kingston Road and Eglinton Avenue. In 1832 it became the first community in Scarborough Township to have its own post office, though by the 1890s it had only approximately a dozen dwellings. The area was built up as part of Scarborough's postwar suburban growth. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Scarborough Village is generally bounded by the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) to the north, Scarborough Golf Club Road and Bethune Boulevard to the east, Lake Ontario and Bellamy Ravine Creek to the south and Bellamy Road to the west, and covers approximately 308 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and Washington Methodist Church Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Scarborough Village includes South Marine Park, Scarborough Village Park and Mason Road Park, and Bellamy Ravine Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools. Other notable landmarks include Christ Church Scarborough Village and Eglinton GO Station (northwest edge).

09.04.0130.t:
Rural Richmond Hill, Richmond Hill

Rural Richmond Hill covers the remaining farm and countryside lands of the city, largely on the Oak Ridges Moraine. These lands were part of the former King, Whitchurch, Markham and Vaughan townships until Richmond Hill was enlarged from 1,700 to approximately 27,000 acres in 1971 with the creation of York Region. Much of the area is now protected under Oak Ridges Moraine policies.

Rural Richmond Hill is generally bounded by Bloomington Road to the north and Highway 404 and Bayview Avenue to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 3,328 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision), the CN rail line, Gormley GO station, Elgin Mills Cemetery and Toronto Muslim Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 404. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Richmond Hill includes Oak Ridges Corridor Conservation Reserve, Richmond Green and Phyllis Rawlinson Park, and the Rouge River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Bond Lake and St. George Lake. Diamondback Golf Club and Bloomington Downs Golf Course are located in the area. Residents are served by one school and the Richmond Green branch of the Richmond Hill Public Library, and transit is provided by the Gormley and Bloomington GO stations.

10.04.0020.t:
Rural Scugog, Scugog

Rural Scugog covers the countryside of the former Reach, Cartwright and Scugog townships around Lake Scugog. The lake was created by a dam at Lindsay in 1834, which also formed Scugog Island. Scugog Township was formed in 1856, and the present Township of Scugog was created on January 1, 1974 by merging the three townships with Port Perry.

Rural Scugog is generally bounded by Brock-Scugog Townline Road to the north, Lake Scugog to the east, the Clarington boundary to the south and Lake Ridge Road to the west, and covers approximately 51,692 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Illumination, a hydro transformer station, a landfill site, Greenbank Airport, Marsh Hill Solar Farm, Prince Albert Cemetery and Immaculate Conception Borelia Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision) and a quarry or aggregate pit. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Scugog includes Port Perry Fair Ground, Cartwright Fields and Port Perry Waterfront, and Port Perry Lagoons and the Nonquon River run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Scugog. Oakridge Golf Club and Summerlea Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Scugog Public Library. Lakeridge Health - Port Perry is also located in the community.

04.18.0040.t:
Rural Severn, Severn

Rural Severn covers the countryside and waterfront areas of the Township of Severn, between Lake Couchiching and the Severn River. Lumbering drove early settlement, including the Severn Mills sawmill from approximately 1850, and the economy turned toward tourism after the Trent-Severn Waterway was completed in the area in 1915. The Township of Severn was formed on January 1, 1994 from the Village of Coldwater, the townships of Matchedash and Orillia, and parts of Medonte and Tay.

Rural Severn is generally bounded by Highway 400 to the north, Sparrow Lake to the east, Lake Couchiching to the south and Georgian Bay and the Oro-Medonte boundary to the west, and covers approximately 51,337 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision), the CN rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), Highway 400, Highway 11, Highway 12, a quarry or aggregate pit, a hydro transformer station (Severn TS), Waubaushene 4, Waubaushene 5 and a landfill site. Along or just beyond its edges are Saint Michael's Roman Catholic Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Severn includes Matchedash Bay Provincial Wilderness Area and Grant's Woods, and the North River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Couchiching and Sparrow Lake. Hawk Ridge Golf & Country Club and Bonaire Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by one school and the Severn Township Public Library. Shopping is available at Orillia Square Mall. Other notable landmarks include Trent-Severn Waterway.

04.09.0040.t:
Rural Springwater, Springwater

Rural Springwater covers the farmland and countryside of the former Flos and Vespra townships and part of Medonte, north and west of Barrie. The area was settled for farming in the 19th century, near the earlier Wendat settlement of Ossossane. On January 1, 1994 it became part of the Township of Springwater, formed from Flos and Vespra townships, the villages of Elmvale and Hillsdale, and part of Medonte. In 2026 Barrie annexed two portions of the township.

Rural Springwater is generally bounded by the Wasaga Beach boundary and Tiny Flos Townline to the north, Penetanguishene Road and Scarlett Line to the east, County Road 90 and the Barrie boundary to the south and the Clearview boundary to the west, and covers approximately 53,877 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), Highway 400, Highway 11, Midhurst 6, a quarry or aggregate pit, Aria Solar, Midhurst 2, a hydro transformer station (Midhurst TS), a hydro transformer station (Essa TS), Elmvale Presbyterian Cemetery, Minesing Union Cemetery and Saint Patrick's Roman Catholic Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Barrie Landfill (landfill) and Barrie Landfill Borrows Area (landfill). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Springwater includes Minesing Wetlands Conservation Area, Springwater Provincial Park and Edenvale Conservation Area, and Willow Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Orr Lake and Little Lake. Barrie Golf & Country Club and Landings of Willow Creek golf Course are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools, the Elmvale branch of the Springwater Public Library and the Midhurst branch of the Springwater Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Simcoe County Museum.

01.E05.1010.t:
Steeles, City of Toronto (TRREB district E05)

Steeles takes its name from Steeles Avenue, its northern boundary. The area held a Huron-Wendat village, the Alexandra site, in approximately 1400 CE, and was later cleared for farmland after European settlement in Scarborough Township. Most residential development was complete by the early 1980s, and the last farm was built over in 2001. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Steeles is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Kennedy Road to the east, a hydro corridor to the south and Victoria Park Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 469 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Steeles includes L'Amoreaux Park, Huntsmill Park and Terry Fox Park. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools and the Steeles branch of the Toronto Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Bamburgh Gardens Shopping Plaza and Dr. Norman Bethune Collegiate Institute.

07.01.0230.t:
Rural Stoney Creek, Hamilton

Rural Stoney Creek covers the farmland of the former Saltfleet Township, much of it above the Escarpment. Saltfleet was settled by Loyalists in the late 1700s, and fruit growing was the main industry for decades. Saltfleet merged with the village of Stoney Creek in 1974 to form the Town of Stoney Creek, which became a city in 1984 and joined Hamilton in 2001.

Rural Stoney Creek is generally bounded by the Grimsby boundary to the south and the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision) and Regional Road 20 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 5,454 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision), Waterford Vinemount Quarries (quarry), Stoney Creek Airport and Tapleytown Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Chapel Hill Memorial Gardens (cemetery). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Stoney Creek includes Saltfleet Conservation Area and Tapleytown Men's Club Park, and Forty Mile Creek and Stoney Creek run through or along the community. Pros Golf Centre is located in the area. Residents are served by one school.

04.08.0020.t:
Rural Tay, Tay

Rural Tay covers the countryside and smaller hamlets of the Township of Tay, such as Sturgeon Bay, Ogden's Beach and Paradise Point. The township was named in 1822 after a pet dog of Lady Sarah Maitland, wife of Lieutenant Governor Sir Peregrine Maitland. Tay was part of the United Townships of Tiny and Tay from 1851 and became a separate township in 1869. The current township took its present form in 1994.

Rural Tay is generally bounded by Georgian Bay to the east and Vasey Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 12,644 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a quarry or aggregate pit, a hydro transformer station (Waubaushene TS), RayLight Solar Park, a landfill site and Vasey United Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 400 and Waubaushene Protestant Cemetery/St. John's Catholic Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Tay includes Wye Marsh Provincial Wildlife Area, Wye Marsh and Waubashene Beaches Provincial Park, and Hog Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Mud Lake and Georgian Bay. Other notable landmarks include Sainte Marie among the Hurons.

04.04.0020.t:
Rural Tiny, Tiny

Rural Tiny covers the farmland, shoreline and beach communities of the Township of Tiny, including Balm Beach, Sandy Bay and Woodland Beach. The area was part of the Huron-Wendat homeland before 1650. The Township of Tiny was named in 1822 after a pet dog of Lady Sarah Maitland, wife of Lieutenant Governor Sir Peregrine Maitland. It was part of the United Townships of Tiny and Tay from 1851 and became a separate township in 1869.

Rural Tiny is generally bounded by Georgian Bay to the north, the Midland boundary to the east and Tiny Flos Townline to the south, and covers approximately 32,639 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a quarry or aggregate pit, Huronia Airport, a landfill site, Church of the Good Shepherd Cemetery and St. Andrew's Presbyterian Cemetary (cemetery). Along or just beyond its edges are Aria Solar. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Tiny includes Awenda Provincial Park, Tiny Marsh Provincial Wildlife Area and Lafontaine Park, and the Wye River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Farlain Lake and Georgian Bay. Brooklea Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

10.01.0010.t:
Rural Uxbridge, Uxbridge

Rural Uxbridge covers the countryside and hamlets of the Township of Uxbridge, including Goodwood, Leaskdale and Siloam. The township was named after Uxbridge, England, and was first settled by Quakers from Pennsylvania in 1806. It was incorporated in 1850. In 1974 Uxbridge Township, the Town of Uxbridge and Scott Township were combined into the present Township of Uxbridge.

Rural Uxbridge is generally bounded by Ravenshoe Road to the north, Lake Ridge Road to the east, Uxbridge-Pickering Townline Road to the south and York Durham Line to the west, and covers approximately 42,331 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision), the Uxbridge Brook Water Pollution Control Plant, J Chefero Sand & Gravel Ltd (quarry), Roseplain Solar Farm, Foster Memorial Cemetery, Quaker Hill Cemetery and Secord Pet Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are GO Lincolnville Yard and Lafarge Stouffville (quarry). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Uxbridge includes Uxbridge Urban Provincial Park, Rouge National Urban Park and Durham Regional Forest, and Pefferlaw Brook runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Mud Lake and Secord's Pond. Wyndance Golf Club and Coppinwood Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools, the Main branch of the Uxbridge Public Library and the Zephyr branch of the Uxbridge Public Library. Uxbridge Cottage Hospital is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Thomas Foster Memorial Temple, Leaskdale Manse (Lucy Maud Montgomery) and Barnyard Playland.

09.01.0010.t:
Schomberg, King

Schomberg was first settled as Brownsville after founder Thomas Brown, who built its flour mill in 1836. It was renamed Schomberg in 1862, likely after the 3rd Duke of Schomberg, because another Brownsville post office existed. It became a police village in 1899, and the Schomberg and Aurora Railway ran from 1902 to 1927. Housing grew in the 1950s and 1960s, in the 1990s and again in the 2010s.

Schomberg is generally bounded by Highway 9 to the north, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 268 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Schomberg Wellhouse, a cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 7% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Schomberg includes Osin Lions Park, Schomberg Fair Grounds and Hickstead Memorial Park, and the Holland River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Schomberg branch of the King Township Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Main Street Schomberg.

04.16.0060.t:
Shanty Bay, Oro-Medonte

Shanty Bay is a lakeside village on Kempenfelt Bay of Lake Simcoe, founded in the 1830s by the family of painter Lucius Richard O'Brien. The name is said to come from the shanties of early Black settlers in the area. St. Thomas Anglican Church, built of rammed earth between 1838 and 1841, was dedicated in 1842. Shanty Bay became part of the Township of Oro-Medonte in 1994.

Shanty Bay is generally bounded by Oro-Medonte Line 2 and Red Oak Crescent to the north, Oro-Medonte Rail Trail and Ridge Road to the east and Lake Simcoe to the south, and covers approximately 189 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Shanty Bay includes Shanty Bay Park, Emily Park and Arbourwood Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. Residents are served by one school.

09.08.0030.t:
Sharon, East Gwillimbury

Sharon grew around the farm of David Willson, leader of the Children of Peace, a group that broke away from the Quakers. The community was first called Hope and was renamed Sharon in 1841, after the Sharon Temple, so it could obtain a post office. The Temple was built between 1825 and 1831. Housing subdivisions were added from the mid-1980s, and Sharon is now home to the Town of East Gwillimbury's civic centre.

The boundary of Sharon follows local streets, lot lines and natural features rather than major roads, and the community covers approximately 529 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 404. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Sharon includes East Gwillimbury Sports Complex and Children of Peace Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

03.02.0010.t:
Shelburne, Shelburne

Shelburne grew from settlement in the 1860s along the Toronto-Sydenham Road, now Highway 10, in Melancthon Township. Founder William Jelly opened the British Canadian Hotel in 1865, and the post office was named after the Earl of Shelburne. New railways helped the population grow from approximately 70 in 1869 to 750 by 1877. Shelburne was incorporated as a village in 1879, later became a town, and has grown with new subdivisions in recent decades.

Shelburne is generally bounded by County Road 11 and County Road 124 to the east, the Amaranth boundary to the south and the Melancthon boundary to the west, and covers approximately 371 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 10, the Shelburne Wastewater Treatment Plant and industrial lands (approximately 11% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Shelburne Public Library.

07.01.1820.t:
Sheldon, Hamilton

Sheldon is a residential neighbourhood on the south Hamilton Mountain. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. It is one of the newer Mountain neighbourhoods, with most homes built in the 2000s and early 2010s.

Sheldon is generally bounded by Stone Church Road to the north, West 5th Street to the east, Rymal Road to the south and Garth Street to the west, and covers approximately 128 hectares.

The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 2.7 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Sheldon includes William Connell City-Wide Park, Garth Reservoir Park and Bishop A. Tonnos Park.

10.06.0010.t:
Rural Whitby, Whitby

Rural Whitby covers the farmland and countryside of the former Whitby Township north of the urban area. The township was surveyed in 1792 and settled from approximately 1800; its eastern half became East Whitby Township in 1857. The township merged with the Town of Whitby in 1968. Highways 407 and 412 opened through the area in 2016.

Rural Whitby is generally bounded by Townline Road to the north, the Oshawa boundary to the east and Lake Ridge Road to the south, and covers approximately 8,369 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision), the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), Highway 412, Highway 407 ETR, Highway 401, a hydro transformer station (Whitby TS) and a quarry or aggregate pit. Along or just beyond its edges are a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Whitby includes Cullen Central Park, Lynde Creek Park and Whitby Meadows Park, and Lynde Creek and Oshawa Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Cranberry Marsh. Lakeridge Links & Whispering Ridge Golf Courses and Royal Ashburn Golf Club are located in the area.

09.05.0010.t:
Rural Whitchurch-Stouffville, Whitchurch-Stouffville

Rural Whitchurch-Stouffville covers the countryside of the former Whitchurch Township. The township was created in 1792 and named after a village in Herefordshire, England, linked to Elizabeth Simcoe's family; it was surveyed in 1800 to 1802. Clearing of the thin northern soils led to reforestation from 1911 onward. On January 1, 1971, the township merged with the Village of Stouffville to form the Town of Whitchurch-Stouffville.

Rural Whitchurch-Stouffville is generally bounded by Davis Drive to the north, York Durham Line to the east, the Markham boundary to the south and Highway 404 to the west, and covers approximately 19,395 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (CN Bala Subdivision), Highway 404, a hydro transformer station, Brock Aggregates (quarry), York Sanitation Site #4 (landfill), Lafarge Stouffville (quarry), Highland Hills Memorial Gardens (cemetery), Pine Orchard Cemetery and Heise Hill Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision) and GO Lincolnville Yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Whitchurch-Stouffville includes North Tract, Eldred King Tract and Bruce's Mill Conservation Area, and the Holland River East Branch runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Musselman Lake and Preston Lake. Spring Lakes Golf Club and Station Creek Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools, and transit is provided by the Old Elm GO Station.

07.01.1760.t:
Rushdale, Hamilton

Rushdale is a residential neighbourhood on the south Hamilton Mountain. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most of its homes were built in the 1980s.

Rushdale is generally bounded by the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the north, Upper Sherman Avenue to the east, Stone Church Road to the south and Upper Wentworth Street to the west, and covers approximately 74 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rushdale includes T. B. McQuesten Park.

05.03.0100.t:
Sheridan, Mississauga

Sheridan takes its name from the former village of Sheridan, which grew around the crossing of Winston Churchill Boulevard and Middle Road (now the Queen Elizabeth Way). First called Hammondsville, the village was renamed in 1857 after the playwright Richard Brinsley Sheridan. The farmland was developed with suburban housing after the area became part of Mississauga in 1968 and the City in 1974.

Sheridan is generally bounded by the Credit River and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the east and Dundas Street and Winston Churchill Boulevard to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 787 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and St. Peter's Anglican Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Sheridan includes Springbank Meadows Park, Bruce Reynolds Park and Thornlodge Park, and Loyalist Creek, Glen Erin Brook and the Irrigation Canal run through or along the community. Mississaugua Golf & Country Club and Credit Valley Golf & Country Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Sheridan branch of the Mississauga Library. Shopping is available at Sheridan Centre.

09.03.0340.t:
Sherwood-Amberglen, Markham

Sherwood-Amberglen is a residential area of east Markham, next to historic Markham Village. The land was part of Markham Township, settled from the early 1800s by Mennonite and later British settlers. It was built up as part of Markham's suburban growth in the later 20th century.

Sherwood-Amberglen is generally bounded by Highway 7 to the north, Ninth Line to the east, Highway 407 to the south and the Rouge River and Mount Joy Creek to the west, and covers approximately 137 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Sherwood-Amberglen includes Rouge Valley Park, Armstrong Park and Sherwood Forest, and the Rouge River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

06.02.0170.t:
Shoreacres, Burlington

Shoreacres is a lakeside residential area in east Burlington, in the former Nelson Township. The land was originally granted to Laura Secord after the War of 1812. In 1930 Edythe MacKay, daughter of Hamilton industrialist Cyrus Birge, built a stone lakefront mansion on the "Shore Acres" estate. The city bought the estate in 1990, and the surrounding area was built up with estate and suburban housing through the 20th century.

Shoreacres is generally bounded by Fairview Street to the north, Appleby Line to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Walkers Line to the west, and covers approximately 455 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Shoreacres.

Green space in Shoreacres includes Nelson Park, Paletta Lakefront Park and Iroquois Park, and Shoreacres Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the New Appleby branch of the Burlington Public Library.

04.02.0010.t:
Singhampton, Clearview

Singhampton is a village in the southwest part of Clearview Township, below the Niagara Escarpment. It lies in the former Nottawasaga Township, which was incorporated in 1851. Clearview Township was formed on January 1, 1994, by merging the Town of Stayner, the Village of Creemore and the townships of Nottawasaga and Sunnidale. Singhampton remains a small village surrounded by farmland and escarpment lands.

Singhampton is generally bounded by County Road 124/124 and County Road 31/95 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 79 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Singhampton is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

09.02.0030.t:
Sonoma Heights, Vaughan

Sonoma Heights is a residential area of Woodbridge near Islington Avenue and Rutherford Road. Woodbridge began as the mill village of Burwick after 1837 and was incorporated as a village in 1882. Sonoma Heights was among the subdivisions built north of the old village during the 1990s. The area has been part of the Town, now City, of Vaughan since 1971.

Sonoma Heights is generally bounded by Major MacKenzie Drive to the north, Islington Avenue and Canada Company Avenue to the east, Rutherford Road to the south and the Humber River to the west, and covers approximately 414 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Sonoma Heights includes Sonoma Heights Community Park, Napa Valley Park and Sunset Ridge Park, and the Humber River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools.

10.05.0070.t:
South East, Ajax

This community covers southeastern Ajax along Lake Ontario, including Pickering Beach. Pickering Beach was developed by James Tuckett from 1926 as a lakeshore cottage community that later became permanent. Ajax was named after the Royal Navy cruiser HMS Ajax, and grew from a Second World War munitions plant and its workers' village built on farmland in Pickering Township from 1939. It became a town in 1955 and joined the Regional Municipality of Durham in 1974, when its boundaries were expanded to include Pickering Village, Pickering Beach and Audley.

South East is generally bounded by the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision) to the north, Lake Ridge Road to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Harwood Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 1,191 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Ajax Water Supply Plant and industrial lands (approximately 5% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision) and Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in South East includes Lakeside Park, Paradise Park and Kinsman Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Main branch of the Ajax Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Pickering Beach.

07.01.0220.t:
Stoney Creek Mountain, Hamilton

Stoney Creek Mountain is the part of Stoney Creek above the Niagara Escarpment, on land of the former Saltfleet Township. Areas on the Escarpment west of Highway 20 became known as Upper Stoney Creek. Housing was built steadily from the 1960s onward, with strong growth in the 1990s and 2000s. Stoney Creek was amalgamated into Hamilton in 2001.

Stoney Creek Mountain is generally bounded by Upper Centennial Parkway to the east and Rymal Road to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,189 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a quarry or aggregate pit and Hannon Free Methodist Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision), the Red Hill Valley Parkway and Trinity United Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Stoney Creek Mountain includes Eramosa Karst Conservation Area, Heritage Green Sports Park and Valley Park, and Davis Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools and the Valley Park branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

07.01.1480.t:
Vincent, Hamilton

Vincent is named after John Vincent (1764-1848), the British army officer at the Battle of Stoney Creek in 1813. It is a mainly residential neighbourhood in east Hamilton, with shops along Quigley Road. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most homes were built between 1961 and 1980.

Vincent is generally bounded by King Street to the north and Davis Creek and Country Club Drive to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 198 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Vincent includes Veevers Park. Residents are served by one school.

01.W01.0480.t:
South Parkdale, City of Toronto (TRREB district W01)

South Parkdale is the part of Parkdale south of Queen Street West. Parkdale grew as a lakeside suburb after the railway station opened in 1856, was incorporated as a village in 1879, and was annexed by the City of Toronto in 1889. Large Victorian houses were built in the 1880s and 1890s. After the Gardiner Expressway was built from 1955, many blocks were replaced by apartment buildings in the 1950s to 1970s, and many older houses were converted to multiple units.

South Parkdale is generally bounded by Queen Street to the north and Lake Ontario and the Gardiner Expressway to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 211 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Gardiner Expressway and a rail yard. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Galt Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in South Parkdale includes Sir Casimir Gzowski Park, Marilyn Bell Park and Budapest Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. E.W. Bickle Centre for Complex Continuing Care is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Masaryk Park and Sunnyside Pavillion.

09.04.0060.t:
South Richvale, Richmond Hill

South Richvale is part of Richvale, a residential area in southwest Richmond Hill, lying south of Carrville Road. The land was rural until it became part of Richmond Hill with the 1971 municipal expansion. Hillcrest Mall serves as Richvale's main shopping centre.

South Richvale is generally bounded by Carrville Road to the north, Yonge Street to the east, Highway 7 to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 441 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 407 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in South Richvale includes Morgan Boyle Park, Chapman Park and Sunnywood Park, and the Don River East Branch and Patterson Creek run through or along the community. Richmond Hill Golf and Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Richvale branch of the Richmond Hill Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Hillcrest Mall.

01.E01.1400.t:
South Riverdale, City of Toronto (TRREB district E01)

South Riverdale covers the southern half of Riverdale, from Gerrard Street to Lake Shore Boulevard, and includes Leslieville. Leslieville began as a small village in the 1850s around the Toronto Nurseries of George Leslie, and the area was annexed to the City of Toronto in 1884. It developed in the late 1800s and early 1900s as a working-class district of houses and light industry. Since the 1990s many former industrial buildings have been converted to housing and film studios.

South Riverdale is generally bounded by Lake Ontario and Ship Channel to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 876 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision), Portlands Energy Centre, David Miller Carhouse, the Ashbridges Bay Wastewater Treatment Plant, a hydro transformer station (Portlands Energy Center Substation), a hydro transformer station (Basin TS), Holy Blossom Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 13% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision), the Don Valley Parkway, the Gardiner Expressway, GO Don Yard and TTC Greenwood Yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in South Riverdale includes Tommy Thompson Park, Cherry Beach Clarke Beach Park and Biidaasige Park, and the Don River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools, the Jones branch of the Toronto Public Library and the Queen/Saulter branch of the Toronto Public Library. Shopping is available at Gerrard Square. Other notable landmarks include Jimmie Simpson Park and Hennick Bridgepoint Hospital and the former Don Jail.

04.15.0260.t:
South Shore, Barrie

South Shore runs along the south side of Kempenfelt Bay, east of Allandale. The shoreline here was part of Innisfil Township, which included the early settlements of Tollendal and Minets Point. Much of Barrie's south end was part of Innisfil Township until January 1, 1982, when approximately 8,623 acres were annexed to the city. The area mixes older lakeside homes with newer subdivisions.

South Shore is generally bounded by Lake Simcoe to the east and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 534 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision). Along or just beyond its edges are a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in South Shore includes The Gables Park, Tyndale Park and Dock Road Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe.

10.05.0030.t:
South West, Ajax

This community covers southwestern Ajax along Lake Ontario, part of the lands where the Defence Industries Limited munitions plant was built in 1939. Ajax was named after the Royal Navy cruiser HMS Ajax, and grew from a Second World War munitions plant and its workers' village built on farmland in Pickering Township from 1939. It became a town in 1955 and joined the Regional Municipality of Durham in 1974, when its boundaries were expanded to include Pickering Village, Pickering Beach and Audley.

South West is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Harwood Avenue to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Church Street and Duffins Creek to the west, and covers approximately 902 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision), the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), Kennedy Detention Centre and industrial lands (approximately 27% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401 and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in South West includes Ajax Lion's Park, and Duffins Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools, and transit is provided by the Ajax GO Station. Lakeridge Health - Ajax Pickering Hospital is also located in the community.

05.03.0110.t:
Southdown, Mississauga

Southdown is mainly an industrial area in the southwest of Mississauga, next to Clarkson and along Southdown Road. Industrial uses here include a cement plant and an oil refinery, with the cement plant's smokestack, built in 1956, being the city's tallest structure until 2011. The area was part of the former Toronto Township and became part of Mississauga in 1968.

Southdown is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) and Southdown Road to the north, Orr Road to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Winston Churchill Boulevard to the west, and covers approximately 724 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Clarkson Wastewater Treatment Plant and industrial lands (approximately 52% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) and a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Southdown includes Lakeside Park and Petro Canada Park, and Avonhead Creek runs through or along the community. Transit is provided by the Clarkson GO Station.

05.02.0330.t:
Southgate, Brampton

Southgate is a residential area in the southern part of Bramalea in east Brampton. Bramalea was developed from the late 1950s and 1960s as a planned satellite town in the former Chinguacousy Township by Bramalea Limited, with streets named in alphabetical phases. Construction began in the 1960s and continued into the early 1970s. Bramalea became part of the City of Brampton in 1974.

Southgate is generally bounded by Queen Street to the north, Torbram Road to the east, Steeles Avenue to the south and Bramalea Road to the west, and covers approximately 410 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 17% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Old Methodist Cemetery Grahamsville. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Southgate includes Earnscliffe Park, Fallingdale Park and Dearbourne Park, and West Mimico Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools.

01.C12.0640.t:
St. Andrew-Windfields, City of Toronto (TRREB district C12)

The name comes from the former St. Andrew's Golf Course (1927 to the 1950s) and from Windfields, the estate E.P. Taylor founded in 1937, which became a well-known thoroughbred horse farm. Taylor sold most of the estate to developers in 1968 and donated land for Windfields Park. Most houses in the Windfields area were built in the 1970s and 1980s. The area was part of North York until it joined the City of Toronto in 1998.

St. Andrew-Windfields is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, York Mills Road to the east and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 717 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision), St. John's York Mills (cemetery) and industrial lands (approximately 7% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in St. Andrew-Windfields includes Moatfield Farm Park, St. Andrew’s Park and Mossgrove Park, and the Don River East Branch runs through or along the community. Donalda Golf and Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools, and transit is provided by the York Mills subway station and the Oriole GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Wilket Creek.

07.01.1290.t:
St. Clair, Hamilton

St. Clair is a small residential neighbourhood at the foot of the Escarpment in east-central Hamilton, with shops along Main Street East. It lies on former Barton Township land that was brought into the city as Hamilton grew east. Most of its homes were built before 1960.

St. Clair is generally bounded by Main Street to the north, Sherman Avenue to the east, Sherman Access and Mountain Park Avenue to the south and Wentworth Street to the west, and covers approximately 70 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in St. Clair includes Myrtle Park and Lifesavers Park.

05.02.0280.t:
Steeles Industrial, Brampton

Steeles Industrial is an employment area along Steeles Avenue in south Brampton, near the Mississauga boundary. The land was part of Chinguacousy Township. Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships were merged with the Town of Brampton in 1974 to form the City of Brampton. Industrial development here grew mainly in the second half of the 20th century.

Steeles Industrial is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue and Highway 407 to the east and Etobicoke Creek to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 568 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), Highway 410 and industrial lands (approximately 50% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407 and Emerald Energy from Waste. The community is also close to Toronto Pearson International Airport, approximately 2.2 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Steeles Industrial includes Kennedy Valley Park, and Etobicoke Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school, and transit is provided by the Bramalea GO Station.

09.02.0110.t:
Steeles West Industrial, Vaughan

Steeles West Industrial is an employment area in the southern part of Vaughan, along Steeles Avenue. Concord, the main industrial district of Vaughan, began to industrialize in the 1950s after Highway 400 and the CN MacMillan Yard were built. Industrial development along Steeles Avenue was largely built in the 1980s. The area has been part of the Town, now City, of Vaughan since 1971.

Steeles West Industrial is generally bounded by Highway 400 to the east and Highway 407 and Steeles Avenue to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 392 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 40% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407 and Highway 400. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Steeles West Industrial is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

10.07.0090.t:
Stevenson, Oshawa

Stevenson is in southwest Oshawa and takes its name from Stevenson Road, named after a family that once held large landholdings in the area. The land was originally part of Whitby Township (later East Whitby). It was annexed by the City of Oshawa in the 1950s. The area is now largely an industrial and commercial corridor, with some residential pockets and lakefront parkland at its south end.

Stevenson is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Park Road to the east, Lake Ontario and Phillip Murray Avenue to the south and Boundary Road and the Whitby boundary to the west, and covers approximately 582 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision), a hydro transformer station, CN Oshawa Yard and industrial lands (approximately 68% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Stevenson includes Lakefront West Park, Gold Point Wildlife Reserve and Fenelon / Venus Park. Transit is provided by the Oshawa GO Station.

07.01.1280.t:
Stinson, Hamilton

Stinson is named after Thomas Stinson (1798-1864), a merchant, banker and landowner. It is a mainly residential neighbourhood in the lower city south-east of downtown, with businesses along Stinson Street and Main Street East. The area was within city limits by the end of the 19th century, when Hamilton had expanded to roughly the Mountain brow and Gage Avenue. Most of its homes were built before 1960.

Stinson is generally bounded by Main Street to the north, Wentworth Street to the east, Mountain Park Avenue to the south and Wellington Street to the west, and covers approximately 71 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Stinson includes Bruce Trail Park, Rail Trail Park and Carter Park.

09.07.0030.t:
Summerhill Estates, Newmarket

Summerhill Estates is a residential neighbourhood in southwest Newmarket, between Yonge Street and Bathurst Street, south of Mulock Drive. It was largely built from the 1990s onward. Newmarket was settled by Quakers between 1801 and 1803 and was incorporated as a town in 1880.

Summerhill Estates is generally bounded by McCaffrey Road to the north, Yonge Street to the east, the Aurora boundary to the south and Bathurst Street and Old Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 547 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Religious Society of Friends Burial Ground. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Summerhill Estates includes Whipper Watson Park, Jim Bond Park and George Luesby Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools.

01.W07.0160.t:
Stonegate-Queensway, City of Toronto (TRREB district W07)

Stonegate-Queensway lies in southeast Etobicoke near the mouth of the Humber River, which was the site of early trading and the first community in southern Etobicoke. Parts of the area were subdivided in 1883 and 1926, but most of the northern part was developed after the Second World War, starting with veterans' houses at The Queensway and Royal York Road. The Queensway itself was named in the 1950s, after Queen Elizabeth II came to the throne. Etobicoke became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Stonegate-Queensway is generally bounded by Bloor Street to the north, the Humber River to the east, the Gardiner Expressway to the south and Islington Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 799 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Gardiner Expressway, the Humber Wastewater Treatment Plant, Park Lawn Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Stonegate-Queensway includes King's Mill Park, South Humber Park and Berry Road Park, and Mimico Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 11 schools and the Humber Bay branch of the Toronto Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Ontario Food Terminal.

09.07.0090.t:
Stonehaven-Wyndham, Newmarket

Stonehaven-Wyndham is a residential neighbourhood in southeast Newmarket, between Bayview Avenue and Highway 404, south of Mulock Drive. It was developed as development in Newmarket moved east toward Highway 404. Many of its streets are named after famous racehorses, and Copper Hills is its newest section.

Stonehaven-Wyndham is generally bounded by Mulock Drive to the north, Highway 404 to the east and the Aurora boundary and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 640 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and industrial lands (approximately 7% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), Highway 404 and a hydro transformer station (Armitage TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Stonehaven-Wyndham includes Ken Sturgeon Park, Art Ferguson Park and Best Family Park, and the Holland River East Branch and Bogart Creek run through or along the community. St. Andrews Valley Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Other notable landmarks include Magna Centre.

07.01.0240.t:
