Stoney Creek, Hamilton

Stoney Creek takes its name from the creek that runs from the Devil's Punch Bowl to Lake Ontario. The area was settled by Loyalists in the late 1700s and was the site of the Battle of Stoney Creek on June 6, 1813. The village merged with Saltfleet Township in 1974 to form the Town of Stoney Creek, which became a city in 1984. Residential growth in the lower city was strong in the 1970s and 1980s, and Stoney Creek was amalgamated into Hamilton in 2001.

Stoney Creek is generally bounded by Barton Street to the north, Fruitland Road to the east, the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision) to the south and Queenston Road to the west, and covers approximately 1,038 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision) and Fruitland Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Stoney Creek Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Stoney Creek includes Green Acres Park, Sherwood Park and Hunter Estates Park, and Battlefield Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 11 schools and the Saltfleet branch of the Hamilton Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Eastgate Square (edge).

07.01.0270.t:
Stoney Creek Industrial, Hamilton

Stoney Creek Industrial is the industrial and employment area of the former City of Stoney Creek. Lower land costs than in Hamilton made Stoney Creek a centre for light industry and road transportation. Stoney Creek was formed from the village and Saltfleet Township in 1974, became a city in 1984, and was amalgamated into Hamilton in 2001.

Stoney Creek Industrial is generally bounded by the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and Barton Street to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 762 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision), a hydro transformer station and industrial lands (approximately 71% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Glover Golf and Sports Park is located in the area. Residents are served by one school. Mohawk College - Stoney Creek Campus is also located in the community.

09.05.0030.t:
Stouffville, Whitchurch-Stouffville

Stouffville is named after Abraham Stouffer, a Mennonite settler from Pennsylvania who arrived in 1804 and built saw and grist mills on Duffins Creek. The name was shortened to Stouffville when the post office opened in 1832. The Toronto and Nipissing Railway arrived in 1871, and the village was incorporated in 1877. It joined Whitchurch Township in 1971 to form Whitchurch-Stouffville, and grew rapidly after 2005, nearly doubling in population between 2006 and 2011.

Stouffville is generally bounded by Bethesda Sideroad to the north, York Durham Line to the east, the Markham boundary to the south and Highway 48 to the west, and covers approximately 1,602 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision), GO Lincolnville Yard and a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transformer station. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Stouffville includes Stouffville Arena Park, Stouffville Leisure Centre Memorial Park and Sunnyridge Park, and Stouffville Creek runs through or along the community. Timber Creek Golf & Family Fun Centre is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 11 schools and the Whitchurch-Stouffville Public Library, and transit is provided by the Old Elm GO Station.

07.01.1080.t:
Strathcona, Hamilton

Strathcona is a lower-city neighbourhood west of downtown Hamilton, bounded by Highway 403, the CN rail line, Queen Street, York Boulevard and Main Street. Many of its homes were built in the late 19th century. It includes Dundurn Castle, built between 1832 and 1835 for Sir Allan Napier MacNab. Victoria Park was the site of the Crystal Palace exhibition hall from 1860 to 1891.

Strathcona is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) to the north, Queen Street to the east, Main Street to the south and Highway 403 and Lake Ontario to the west, and covers approximately 185 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision), Highway 403, Hamilton Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 3% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line and the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Strathcona includes Dundurn Park, Kay Drage Park and Victoria Park. Residents are served by one school.

09.09.0050.t:
Sutton   Jackson's Point, Georgina

Sutton began with James O'Brien Bourchier, who settled in 1821 and built saw and grist mills, and was first called Bourchier's Mills. It was renamed Sutton West in 1885 and was a village until it joined the Town of Georgina in 1971. Jackson's Point, on the lake to the north, is named after John Mills Jackson, who settled there in the late 1820s. Railway service from 1877 and the radial railway to Toronto in the early 1900s made Jackson's Point an early cottage and resort area.

Sutton   Jackson's Point is generally bounded by Lake Simcoe to the north, Park Road to the east, Old Homestead Road to the south and McCowan Road to the west, and covers approximately 3,680 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Briar Hill Cemetary (cemetery), Briar Hill Cemetery and St. George's Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Sutton   Jackson's Point includes Sibbald Point Provincial Park, De La Salle Park and Bonnie Park, and the Black River runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. The Briars Golf Club and Briars Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Peter Gzowski branch of the Georgina Public Library.

05.03.0060.t:
Streetsville, Mississauga

Streetsville is named after Timothy Street, a surveyor who built saw and grist mills on the Credit River. The first settler, James Glendinning, arrived in 1819. The village was incorporated in 1858 and became a town in 1962. Suburban growth began in the mid-1950s and continued through the 1960s, with further building in the late 1980s. Streetsville was amalgamated into the City of Mississauga in 1974.

Streetsville is generally bounded by the Credit River to the east, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision) to the south and Erin Mills Parkway and Britannia Road to the west, and covers approximately 481 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), Streetsville Memorial Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Streetsville Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Streetsville includes Credit Meadows Park, Streetsville Memorial Park and Turney Woods, and Mullet Creek and the Credit River run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Streetsville branch of the Mississauga Library, and transit is provided by the Streetsville GO Station. Other notable landmarks include Historic Queen Street South main street.

07.01.1130.t:
Stipley, Hamilton

Stipley (also spelled Stipeley) is a neighbourhood in Hamilton's lower east end, with shops along Barton Street East, King Street East and Main Street East. It lies on former Barton Township land that was brought into the city as Hamilton grew east. Most of its homes were built before 1960.

Stipley is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) to the north, Gage Avenue to the east, Main Street to the south and Sherman Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 120 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include industrial lands (approximately 12% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Stipley includes Lucy Day Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

04.14.0030.t:
Stroud, Innisfil

Stroud was first called Meyer's Corners and later Victoria. It was renamed Stroud in 1875 after Stroud, England, the hometown of local MP W.C. Little. Settlers began building homes in approximately 1825, and Innisfil Township's first school (1838) and first church were here. It became part of the Town of Innisfil on January 1, 1991.

Stroud is generally bounded by Nelson Crescent to the north and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 240 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school and the Stroud branch of the Innisfil Public Library.

10.03.0030.t:
Sunderland, Brock

Sunderland was first called Jones Corners, after Arch and Lorenzo Jones, who owned property in the village core. It grew around the Brock Hotel, a stopping place run by Lorenzo Jones, and was renamed Sunderland by 1871. The land was granted to settlers in the early 1820s. Since 1974 it has been part of the Township of Brock in Durham Region.

Sunderland is generally bounded by Beaver River Wetland Trail to the east and Highway 7/12 to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 135 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Sunderland Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school and the Brock Libraries - Sunderland Branch.

04.15.0050.t:
Sunnidale, Barrie

Sunnidale is a residential area in northwest Barrie named after Sunnidale Road. Sunnidale Park was a golf course from 1911 to the 1960s before the city acquired it as a public park in the late 1960s. Much of the surrounding area was built up with housing in the second half of the 20th century.

Sunnidale is generally bounded by Livingstone Street to the north, Highway 400 to the south and Anne Street to the west, and covers approximately 246 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 400, Barrie Union Cemetery and St. Mary's Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Sunnidale includes Sunnidale Park, Sunnidale Dog Off Leash Recreation Area and Riverwood Park. Residents are served by one school.

01.E05.1080.t:
Tam O'Shanter-Sullivan, City of Toronto (TRREB district E05)

The name comes from the Tam O'Shanter Golf Course and from O'Sullivan's Corners at Victoria Park and Sheppard avenues, named after Patrick O'Sullivan, where a post office opened in 1892. The land was farmland in Scarborough Township, and Harry C. Hatch trained racehorses on his farm at Pharmacy and Sheppard from 1927 to 1946. Residential growth began in the 1950s, and in the 1960s the Robert McClintock Company built the Bridlewood development. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Tam O'Shanter-Sullivan is generally bounded by Huntingwood Drive to the north, Kennedy Road to the east, Highway 401 to the south and Victoria Park Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 554 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) and Highway 401. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Tam O'Shanter-Sullivan includes Ron Watson Park, Wishing Well Park and Stephen Leacock Park. Tam O'Shanter Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools and the Agincourt branch of the Toronto Public Library. Shopping is available at Agincourt Mall.

10.06.0060.t:
Taunton North, Whitby

Taunton North is a residential area in north Whitby, named after Taunton Road. Whitby Township was surveyed in 1792, and the town and township merged in 1968. Since at least the mid-1990s, new subdivision growth in Whitby has moved northward, and this area was built out in that period.

Taunton North is generally bounded by Conlin Road and a hydro corridor to the north, the Oshawa boundary to the east, Taunton Road to the south and Lynde Creek to the west, and covers approximately 907 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Resurrection Catholic Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Taunton North includes Cullen Central Park, Hannam Park and McKinney Park, and Pringle Creek and Lynde Creek run through or along the community. Lyndebrook Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

07.01.1880.t:
Templemead, Hamilton

Templemead is a residential neighbourhood on the south-east Hamilton Mountain, with shopping along Rymal Road East and at Stone Church Road and Upper Ottawa Street. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most homes were built between 1961 and 2000, with the largest share from the 1980s.

Templemead is generally bounded by Stone Church Road to the north, Upper Ottawa Street to the east, Rymal Road to the south and Upper Gage Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 85 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Templemead.

Green space in Templemead includes Templemead Park. Residents are served by one school.

01.C11.0790.t:
Thorncliffe Park, City of Toronto (TRREB district C11)

The name comes from Thorn Cliff House, home of the Taylor family, who bought farmland at the forks of the Don River in 1831. The land later became a horse farm and, from 1920, the Thorncliffe Park racetrack. Leaside annexed the former racetrack in 1954 and planned a new community. Most of its apartment buildings were built in the 1960s and early 1970s, and it became part of East York in 1967 and the City of Toronto in 1998.

Thorncliffe Park is generally bounded by Eglinton Avenue to the north, the Don River West Branch to the east, the Don River to the south and Laird Drive and Millwood Road to the west, and covers approximately 313 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision), a hydro transformer station (Leaside Transformer Station) and industrial lands (approximately 27% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Don Valley Parkway and the North Toronto Wastewater Treatment Plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Thorncliffe Park includes E. T. Seton Park, Lower Don Parklands and Leaside Park, and the Don River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Thorncliffe branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Laird LRT station. Shopping is available at East York Town Centre. Other notable landmarks include Overlea Boulevard.

01.E02.1390.t:
The Beaches, City of Toronto (TRREB district E02)

The Beaches takes its name from the Lake Ontario beaches along its shore, including Balmy, Kew, Scarboro and Woodbine beaches. The area was originally wooded, with summer cottages and amusement parks such as Victoria Park (1878 to 1906) and Scarboro Beach Park (1907 to 1925). It grew as a residential district in the early 1900s, served by streetcar service on Queen Street East. The public boardwalk opened in 1932 after the shoreline was enlarged.

The Beaches is generally bounded by Kingston Road to the north, Lake Ontario to the south and Eastern Avenue and Lake Shore Boulevard to the west, and covers approximately 393 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but David Miller Carhouse, the Ashbridges Bay Wastewater Treatment Plant, the R.C. Harris Water Treatment Plant and St. John's Norway Cemetery & Crematorium lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in The Beaches includes Woodbine Beach Park, Ashbridges Bay Park and Woodbine Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Beaches branch of the Toronto Public Library. Other notable landmarks include R. C. Harris Water Treatment Plant and Queen Street East.

01.C01.1003.t:
The Islands, City of Toronto (TRREB district C01)

The Toronto Islands were once a sand peninsula. A storm on April 13, 1858 cut a channel and separated them from the mainland. The City of Toronto acquired the islands in 1867 and leased lots for summer homes, hotels and a tent community at Ward's Island. Year-round living was approved in 1947, and the remaining residential community on Ward's and Algonquin Islands was secured by provincial legislation in 1993.

The Islands is generally bounded by Lake Ontario to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 313 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Island Water Treatment Plant and Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in The Islands includes Toronto Island Park, Environmentally Significant Area and Ward's Island Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Gibraltar Point Lighthouse (1809), Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport and Centreville.

01.W10.0030.t:
Thistletown-Beaumonde Heights, City of Toronto (TRREB district W10)

Thistletown was planned in 1847 as a postal village serving farms in Etobicoke Township. It was first called St. Andrew's and was later renamed after local physician Dr. William Thistle. The area stayed largely agricultural until the 1950s, and residential subdivisions replaced the farmland from the late 1950s into the 1970s. Beaumonde Heights is the part west of Islington Avenue. The area became part of the amalgamated City of Toronto in 1998.

Thistletown-Beaumonde Heights is generally bounded by Finch Avenue to the north, the Humber River to the east, the West Humber River to the south and Kipling Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 341 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and surface light rail transit (LRT) tracks. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Thistletown-Beaumonde Heights includes West Humber Parkland, Thistletown Park and Summerlea Park, and the West Humber River, the Humber River and Albion Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools, and transit is provided by the Mount Olive and Rowntree Mills LRT stations.

09.03.0030.t:
Thornhill, Markham

Thornhill was founded in 1794 along Yonge Street, with the first Markham-side settler being Nicholas Miller. It is named after Benjamin Thorne, who ran a gristmill, sawmill and tannery from 1820; the area was known as Thorne's Mills and later Thorne's Hill. Thornhill was a police village from 1931 until 1971, when it was divided between Markham and Vaughan. The John Street area keeps 19th-century buildings in a heritage district.

Thornhill is generally bounded by the Don River East Branch to the north, Bayview Avenue and John Street to the east, the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 212 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Thornhill Cemetery and Saint Luke’s Roman Catholic Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (York Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Thornhill includes Woodland Park, John Honsberger Field Park and Sprucewood Park, and the Don River East Branch runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Thornhill Village branch of the Markham Public Library.

10.02.0150.t:
Village East, Pickering

Village East is a residential neighbourhood in Pickering. Its name refers to its position near the historic Pickering Village area, which became part of Ajax in 1974. The neighbourhood was developed in stages beginning in the 1940s and 1950s. Townhomes and apartment buildings were added in the 1970s and 1980s.

Village East is generally bounded by the Ajax boundary and Finch Avenue to the north, Notion Road to the east, Highway 401 to the south and a hydro corridor to the west, and covers approximately 180 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 401 and Post Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision), the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and the CN rail line (York Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Village East includes Village East Park and Denmar Park.

09.03.0070.t:
Thornlea, Markham

Thornlea lies in the Thornhill area of west Markham, near Bayview Avenue. The name is shared with the John Welsh House, known as Thornlea, on John Street, and with Thornlea Secondary School, which opened in 1968. The area developed as part of Thornhill's suburban growth from the 1960s and 1970s and joined the Town of Markham in 1971.

Thornlea is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, Highway 404 to the east, the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the south and German Mills Creek to the west, and covers approximately 307 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (York Subdivision), Highway 407 and Highway 404. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Thornlea includes Valley View Park, Huntington Park and Thornlea East Park, and German Mills Creek and the Summerdale River run through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

04.10.0050.t:
Thornton, Essa

Thornton was founded in the 1820s and was established as Henrysville, also called Henry's Corners, in 1833, after settler John Henry. When a post office opened in 1854, the name was changed to Thornton, after local mill owner Henry Thornton. It was a police village until 1991, when it merged into the Township of Essa. New subdivisions have been added since the 2010s.

Thornton is generally bounded by Innisfil Beach Road to the north, the Innisfil boundary to the east, 7th Line to the south and 11th Line to the west, and covers approximately 202 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Thornton.

Green space in Thornton includes Thornton Community Park, Thornton Hill Soccer Park and Kevin Crescent Park. Residents are served by the Thornton branch of the Essa Public Library.

05.02.0420.t:
Toronto Gore Rural Estate, Brampton

Toronto Gore Rural Estate is an area of large residential lots in northeast Brampton, in the former Toronto Gore Township. Toronto Gore was formed in 1819 and included hamlets such as Castlemore and Ebenezer. The remainder of the township was merged into the City of Brampton in 1974. Larger lots were developed in the Castlemore area in the 1970s and 1980s, and estate lot development continued into the 2000s.

Toronto Gore Rural Estate is generally bounded by Mayfield Road to the north, The Gore Road to the east, Castlemore Road to the south and Goreway Drive to the west, and covers approximately 1,278 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include St. Patrick's Catholic Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Toronto Gore Rural Estate includes Gore Meadows Community Park East, and the West Humber River and Salt Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Gore Meadows branch of the Brampton Library.

04.12.0020.t:
Tottenham, New Tecumseth

Tottenham is named after its first postmaster, Alexander Totten. It was incorporated as a village in 1884. A fire in 1895 destroyed approximately 80 buildings in the village. Tottenham became part of the Town of New Tecumseth in 1991.

The boundary of Tottenham follows local streets, lot lines and natural features rather than major roads, and the community covers approximately 457 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), a wastewater treatment plant and industrial lands (approximately 8% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Tottenham includes Tottenham Conservation Area, Eastern Avenue Park and Joan Sutherland Park. The community includes or fronts onto Tottenham Pond. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Pam Kirkpatrick branch of the New Tecumseth Public Library. Other notable landmarks include South Simcoe Railway (heritage line to Beeton).

10.02.0110.t:
Town Centre, Pickering

Town Centre is Pickering's central commercial and civic area, along Highway 401 between Liverpool Road and Brock Road. It is built around Pickering Town Centre, a two-storey shopping mall, and the city's civic complex. An enclosed pedestrian bridge over Highway 401, opened in 2012, links the area to Pickering GO Station. Since then the area has seen new high-density residential development. Pickering became a town in 1974 and a city in 2000.

Town Centre is generally bounded by a hydro corridor to the east and Highway 401 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 167 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 401. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision), the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the CN rail line (York Subdivision), the CN rail line (CN Kingston Subdivision) and the CN rail line (Metrolinx Kingston Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Town Centre includes Diana Princess of Wales Park. Residents are served by the Central branch of the Pickering Public Library. Shopping is available at Pickering City Centre.

07.01.1790.t:
Trenholme, Hamilton

Trenholme is named after Clementina Trenholme (1844-1918), an author and social organizer and the mother of radio pioneer Reginald Fessenden. It is a mainly residential neighbourhood on the East Mountain, with shops along Stone Church Road East. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most homes were built in the 1980s, with the rest from the 1960s, 1970s and 1990s.

Trenholme is generally bounded by Limeridge Road to the north, Escarpment Rail Trail to the east, Stone Church Road to the south and Upper Ottawa Street to the west, and covers approximately 109 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway, the Red Hill Valley Parkway and industrial lands (approximately 10% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Trenholme includes Trenholme Park, and Redhill Creek runs through or along the community.

01.C01.0970.t:
Trinity-Bellwoods, City of Toronto (TRREB district C01)

The area is named after Trinity Bellwoods Park, which was the site of Trinity College from 1852 for just over 100 years. The park lies in the former Garrison Creek ravine. By 1900 the surrounding streets were filled with Bay-and-gable and Gothic Revival houses. Polish and Ukrainian immigrants settled here in the early 1900s, followed by Portuguese immigrants from the 1960s.

Trinity-Bellwoods is generally bounded by College Street to the north, Bathurst Street to the east, Queen Street to the south and Dovercourt Road to the west, and covers approximately 173 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Trinity-Bellwoods.

Green space in Trinity-Bellwoods includes Trinity Bellwoods Park, Fred Hamilton Playground and Osler Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools. Other notable landmarks include Ossington Avenue.

07.01.1970.t:
Twenty Place, Hamilton

Twenty Place is an adult lifestyle community in Mount Hope, in the Glanbrook area of Hamilton, built around Twentyplace Boulevard. Some of its homes were built in the late 1990s. Mount Hope lies in the former Glanford Township, which merged with Binbrook in 1974 to form Glanbrook, amalgamated into Hamilton in 2001.

Twenty Place is generally bounded by a hydro corridor to the east, Twenty Road to the south and Garth Street to the west, and covers approximately 86 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 1.4 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Twenty Place is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

06.02.0050.t:
Tyandaga, Burlington

Tyandaga is a residential area in north Burlington, around the municipal Tyandaga golf course. The name comes from Thayendanegea, the Mohawk name of Joseph Brant, who settled at Burlington Bay around 1802. The golf club was founded in 1963, and the surrounding neighbourhood was built up around it in the following decades.

Tyandaga is generally bounded by Dundas Street to the north, Brant Street to the east, Highway 403 to the south and a hydro corridor to the west, and covers approximately 419 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 403. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407, a hydro transformer station (Burlington Transformer Station) and a quarry or aggregate pit. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Tyandaga includes Kerns Park, Westbury Park and Fairchild Park, and Rambo Creek runs through or along the community. Tyandaga Municipal Golf Course is located in the area.

09.03.0190.t:
Unionville, Markham

Unionville takes its name from Union Mills, built in approximately 1839-1840 and named for the 1840 Act of Union. The area was first settled by William Berczy's German settlers from 1794. It was a police village in Markham Township until 1971, when it became part of the Town of Markham. Major housing development began in the 1960s.

Unionville is generally bounded by 16th Avenue to the north, Kennedy Road to the east, Highway 407 to the south and Rodick Road and a hydro corridor to the west, and covers approximately 1,223 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Uxbridge Subdivision) and a hydro transformer station (Buttonville TS). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407 and a hydro transformer station (D. H. Cockburn Transformer Station). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Unionville includes Austin Drive Park, Bruce Creek and Mildred Temple Park, and the Rouge River, Bruce Creek and Berczy Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools and the Unionville branch of the Markham Public Library. York University Markham Campus is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Main Street Unionville, Toogood Pond and Varley Art Gallery.

01.C01.0890.t:
University, City of Toronto (TRREB district C01)

The area is named after the University of Toronto, whose St. George campus makes up most of it. The university was chartered as King's College in 1827, and University College was built in 1857. The land was originally park lots and estates north of Queen Street, and the university grounds were known as University Park. Houses on the streets west of the campus were mainly built in the late 1800s and early 1900s.

University is generally bounded by Bloor Street to the north, Queen's Park Crescent and Queen's Park to the east, College Street to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 140 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of University.

Green space in University includes Robert Street Playground, Huron & Washington Parkette and Margaret Fairley Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools, and transit is provided by the Queen's Park and Museum subway stations. Centre For Addiction and Mental Health - College Street Site, University of Toronto St. George and University College are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Spadina Avenue and Royal Ontario Museum.

09.02.0210.t:
Uplands, Vaughan

Uplands is a residential area in the Thornhill part of Vaughan. Thornhill was founded in 1794 and named after Benjamin Thorne, who ran mills there from 1820. The area takes its name from the Uplands Golf Course, opened in 1922 to a Stanley Thompson design. In the 1980s approximately half of the golf course land was developed for housing, and the Uplands Ski Centre opened on part of the remaining land in 1989.

Uplands is generally bounded by Highway 7 to the north, Yonge Street to the east, Centre Street to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 440 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 407. Along or just beyond its edges are Holy Cross Catholic Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Uplands includes Rosedale North Park, Oakbank Park and Newport Square Park, and the Don River East Branch runs through or along the community. Thornhill Country Club and Uplands Golf & Ski Center are located in the area. Residents are served by one school.

06.02.0200.t:
Uptown, Burlington

Uptown is in northeast Burlington, centred on Appleby Line north of the QEW. The area was farmland of the former Nelson Township, known for market gardens and fruit farms, and was annexed by Burlington in 1958. In 1994 the city designated it as Uptown, a secondary urban centre. Farmland has since been replaced by housing, shopping plazas and business parks, mostly from the 1990s onward.

Uptown is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and Appleby Line to the north, Sheldon Creek to the east, Mainway to the south and Appleby Creek to the west, and covers approximately 122 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and industrial lands (approximately 10% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Uptown includes Des Jardines Park and Lampman Park, and Sheldon Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Corpus Christi Catholic Secondary School.

10.01.0020.t:
Uxbridge, Uxbridge

The town of Uxbridge grew up near the Quaker settlement that began in 1806, and is named after Uxbridge, England. The Toronto and Nipissing Railway arrived in 1871, and the village was incorporated on its own in 1872. In 1974 it was combined with Uxbridge and Scott townships into the present Township of Uxbridge.

Uxbridge is generally bounded by Elgin Park Drive to the south and Concession Road 6 to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 770 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Uxbridge Brook Water Pollution Control Plant and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Uxbridge includes Elgin Park, Quaker Hill and Quaker Common, and Uxbridge Brook runs through or along the community. Fox Bridge Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Main branch of the Uxbridge Public Library. Uxbridge Cottage Hospital is also located in the community.

05.02.0360.t:
Vales of Castlemore North, Brampton

The Vales of Castlemore North is the northern part of the Vales of Castlemore area in northeast Brampton, named after the former hamlet of Castlemore in Toronto Gore Township. The remainder of the township was merged into the City of Brampton in 1974. The area was mainly farmland, with large-lot homes from the 1970s and 1980s. Suburban development has been active since the early 1990s and through the 2000s.

Vales of Castlemore North is generally bounded by Mayfield Road to the north, Goreway Drive to the east and Countryside Drive to the south, and covers approximately 201 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Vales of Castlemore North includes Lillie Roberts Park, Barbreh Brown Park and Lauderhill Valley Park, and the West Humber River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.03.0250.t:
Village Green-South Unionville, Markham

This area lies south of historic Unionville, between Highway 7 and Highway 407, roughly from Kennedy Road to McCowan Road. It was farmland of Markham Township; the older northern part was built in the later 20th century, and the newer South Unionville sections were built from 2000 to approximately 2003.

Village Green-South Unionville is generally bounded by Highway 7 to the north, McCowan Road to the east, Highway 407 to the south and Kennedy Road to the west, and covers approximately 223 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 407 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Village Green-South Unionville includes South Unionville Park, Ray Street Park and Caboto Trail Parkette, and the Rouge River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

10.07.0080.t:
Vanier, Oshawa

Vanier is named after its first school, General Vanier Secondary School, which honours Georges Vanier, Governor General of Canada from 1959 to 1967. The area in west Oshawa was part of East Whitby Township and was annexed by Oshawa in 1950. Most of its housing dates from the mid to late 20th century. The Oshawa Shopping Centre (now Oshawa Centre), which opened in 1956, anchors the area.

Vanier is generally bounded by King Street to the north, Oshawa Creek to the east, Highway 401 to the south and the Whitby boundary to the west, and covers approximately 501 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), Highway 401 and a hydro transformer station. Along or just beyond its edges are Mount Lawn Memorial Garden (cemetery), Union Cemetery and Pioneer Memorial Garden (cemetery). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Vanier includes Oshawa Civic Recreation Complex, Warne Park and Storie Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools. Shopping is available at Oshawa Centre and Midtown Mall. Trent University - Durham GTA Campus is also located in the community.

09.02.0120.t:
Vaughan Corporate Centre, Vaughan

Vaughan Corporate Centre was the original name of the area now known as the Vaughan Metropolitan Centre, at Highway 7 and Jane Street. It occupies the site of Edgeley, a historic farming hamlet in Vaughan Township. The city planned a new business core here under an official plan amendment approved in 1998, and the name was changed in 2009. High-rise development followed the opening of the subway extension in December 2017.

Vaughan Corporate Centre is generally bounded by Portage Parkway to the north, Creditstone Road and Highway 7 to the east, Highway 407 to the south and Weston Road to the west, and covers approximately 314 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 407, Highway 400 and industrial lands (approximately 16% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Beechwood Cemetery and Mausoleum. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Transit is provided by the Vaughan Metropolitan Centre subway station.

09.02.0070.t:
Vaughan Grove, Vaughan

Vaughan Grove is a residential area in Woodbridge. Woodbridge began as the mill village of Burwick after 1837 and was incorporated as a village in 1882. Suburban growth spread outward from the old village from the 1950s through the 1990s. In 1971 Woodbridge was amalgamated into the Town of Vaughan, now the City of Vaughan.

Vaughan Grove is generally bounded by Highway 7 to the north, the Humber River to the east, the City of Toronto boundary and Steeles Avenue to the south and Martin Grove Road to the west, and covers approximately 392 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) and Highway 407. Along or just beyond its edges are a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Vaughan Grove includes Thackeray Park, Vaughan Grove Sports Park and Steeles West Common Park, and Plunkett Creek and the Humber River run through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

09.03.0110.t:
Victoria Square, Markham

Victoria Square began in 1805 at the crossroads of the former 4th Line (now Victoria Square Boulevard), settled mainly by Pennsylvania Mennonites; it was first called Heise Hill. A post office opened in 1854 and closed in 1914, after which the corners became residential. The Woodbine Avenue bypass opened in 2010, and farmland has since been giving way to new housing.

Victoria Square is generally bounded by the Whitchurch-Stouffville boundary to the north, Warden Avenue to the east, Elgin Mills Road to the south and Highway 404 to the west, and covers approximately 820 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Victoria Square United Church Cemetery, East Victoria Square United Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 404 and Elgin Mills Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Victoria Square includes Victoria Square Park, The Arboretum and Heritage Orchard and West Cathedral Pond, and Berczy Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

07.01.1960.t:
Villages of Glancaster, Hamilton

The Villages of Glancaster is an adult lifestyle community in the Glanbrook area of south Hamilton. Glancaster Road marks the boundary between the former Glanford and Ancaster townships. Most homes were built between 1991 and 2005, with some added in the 2010s. Glanford merged with Binbrook in 1974 to form Glanbrook, which was amalgamated into Hamilton in 2001.

Villages of Glancaster is generally bounded by a hydro corridor to the north, Garth Street to the east, Twenty Road to the south and Glancaster Road to the west, and covers approximately 105 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. The community is also close to John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport, approximately 1.5 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Villages of Glancaster includes St. Mary Park.

06.04.1012.t:
Northwest, Oakville

Northwest Oakville includes land around Dundas Street and Bronte Road, near the former hamlet of Palermo. Palermo was founded as Hagartown by Lawrence Hagar in 1805 and was renamed Palermo in 1836. The area was part of Trafalgar Township, which joined the Town of Oakville in 1962. It stayed largely rural until recent residential development in North Oakville.

Northwest is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, Dundas Street and Sixteen Mile Creek to the east and Tremaine Road to the west, and covers approximately 821 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 407 and Palermo Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Northwest includes Palermo Park and Travertine Park. Oakville Trafalgar Memorial Hospital is also located in the community.

09.02.0080.t:
Vellore Village, Vaughan

Vellore Village is built around the former hamlet of Vellore, near Weston Road and Rutherford Road. Vellore was one of the historic hamlets of Vaughan Township, where the township hall was located. The area remained farmland until suburban housing was built from the late 1990s and 2000s, with growth north of Major Mackenzie Drive continuing into the 2020s. It has been part of the Town, now City, of Vaughan since 1971.

Vellore Village is generally bounded by Teston Road to the north, Jane Street and Highway 400 to the east, Rutherford Road to the south and Major MacKenzie Drive to the west, and covers approximately 2,205 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 400 and Wesleyan Methodist Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Photo added by SD Cowan St. Paul's Presbyterian Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Vellore Village includes Kortright Centre for Conservation, Matthew Park and Chatfield District Park, and the East Humber River and Purpleville Creek run through or along the community. Harry Putter Driving Range is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 17 schools. Shopping is available at Vaughan Mills. Cortellucci Vaughan Hospital is also located in the community.

01.C13.0810.t:
Victoria Village, City of Toronto (TRREB district C13)

The area lies along Victoria Park Avenue north of Eglinton Avenue. Much of the land was owned by the Herron family, who ran an orchard here. Investors led by MP Robert Henry McGregor developed the area in the 1950s, and most homes were built from the late 1950s into the 1960s. It was part of York Township, then North York, and became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Victoria Village is generally bounded by Lawrence Avenue to the north, Victoria Park Avenue to the east and the Don River East Branch to the west, and covers approximately 474 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision), surface light rail transit (LRT) tracks, a hydro transformer station (Bermondsey TS) and industrial lands (approximately 28% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Don Valley Parkway and Saint Jude's Anglican Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Victoria Village includes Anewan Greenbelt, Wigmore Park and Sweeney Drive, and the Don River East Branch runs through or along the community. Flemingdon Park Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Victoria Village branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Sloane LRT station.

06.04.1021.t:
Winston Park, Oakville

This community lies within the Town of Oakville. Trafalgar Township ran east to what is now Winston Churchill Boulevard, and in 1974 land east of Ninth Line north of Dundas Street was transferred to Mississauga. The area was part of Trafalgar Township, which was created in 1806 and named after the Battle of Trafalgar. Trafalgar Township was amalgamated with the Town of Oakville in 1962.

Winston Park is generally bounded by Dundas Street to the north, Winston Churchill Boulevard to the east, Sherwood Heights Drive to the south and Ninth Line to the west, and covers approximately 466 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 403, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and industrial lands (approximately 42% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Glen Oaks Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Winston Park includes Winston Woods Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

09.03.0330.t:
Vinegar Hill, Markham

Vinegar Hill is one of Markham's earliest settled areas, established in approximately 1805 just south of the historic Markham village along the Rouge River. Its name is believed to come from a cider mill on the east side of the Rouge valley. Older streets have seen infill, and newer housing was built at the south end near Highway 407.

Vinegar Hill is generally bounded by Main Street Markham to the north, the Rouge River to the east and Highway 407 and Markham Road to the south, and covers approximately 53 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include St. Patrick ’s Roman Catholic Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Vinegar Hill includes Rouge Valley Park and Milne Dam Conservation Park, and the Rouge River runs through or along the community.

09.09.0060.t:
Virginia, Georgina

Virginia is a small lakeside community on the south shore of Lake Simcoe in eastern Georgina. It was originally known as Frenchtown, after the French Canadian settlers who came from Quebec from the 1830s. By the 1850s they had established Saint Anthony's Church, which was rebuilt in its present form in 1903. The area became part of the Town of Georgina in 1971.

Virginia is generally bounded by Lake Simcoe to the north, Highway 48 to the south and Park Road to the west, and covers approximately 2,943 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but St. George's Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Virginia includes Sibbald Point Provincial Park and Duclos Point Provincial Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Simcoe. Residents are served by one school.

04.08.0040.t:
Victoria Harbour, Tay

Victoria Harbour is a lakeside community on Georgian Bay in the Township of Tay. It separated from Tay Township as an incorporated village on December 31, 1910. The village was amalgamated back into Tay on January 1, 1994, as part of the restructuring of Simcoe County.

Victoria Harbour is generally bounded by Georgian Bay and Robins Point Road to the east and Highway 12 and Tay Shore Trail to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 491 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a wastewater treatment plant and Victoria Harbour Union Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Victoria Harbour includes Oakwood Park. The community includes or fronts onto Georgian Bay. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Theo & Elaine Bernard branch of the Tay Township Public Library.

09.03.0140.t:
Victoria Manor-Jennings Gate, Markham

Victoria Manor-Jennings Gate lies north of Major Mackenzie Drive, east of the historic hamlet of Victoria Square, which was settled from 1805 by Pennsylvania Mennonite families and first called Heise Hill. The area was farmland until modern development began with nearby Cathedraltown in 2006. Victoria Manor was built mainly after 2005, while Jennings Gate has custom estate homes on large lots.

Victoria Manor-Jennings Gate is generally bounded by Major MacKenzie Drive to the south and Victoria Square Boulevard to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 168 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Victoria Manor-Jennings Gate includes Artisan Trail, John Payne Park and Joseph Ellerby Park. Residents are served by one school.

01.C08.1002.t:
Waterfront Communities C8, City of Toronto (TRREB district C08)

This area includes the St. Lawrence neighbourhood, close to the original Town of York laid out in 1793. Much of it was harbour that was filled in for railways and industry by the 1860s. Industry declined by the 1960s, and the St. Lawrence housing community was built from the 1970s into the 1990s. The former Gooderham and Worts distillery (founded 1832) reopened as the Distillery District in 2003, and the nearby West Don Lands were redeveloped from 2015.

Waterfront Communities C8 is generally bounded by Keating Channel and Eastern Avenue to the east, Merchants' Wharf to the south and Lake Ontario and Front Street to the west, and covers approximately 170 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Union Station Rail Corridor rail line, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Bala Subdivision), the Gardiner Expressway, a rail yard, a hydro transformer station (Esplanade TS), Cherry Street Stormwater Management Facility, GO Don Yard and industrial lands (approximately 5% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and the Don Valley Parkway. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Waterfront Communities C8 includes Corktown Common, Sherbourne Common and 50 Queens Quay East Park, and Keating Channel and the Don River run through or along the community. Residents are served by one school. George Brown College - Waterfront Campus is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include St. Lawrence Market, Distillery District (National Historic Site) and Gooderham (Flatiron) Building (1892).

04.03.0010.t:
Wasaga Beach, Wasaga Beach

Wasaga is a short form of Nottawasaga, the name of the river and bay. Sandy soil delayed farm settlement, and the first permanent settler, John Van Vlack, arrived in 1869; logging was the main industry for the rest of the 1800s. The area became a cottage and beach resort from the early 1900s. It was incorporated as a village in 1951 and as a town in 1974, and its permanent population roughly doubled between 2001 and 2021.

Wasaga Beach is generally bounded by the Springwater boundary to the east, the Clearview boundary to the south and Georgian Bay to the west, and covers approximately 6,034 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 26, a wastewater treatment plant and a landfill site. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Wasaga Beach includes Wasaga Beach Provincial Park, Wasaga Sports Park and Oakview Woods Community Park, and the Nottawasaga River and McIntyre Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Marl Lake. Marlwood Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Wasaga Beach Public Library.

07.01.0120.t:
Waterdown, Hamilton

Waterdown began in 1805 when Alexander Brown built a sawmill at the Great Falls in Smokey Hollow on Grindstone Creek. Ebenezer Culver Griffin surveyed village lots in 1830, and a post office opened in 1840. Waterdown became an incorporated village in 1879. It joined the Town of Flamborough in 1974 and was amalgamated into Hamilton in 2001, and it has grown quickly as a suburban community since the late 1990s.

Waterdown is generally bounded by Parkside Drive to the east and the Burlington boundary to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,315 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision), Highway 6, Water Treatment Plant, Waterdown Union Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Waterdown includes Waterdown Memorial Park, Gatesbury Park and Arrowhon Natural Area, and Grindstone Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Waterdown branch of the Hamilton Public Library.

01.C01.1001.t:
Waterfront Communities C1, City of Toronto (TRREB district C01)

Much of this area is reclaimed land along the harbour that was used for railway yards and port uses from the late 1800s. The Canadian National Spadina yards and the wider Railway Lands were cleared after rail operations moved out from 1965. The CN Tower was built in the 1970s and SkyDome (now Rogers Centre) opened in 1989. High-rise condominium communities such as CityPlace were built out from approximately 2000.

Waterfront Communities C1 is generally bounded by Queen Street to the north, Front Street and Simcoe Street to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 243 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Union Station Rail Corridor rail line, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line, the Gardiner Expressway, a hydro transformer station (Clare R. Copeland Transformer Station) and a hydro transformer station (John TS). Along or just beyond its edges are a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Waterfront Communities C1 includes Roundhouse Park, Canoe Landing Park and Harbour Square Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Fort York branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Union subway station. Other notable landmarks include CN Tower, Rogers Centre and Harbourfront Centre.

04.08.0050.t:
Waubaushene, Tay

Waubaushene is a community on Georgian Bay in the Township of Tay. Tay was named in 1822 and became a separate township in 1869, after being part of the United Townships of Tiny and Tay from 1851. The present Township of Tay was formed through county restructuring in 1994.

Waubaushene is generally bounded by Tay Shore Trail and King Road to the north, Georgian Bay to the east, Highway 400 and Sandhill Road to the south and Albin Road to the west, and covers approximately 153 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 400 and Waubaushene Protestant Cemetery/St. John's Catholic Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Waubaushene includes Waubashene Beaches Provincial Park. Residents are served by the Waubaushene branch of the Tay Township Public Library.

04.08.0010.t:
Waverley, Tay

Waverley is a community in the Township of Tay in Simcoe County. Tay was named in 1822 after a pet dog of Lady Sarah Maitland, wife of Lieutenant Governor Sir Peregrine Maitland. It became a separate township in 1869. The present township took its current form in 1994.

Waverley is generally bounded by the Tiny boundary to the north, Vasey Road to the east and the Springwater boundary to the south, and covers approximately 126 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Waverley Gospel Hall Cemetery, Waverley United Cemetery and Saint John's Anglican Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Waverley includes Waverley Park.

04.15.0130.t:
Wellington, Barrie

Wellington is an established residential area in central Barrie, northeast of downtown, named after Wellington Street. Barrie grew from a supply depot at the end of the Nine Mile Portage and was named in 1833 after Commodore Sir Robert Barrie. It became a village in 1854, a town in 1871 and a city in 1959.

Wellington is generally bounded by Ottaway Avenue to the north, Duckworth Street and Bell Farm Road to the east, Wellington Street to the south and Bayfield Street and Highway 400 to the west, and covers approximately 180 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 400 lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school.

04.15.0040.t:
West Bayfield, Barrie

West Bayfield is a residential area in north Barrie on the west side of Bayfield Street (formerly Highway 26). Barrie's northern limit was Cundles Road until 1984, when the city annexed approximately 2,200 acres from Vespra Township, including the Bayfield Street commercial strip. Most of the area was built up with suburban housing after that annexation.

West Bayfield is generally bounded by Livingstone Street to the south and the Springwater boundary to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 113 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Barrie Union Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in West Bayfield includes West Bayfield Park and Hanmer Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

09.02.0060.t:
West Woodbridge, Vaughan

West Woodbridge covers part of the western side of Woodbridge. The village began as Burwick after 1837 and was renamed Woodbridge before 1855. Western growth reached Martin Grove Road in the 1960s and extended to Highway 27 in the late 1980s and early 1990s. In 1971 Woodbridge was amalgamated into the Town of Vaughan, now the City of Vaughan.

West Woodbridge is generally bounded by Robinson Creek to the north, the Humber River to the east, Highway 7 to the south and Highway 27 to the west, and covers approximately 578 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), a cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 5% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in West Woodbridge includes Rainbow Creek Park, Michael Barrasso Park and Fred Armstrong Parkette, and Robinson Creek, the Humber River and Rainbow Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Vaughan Public Libraries - Woodbridge Branch.

01.E10.1160.t:
West Hill, City of Toronto (TRREB district E10)

West Hill takes its name from its position on the high ground west of the Highland Creek valley in the former Scarborough Township. A post office named West Hill opened in 1879, and the area remained largely rural until after the Second World War. Subdivisions were built around Kingston Road from the 1950s, with larger curving-street subdivisions and some high-rise apartments added through the 1960s and 1970s. It was part of the City of Scarborough until amalgamation into the City of Toronto in 1998.

West Hill is generally bounded by Highland Creek to the north, Lake Ontario and the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision) to the south and West Highland Creek and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 951 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), Highland Creek Treatment Plant, St. Margaret's In The Pines (cemetery) and industrial lands (approximately 5% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and Asbestos Waste Site (John’s Manville Plant) (landfill). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in West Hill includes Highland Creek Ravine, East Point Park and Morningside Park, and Thornton Creek, West Highland Creek and Highland Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 11 schools and the Morningside branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Guildwood GO Station. University of Toronto Scarborough is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Colonel Danforth Park.

07.01.1070.t:
Westdale, Hamilton

Westdale was planned in the early 1920s as a Garden City style suburb, first called Hamilton Gardens, on former farmland. The name Westdale was chosen through a public contest in 1923. In 1927 land was sold to the city for McMaster University and the Royal Botanical Gardens. The neighbourhood is laid out around oval streets centred on Westdale Village on King Street West.

Westdale is generally bounded by Lake Ontario to the north, Highway 403 to the east, Main Street to the south and Forsyth Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 211 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 403 and a hydro transformer station (Newton TS) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Westdale includes Royal Botanical Gardens, Coronation Park and The Oval. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the Westdale branch of the Hamilton Public Library. Other notable landmarks include McMaster University and Cootes Paradise (edge).

01.C14.0580.t:
Willowdale East, City of Toronto (TRREB district C14)

Willowdale takes its name from the willow trees that once grew in the district; it began as the postal village of Willow Dale, with a post office opened in 1851. Jacob Cummer, the area's first settler, arrived in 1797, and David Gibson's farmhouse (now Gibson House) was built in 1851. The area was part of York Township, became part of North York in 1922 and joined the City of Toronto in 1998. Single-family homes were built mainly in the 1950s, and the Yonge Street corridor has since been redeveloped with high-rise buildings as part of North York Centre.

Willowdale East is generally bounded by Finch Avenue to the north, Bayview Avenue to the east, Highway 401 to the south and Yonge Street to the west, and covers approximately 509 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 401 and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Willowdale East includes Glendora Park, Sheppard East Park and Willowdale Park. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools, and transit is provided by the North York Centre, Bayview and Sheppard-Yonge subway stations. Shopping is available at Yonge Sheppard Centre. Other notable landmarks include Gibson House Museum.

01.W10.0010.t:
West Humber-Clairville, City of Toronto (TRREB district W10)

Claireville began as a hamlet at the meeting of Albion Road, Indian Line and Steeles Avenue, with an early post office first called Humber. It was named after Claire Elizabeth, the eldest daughter of landowner Jean du Petit Pont de la Haye, and was laid out in approximately 1850. A flood control dam on the West Humber River created the Claireville reservoir in 1957. Highway 427 and nearby rail lines later made much of the area industrial, with suburban housing built from the 1960s onward.

West Humber-Clairville is generally bounded by Martin Grove Road and Steeles Avenue to the north, Kipling Avenue and the West Humber River to the east, Highway 401 to the south and Highway 427 to the west, and covers approximately 3,013 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), the GO Transit Weston Subdivision rail line, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Pearson Subdivision), the Union Pearson Express rail line, Highway 427, Highway 401, Highway 409, surface light rail transit (LRT) tracks, Toronto Pearson International Airport, Greater Toronto Area Immigration Holding Centre, a rail yard, a hydro transformer station (Richview Transformer Station), a hydro transformer station (Rexdale TS), Glendale Funeral Home & Cemetery, Sharon Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 37% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in West Humber-Clairville includes Humber Arboretum, West Humber Parkland and Claireville Conservation Area, and the West Humber River, Mimico Creek and Berry Creek run through or along the community. Royal Woodbine Golf Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 10 schools, the Humberwood branch of the Toronto Public Library and the Northern Elms branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Etobicoke North GO Station and the Humber College, Westmore and Martin Grove LRT stations. Shopping is available at Woodbine Mall. Etobicoke General Hospital and Humber Polytechnic are also located in the community.

10.02.0080.t:
West Shore, Pickering

West Shore is on the Lake Ontario shoreline in south Pickering, west of Frenchman's Bay. Settlers were drawn to the shoreline from the 1800s, and cottage-style homes were built near the lake in the early 1900s. Most of the neighbourhood was built in the 1960s, when the first subdivisions went up. The Nesbitt-Newman House, an 1850s Georgian stone farmhouse, survives from the earlier period.

West Shore is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Lake Ontario to the east and Petticoat Creek to the west, and covers approximately 356 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CN rail line (Metrolinx Kingston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision), the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the CN rail line (CN Kingston Subdivision) and industrial lands (approximately 9% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (York Subdivision) and Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in West Shore includes Rotary Park, Petticoat Creek Conservation Area and West shore park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Ontario. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. Other notable landmarks include Frenchman's Bay.

04.18.0080.t:
West Shore, Severn

West Shore covers communities along the western shore of Lake Couchiching, north of Orillia, in the former Orillia Township. The shoreline developed with cottages and later year-round homes in the 20th century. The Township of Severn was formed on January 1, 1994 from the Village of Coldwater, the townships of Matchedash and Orillia, and parts of Medonte and Tay.

West Shore is generally bounded by Goldstein Road to the east, Lake Couchiching to the south and Menoke Beach Road and Brennan Line to the west, and covers approximately 1,337 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 11. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in West Shore includes Timberline Park and Ardtrea Park. The community includes or fronts onto Lake Couchiching. Residents are served by one school.

01.W03.0400.t:
Weston-Pellam Park, City of Toronto (TRREB district W03)

Weston-Pellam Park lies around Weston Road and Rogers Road in the former York Township, north of the West Toronto Junction rail lands. Weston Road was first laid out in the early 1800s to link Dundas Street with the village of Weston, and part of its original route is now Rogers Road. Most housing is modest detached and semi-detached homes from the first half of the 20th century. The area was part of the Township, later Borough and City, of York until amalgamation into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Weston-Pellam Park is generally bounded by Rowntree Avenue to the north, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the east, the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision) to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 144 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, a rail yard, a hydro transformer station (Wiltshire TS) and industrial lands (approximately 15% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Galt Subdivision) and the CPKC rail line. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Weston-Pellam Park includes Wadsworth Park, S.A.D.R.A. Park and Pelham Avenue Playground. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the St. Clair/Silverthorn branch of the Toronto Public Library.

04.04.0040.t:
Wyevale, Tiny

Wyevale is a small community in the southern part of the Township of Tiny. The Wye River rises in the nearby Tiny Marsh. The Township of Tiny was named in 1822 after a pet dog of Lady Sarah Maitland, wife of Lieutenant Governor Sir Peregrine Maitland. It was part of the United Townships of Tiny and Tay from 1851 and became a separate township in 1869.

Wyevale is generally bounded by Withall Grove to the north, Mary Jane Road to the east and County Road 6 to the south, and covers approximately 135 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Wyevale.

Green space in Wyevale includes Reynolds Park. Residents are served by one school.

05.03.0030.t:
Western Business Park, Mississauga

Western Business Park is an employment area in western Mississauga, on lands of the former Toronto Township. Toronto Township was formed in 1805 after the Treaty 14 land purchase from the Mississaugas, and it remained largely agricultural until suburban growth began after the Second World War.
