The area became part of the Town of Mississauga in 1968, which became a city in 1974. It was developed mainly for industrial and business uses as the city grew.

Western Business Park is generally bounded by Ridgeway Drive and Highway 403 to the north, Dunwin Drive to the east, Dundas Street to the south and Ninth Line to the west, and covers approximately 405 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 403 and industrial lands (approximately 38% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Glen Oaks Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Western Business Park includes Ninth Line Sports Park, and Glen Erin Brook runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

05.02.0250.t:
Westgate, Brampton

Westgate is a residential area in north-central Brampton, crossed by Williams Parkway. The land was rural farmland before suburban development. Chinguacousy and Toronto Gore townships were merged with the Town of Brampton in 1974 to form the City of Brampton. Most homes in the area were built in the 1980s and 1990s.

Westgate is generally bounded by Bovaird Drive to the north, Dixie Road to the east, Lambeth Street to the south and Highway 410 to the west, and covers approximately 393 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 410. Along or just beyond its edges are Lundy Burial Ground Cemetery/Mount Olivet Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Westgate includes Bramalea Limited Community Park, Northampton Park and Laurelcrest Park North. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

09.02.0010.t:
West Woodbridge Industrial Area, Vaughan

West Woodbridge Industrial Area is an employment area on the western edge of Woodbridge. The land was farmland in Vaughan Township, which was incorporated in 1850 and became the Town of Vaughan in 1971. Industrial development west of Highway 27 began in the 2000s in anticipation of the Highway 427 extension, which opened in 2021. Development is ongoing.

West Woodbridge Industrial Area is generally bounded by Major MacKenzie Drive and the Humber River to the north, Highway 27 to the east, Steeles Avenue and Martin Grove Road to the south and Highway 50 to the west, and covers approximately 2,479 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), Highway 427, Highway 407, CPKC Vaughan Intermodal Yard, a hydro transformer station (Claireville TS), a hydro transformer station (Woodbridge TS), Queen of Heaven Catholic Cemetery, Glenview Memorial Gardens (cemetery), Knox Presbyterian Church Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 29% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and a rail yard. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in West Woodbridge Industrial Area includes Milani Boulevard Soccer Facility, and West Robinson Creek, the Humber River and Robinson Creek run through or along the community.

09.04.0030.t:
Westbrook, Richmond Hill

Westbrook is in north Richmond Hill near Bathurst Street, at the edge of the Oak Ridges Moraine. Part of the area was Twickenham Farm, bought by Captain Larratt Smith in 1836. The land remained rural until it was developed as a newer subdivision area in recent decades.

Westbrook is generally bounded by Gamble Road to the north, Yonge Street to the east, Elgin Mills Road to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 443 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Westbrook.

Green space in Westbrook includes Tollbar Park, Larratt Lea Park and Rouge Crest Park. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools.

07.01.1370.t:
Westcliffe, Hamilton

Westcliffe is a residential neighbourhood on the west Hamilton Mountain, with Westcliffe Mall on Mohawk Road West. The area was once part of Barton Township. Hamilton annexed the township in stages, and the last of it was absorbed in 1960. Most homes were built before 1960, with the rest mainly from 1961 to 1980.

Westcliffe is generally bounded by Scenic Drive to the north, Garth Street to the east, Mohawk Road to the south and Sanatorium Road to the west, and covers approximately 179 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include St. Peter's Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Westcliffe includes Colquhoun Park, Holbrook Park and Cliffview Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

07.01.1620.t:
Yeoville, Hamilton

Yeoville is a residential neighbourhood on the west Hamilton Mountain. The Mountain was originally part of Barton Township, and its first European settlement was by Pennsylvania Dutch Loyalists along what is now Mohawk Road, west of Upper James Street. The area was later absorbed into the City of Hamilton, which was amalgamated with five neighbouring municipalities on January 1, 2001.

Yeoville is generally bounded by Mohawk Road to the north, Upper James Street to the east, the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway to the south and West 5th Street to the west, and covers approximately 47 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Lincoln M. Alexander Parkway lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school.

01.C07.0500.t:
Westminster-Branson, City of Toronto (TRREB district C07)

The area lies near Bathurst Street and Finch Avenue and is also known as Fisherville, after a former settlement on the site. It was part of York Township, then North York from 1922, and the City of Toronto from 1998. The area was largely developed from the 1950s onward with houses, apartments and condominiums.

Westminster-Branson is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Bathurst Street to the south and the Don River West Branch to the west, and covers approximately 368 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Beth Tzedec Memorial Park (cemetery) and industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Bathurst Lawn Memorial Park (cemetery). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Westminster-Branson includes G. Ross Lord Park, Rockford Park and Antibes Park, and the Don River West Branch and Westminster Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Centennial branch of the Toronto Public Library. North York General Hospital - Finch Site is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Esther Shiner Stadium.

01.W04.0300.t:
Weston, City of Toronto (TRREB district W04)

Weston was named in 1815 by mill owner James Farr after his birthplace, Weston in Hertfordshire, England. Settlement began in the 1790s with a sawmill on the Humber River, and the Grand Trunk Railway arrived in 1856. Weston was incorporated as a village in 1881 and as a town in 1914, and much of its Victorian housing east of the railway dates from that period. It joined the Borough of York in 1967 and became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Weston is generally bounded by Woodward Avenue to the north, Jane Street to the east, the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision) to the south and the Humber River to the west, and covers approximately 272 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Weston Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (MacTier Subdivision), St. John's on the Humber Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 5% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Weston includes Mallaby Park, Cruickshank Park and Denison Park, and the Humber River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools and the Weston branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Weston GO Station.

01.E04.1090.t:
Wexford-Maryvale, City of Toronto (TRREB district E04)

Wexford is named for County Wexford in Ireland and began as a small village, whose Anglican Church of St. Jude dates from 1848. Maryvale is named after the Maryvale farm that once covered part of the area. Both were rural parts of Scarborough Township until they were built up as suburbs in the 1950s, mainly with bungalows, apartments and retail plazas. Scarborough joined Metropolitan Toronto in 1953 and the City of Toronto in 1998.

Wexford-Maryvale is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Birchmount Road to the east, Eglinton Avenue to the south and Victoria Park Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 1,017 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision), Saint Jude's Anglican Church Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 23% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Wexford-Maryvale includes Ashtonbee Reservoir Park, Wexford Park and Terraview Park, and Taylor-Massey Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 12 schools and the Maryvale branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the O'Connor, Pharmacy, Hakimi Lebovic and Golden Mile LRT stations. Shopping is available at Parkway Mall and Golden Mile Mall. Centennial College - Ashtonbee Campus is also located in the community.

06.01.1023.t:
Beaty, Milton

Beaty is named after the Beaty family, who farmed the land for generations when it was part of Trafalgar Township; John Beaty came from County Cavan, Ireland. The Town of Milton created the neighbourhood in 1998 as part of the Bristol Survey urban expansion, and construction began in 2001. It was among the first areas of 'new Milton', which grew quickly after the Big Pipe water project of approximately 2002.

Beaty is generally bounded by Derry Road to the north, James Snow Parkway to the east, Louis St. Laurent Avenue to the south and Thompson Road to the west, and covers approximately 316 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Beaty.

Green space in Beaty includes Beaty Neighbourhood Park (North), Beaty Neighbourhood Park (South) and Bennet Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Beaty branch of the Milton Public Library.

06.01.1024.t:
Bronte Meadows, Milton

Bronte Meadows takes its name from Bronte Street, its west boundary, and from the hay meadows that covered the land before development. It lies north of Derry Road between Bronte Street and Ontario Street, on land of the former Trafalgar Township near Sixteen Mile Creek. It was developed from the 1970s, with much of it built in the early 1980s.

Bronte Meadows is generally bounded by Bell Street and Woodlawn Crescent to the north, Derry Road to the south and Bronte Street to the west, and covers approximately 47 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Bronte Meadows.

Green space in Bronte Meadows includes Bronte Meadows Park. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include John Tonelli Sports Centre.

10.06.0110.t:
Whitby Industrial, Whitby

Whitby Industrial is an employment area in the Town of Whitby. Whitby Township was surveyed in 1792, and the Town of Whitby was incorporated in 1855. The town and township merged in 1968, and Whitby became part of Durham Region in 1974. Industrial land was developed as the town grew in the decades after the merger.

Whitby Industrial is generally bounded by the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) to the north, the Oshawa boundary and Boundary Road to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Highway 401 to the west, and covers approximately 987 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Kingston Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Subdivision), Highway 401, the Corbett Creek Water Pollution Control Plant, CN Oshawa Yard, a hydro transformer station and industrial lands (approximately 48% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Whitby Industrial includes Ronald C. Deeth Park, Gordon Richards Park and Intrepid Park, and Corbett Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school. Durham College - Whitby Campus is also located in the community.

10.06.0020.t:
Williamsburg, Whitby

Williamsburg is a residential area in Whitby. Whitby Township was surveyed in 1792 and named after Whitby in Yorkshire, England. The town and township merged in 1968. Since at least the mid-1990s, new subdivision growth in Whitby has moved northward, and this area was built out in that period.

Williamsburg is generally bounded by Taunton Road to the north, Brock Street to the east, the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) to the south and Otter Creek to the west, and covers approximately 529 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CPKC rail line (Belleville Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Williamsburg includes Medland Park, Whitburn Park and Sato Street Park, and Lynde Creek and Otter Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools.

06.04.1022.t:
West Oak Trails, Oakville

West Oak Trails lies in north-central west Oakville, north of Upper Middle Road. The land was farmland in Trafalgar Township until the township joined the Town of Oakville in 1962. It is newer than most other Oakville communities and was built up after the older suburbs to the south.

West Oak Trails is generally bounded by Dundas Street to the north, Sixteen Mile Creek to the east, Upper Middle Road to the south and Third Line to the west, and covers approximately 370 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in West Oak Trails includes Sixteen Hollow Park, Dashwood Parkette and merry- go-rounds, and Sixteen Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

01.C03.0750.t:
Yonge-Eglinton, City of Toronto (TRREB district C03)

The area began as the farming village of Eglinton in the early 1800s. A horse-drawn streetcar reached it in 1884, and housing development followed. Eglinton became part of the Town of North Toronto in 1890, which was annexed to the City of Toronto in 1912. The Yonge subway opened to Eglinton in 1954, and the area has since grown into a midtown office and high-rise residential centre.

Yonge-Eglinton is generally bounded by Briar Hill Avenue and Avenue Road to the north, Yonge Street to the east, Kay Gardiner Beltline Trail to the south and Elmsthorpe Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 161 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Davisville Yard. Along or just beyond its edges are Mount Pleasant Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Yonge-Eglinton includes Eglinton Park, Oriole Park and Fiona Nelson Parkette. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Northern District branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the Davisville and Eglinton subway stations and the Avenue LRT station. Other notable landmarks include Canada Square office complex.

01.C07.0590.t:
Willowdale West, City of Toronto (TRREB district C07)

Willowdale is named for the willow trees that once grew in the district; David Gibson helped establish the 'Willow Dale' post office. The area was settled by Jacob Cummer and others from the late 1700s. It was part of York Township, then North York from 1922, and its original single-family homes were built from the 1910s to the 1950s. In recent decades, the Yonge Street frontage has been redeveloped as part of the high-rise North York Centre.

Willowdale West is generally bounded by Finch Avenue to the north, Yonge Street to the east and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 323 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include York Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Willowdale West includes Hinder Area, Edithvale Park and Stafford Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools and the North York Central Library branch of the Toronto Public Library, and transit is provided by the North York Centre subway station. Other notable landmarks include Gibson House Museum (1851) and Mel Lastman Square and North York Civic Centre.

01.W09.0070.t:
Willowridge-Martingrove-Richview, City of Toronto (TRREB district W09)

The area was first known as Kit's Corners, after early settler Christopher Kit Thirkle. The name Richview comes from a post office opened in 1852, when the area was a farming community in Etobicoke Township. It was built up as part of suburban Etobicoke, mainly in the 1950s and 1960s. Etobicoke became part of the amalgamated City of Toronto in 1998.

Willowridge-Martingrove-Richview is generally bounded by Kipling Avenue and Dixon Road to the north, The Westway and Royal York Road to the east, Eglinton Avenue to the south and Highway 401 to the west, and covers approximately 547 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401, Highway 27, a hydro transformer station (Richview Transformer Station), Sanctuary Park Cemetery and Riverside Cemetery. The community is also close to Toronto Pearson International Airport, approximately 1.2 km away (possible aircraft noise). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Willowridge-Martingrove-Richview includes Richview Park, Silver Creek Park and Westgrove Park, and Mimico Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 10 schools and the Richview branch of the Toronto Public Library.

10.07.0040.t:
Windfields, Oshawa

Windfields is named after Windfields Farm, the thoroughbred breeding farm of E. P. Taylor. The land was first Parkwood Stable, owned by Colonel R. S. McLaughlin, and Taylor bought it in 1950. The farm was the birthplace of the racehorse Northern Dancer, and its breeding operations wound up in 2009. Parts of the farm went to Ontario Tech University and Durham College, and the rest has been developed for housing since the 2000s, with a larger new neighbourhood under construction from 2018.

Windfields is generally bounded by Winchester Road to the north, East Oshawa Creek to the east, Conlin Road to the south and Oshawa Creek to the west, and covers approximately 573 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Highway 407 ETR. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Windfields includes Steeplechase Park, Bridle Park and Gulfstream Park, and Oshawa Creek runs through or along the community. Kedron Dells Golf Course is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools. Ontario Tech University is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Former Windfields Farm and Durham College.

07.01.0260.t:
Winona, Hamilton

Winona began as a farming hamlet called "the Fifty" near Fifty Creek in Saltfleet Township. In the late 1800s its centre moved inland around the railway. E.D. Smith founded his food company here in 1882, and it dominated the local economy until approximately 1980. Winona became part of Stoney Creek in 1974 and of the City of Hamilton in 2001.

Winona is generally bounded by Tuscani Drive to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 78 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but a hydro transmission corridor and the CN rail line (Grimsby Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Winona is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

07.01.0290.t:
Winona Park, Hamilton

Winona Park is a residential area along the Lake Ontario shore in the Winona area of Stoney Creek. Winona began as a farming hamlet near Fifty Creek in Saltfleet Township, and it became part of Stoney Creek in 1974 and of Hamilton in 2001. Most homes in Winona Park were built in the 2000s.

Winona Park is generally bounded by Fifty Creek and Baseline Road to the east and Lake Ontario and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 206 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Winona Park includes Fifty Point Conservation Area, John Willison Park and Lake Vista Park.

09.03.0220.t:
Wismer, Markham

Wismer Commons is named after the Wismer family; David Wismer arrived in Markham Township in 1806 from Pennsylvania. The family later donated land for the area's first school near 16th Avenue and Markham Road. The area, north of 16th Avenue between McCowan Road and Markham Road, was farmland and has been developed in stages as part of Markham's recent northward growth.

Wismer is generally bounded by Major MacKenzie Drive to the north, Markham Road to the east, 16th Avenue to the south and McCowan Road to the west, and covers approximately 429 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Wismer.

Green space in Wismer includes Wismer Park, Ross Brown Park and Sinclair Holden Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools. Other notable landmarks include Markham Museum.

01.E09.1120.t:
Woburn, City of Toronto (TRREB district E09)

Woburn began as a small crossroads community at Markham Road and Danforth's Road (now Painted Post Drive), with a post office, schoolhouse and the Woburn Hotel. The hotel hosted the first Scarborough Township council meetings from 1850 until 1922. The area was built up as a suburb from the mid-1950s, with schools opening between 1956 and 1969. Scarborough became part of the City of Toronto in 1998.

Woburn is generally bounded by Highway 401 and Highland Creek to the north, West Highland Creek to the east, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and Bellamy Road to the south and McCowan Road to the west, and covers approximately 1,224 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Tabor Hill Ossuary (cemetery) and industrial lands (approximately 6% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision), Highway 401 and a hydro transformer station (Ellesmere TS). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Woburn includes Morningside Park, Highland Creek and Cedarbrook Park, and West Highland Creek, Highland Creek and Curran Hall Creek run through or along the community. Scarborough Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 17 schools and the Cedarbrae branch of the Toronto Public Library. Shopping is available at Cedarbrae Mall. Centennial College is also located in the community.

04.04.0050.t:
Wyebridge, Tiny

Wyebridge is a small community in the Township of Tiny near the Wye River. The Township of Tiny was named in 1822 after a pet dog of Lady Sarah Maitland, wife of Lieutenant Governor Sir Peregrine Maitland. It was part of the United Townships of Tiny and Tay from 1851 and became a separate township in 1869. Midland and Penetanguishene separated from the township in the 1870s.

Wyebridge is generally bounded by the Wye River and Catherine Street to the north and Sarah Burke Memorial Highway to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 26 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Church of the Good Shepherd Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Wyebridge is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

01.E02.1280.t:
Woodbine Corridor, City of Toronto (TRREB district E02)

The area between Coxwell Avenue and Woodbine Avenue began as the village of Norway, which formed in the 1840s around a toll gate, the Norway steam saw mill (1835) and a post office on Kingston Road. St. John's Church Norway and its cemetery date from 1850 and 1853. The Toronto Golf Club occupied open land between Woodbine and Coxwell from 1876 to 1909. Norway and Midway were annexed to the City of Toronto in 1909, and the land was then subdivided for housing in the 1910s.

Woodbine Corridor is generally bounded by Danforth Avenue to the north, Woodbine Avenue to the east, Kingston Road to the south and Coxwell Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 159 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Kingston Subdivision) and St. John's Norway Cemetery & Crematorium. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Woodbine Corridor includes Fairmount Park, Merrill Bridge Road Park and Orchard Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools. Other notable landmarks include St. John's Norway Cemetery.

01.E03.1380.t:
Woodbine-Lumsden, City of Toronto (TRREB district E03)

Woodbine-Lumsden takes its name from Woodbine Avenue and Lumsden Avenue, and lies north of Danforth Avenue in the former East York. The area includes Woodbine Heights, which developed early around a railway station and horse-racing facilities near Main and Danforth. It was part of York Township until East York was formed in 1924, and its housing is largely older East York homes from the first half of the 20th century. East York joined the City of Toronto in 1998.

Woodbine-Lumsden is generally bounded by Taylor-Massey Creek and Taylor Massey Creek to the north, Main Street to the east, Newmarket Avenue to the south and Woodbine Avenue to the west, and covers approximately 132 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Woodbine-Lumsden includes Taylor Creek Park, Stan Wadlow Park and Everett Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools, and transit is provided by the Woodbine subway station.

07.01.0210.t:
Woodburn, Hamilton

Woodburn is a small rural community in the Glanbrook area of Hamilton, in the former Binbrook Township. Binbrook was surveyed in the 1790s and named in 1792 after a town in Lincolnshire, England. It merged with Glanford in 1974 to form Glanbrook, which was amalgamated into Hamilton in 2001. The area remains largely agricultural.

Woodburn is generally bounded by Golf Club Road to the east, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 71 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Christ Church Cemetery, Woodburn. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Woodburn is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

09.07.0010.t:
Woodland Hill, Newmarket

Woodland Hill is in northwest Newmarket, west of Yonge Street and north of Davis Drive. The area was part of King Township until 1971, when York Region was formed and Newmarket's boundaries were expanded. It stayed rural until the late 1990s, and most of its homes were built in the early 2000s.

Woodland Hill is generally bounded by the East Gwillimbury boundary to the north, Yonge Street to the east, Davis Drive to the south and Bathurst Street to the west, and covers approximately 376 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Woodland Hill includes Bonshaw Park, Environmental Park and Woodland Hills Labyrinth Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools. Shopping is available at Upper Canada Mall.

10.02.0070.t:
Woodlands, Pickering

Woodlands is a residential neighbourhood in Pickering on land that was farmland and woodlots in Pickering Township. It was developed in stages between approximately 1940 and 2000. Pickering became a town in 1974 and a city in 2000.

Woodlands is generally bounded by the CN rail line (York Subdivision) to the north, Highway 401 to the south and Petticoat Creek to the west, and covers approximately 152 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Highway 401. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (York Subdivision) and the CN rail line (Metrolinx Kingston Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Petticoat Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Rougemount branch of the Pickering Public Library.

01.C02.0850.t:
Wychwood, City of Toronto (TRREB district C02)

The name comes from Wychwood Park, an artists' colony founded in the late 1800s by painter Marmaduke Matthews and Alexander Jardine. Matthews named it after Wychwood forest in Oxfordshire, England. The park was joined to the City of Toronto in 1909, and in 1985 it became the first residential heritage conservation district in Ontario. The surrounding streets were largely built up in the early 1900s.

Wychwood is generally bounded by St. Clair Avenue to the north, Bathurst Street to the east, the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision) to the south and Oakwood Avenue and Dovercourt Road to the west, and covers approximately 159 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and industrial lands (approximately 9% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Wychwood includes Hillcrest Park, Wychwood Barns Park and Frankel Lambert Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Davenport branch of the Toronto Public Library. Other notable landmarks include Artscape Wychwood Barns (former St. Clair streetcar carhouse).

01.C02.0830.t:
Yonge-St. Clair, City of Toronto (TRREB district C02)

The area grew around the Deer Park estate, 40 acres at Yonge and St. Clair bought by the Heath family in 1837. The estate was subdivided from 1846 and fully sold by 1874. Deer Park was annexed by the City of Toronto in 1908. It became an upper-middle-class residential district by the 1930s, and offices and apartments were later built around the Yonge and St. Clair intersection.

Yonge-St. Clair is generally bounded by Kay Gardiner Beltline Trail and Oriole Parkway to the north, Yonge Street to the east and Avenue Road and the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision) to the south, and covers approximately 117 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Davisville Yard and St. Michael's Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (North Toronto Subdivision) and Mount Pleasant Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Yonge-St. Clair includes Lionel Conacher Park, Robertson Davies Park and Amsterdam Square. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools, and transit is provided by the St. Clair subway station. Other notable landmarks include St. Michael's Cemetery (1855).

01.W05.0230.t:
York University Heights, City of Toronto (TRREB district W05)

York University Heights, also known as Northwood Park, is named after York University, whose main Keele campus lies within it. The area was farmland in York Township and became part of North York in 1922. Suburban housing and the university campus were built in the decades after the Second World War, and The Village at York University was added from 2005. North York was amalgamated into the City of Toronto in 1998.

York University Heights is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Dufferin Street to the east, Sheppard Avenue to the south and Black Creek to the west, and covers approximately 1,316 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (GO Transit Newmarket Subdivision), surface light rail transit (LRT) tracks and industrial lands (approximately 39% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in York University Heights includes Derrydowns Park, Black Creek Parkland and Sentinel Park, and Black Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools, and transit is provided by the Sentinel LRT station and the Finch West, Pioneer Village and York University subway stations. York University, Keele Campus and Seneca @ York Campus are also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include The Village at Black Creek.

01.W04.0320.t:
Yorkdale-Glen Park, City of Toronto (TRREB district W04)

Yorkdale-Glen Park lies south of Highway 401 between the rail line and Allen Road in the former North York, which separated from York Township in 1922. Homes south of Lawrence Avenue were mostly built in the 1950s and 1960s, largely bungalows and backsplits. Yorkdale Shopping Centre opened in the north of the area in 1964. North York was amalgamated into the City of Toronto in 1998.

Yorkdale-Glen Park is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Allen Road to the east, Briar Hill Avenue to the south and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 594 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Allen Road and industrial lands (approximately 30% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Newmarket Subdivision) and Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Yorkdale-Glen Park includes Caledonia Park, Glen Long Park and Wenderly Park. Residents are served by approximately 9 schools, and transit is provided by the Glencairn, Lawrence West and Yorkdale subway stations. Shopping is available at Yorkdale Shopping Centre and Lawrence Allen Centre.

06.04.1007.t:
Glen Abbey, Oakville

Glen Abbey lies in west Oakville, with Third Line and Dorval Drive as its main roads. It takes its name from the Glen Abbey Golf Course, a Jack Nicklaus design that opened in 1977 and has hosted the Canadian Open 30 times. The land was part of Trafalgar Township until it joined the Town of Oakville in 1962. The residential community was built around the golf course in the following decades.

Glen Abbey is generally bounded by Upper Middle Road and Sixteen Mile Creek to the east and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and Burloak Drive to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,382 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the Mid Halton Wastewater Treatment Plant and Merton Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Glen Abbey includes Bronte Creek Provincial Park, Glen Abbey Park and Heritage Way Park, and Bronte Creek, Fourteen Mile Creek and McCraney Creek run through or along the community. Glen Abbey and Deerfield Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Glen Abbey branch of the Oakville Public Library.

06.04.1008.t:
Glenorchy, Oakville

Glenorchy is named after a 19th-century hamlet in Trafalgar Township, north of Dundas Street. A schoolhouse was built there in 1850, George Halliday ran a mill in the 1850s, and a post office operated from 1894 to 1912. The area stayed rural after Trafalgar Township joined Oakville in 1962. It has been developed as part of North Oakville in recent years.

Glenorchy is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, Trafalgar Road to the east, Dundas Street to the south and Neyagawa Boulevard to the west, and covers approximately 954 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Highway 407 and Munn's Pioneer Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Glenorchy includes Fowley Park, Isaac Park and Bowbeer Parkette. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

06.04.1009.t:
Joshua Creek, Oakville

Joshua Creek takes its name from Joshua Creek, a watercourse in east Oakville. The land was farmland in Trafalgar Township until the township joined the Town of Oakville in 1962. The area was later developed as a suburban residential community.

Joshua Creek is generally bounded by Dundas Street to the north, Ninth Line to the east, Upper Middle Road and Grand Boulevard to the south and Eighth Line and Glenashton Drive to the west, and covers approximately 347 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Glen Oaks Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Joshua Creek includes Bayshire Woods Park, Pinery Park and North Ridge Trail Park, and Joshua's Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools and the Oakville Public Library.

06.04.1001.t:
Bronte, Oakville

Bronte began in 1834 as a small fishing village at the mouth of Twelve Mile Creek (now Bronte Creek). It was named for Horatio Nelson, who held the title Duke of Bronte. Its first harbour was completed in 1856, and it was a separate village from 1951 to 1959 before returning to Trafalgar Township. Bronte became part of the Town of Oakville in 1962, and suburban housing replaced farmland south of the QEW from the 1950s to the 1970s.

Bronte is generally bounded by Rebecca Street to the east and Lake Ontario and Burloak Drive to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 531 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bronte includes Shell Park, Nautical Woods and Creekpath Woods Park, and Bronte Creek and Sheldon Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

06.04.1002.t:
Central, Oakville

This community lies in the central part of the Town of Oakville. Oakville itself was founded after William Chisholm bought 960 acres at the mouth of Sixteen Mile Creek at a Crown auction in 1827, and it was incorporated as a town in 1857. The area was part of Trafalgar Township, which was created in 1806 and named after the Battle of Trafalgar. Trafalgar Township was amalgamated with the Town of Oakville in 1962. The opening of the QEW in 1939 made commuting to Toronto practical and led to steady suburban growth.

Central is generally bounded by Speers Road to the north, Sixteen Mile Creek to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Dorval Drive to the west, and covers approximately 240 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Oakville Water Purification Plant and St. Jude's Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Central includes Trafalgar Park, Water Works Park and Shipyard Park, and Sixteen Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

06.04.1003.t:
College Park, Oakville

College Park lies between Sixteen Mile Creek and Trafalgar Road, from the QEW north to Upper Middle Road. It takes its name from Sheridan College, whose Trafalgar Road campus opened in 1970. The land was part of Trafalgar Township, which joined the Town of Oakville in 1962, and the area was built up as a suburban community after that time.

College Park is generally bounded by Upper Middle Road to the north, Trafalgar Road to the east, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the south and Sixteen Mile Creek to the west, and covers approximately 435 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) and Oakville/St. Mary's Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in College Park includes Oxford Park, Oakdale Park and Ridgeview Park, and Sixteen Mile Creek, West Morrison Creek and Munn's Creek run through or along the community. Oakville Golf Club and Glen Abbey are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the White Oaks branch of the Oakville Public Library. Sheridan College - Trafalgar Campus is also located in the community.

06.04.1004.t:
Clearview, Oakville

Clearview lies in east Oakville on the border with Mississauga. It was part of the former hamlet of Sheridan, founded as Hammondville in 1812 and renamed Sheridan in 1857. Much of the old hamlet was removed when roads were widened and the QEW was built. The area became part of the Town of Oakville in 1962 and was later developed as a suburban community.

Clearview is generally bounded by Sherwood Heights Drive to the north, Winston Churchill Boulevard to the east, Sheridan Garden Drive to the south and Ford Drive to the west, and covers approximately 193 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Clearview.

Green space in Clearview includes Kingsford Park, Clearview Park and Wynten Way Park. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Clearview branch of the Oakville Public Library.

06.04.1005.t:
Falgarwood, Oakville

Falgarwood lies in northeast Oakville, at the southern end of the area known as Iroquois Ridge South. The land was farmland in Trafalgar Township until the township joined the Town of Oakville in 1962. The area was then developed as a suburban residential community.

Falgarwood is generally bounded by Upper Middle Road to the north and Trafalgar Road to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 353 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but Syl Apps Youth Centre lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Falgarwood includes Iroquois Shoreline Woods Park, Holton Heights Park and Sheridan Woods Park, and Morrison Creek and East Wedgewood Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

06.04.1006.t:
Ford, Oakville

The Ford community in southeast Oakville is named after the Ford Motor Company of Canada, whose Oakville Assembly plant opened on The Canadian Road in 1953. Ford's Canadian headquarters is also located here. The land was part of Trafalgar Township until it joined the Town of Oakville in 1962, and housing in the area grew alongside the plant from the 1950s onward.

Ford is generally bounded by Cornwall Road to the north, Winston Churchill Boulevard to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Maple Grove Drive to the west, and covers approximately 354 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Oakville South East Wastewater Treatment Plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Ford includes Southend Sports Fields, Charnwood Park and Maplegrove Park, and Joshua's Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

06.04.1013.t:
Old Oakville, Oakville

Old Oakville is the town's original downtown, on the Lake Ontario shore east of Sixteen Mile Creek. William Chisholm bought 960 acres at the mouth of the creek at a Crown auction in 1827, and his agents built the harbour, a shipyard and town lots. Oakville was incorporated as a town in 1857 and shipped wheat and lumber from its harbour. Many of the area's older homes and commercial buildings date from the 19th and early 20th centuries.

Old Oakville is generally bounded by Cornwall Road to the north, Chartwell Road to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Sixteen Mile Creek to the west, and covers approximately 246 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line and a rail yard lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Old Oakville includes Post Park, Wallace Park and Perkins Passage, and Sixteen Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools and the Oakville Public Library.

06.01.1030.t:
Derry Green, Milton

Derry Green is in east Milton, on former Trafalgar Township farmland near Highway 401 and James Snow Parkway. It is mainly planned as the Derry Green Corporate Business Park, an employment area of approximately 800 hectares within Milton's urban expansion. Its secondary plan was adopted by council in 2010 and approved in 2014-2015, and development has been underway since the late 2010s.

Derry Green is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Sixth Line to the east and James Snow Parkway to the west, and covers approximately 814 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), Highway 401, GO Milton Yard, a hydro transformer station (Halton TS), a hydro transformer station (Milton SS) and industrial lands (approximately 4% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Derry Green is primarily residential, with no major landmarks identified from available map data.

06.04.1000.t:
Bronte Creek, Oakville

This area takes its name from Bronte Creek, the local name for Twelve Mile Creek, which flows to Lake Ontario at Bronte. Bronte was named after Horatio Nelson, Duke of Bronte, and was founded as a fishing village in 1834. The area was part of Trafalgar Township, which was joined with Bronte and Oakville to form the Town of Oakville in 1962. Bronte Creek Provincial Park was established in 1975.

Bronte Creek is generally bounded by Dundas Street to the north, Bronte Road to the east, Upper Middle Road to the south and a hydro corridor and the Burlington boundary to the west, and covers approximately 390 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Bronte Creek includes Bronte Creek Provincial Park and Valleyridge Park, and Fourteen Mile Creek and Bronte Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

06.04.1010.t:
Joshua Meadows, Oakville

Joshua Meadows is a newer community in north Oakville, named after Joshua Creek. The land was farmland in Trafalgar Township, which was created in 1806 and amalgamated with the Town of Oakville in 1962. The area stayed largely agricultural until recent residential development north of Dundas Street.

Joshua Meadows is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, Ninth Line to the east, Dundas Street to the south and Trafalgar Road to the west, and covers approximately 910 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Glen Oaks Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407 and Highway 403. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Joshua Meadows includes William Rose Park. Vic Hadfield Golf & Learning Centre is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools.

06.04.1011.t:
Morrison, Oakville

Morrison lies in southeast Oakville, in the lakeside area often called Eastlake. In the early 1900s, wealthy city residents built summer homes along Lakeshore Road, and many later became permanent residences. The area was part of Trafalgar Township until 1962, when the township joined the Town of Oakville. Oakville's Jewish community dedicated the Shaarei Beth El Synagogue on Morrison Road in 1962.

Morrison is generally bounded by Cornwall Road to the north, Maple Grove Drive to the east, Lake Ontario to the south and Chartwell Road to the west, and covers approximately 407 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision) and a rail yard lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Morrison includes Pinewood Park, Wedgewood Park and Gairloch Gardens, and Morrison Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 8 schools.

06.04.1014.t:
Queen Elizabeth, Oakville

This community lies within the Town of Oakville. The Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) opened through Oakville in 1939 and made commuting to Toronto and Hamilton practical. The area was part of Trafalgar Township, which was created in 1806 and named after the Battle of Trafalgar. Trafalgar Township was amalgamated with the Town of Oakville in 1962. Much of south Oakville was built up with suburban housing from the 1950s onward.

Queen Elizabeth is generally bounded by Cornwall Road to the east and the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW) to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,915 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Oakville Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line, the Queen Elizabeth Way (QEW), Highway 403, Syl Apps Youth Centre, a rail yard, a hydro transformer station (Oakville TS #2), a hydro transformer station (Bronte TS), Oakville/St. Mary's Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 43% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are the Mid Halton Wastewater Treatment Plant and Merton Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Queen Elizabeth includes Cornwall Road Park, and Bronte Creek, Sixteen Mile Creek and McCraney Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 2 schools, and transit is provided by the Bronte and Oakville GO stations. Shopping is available at Oakville Place.

06.04.1015.t:
River Oaks, Oakville

River Oaks lies in north-central Oakville and includes the Oak Park development. The land was farmland in Trafalgar Township until the township joined the Town of Oakville in 1962. It was later built up as a suburban residential community.

River Oaks is generally bounded by Dundas Street to the north, Trafalgar Road to the east, Upper Middle Road to the south and Sixteen Mile Creek to the west, and covers approximately 700 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Munn's Pioneer Cemetery and Knox Sixteen Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Trafalgar Lawn Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in River Oaks includes Memorial Park, Neyagawa Park and River Glen Park, and Sixteen Mile Creek, West Morrison Creek and Shannon's Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools.

06.04.1016.t:
Sixteen Hollow, Oakville

Sixteen Hollow is named after an early settlement where Dundas Street crosses Sixteen Mile Creek. In 1827 George Chalmers built a grist and sawmill, a store and an ashery there, and the area became known as Sixteen Hollow. John Proudfoot bought the settlement in 1840, after which it was called Proudfoot's Hollow, and Knox Presbyterian Church was built there in 1845. The area stayed rural after Trafalgar Township joined Oakville in 1962 and has been developed as part of North Oakville in recent years.

Sixteen Hollow is generally bounded by Highway 407 to the north, Neyagawa Boulevard to the east, Dundas Street to the south and Sixteen Mile Creek to the west, and covers approximately 485 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a landfill site and Trafalgar Lawn Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 407 and Knox Sixteen Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Sixteen Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school and the Sixteen Mile branch of the Oakville Public Library.

06.04.1017.t:
Southwest, Oakville

Southwest Oakville lies along Lake Ontario near the former village of Bronte. Bronte began in 1834 as a fishing village at the mouth of Twelve Mile Creek and joined the Town of Oakville in 1962. Farmland in this part of town was replaced by suburban housing from the 1950s to the 1970s. The Lakeshore Woods community was later built on the former Shell Research Centre lands.

Southwest is generally bounded by Rebecca Street and Lake Ontario to the east and Third Line to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 304 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Oakville Wastewater Treatment Plant and St. Jude's Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Southwest includes Coronation Park, Sir John Colbourne Park and Birch Hill Promenade, and Fourteen Mile Creek runs through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Woodside branch of the Oakville Public Library.

06.04.1018.t:
Wedgewood Creek, Oakville

This community lies within the Town of Oakville. The area was part of Trafalgar Township, which was created in 1806 and named after the Battle of Trafalgar. Trafalgar Township was amalgamated with the Town of Oakville in 1962. The area was farmland before it was developed as a suburban residential community.

Wedgewood Creek is generally bounded by Eighth Line and Dundas Street to the north, Glenashton Drive and Grand Boulevard to the east, Upper Middle Road to the south and Trafalgar Road to the west, and covers approximately 235 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of Wedgewood Creek.

Green space in Wedgewood Creek includes Valleybrook Park, Postridge Park and Laurelwood Park, and Morrison Creek runs through or along the community.

06.04.1019.t:
Westmount, Oakville

Westmount is a residential community in west Oakville. The land was farmland in Trafalgar Township, which was created in 1806 and amalgamated with the Town of Oakville in 1962. It is one of the town's newer suburban areas, built up after the older communities to the south.

Westmount is generally bounded by Dundas Street to the north, Third Line to the east, Upper Middle Road to the south and Bronte Road to the west, and covers approximately 417 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include Palermo Cemetery. Along or just beyond its edges are a hydro transmission corridor. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Westmount includes Millstone Park and Fairmount Park. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools.

06.04.1020.t:
West, Oakville

This community lies in the western part of the Town of Oakville. The area was part of Trafalgar Township, which was created in 1806 and named after the Battle of Trafalgar. Trafalgar Township was amalgamated with the Town of Oakville in 1962. The area was farmland before it was developed for suburban housing.

West is generally bounded by Rebecca Street to the east and Bronte Creek to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 599 hectares.

No major adverse influences, such as hydro corridors, rail lines, highways, cemeteries, treatment plants or industrial lands, were identified within or along the edges of West.

Green space in West includes Brookdale Park, Morden Park and Westgate Park, and Fourteen Mile Creek and Bronte Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 6 schools. Shopping is available at South Oakville Centre.

06.01.1031.t:
Dorset Park, Milton

Dorset Park was registered as a subdivision in 1973 by the British builder Wimpey Homes. The name is reported to come from the county of Dorset in southern England. It was one of the first suburban neighbourhoods built next to Old Milton, with most homes dating from the 1970s and 1980s.

Dorset Park is generally bounded by Steeles Avenue to the north, Thompson Road to the east, Main Street to the south and Ontario Street to the west, and covers approximately 173 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Dorset Park includes Kinsmen Park, Melanie Park and Baldwin Park. Residents are served by approximately 3 schools.

06.01.1032.t:
Ford, Milton

Ford is named after the Ford family, who settled in the area in the 1830s and farmed in what was then Trafalgar Township. The neighbourhood was planned by the Town of Milton in 2004 as part of the Boyne Survey, together with Bowes, Cobban and Walker. Home construction began in approximately 2015 and the area is still being built out.

Ford is generally bounded by Louis St. Laurent Avenue to the north, Regional Road 25 to the east, Britannia Road to the south and the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the west, and covers approximately 286 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) and Bowes Cemetery lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Ford includes Raspberry Park and Benjamin Chee Chee Park. Residents are served by approximately 5 schools.

06.04.1023.t:
Rural Oakville, Oakville

Rural Oakville covers the remaining agricultural land in the north part of the town. This land was part of Trafalgar Township, created in 1806, where wheat was the main crop for most of its history. The township was amalgamated with Oakville in 1962. In 1974 the new Halton Region boundaries moved Oakville's northern limit south to just north of the future Highway 407.

Rural Oakville is generally bounded by Lower Base Line to the north, Highway 407 to the east and Bronte Road and Burnhamthorpe Road to the west, and covers approximately 861 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, Highway 407, a hydro transformer station (Palermo TS) and W.A Bill Johnson Biosolids Management Centre. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Sixteen Mile Creek and East Sixteen Mile Creek run through or along the community. Oakville Executive Golf Course and Tee Zone Driving Range are located in the area.

06.01.1070.t:
Rural Nassagaweya, Milton

Nassagaweya Township was created in 1819. Its name comes from a Mississauga word meaning "river with two outlets", because its streams drain both to Lake Ontario and to the Grand River. It was a farming township with small hamlets such as Campbellville, Brookville, Moffat and Haltonville. In 1974 the township became part of the Town of Milton.

Rural Nassagaweya is generally bounded by Fourth Line Nassagaweya to the north, Nassagaweya-Esquesing Town Line to the east and the Halton Hills boundary and Highway 401 to the south, and covers approximately 6,706 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and Dufferin Aggregates (quarry). Along or just beyond its edges are the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision) and Highway 401. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Nassagaweya includes Hilton Falls Conservation Area, and Sixteen Mile Creek and Blue Springs Creek run through or along the community.

06.01.0010.t:
Moffat, Milton

Moffat is a small rural hamlet in the former Nassagaweya Township. Nassagaweya was created in 1819 and was a farming township with several small crossroads hamlets. The township became part of the Town of Milton in 1974. Specific history for the hamlet was not found.

Moffat is generally bounded by Second Line Nassagaweya and 15 Side Road to the east and Mountsberg Creek to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 179 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Goderich Subdivision rail line and a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Mountsberg Creek runs through or along the community.

06.01.1072.t:
Rural Trafalgar, Milton

Trafalgar Township was created in 1806, after the Mississaugas sold the land in 1805, and was named after the Battle of Trafalgar. It was surveyed by Samuel Street Wilmot and settled as a farming township, with wheat as the main crop for much of its history. In 1974 the northern part of the former township became part of the Town of Milton, and this rural area remains largely agricultural.

Rural Trafalgar is generally bounded by Highway 401 to the north, Highway 407 to the east and Britannia Road and Tremaine Road to the west, and covers approximately 7,232 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), Highway 407, a landfill site, CPKC Milton Yard, a hydro transformer station (Trafalgar TS) and a hydro transformer station (Glenorchy Municipal TS). Along or just beyond its edges are Highway 401, a quarry or aggregate pit and Omagh Presbyterian Church Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Trafalgar includes Drumquin Park, and Sixteen Mile Creek, East Sixteen Mile Creek and Middle Sixteen Mile Creek run through or along the community. Rattle Snake Point Golf & County Club and Piper's Heath Golf Club are located in the area.

06.03.1045.t:
Acton, Halton Hills

Acton was settled in 1825 by the Adams brothers, Methodist preachers who farmed along a branch of the Credit River. The settlement was first called Danville and then Adamsville, and in 1844 it was named Acton after Acton in London, England. Tanning became the main industry, and the Beardmore tannery was once the largest in Canada, giving Acton the nickname "Leathertown". Acton became a village in 1874 and a town in 1950, and joined Halton Hills in 1974.

Acton is generally bounded by Fairy Lake to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 766 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision), the Acton Wastewater Treatment Plant, Fairview Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 8% of the community area). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Acton includes Prospect Park, Acton Sports Park and Rotary Park, and Black Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Fairy Lake. Residents are served by approximately 4 schools and the Acton branch of the Halton Hills Public Library, and transit is provided by the Acton GO Station.

06.03.0060.t:
Glen Williams, Halton Hills

Glen Williams is a hamlet on the Credit River, named after Benajah Williams, who acquired the land and built a sawmill with his sons in 1825. The river powered saw, flour and woollen mills, and the woollen mill operated until 1982. The hamlet was part of Esquesing Township and joined Halton Hills in 1974.

Glen Williams is generally bounded by the Credit River to the south and Silver Creek to the west, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 356 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Glen Williams includes Glen Williams Park, and the Credit River runs through or along the community. Residents are served by one school.

06.03.0020.t:
1048 - Limehouse, Halton Hills

Limehouse is a hamlet in the former Esquesing Township. The first Crown grant in the area was made in 1820, and around 1840 the settlement was called Fountain Green. When the post office opened in 1857 it was renamed Limehouse after its lime-burning industry, which used local limestone and continued until 1917. The Grand Trunk Railway was built through the village in 1856. Esquesing became part of Halton Hills in 1974.

1048 - Limehouse is generally bounded by 22 Side Road to the east and the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision) and Black Creek to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 60 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a quarry or aggregate pit. Along or just beyond its edges are the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision). Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 1048 - Limehouse includes Limehouse Memorial Garden. Residents are served by one school.

06.03.0040.t:
1050 - Stewarttown, Halton Hills

Stewarttown is a hamlet just south of Georgetown in the former Esquesing Township. First settlers arrived in 1819, and the name came into use around 1846 after brothers John and Duncan Stewart, who settled there in 1842. A brick town hall built around 1850 served as Esquesing's municipal office for many years, and a railway line opened through the village in 1873. Esquesing became part of Halton Hills in 1974.

1050 - Stewarttown is generally bounded by the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the north, 15 Side Road to the south and Mill Pond Drive to the west, and covers approximately 106 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

The Club at North Halton is located in the area. Residents are served by one school.

06.01.1073.t:
1051 - Walker, Milton

Walker is named after the family of Philip Walker, a United Empire Loyalist who came to the area in 1816; his descendants farmed this land for generations. The neighbourhood was planned by the Town of Milton in 2004 as part of the Boyne Survey. Home construction began in approximately 2015 and the area is still being built out.

1051 - Walker is generally bounded by Louis St. Laurent Avenue to the north, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) to the east, Britannia Road to the south and Tremaine Road to the west, and covers approximately 147 hectares.

There are no major adverse influences within the community itself, but the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision) lie along or just beyond its edges. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Residents are served by one school.

06.01.1060.t:
Rural Milton West, Milton

Rural Milton West is the rural western part of the Town of Milton. This area was farmland in the former townships of Trafalgar, Nassagaweya and Nelson until 1974, when these lands became part of the present Town of Milton. It remains largely rural. Specific history for this community was not found.

Rural Milton West is generally bounded by Fourth Line Nassagaweya and Nassagaweya-Puslinch Townline to the north, Highway 401 to the east and Derry Road and Milburough Line to the south, and covers approximately 15,120 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CPKC rail line (Galt Subdivision), the Goderich Subdivision rail line, the CPKC rail line (Hamilton Subdivision), the CPKC rail line, Highway 401, surface light rail transit (LRT) tracks, Sherman Sand & Gravel Ltd. (quarry), Saint John's Anglican Cemetery, Ebenezer United Church Cemetery and DeForest Pioneer Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Rural Milton West includes Crawford Lake Conservation Area, Kelso Conservation Area and Area 8, and Mountsberg Creek runs through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Kelso Lake and Area 8 Lake. Residents are served by one school. Other notable landmarks include Iroquoian Village.

06.03.0030.t:
1049 - Rural Halton Hills, Halton Hills

This community covers rural lands of Halton Hills outside the main urban areas. Most of it lies in the former Esquesing Township, which was surveyed in 1818 and opened to settlement in 1819. The area has remained largely agricultural, with small hamlets that grew along early roads. Halton Hills was formed in 1974 from Georgetown, Acton and most of Esquesing Township.

1049 - Rural Halton Hills is generally bounded by Sideroad 32 to the north, Winston Churchill Boulevard to the east, Highway 401 to the south and Fourth Line and 22 Side Road to the west, and covers approximately 22,668 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor, the CN rail line (Halton Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision), the CN rail line (Metrolinx Guelph Subdivision), the Metrolinx (GO Transit) rail line, Highway 401, Highway 407, Halton Hills Generating Station, a hydro transformer station, a quarry or aggregate pit, the Acton Wastewater Treatment Plant, the Georgetown Wastewater Treatment Plant, Fairview Cemetery, Holy Redeemer Catholic Cemetery and Greenwood Cemetery. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in 1049 - Rural Halton Hills includes Silver Creek Conservation Area, Scotsdale Farm and Terra Cotta Conservation Area, and the Credit River and Silver Creek run through or along the community. The community includes or fronts onto Fairy Lake. Blue Springs Golf Club and Eagle Ridge Golf Club are located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 25 schools, the Acton branch of the Halton Hills Public Library and the Georgetown branch of the Halton Hills Public Library, and transit is provided by the Georgetown and Acton GO stations. Shopping is available at Toronto Premium Outlets and Georgetown Market Place. Georgetown Hospital is also located in the community.

12.04.0051.t:
Otonabee Ward 1, Peterborough

Otonabee Ward covers the south end of Peterborough and takes its name from the Otonabee River and the former Otonabee Township, which bordered the city on the south and east. Peterborough was founded in 1825 and grew as a timber and later manufacturing centre, with large employers such as Canadian General Electric and Quaker Oats. Most township land in this area was annexed after the Second World War. Residential growth later shifted toward the west and south of the city.

Otonabee Ward 1 is generally bounded by Sherbrooke Street to the north, Lansdowne Street and the Otonabee River to the east and the Cavan Monaghan boundary to the south, and covers approximately 1,376 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include the CPKC rail line (Havelock Subdivision), Highway 7, St. Peter's Cemetery and industrial lands (approximately 14% of the community area). Along or just beyond its edges are John M. Turner Memorial Highway and the City Of Peterborough Wastewater Treatment Plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Otonabee Ward 1 includes Bowers Park, Morrow Park and Kinsmen Park. Kawartha Golf & Country Club is located in the area. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools and the Delafosse branch of the Peterborough Public Library. Shopping is available at Lansdowne Place. Fleming College is also located in the community. Other notable landmarks include Little Lake (Otonabee River).

12.04.0052.t:
Northcrest Ward 5, Peterborough

Northcrest Ward covers the north end of Peterborough. Much of it was township farmland until it was annexed by the city after the Second World War. Residential growth moved north from the 1960s, around the same time Trent University was established in 1964 with its main campus in the far north end. The area was largely built out from the 1960s onward.

Northcrest Ward 5 is generally bounded by the Selwyn boundary and the Otonabee River to the east and Parkhill Road and Water Street to the south, with its remaining edges following local streets, lot lines or natural features. It covers approximately 1,205 hectares.

Adverse influences within the community include a hydro transmission corridor and a wastewater treatment plant. Properties near these influences may be affected by noise, traffic, views or market appeal, and should be considered on an individual basis.

Green space in Northcrest Ward 5 includes Riverview Park & Zoo, Jackson Park and Inverlea Park, and the Otonabee River and Jackson Creek run through or along the community. Residents are served by approximately 7 schools. Shopping is available at Portage Place. Trent University and Master's College are also located in the community.

12.04.0053.t:
Town Ward 3, Peterborough

Town Ward covers downtown and the older central part of Peterborough on the west bank of the Otonabee River. The settlement began as Scott's Plains, after Adam Scott, who built mills here from 1818-1819. It was renamed Peterborough after Peter Robinson, who led Irish settlers to the area in 1825. Peterborough became a town in 1850 and a city in 1905, and the central area was largely built up in the 19th and early 20th centuries.
